10011-365-foreign-dishes-a-foreign-dish-:
This 1908 cookbook offers a foreign dish for every day of the year, arranged month by month. January alone runs from Austrian goulash, made with calves' heads, onions, potatoes, and paprika, to East India fish with salmon, butter, onion, and coconut.

Each recipe is short and practical, meant for a home cook willing to try new flavors. The year's tour crosses Europe, Asia, and beyond, one dish at a time. Cooks get a daily invitation to travel by taste, and a snapshot of what adventurous American tables looked like in 1908. The book invites cooks to try one new country at every meal.
10062-the-iron-game-a-tale-of-the-war:
Henry F. Keenan's 1898 tale of the war, dedicated to Bernard John McGrann, takes its epigraph from a poem of marching columns and the cold, grim dice of the iron game. Book one, The Caribeans, opens with a boy in blue, flag and faith, and Marlbrook marching off to war.

Chapters follow the army on the Potomac, the step that costs, an army with banners, blood and iron, and the legions of Varus, in the manner of Civil War fiction. Keenan writes of soldiers and strategy with feeling. Readers get a war novel where battle is a game played with lives, and no move is free.
10159-england-and-the-war:
Walter Raleigh gathered these wartime addresses in 1918, after giving them between 1914 and 1918. Raleigh, an Oxford scholar, spoke to institutes, colleges, and societies about what the First World War meant for England. The book collects his case in one place, from early pamphlets to late lectures.

Talks treat might versus right, the war of ideas, the faith of England, gains from war, the press, and Shakespeare as a national voice. Raleigh argues that Germany's armed doctrine, not one ruler alone, was the foe. Readers get a learned, patriotic survey of wartime thought at Oxford and beyond.
10409-the-crisis-of-the-naval-war:
Admiral of the Fleet Viscount Jellicoe of Scapa published this naval history in 1920, with plates and charts. Jellicoe, who had commanded the Grand Fleet, writes on the crisis of 1917, when German submarines threatened Britain's lifelines. His tone is official, plain, and concerned with facts and organization.

Chapters treat Admiralty changes, the submarine campaign, anti-submarine work, and the introduction and working of the convoy system. American entry, patrol craft, minesweeping, and the Dover and Harwich forces follow. Readers get a first-hand, authoritative account of how Britain met the U-boat danger.
10712-white-jacket-or-the-world-on-a-man:
Herman Melville, already known for Typee and Omoo, drew on his own naval service for White-Jacket, published in 1850. In 1843 he shipped as an ordinary seaman on a United States frigate in the Pacific and served more than a year before discharge on reaching home. The book turns that voyage into a picture of life aboard a man-of-war.

Chapters describe the jacket that gives the book its name, the divisions of the crew, daily routine, discipline, and the hardships of common sailors. Melville mixes story with protest, especially against flogging. Readers get both a sea tale and a reformer's case, from the author who would soon publish Moby-Dick.
1120-julius-caesar:
Brutus, a Roman noble torn between love of Caesar and love of Rome, joins Cassius in the plot to kill the dictator on the Ides of March. William Shakespeare's tragedy follows the murder, Mark Antony's funeral speech that turns the crowd, and the civil war that ends at Philippi with Brutus dead by his own sword.

The play weighs honor against ambition and asks whether a noble murder can ever stay clean. Its speeches, from "Friends, Romans, countrymen" to Brutus's farewell, are among the most quoted in English. The tragedy still frames how we talk about power, conspiracy, and the crowd.
11289-what-is-coming-a-forecast-of-thing:
H. G. Wells wrote this 1916 forecast while the First World War was still raging, asking what peace would bring. Chapters predict the war's end, nations in liquidation, Europe's drift toward socialism, new education, the war's effect on women. A new map of Europe, with separate essays on the United States, France, Britain, Russia, and the outlook for Germans. Wells opens by defending prophecy as a scientific habit of mind.

His forecasts mix shrewd guesses with Edwardian optimism, and reading them now means measuring hits against misses. The book's value is less as prediction than as evidence: it shows what a leading progressive thinker hoped the war would force the world to become. Its final chapters argue that the old order cannot return.
11352-germany-and-the-next-war:
Friedrich von Bernhardi's Germany and the Next War, in English translation, argues that Germany must prepare for a coming European war and embrace power politics. Written by a German general before the First World War, the book became notorious in Britain as evidence of German militarism, quoted by those warning that Berlin sought war. Its chapters treat Germany's place among nations, the necessity of expansion, and the moral justification of force.

Reading it now means separating Bernhardi's argument from its later reputation. The book did not cause the war, but it shaped how enemies understood German intentions. For historians of the war's origins, it is an essential, unsettling primary source, best read beside the diplomatic record.
11565-friends-though-divided-a-tale-of-t:
G. A. Henty's tale of the Civil War, as the English call their seventeenth-century conflict, opens in July 1642 with three young people on a shady bank near Oxford. Chapters follow the eve of war, a brawl at Oxford, breaking prison, a mission of state, and a stubborn defence.

Later chapters bring Montrose, an attempt to rescue the king, a riot in the city, the execution of Charles, the siege of Drogheda, slaves in the Bermudas, and the battle of Worcester. Friends divide between king and Parliament, and the story follows their loyalties through prison, escape, and a plot overheard.
11571-mr-punch-s-history-of-the-great-wa:
Mr. Punch's History of the Great War, first printed in July 1919, gathers five hectic years of cartoons and verse into a mixed record of heroes, heroines, and others. The editor credits O. S. and his band of brothers, who took their cue from the gay courage of fighting men.

A prologue traces Punch from the Afghan campaign and the Crimea, through the first Victoria Crosses in 1857 and the Indian Mutiny, to the volunteer movement. Later pages mock Lord Devonport over the official Bath bun and note a war saying on Germans blowing up hospitals. The book is satire as history.
11682-the-soul-of-the-war:
Philip Gibbs, with an introduction by Anthony Langley, wrote The Soul of the War from the first months of fighting. Chapters run from foreboding and mobilisation through retreat, invasion, and the last stand of the Belgians to the soul of Paris and the men in khaki.

Gibbs asks what man could lay bare England's soul in July 1914, when war threatened all that seemed safe and certain. Later scenes bring shell fire on a town hall square, a furnace glow, and wounded men carried on stretchers past a doctor and a lieutenant. The book is a correspondent's record of feeling as much as of battle.
11688-history-of-julius-caesar:
Jacob Abbott's History of Julius Caesar, with engravings, follows Caesar from Marius and Sylla through early years to the consulship. The conquest of Gaul, Pompey, and the crossing of the Rubicon follow in order.

Later chapters cover Pharsalia, the flight and death of Pompey, Caesar in Egypt, Caesar as imperator, the conspiracy, and the assassination. One passage shows Caesar addressing troops before the Rubicon, urging them to stand faithful and promising ample rewards. The first town on the Roman side, Ariminum, then surrenders. The book is a young reader's life of Rome's great general.
11895-peace-theories-and-the-balkan-war:
Norman Angell, author of The Great Illusion, published Peace Theories and the Balkan War in 1912, as war in the Balkans tested arguments about war and peace. Angell opens by insisting that blame, criticism, or sackcloth matters little at the present moment, and turns instead to the ideas that shape how nations judge war.

The book examines peace theories against a real, unfolding war, asking whether the doctrines of pacifists, militarists, and critics survive contact with events. Angell, already famous for arguing that conquest no longer paid, uses the Balkan conflict as a case study. He presses readers to separate moral feeling from the political and economic facts of modern warfare.
11979-the-diverting-history-of-john-gilp:
William Cowper's Diverting History of John Gilpin, in R. Caldecott's Picture Book edition of 1878, tells how Gilpin went farther than he intended and came safe home again. Caldecott's drawings accompany Cowper's verses about John Gilpin, a citizen of credit and renown and a train-band captain.

Gilpin's holiday ride becomes a runaway comedy, as horse, hat, and cloak conspire against a respectable tradesman out for a day's pleasure. Cowper's ballad, light and humane, has outlived its occasion to become a classic of English comic verse. Caldecott's pictures, with their lively line, made it a favorite picture book for children and adults alike.
12068-camp-fire-and-cotton-field-souther:
Thomas W. Knox's 1865 book Camp-Fire and Cotton-Field, subtitled Southern Adventure in Time of War, recounts life with the Union armies and residence on a Louisiana plantation. Knox, a Herald correspondent, dedicates the volume to representatives of the press who followed the national armies and recorded deeds of valor that secured the perpetuity of the republic.

With illustrations, Knox moves from campfires and marches to plantation life under occupation, describing soldiers, freedpeople, planters, and correspondents. His account, written in the war's final year, offers a journalist's view of the Civil War's western and southern theaters, where war, emancipation, and everyday survival met.
12233-stonewall-jackson-and-the-american:
Colonel G. F. R. Henderson wrote this military biography of Stonewall Jackson, published in two volumes with an introduction by Field Marshal Wolseley. This first volume follows Jackson from West Point and the Mexican War through Lexington teaching, secession, and the early Civil War campaigns.

Chapters cover Harper Ferry, First Manassas, the Romney expedition, Kernstown, the Valley Campaign, the Seven Days, Cedar Run, Second Manassas, Sharpsburg, Fredericksburg, and Chancellorsville, with maps and plans. Henderson, a British staff officer, praises Jackson speed, secrecy, and religious conviction, while judging his tactics with a soldier eye. The book shaped how generations read Jackson, and it remains a detailed campaign study.
12384-battle-pieces-and-aspects-of-the-w:
Herman Melville published Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War in 1866, his poems on the Civil War, dedicated to the three hundred thousand who fell for the maintenance of the Union. Melville, author of Moby-Dick, wrote the pieces after the fall of Richmond.

The poems follow the war in order, from early battles through Sherman march and Lincoln death, with prose notes on events. A mid-book poem pictures a field long slept in pastoral green, where a goblin mountain of marl and slag upheaves. Melville honors both sides courage while defending the Union cause. The volume is uneven as verse, but its moral gravity and historical notes make it a major Civil War book.
12418-the-land-of-deepening-shadow-germa:
D. Thomas Curtin published The Land of Deepening Shadow in 1917, a report on Germany at war, dedicated to Lord Northcliffe. Curtin, an American correspondent, entered Germany and wrote of what he saw under censorship and blockade.

Chapters cover getting in, when skies were blue, the crime against the children, pulpits of hate, puppet professors, the lie on the film, and the idea factory. Later chapters treat correspondents in shackles, Anton Lang of Oberammergau, submarine motives, and a land of substitutes. A mid-book scene has Liebknecht driven from the speakers tribune by red-faced deputies. Curtin book is wartime propaganda as well as report, and modern readers weigh its claims with care.
12427-neutral-rights-and-obligations-in-:
Robert Granville Campbell's 1908 essay grew from work in the political science seminary at Johns Hopkins, as part of a larger study of the Anglo-Boer War and its questions of international law. At first Britain treated the contest as one that need not call neutrality laws into play.

By late November, however, Britain's declaration, with retroactive effect, put the war on a belligerent basis, dating it from the Transvaal ultimatum of 11 October 1899. Campbell traces what that shift meant for neutrals: trade, contraband, blockade and the duties of third parties. The essay is a careful, academic study of law in war, written close to its events.
12541-the-american-indian-as-participant:
Annie Heloise Abel, professor of history at Smith College, published this 1919 study of the American Indian as participant in the Civil War. It is dedicated to former colleagues and students at Goucher and Johns Hopkins. Contents open with Pea Ridge, or Elkhorn, and its effects, and Lane's brigade. Indian refugees in southern Kansas, and the first Indian expedition, follow.

Later chapters follow the march to Tahlequah, and General Pike in controversy with Hindman. The Arkansas and Red River superintendency, Pike's retirement, removal to the Sac and Fox agency, and negotiations with Union Indians follow. Abel writes as a scholarly historian, close to documents. The book remains a foundational study of Native nations caught between Union and Confederacy.
1272-the-riddle-of-the-rhine-chemical-st:
LeFebure examines chemical strategy in peace and war, using the Rhine as the riddle at the centre of European security after the First World War. German chemical industry, he argues, held power that treaties could not erase. LeFebure, a British officer, wrote after seeing gas warfare in the First World War.

The book warns that factories built for dyes and drugs could turn to poison gas, and it urges control of chemical capacity. Written in the shadow of gas warfare, it remains a sober early study of dual-use industry and arms control. The Rhine, border and highway, stood for the chemical power that treaties tried to bind.
13007-the-edda-volume-1-the-divine-mytho:
Winifred Faraday's 1902 study, number twelve in the Popular Studies in Mythology, Romance, and Folklore series, retells the divine mythology of the Norse Edda for general readers. Faraday explains her plain spelling of Norse names, dropping marks of vowel length and most case endings so newcomers can follow the gods. Her focus is the Aesir, the ruling powers of the Viking world.

Odin travels in disguise to gain wisdom, while Thor marches east to fight giants, his hammer the champion's weapon against the World-Snake at Ragnarok. The whole tale, Faraday stresses, is shadowed by that coming doom, when gods and foes meet in final battle. Short, clear, and keyed to the old poems, the book serves as a first guide to Norse myth.
13008-the-edda-volume-2-the-heroic-mytho:
Winifred Faraday's Edda II: The Heroic Mythology of the North, published in 1902 as Popular Studies number thirteen, follows her volume on divine mythology. Heroes like Sigemund the Waelsing, Fitela, Aetla, Eormanric the Goth, and Weland the Smith were known to early English writers, often by a name alone. Saxon poets had turned toward saints' legends and Bible paraphrase.

A Gudrun passage shows the tragic thread: Svanhild, like a sunbeam in her hall, is trodden into dust under horses' hoofs, and her brothers die avenging her, leaving only Aslaug alive. Faraday writes with scholarly care for general readers. The study suits lovers of Norse and Germanic legend.
13549-the-art-of-war:
Baron de Jomini, general and aide-de-camp to the Emperor of Russia, sets out the art of war in this work translated from French by Capt. G. H. Mendell and Lieut. W. P. Craighill, first published in English in 1862. The translators warn against two extremes: rigid word-for-word rendering and too free a pen, either of which may lose the author's sense.

Jomini teaches strategy, tactics, and logistics as a system. An army on the offensive must plan for defence, posting a reserve between base and front to support menaced points without weakening the active army. Logistics, he asks, is no mere detail but a general science, the practical art of moving armies and carrying out staff duty. The book shaped American military thinking in the Civil War era.
13789-great-britain-and-the-american-civ:
Ephraim Douglass Adams wrote this two-volume study, bound as one, of Britain and the American Civil War. Volume one opens with backgrounds, then follows British policy from 1860 onward. Chapters treat suspicion of Seward, the Declaration of Paris, Bull Run, cotton, and the Trent affair. The blockade and the entry of Mr. Lindsay follow.

Adams draws on diplomatic papers to show how London weighed neutrality, trade, and public opinion. He traces impressment, naval policy, and the cotton famine's effect on Lancashire. British leaders feared both American anger and French moves. The study remains a standard account of Anglo-American relations in wartime. It suits readers of diplomatic and Civil War history.
13790-life-and-letters-of-john-gay-1685-:
Lewis Melville wrote this 1921 life of John Gay, author of The Beggar's Opera. Gay, born in 1685, rose from a Devon childhood to London literary circles. He befriended Pope and Swift, wrote poems and plays, and won fame with his 1728 ballad opera. Melville draws on letters and memoirs to trace that rise.

The book follows Gay's hopes, patrons, and disappointments. It explains how The Beggar's Opera mocked Italian opera and Walpole's politics at once. Later chapters cover his final years and early death in 1732. A portrait from Kneller fronts the volume. The biography suits readers of Augustan literature and theatre history.
13918-secret-chambers-and-hiding-places-:
Allan Fea wrote Secret Chambers and Hiding-Places, in a third revised edition with eighty illustrations. It gathers historic, romantic, and legendary stories of hiding holes and secret rooms. Moseley Hall fronts the volume. Chapters treat priest's holes, Hindlip Hall, and priest-hunting at Braddocks, plus Gunpowder Plot conspirators.

Later chapters follow king-hunting at Boscobel, Moseley, Trent, and Heale, and cavalier-hunting elsewhere. Fea explains how priests hid from sanguinary laws after the Gunpowder Plot, when saying Mass could mean death. Houses like Harvington, Oxburgh, and Parham hide their secrets in walls and floors. The book blends antiquarian research with romance. It delights readers who love old houses and escapes.
14299-native-races-and-the-war:
Josephine E. Butler published Native Races and the War in 1900, arguing future peace must rest on justice to colored as well as white men. Dedicated to her children and grandchildren, the book opens with an apology for yet another volume on the South African question, then distinguishes legalized slavery from native subjection by individuals. Transvaal bankruptcy, annexation, and liberation frame the history.

Native voices carry the protest. British commissioners met three hundred native chiefs, hearing sorrowful speeches against annexation, while a royal commission took evidence on slavery. Christian King Khama appealed for his people, and M'Plaank, nephew of Cetewayo, wrote in their cause. A closing scene shows a governor leaving African soil amid flags, salutes, and Malays in bright clothing at the docks. Butler writes as a reformer: empire judged by how it treats those it rules, not by flags alone.
15006-historic-papers-on-the-causes-of-t:
Eugenia Dunlap Potts was historian of the Lexington, Kentucky, chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy. She gathers historic papers on the causes of the Civil War, printed at Ashland in Lexington. The Old South, read before the Lexington chapter in February 1909, opens the volume.

Potts argues that no pen or brush can picture ante-bellum life in the old Southern states. That period ran two hundred and fifty years without parallel, with a separate way of life that can never be reproduced. Socially, intellectually, politically and religiously, she claims, the South stood pre-eminent, led by the spirit of the cavalier. The papers are a partisan Southern view, valuable as evidence of Lost Cause memory.
1522-julius-caesar:
Shakespeare's Roman tragedy opens with Caesar's triumph in Rome and the fears of Brutus, Cassius. Their fellow conspirators, who kill him on the Ides of March for the sake of the republic. Mark Antony's funeral speech then turns the crowd, and Rome slides into civil war.

Brutus, honourable but politically blind, loses to Antony and Octavius at Philippi, and dies by his own sword with his honour intact. The play weighs liberty against loyalty and rhetoric against reason. It is a taut, public drama, still quoted wherever power and conspiracy are discussed.
1532-king-lear:
King Lear opens with an old king dividing his kingdom between his daughters according to their flattery. Cordelia, who loves in silence, is cast out, and Lear soon learns the cost of his folly as Goneril and Regan strip him of power, followers. Shelter, driving him mad onto a stormy heath.

Beside Lear's fall runs Gloucester's tragedy, as a bastard son blinds his father and a loyal son restores him. The play ends in death upon death, with Lear cradling Cordelia. It is Shakespeare's bleakest tragedy, a towering study of age, pride, ingratitude, and love that comes too late.
15522-the-war-chief-of-the-ottawas-a-chr:
Thomas Guthrie Marquis wrote this chronicle of the Pontiac War as volume fifteen of the Chronicles of Canada, edited by George Wrong and H. H. Langton, published in Toronto in 1915. Eight chapters move from the times and the men through Pontiac and the tribes of the hinterland, the gathering storm, and the siege of Detroit.

Later chapters cover the fall of the lesser forts, the relief of Fort Pitt, Detroit once more, and the winding up of the Indian war. The opening sets the scene in September 1760, when news of Montreal's capitulation brought bonfires and prayers across the Thirteen Colonies. Marquis tells a compact, clear story of a frontier rising after French defeat, in the series' popular history style.
15528-the-tale-of-cuffy-bear:
Arthur Scott Bailey published this animal tale for children in New York in 1915, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. It belongs to his Sleepy-Time Tales, beside Frisky Squirrel, Tommy Fox, Fatty Coon, and Billy Woodchuck. The frontispiece shows Cuffy giving one good, hard cuff, a hint of the young bear's temper and play.

Twenty-three chapters follow Cuffy through a bear's year: waking up, finding a porcupine, learning to swim, climbing Blue Mountain, going to market, hunting a bee tree, and getting stung. A forest fire, rain, and growing sleepiness close the seasons. Bailey writes short, clear chapters for bedtime reading, with animal manners standing in for childish lessons about caution, courage, and getting along with neighbors.
15561-the-boer-in-peace-and-war:
Arthur M. Mann, author of The Truth from Johannesburg, published this account of the Boers in London in 1900, with sixteen illustrations. Pictures show Boer mounted police, wagons bringing wool to an early market, a Boer homestead and family, Majuba Hill, a Boer encampment, and President Kruger's house and parliament building. The book appeared as war with Britain began.

Mann opens by warning that a Boer may know you, but it will take you some time to know him, and his real nature may prove hard to penetrate. His ways, Mann says, are not the ways of other people. Later pages treat farm life, church, parliament, cattle, and war, mixing observation with the prejudices of an English writer of the day. The book now reads as a wartime portrait, useful and biased in equal measure.
15665-new-latin-grammar:
A full Latin grammar by Charles E. Bennett, Goldwin Smith Professor of Latin at Cornell University. The 1918 revision adds an introduction on the origin and growth of Latin, plus an index of sources for its examples. Bennett keeps rules short, following Horace's advice that teaching should be brief and easy to hold. The book served college students and keen school pupils alike.

Inside, sounds, word forms, and sentence structure are laid out in order, with examples drawn from real Latin writers. Syntax takes the largest share, showing how cases, moods, and clauses work in practice. Tables and a full index help a reader find a rule fast. As a reference it remains clear and practical: a single volume that covers the whole language for study and for translation.
15720-ruth-fielding-in-the-great-northwe:
This 1921 volume, from Cupples and Leon in New York, illustrated, sends Ruth Fielding to the great Northwest. Its author, Alice B. Emerson, also wrote Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill and Ruth Fielding in the Saddle. The subtitle names the plot: the Indian girl star of the movies. A front picture shows timbers pouring down a bluff behind Ruth.

Twenty-five chapters run from Ruth in peril and a perfect shot through the ring, smoking the peace pipe, and inspiration to everybody agreeing but Dakota Joe. Dakota Joe's wrath, a wonderful event, and the plot developing lead to one New York day and evading the traffic police. Bound for the Northwest, the Hubbell ranch, pursuing danger, and a bull and a bear follow. The book ends with Wonota's surprise: a girls' adventure of movies, ranches, and the far Northwest.
15793-an-unpardonable-liar:
A short novel by Gilbert Parker, issued in Chicago by Charles H. Sergel Company in 1900. Parker, a Canadian writer of romance and history, builds the tale on a single moral fault. The opening chapter, called An Echo, sets a singing voice against a wide world. From there the story tests what one lie can cost.

A man whose word cannot be trusted finds love, honour, and friendship slipping from his grasp. Parker writes with brisk, popular skill, keeping the plot moving through talk and incident. The liar's fate unfolds as warning, not mere puzzle. The book holds interest as a period moral tale: plain, swift, and firm that truth, once broken, is hard to mend.
15835-william-lilly-s-history-of-his-lif:
An autobiography by William Lilly, the famous English astrologer, covering 1602 to 1681. Lilly wrote it in his sixty-sixth year for his friend Elias Ashmole. First published from manuscript in London in 1715, it was reprinted for Charles Baldwyn in 1822. Plates show Lilly, Simon Forman, John Booker, and both King Charleses.

Lilly tells of his youth, his rise as an astrologer, and his dealings with Parliament, army, and court. Hugh Peters, the Speaker, and the kings pass through his pages. His voice stays shrewd, gossipy, and frank about his art. The book stands as a firsthand life of Civil War England, seen through the stars and the streets alike.
15910-a-short-view-of-the-frauds-and-abu:
A seventeenth-century pamphlet by Christopher Merrett, Doctor in Physic and Fellow of the College of Physicians, exposing frauds by apothecaries. An imprimatur dated November 13 fronts the text, with errata from the second edition corrected. Merrett's Latin epigraph jeers that all represent themselves as doctors: the uneducated, the priest, the nurse, the barber, the apothecary, and the old woman.

Merrett charges apothecaries with bad drugs, false measures, and meddling in physic beyond their trade. His prose is learned, angry, and precise. The pamphlet shows the old war between physicians and apothecaries for control of medicine. It still fascinates historians: quackery named, shamed, and fought in print, three centuries ago.
16009-valentine-m-clutchy-the-irish-agen:
William Carleton sets this Irish novel in the town of Castle Cumber, with its two long streets, lanes of cabins, church, prison, courthouse, chapel, shops, and public houses. The opening chapters promise an Irish pair, a marriage proposal, an under agent, and an old Irish squire, all under the shadow of the land system. Valentine M'Clutchy himself is the agent at the center of the story.

Through tenants, landlords, and middlemen, Carleton attacks the abuses of Irish estate management with satire and anger. His scenes are crowded, comic, and often bitter, drawn from a countryside he knew well. The novel remains a sharp, readable record of landlord power and tenant life in pre-Famine Ireland.
16231-forward-march-a-tale-of-the-spanis:
Kirk Munroe's 1899 Harper tale for boys follows young Americans into the Spanish-American War. Contents move from a bowl of roses and a declaration of war to Rollo the Terror, the Rough Riders at San Antonio, and Ridge becoming a trooper. A story of Hobson and the Merrimac, a secret mission, the Cuban blockade, and Cuban hospitality carry the action south.

Munroe, author of the Mate series, writes brisk adventure with a frontispiece of Rough Riders fighting an unseen enemy. The book mixes schoolboy heroics with real war episodes of 1898. Young readers who like military adventure will find a rousing, old-fashioned war story.
16338-the-homeric-hymns-a-new-prose-tran:
Andrew Lang gives a fresh prose rendering of the Homeric Hymns in this 1899 volume, with essays on their literary and mythic sides. The hymns themselves are short preludes to gods and heroes, some only a few lines long. Lang asks who gathered them, when, and why, and notes that the great Alexandrian critics did not treat them as Homer's own work.

The essays weigh the poems as art and as myth, not merely as relics. Lang's plain prose keeps the hymns readable for those without Greek. Readers who know the Iliad and Odyssey will find here the smaller songs that once stood at the door of longer poems.
16454-the-upas-tree-a-christmas-story-fo:
Florence L. Barclay's 1912 Christmas story follows Helen, Aubrey, and Ronnie through fog, mirrors, and a shadow called the upas tree. Part one asks which shall speak first, and part two brings the Infant of Prague and Paradise Lost. Part three sends Ronnie into fog and face to face with the upas, while part four lifts the fog toward a child born at Christmas.

Barclay, author of The Rosary, writes with warmth and high feeling, in the popular romantic style of her day. The tale mixes domestic drama with spiritual hope. Readers of old-fashioned Christmas fiction will find it tender, earnest, and meant to be read by firelight.
16480-beechenbrook-a-rhyme-of-the-war:
Margaret J. Preston's 1866 poem tells a Southern woman's sorrow in the Civil War, dedicated to every Southern woman widowed by the war. Beechenbrook Cottage sits bright in May, with birds, bees, and orchard bloom, while grief hangs over the house. The rhyme was first published during the struggle and reissued after it.

Preston writes in flowing, sentimental verse, with nature's beauty set against human loss. The poem is short and elegiac, meant as a memorial that would not let suffering be forgotten. Readers of Civil War verse will find it a moving Southern voice from the war years.
16516-walker-s-appeal-with-a-brief-sketc:
Henry Highland Garnet reprinted David Walker's Appeal in New York in 1848, with a brief sketch of Walker's life and Garnet's own address to the slaves of the United States. The preface calls the Appeal among the first, and the boldest and most direct, appeals for freedom in the early anti-slavery reform. Walker's widow gave permission for the reprint.

The volume preserves a fiery founding text of Black abolitionism, with Garnet's later address beside it. Its language is urgent and prophetic, aimed at enslaved readers themselves. For students of American freedom struggles, it is an essential, uncompromising document.
16521-fanny-goes-to-war:
Pat Beauchamp, of the First Aid Nursing Yeomanry, tells her war service in this 1919 memoir, introduced by Major-General Thompson. She served with the First Army from July 1917 to April 1919. Her path runs from camp before the war through the journey to the front, trenches, typhoid wards, a Zeppelin raid, convoy life, and Christmas 1916.

Beauchamp writes briskly and vividly, with baths, lorries, convoy pets, and goodbyes along the way. The book gives a woman's view of war work close to the front, practical and unsentimental. Readers of Great War memoirs will find it fresh, funny, and deeply human.
16631-the-skipper-and-the-skipped-being-:
Holman Day wrote this 1911 shore tale of Cap'n Aaron Sproul, late master of the Jefferson P. Benn, now ashore and at odds with his kin. It opens by the sickbed of his uncle, One-arm Jerry, who pleads that a shore post is still honorable work. Aaron sees it as a steep fall from command at sea.

Day fills the book with sea talk, shore folk, and comic clashes between old sailors and land ways. Aaron must learn to lead ashore as he once led afloat, and the humor comes from his pride meeting small-town fact. The tale is warm, funny, and full of salt air, a good pick for readers who like sea yarns told on land.
16674-the-pride-of-palomar:
Peter B. Kyne's 1922 novel of old California opens with a dedication to Frank L. Mulgrew of the Bohemian Club. Kyne admits the book is not what he planned, but holds faint echoes of the old California vanishing when he first cried at Mission Dolores and gazed on Sonoma's redwood hills. Don Miguel Farrel fronts the tale.

Kyne writes of ranchos, pride, and a California passing away, with pictures by Ballinger and Cornwell. The story mixes romance with the clash of old and new California. Readers of western fiction will find a rich, nostalgic novel of land, honor, and change.
17064-the-story-of-a-plush-bear:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this 1921 Make Believe story of a plush bear, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Hope also wrote the sawdust doll, the nodding donkey, the china cat, the Bobbsey Twins, Bunny Brown, and Six Little Bunkers series. The plush bear joins a shelf of toy tales, each giving a toy a life, a voice, and a small adventure.

Hope writes for very young children in short, gentle chapters, with a toy hero who learns kindness and courage. The tale is sweet, simple, and full of nursery warmth. Young readers get a charming, old-style toy story, best read aloud, and collectors of Hope will find another piece of her beloved toy shelf.
17211-a-school-history-of-the-great-war:
Albert E. McKinley, Charles A. Coulomb, and Armand J. Gerson wrote this 1918 school history of the Great War for American pupils. Chapters move from Europe before the war and German militarism through the Hague conferences, Balkan states, and the war year by year from 1914 to 1918. The United States in the war and questions of the coming peace close the text, with a chronology and index.

The authors urge pupils to look behind daily news to causes, alliances, and laws. Written while the war still raged, the book speaks with wartime certainty, a point modern readers should note. As a school text of its day, it gives a clear, orderly frame for the war's course and stakes.
17243-full-revelations-of-a-professional:
Ike Matthews, professional rat-catcher of Pendleton, Manchester, sums up twenty-five years of rat-catching, ferreting, and watching rat ways in this blunt manual. He warns never to poison rats in closed buildings: poisoned drain rats die under floors and breed a dreadful stench. His methods, chiefly tested in Manchester, suit all large towns, he says.

Testimonials from corporations, railway firms, and merchants back his record, and his first part clears warehouses, offices, and storerooms. Matthews writes in plain, workmanlike prose, fond of practical detail over theory. Pest controllers and social historians will enjoy a vivid, no-nonsense trade book from the age of steam and sewers.
17245-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers' March 13, 1852 journal leads with The Dinner-Bell, a playful essay on Britain's daily peal. At noon the bell rings in farm and factory, at one in crowded industry, and at two in Scotland. It rings on through gentry houses to fashionable towns at eight, when it stops abrupt, like an air broken off. Webster's morning drum-beat round the empire opens the parallel.

The essay turns dinner hours into a social map, from laborers to fine folk, with humor and observation. More pieces in the same number follow the journal's home mix. As Victorian light prose, the issue charms with its ear for daily ritual and its gentle fun at British habits.
17256-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers' March 6, 1852 journal leads with The Charitable Chums' Benefit Club, a London tale set at the Mother Bunch public house. Landlord Peter Bowley, once butler to the late Sir Plumberry Muggs, married his cook after both gained legacies of five hundred pounds. The opening paints a mews of carts, cabs, rats, goats, and mud-loving children.

The number follows the journal's home mix of story, fact, and wit for a penny-halfpenny. As Victorian light reading, it charms with its eye for London life and its kindly humor. Readers who like period magazines will find a lively, old-style issue, full of character and street color.
17303-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers priced this March 20, 1852 journal at a penny and a half, as ever, for a wide home audience. Its lead piece, Things in Expectation, weighs the passing age: great science gains and wealth beside social lag, meanness, and poverty. The writer looks twenty years ahead, hoping for progress while admitting war or disaster could break the hope.

The piece balances bright and dark views with a cheerful, earnest tone. More items in the same number follow the journal's mix of thought, fact, and home reading. As a sample of mid-Victorian weekly prose, the issue shows a hopeful age pausing to ask where it was really headed.
17389-the-dreamer-a-romantic-rendering-o:
Mary Newton Stanard's 1909 Dreamer offers a romantic rendering of Edgar Allan Poe's life, from Richmond, Virginia. Stanard calls her book a finished picture of the shadowy sketch biographers give, told with the storyteller's license yet true to spirit if not to letter. Poe's own words from letters and works shape many speeches, and she credits Ingram and Woodberry among her sources.

The book follows the poet and man through his gray visions, loves, and losses, with a Poe motto on day-dreamers at its head. Readers who love Poe will find a tender, novelistic life, richer in feeling than a bare chronology. It suits anyone who wants the legend of Poe in story form, honestly framed as romance.
17405-the-art-of-war:
Sun Tzu's Art of War, in Lionel Giles's 1910 translation, is called the oldest military treatise in the world. Thirteen chapters cover laying plans, waging war, attack by stratagem, tactical dispositions, energy, and weak points and strong. Maneuvering, variation of tactics, the army on the march, terrain, the nine situations, attack by fire, and the use of spies complete the set. Five constant factors open the work: moral law, heaven, earth, commander, and method.

Giles's plain, classic English suits generals, managers, and students of strategy alike. The text's brevity hides deep counsel on knowing self, enemy, and ground. Readers who like timeless wisdom will find a short, sharp book that has shaped war, business, and games for over two thousand years.
17649-the-germ-thoughts-towards-nature-i:
The Germ, thoughts towards nature in poetry, literature, and art, was the literary organ of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, published in 1850. This volume gives a facsimile reprint of that organ, with an introduction by William Michael Rossetti, published in London in 1901 by Elliot Stock. Rossetti's introduction reflects on his fate or whim in writing much about the movement's early days.

He writes of the Brotherhood's members, and especially of his brother Dante Gabriel Rossetti and his sister Christina Georgina Rossetti. Readers get the Pre-Raphaelites in their own first pages, with a later guide from inside the circle. The book suits readers of Pre-Raphaelite art and poetry.
17710-the-devil-s-own-a-romance-of-the-b:
Randall Parrish set this 1917 novel in the Black Hawk War on the old Illinois frontier, where white settlers, soldiers, and Native peoples fought over land and pride. The hero serves at Fort Armstrong, takes leave, and is drawn into a tangle of spies, raiders, and a judge's household that hides more than it shows.

Chapters move from fort life to keel-boats, a girl at bay, and a trail of raids, with sword and gun play beside a slow love plot. Parrish wrote fast, crowd-pleasing tales of the frontier, and this one is a good sample: bold action, clear villains, and a young man who must pick his duty. It reads best as a rousing old war romance, not as strict fact.
17833-an-apologie-for-the-royal-party-16:
This 1659 apologie for the Royal Party, with a panegyric to Charles, defends the royalist cause in the last years of the Commonwealth. Its opening address speaks to a friend who stood engaged in the opposing party, urging conversion from the error of his way. The writer recalls the friend's education and early compliance with those who directed him, then the conversions of others on discovering impostures.

Bloody tyrannies and prodigious oppressors, lately beheld, supply the writer's warnings. Readers get a royalist pamphlet from the eve of the Restoration, earnest and partisan. The book suits readers of Civil War polemic and of Restoration politics.
17998-before-the-war:
Viscount Haldane wrote Before the War in 1920, printed in New York and London by Funk and Wagnalls. Haldane served as Secretary of State for War from 1905 to 1912, and as Lord Chancellor to 1915, so he writes from the heart of British power.

Chapters run from diplomacy before the war to the German attitude, military preparations, and an epilogue. Haldane draws on his own diaries and records, and he speaks in the first person without apology. The book is a key insider account of the slide to war, and a defense of a minister who saw the storm coming.
1804-war-and-the-future-italy-france-and:
H. G. Wells wrote these dispatches from the First World War in 1916, after visiting the Italian and Western fronts. The passing of the effigy opens the book. Chapters on the Isonzo front, the mountain war, and the ruins behind the lines follow, with Italy's risk-taking for an idea given a central place.

Wells argues that Italy, with clear-eyed idealism, counted every risk before entering the war, and he contrasts that spirit with the waste he saw in France. The book is journalism with a thesis: war as a test of peoples, and the future as something to be built rather than endured. It reads now as a vivid record of how the war looked to a famous civilian in its middle years.
18125-the-audacious-war:
Clarence W. Barron wrote The Audacious War in 1915, printed in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin. Barron, head of the Boston News Bureau, named his book for the warship Audacious and for the sheer audacity of the war itself.

Chapters run from the world's greatest contest to tariffs, politics, peace plans, France, Belgium's sacrifice, Russia, England, and Germany. Barron treats the war as a contest of finance and trade as much as of arms, and he draws lessons for America. It is a sharp, early American view of 1914, written while the guns still roared.
18160-in-the-world-war:
Count Ottokar Czernin wrote this memoir of the First World War from inside the Austro-Hungarian leadership. Czernin served as the empire's foreign minister during the war, and his chapters follow the decisions he watched at close hand. They open with reflections on the storm that broke over Europe, then turn to Konopischt, Kaiser William II, and Roumania.

Later chapters take up U-boat warfare, attempts at peace, President Wilson, Poland, Brest-Litovsk, and the Peace of Bucharest. Plates show Franz Ferdinand, Count Tisza, and General Hoffmann. A reader gets the war as seen from Vienna: alliances under strain, peace feelers that failed, and an empire trying to hold its place while its world came apart.
18307-the-adventures-of-akbar:
Flora Annie Steel wrote this children's history of Prince Akbar, published by William Heinemann in London in 1913 with pictures by Byam Shaw. Steel calls it the true story of a little lad who lived to be perhaps the greatest king the world has ever seen. The tale follows Akbar among the snowy mountains between Kandahar and Kabul, and Steel warns that the names may puzzle at first, as in geography lessons.

Chapters run from farewell and the first victory, through the royal umbrella, tumbo-down, on the road, and at court, to winter, Down's stratagem, spring, and the night of record. An opening plate shows baby Akbar on a shelving bank of dry sand, rubbing his eyes. Children get a Mughal prince as a boy hero: courts, roads, and mountain passes, told as adventure with history behind it.
18318-crittenden-a-kentucky-story-of-lov:
John Fox Jr. wrote this Kentucky story of love and war, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1911, with copyright in 1900 and pictures by F. Graham Cootes. Fox dedicates the book to the master of Ballyhoo. The novel opens at daybreak on the edge of the Bluegrass, with birds singing the dawn and ten swift minutes changing the world from nervous exaltation to balm and peace.

From grim hills the scene turns to rolling green slopes, young leaves, white ash and sugar trees, and log cabins giving way to brick homesteads. The Bluegrass setting carries a story of Kentucky families, love, and the shadow of war, told in Fox's lyrical mountain and lowland manner. Readers get a regional romance: a Kentucky landscape at dawn, and the people whose lives unfold across it.
18337-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
Number 430 of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, new series, dated Saturday, March 27, 1852, cost a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly, which mixed essays, useful knowledge, and tales for a general readership. Its pages carry the plain, instructive voice that made Chambers a household name in Victorian Britain.

The number opens with Pronouncers, an essay on people who decide every question at once, loudly and without appeal. Such speakers, the writer says, often carry the company by sheer force of manner, even when they are geese. Another piece treats cooling the air of rooms in hot climates. Readers get a mid-century miscellany: character study beside practical advice.
18380-the-war-after-the-war:
Isaac F. Marcosson wrote this 1917 book on the war after the war, published by John Lane in New York, London, and Toronto. Marcosson, co-author of a life of Charles Frohman, dedicates the book to Lord Northcliffe. His foreword, written while Europe had been drenched with blood for nearly three years, looks past the fighting to the peace that must follow.

Millions of men had been killed or maimed, and billions of dollars in property had gone up in smoke. Marcosson argues that the smoke will clear, fields will green again, and armies will return to peaceful pursuits, while time heals wounds. Readers get a wartime book about peacemaking: trade, finance, and the shape of the world that would have to be rebuilt once the guns fell silent.
1842-michael-strogoff-or-the-courier-of-:
At a fête in the New Palace, the Czar learns the wire is cut beyond Tomsk. A courier named Michael Strogoff must carry a dispatch to Irkutsk before the rebels close the road. The novel opens at a palace fête, where word arrives that the wire is cut beyond Tomsk, and the Czar orders hourly telegrams to a city already falling silent.

Strogoff travels by tarantass at twelve to fourteen miles an hour, through steppe, river, and enemy lines. Verne fills the road with Cossacks, spies, and a brave young woman who shares his journey. The book is Verne at his most romantic: a race against time, a hero who will not break, and an empire measured in versts.
18497-my-second-year-of-the-war:
Frederick Palmer wrote this account of his second year of the war. Palmer also wrote The Last Shot and My Year of the Great War. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1917. Palmer, an American war correspondent, returns to the front and follows the fighting through Verdun and the Somme.

Chapters run from back to the front and Verdun and its sequel. A Canadian innovation and ready for the blow follow. Then come the blow itself, first results of the Somme, and out of the hopper of battle. Later chapters give forward the guns, when the French won, the brigade that went through, the storming of Contalmaison, a great night attack, cavalry going in, and the Anzacs. Readers get the Western Front in 1916 as a reporter saw it: battles, guns, and the men who bore them.
18676-our-navy-in-the-war:
Lawrence Perry published this account of the United States Navy in the Great War at New York in 1919, after a 1918 copyright. Dedicated to Navy Secretary Josephus Daniels, it opens with the German U-boat U-53 calling at Newport and sinking ships off Nantucket, then follows American destroyers to Queenstown. Vice Admiral Sims, armed merchant ships, and the first bluejacket deaths in the war zone fill early chapters.

Later chapters cover convoys bearing troops, destroyers working beside British ships, and the submarine's record, with notes on the Confederate Hunley as forebear. Perry writes as a keen observer of ships and men. The book is a vivid popular history of the navy at war.
1876-the-shape-of-fear:
A narrator cut off from the world aches to hear the cheerful little barks Nita used to give him by way of good night, and her absence becomes the haunting. Her amiable eye with its friendly light is missed, and the absence itself becomes the haunting.

Peattie's ghosts are quiet ones, working through loss and loneliness rather than through shocks, and the stories that follow keep that mood. The collection is a good sample of American supernatural fiction at the turn of the century, written by a Chicago journalist who knew how to make a small, sad strangeness linger.
18765-famous-adventures-and-prison-escap:
The Century Company published this set at New York in 1913, gathering pieces first copyrighted from 1885 to 1893. It opens with the war diary of a Union woman in the South, edited by George W. Cable from faint pencil pages copied in ink, with names changed for safety. Her understatement of peril charms the editor throughout.

Other pieces cover the locomotive chase in Georgia, a romance of Morgan's rough riders, Colonel Rose's tunnel at Libby Prison, a hard road out of Dixie, and the escape of General Breckinridge. Maps and pictures aid the tales. The book is a stirring anthology of Civil War daring and escape.
18794-three-years-war:
Christiaan Rudolf de Wet's account of the Three Years' War, published by Scribner's in December 1902, tells the Boer war from inside a commando. In September 1899, under the Commando Law, every burgher from sixteen to sixty had to hold himself ready, with horse, saddle, rifle, thirty cartridges, and eight days' provisions.

De Wet goes out as a private burgher and rises to vechtgeneraal, fighting at Nicholson's Nek, Ladysmith, Paardeberg, Sanna's Post, and Roodewal. Chapters follow blockhouses, night attacks, a commando of seven hundred men, and his cut through sixty thousand troops. Appendices print the Vereeniging and Pretoria negotiations that ended the war, with correspondence to close.
18993-history-of-the-world-war:
Francis A. March wrote this history of the First World War in collaboration with Richard J. Beamish, war correspondent and military analyst, with an introduction by General Peyton C. March, chief of staff of the United States Army. It presents itself as an authentic narrative of the world's greatest war, illustrated with official photographs from the American, British, and French governments.

The narrative runs day by day through campaigns on land and sea, including the American expedition to Murmansk, Archangel, and Vladivostok in 1918. Generals such as Allenby in Palestine appear in the account. Readers get a contemporary American history of the war, written close to events, useful for its chronology and its official pictures.
19136-hayslope-grange-a-tale-of-the-civi:
Emma Leslie wrote this tale of the English Civil War, set at Hayslope Grange. The Drury family faces divided loyalties as Harry plans to join the King's army and friends debate traitor against hero. Cromwell's Ironsides, cavaliers, and a wounded messenger soon enter the plot.

Maud Harcourt walks the fields in happy thought despite danger to Harry, while Bessie and Bertie weigh tales of soldier heroes. Gilbert Clayton, wounded at Chalgrove, talks of Hampden and Granville in quiet garden chats. Young readers get a Sunday-school style historical tale of faith, loyalty, and war in a country house.
19154-with-lee-in-virginia-a-story-of-th:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' tale of the American Civil War, With Lee in Virginia. His preface tells lads that the weaker South, ill-fed and ill-clad, held four years against a foe with sea power and European arms. Rights of secession, he notes, were still disputed by authorities.

The hero serves on a Virginia estate where Major Wingfield, liked by his slaves, supervised work himself, while overseer Jonas Pearson, a Northern man, gains power after the major's death. Mrs. Wingfield trusts his clear accounts. Young readers get stirring war fiction, sympathetic to the South, best read with a modern eye on slavery.
19235-under-the-great-bear:
Kirk Munroe wrote this 1901 northern tale, Under the Great Bear, where Ursa Major sails so low over a far northern sea that it seems like to fall. Cabot, fresh from graduation with no post, accepts a doubtful friend Thorpe's offer of a world trip, then doubts his own fitness and waste of four years. A lobster factory, a frigate, and a false report follow.

Cabot wonders if he truly wants Thorpe's company, since his guardian asked him only to recommend another man for work. Pride and shame spur him on. Readers get a boys' tale of the Labrador coast, sea work, and a young man learning his own worth.
19393-plays-of-near-far:
Lord Dunsany wrote this set of plays, first printed in London in the early nineteen twenties in a limited edition. The pieces range from the King of the Golden Isles, who must strike a bargain to save his realm, to a queen's flight. A comic clerk counting soap and a fancy of Shakespeare alive today round out the set.

Dunsany's stage worlds are near and far at once: fairy kingdoms beside modern offices, poets beside kings. The plays show his gift for short, strange fables, where a single choice, well or ill made, decides a fate.
1946-on-war:
General Carl von Clausewitz's On War, the classic theory of warfare, argues that war is the continuation of politics by other means. Its nature, he says, is shaped by passion, chance, and reason. Clausewitz, a Prussian officer who fought against Napoleon, wrote the book from experience as well as from thought.

The work takes up friction, the fog of war, the center of gravity, and the difference between absolute war in theory and real war in practice. It remains the most quoted book on strategy ever written. Its influence runs through military schools to this day, because it treats war as a human activity, not a machine.
19714-with-frederick-the-great-a-story-o:
G. A. Henty wrote adventure novels that taught boys history through war. With Frederick the Great tells the Seven Years' War. Henty opens by weighing the war's stakes. Had Prussia been crushed, he argues, Protestantism might have vanished from Germany. The whole course of later events would have changed. He adds that the war mattered nearly as much to Britain.

Henty's formula put a young hero beside great events. Readers learned campaigns while following invented lives. Frederick's Prussia, fighting larger coalitions, suited that formula well. Henty wrote dozens of such novels, all confident and brisk. This one shows his method at its clearest. History first, adventure as the delivery truck.
20173-the-romance-of-golden-star:
George Griffith wrote The Romance of Golden Star, a tale of lost Inca treasure. A sleeper who looks like an Inca lord draws the heroes' awe. If he woke, he could tell how that lost wonderland truly was. He could answer riddles, disprove lies, and reveal hidden treasure at once.

Griffith wrote bold tales of empire, war, and hidden gold for eager readers. Peru's past gives this romance its temples, tombs, and perilous quests. Greed and wonder pull the party deep into old Inca lands. Readers get lost-world adventure in the rich, pulpy style of its day.
20207-under-wellington-s-command-a-tale-:
G. A. Henty wrote Under Wellington's Command, a tale of the Peninsular War. Henty admits one book cannot hold that whole war in outline. To try would make a history, not a tale, he tells readers. His earlier tale had closed with the passage of the Douro.

That crossing drove the French from Portugal in a bold stroke. Now the tale takes up the thread where it left off. Young heroes serve under Wellington through sieges and hard marches in Spain. Readers get Henty's usual mix of true campaigns and boys' bravery.
20354-jack-of-both-sides-the-story-of-a-:
Jack of Both Sides tells the story of a school war at Brincliffe. New boys were lawful game at many schools of the era. But these new boys were also day-pupils, a great grievance there. Only last term had the first day-boy been admitted at all.

Wiseacres prophesied that Jim Bacon was the thin end of the wedge. Boarders and day boys line up as two camps in the war. School stories turn such splits into battles of honor and wit. Readers get a lively tale of loyalty, prejudice, and boyish combat.
20404-all-round-the-year:
E. Nesbit, best known for her children's novels, also wrote verse, and All Round the Year moves through the seasons in poems. The poems mark the turning months with flowers, weather, and city streets. Many were written with young readers in mind.

One poem follows a busy, dusty wind along cruel streets. The wind reaches the heart of violets and robs them of their sweets. Nesbit then turns the image on people: cold kindness met in the street can blight a poor heart the same way. The book mixes charm with such sharp little truths.
20724-the-man-with-the-broken-ear:
Edmond About, a French writer famed for wit, wrote the fantastic novel sold in English as The Man with the Broken Ear. The letters in the text speak to Leon, far from home, and hint at illness and longing at home. A strange find soon turns that homesick talk into a much odder tale.

About mixes science talk, satire, and adventure in one fast story. The broken ear of the title points to a dried human relic with a past of its own. Readers who like early science fiction with a sharp comic edge will find a brief, strange, and lively book here.
20729-at-the-point-of-the-bayonet-a-tale:
G. A. Henty wrote boys' adventure tales set inside real wars, and his Mahratta War story is a clear case. The text calls the fall of the Mahratta power one of the most stirring pages in Britain's Indian campaigns. Those campaigns ran from Clive's day to a firm British rule across the peninsula.

A young hero moves through marches, sieges, and fights as great powers clash around him. Henty packs in period detail about camps, arms, and Indian courts. Modern readers can see both the pull of the adventure form and the imperial views of Henty's age, held side by side on the page.
20849-the-big-brother-a-story-of-indian-:
Summer 1813 opens The Big Brother, George Cary Eggleston's tale of Indian war. Creek bands in Alabama and Mississippi had turned hostile that year. Quiet days of peace, Eggleston warns, make such times hard for later minds to grasp.

A big brother's care for the young gives the tale its name and heart. Frontier homes, alarms, and fights test that bond to the edge. Eggleston knew war at first hand from his own service. His tale mixes boyhood adventure with a veteran's sense of what frontier fear truly felt like, day by day.
21046-story-hour-readings-seventh-year:
Each great race keeps a heritage of story and song, E. C. Hartwell tells seventh-year readers. Hero songs, origin tales, moral fables, and pure fancy all share that store. Story Hour Readings gathers such goods for the seventh school year.

Hartwell chose tales to hold pupils in the last grammar years with worthy matter. Myths, ballads, history tales, and nature pieces fill the reader in turns. Notes help teachers draw out each tale's point in class talk. The book shows how schools once fed young minds on the world's old stories, held to be a birthright of every child.
21136-for-fortune-and-glory-a-story-of-t:
Lewis Hough opens at Harton, a boarding school much like Eton, before sending his heroes to the Soudan War. A former employee, an Egyptian, has stolen a will from a Dublin solicitor, along with an earlier version of it. Because of that theft, a family lost its money when an Eastern bank failed before the war.

Two story lines run side by side: the hunt for the stolen wills and the fighting in the Soudan. School slang and cricket give the early chapters their flavour. In the end the wills are tracked down and justice is done for the estate, while the war scenes carry their own weight.
21201-journal-of-a-voyage-to-brazil-and-:
Maria Graham sailed to Brazil and lived there through parts of 1821, 1822, and 1823, during Brazil's break from Portugal. Her journal, published in London in 1824, records the voyage and the residence. She admits in her preface that she cut many pages on public and private events before printing.

Graham writes honestly rather than with perfect impartiality, which she calls no virtue in some cases. She gathers facts that reached Europe one by one and records how events felt on the spot. The result is a sharp English traveller's picture of a new empire forming, its court, ports, and daily life.
21242-on-the-irrawaddy-a-story-of-the-fi:
G. A. Henty's preface warns that few of Britain's little wars killed so many, in proportion, as the first expedition to Burma. Stanley, his young hero, sails up the Irrawaddy as war breaks out. Chapter titles carry him from a new career to capture, a ruined temple, and service on the staff.

Burmese general Bandoola, the fight for the great pagoda, and the advance on Donabew all appear. Stanley is carried off and rescued along the way. Henty notes how Burmese forces stripped the country of boats and food, pinning the British in Rangoon through one wet season. Victory humbles Burma's pride by the end.
21326-the-black-bar:
HMS Nautilus patrols the west coast of Africa in George Manville Fenn's tale. She intercepts American and Portuguese slave ships bound to buy human cargoes for the Atlantic crossing. Two midshipmen serve aboard her, and Mark Vandean is the hero. The black bar of the title is a heraldic mark of shame in a family's arms.

Fenn drops Mark into one dreadful situation after another, solved often by something unexpected. The patrol setting shows British sea power used against the slave trade in African waters. Equatorial calms, glistening seas, and sudden action alternate as the Nautilus works her station and Mark's ancestry shadows his name.
21374-tention-a-story-of-boy-life-during:
Private Penton Gray, called Pen, wakes wounded in a ravine after a volley. In George Manville Fenn's Peninsular War tale, the boy bugler Punch lies hurt beside him. British troops are near, but French soldiers hold the ground where the boys lie. They must heal in hiding and then find their regiment.

Helpers along the way include the deposed king of Spain himself. Once back, the commanding officer learns that Pen has the education of an officer. He uses Pen's knowledge of the mountains to lead the troops against the French rear. The attack routs the French, and Private Gray is promoted to officer rank on the strength of it.
21398-black-bruin-the-biography-of-a-bea:
Black Bruin, Clarence Hawkes's 1908 life story of a bear, follows one animal from cubhood in the deep woods. Hawkes wrote many such lives of wild creatures, among them a beaver's tale. Charles Copeland's drawings show the bear's world of forest, stream, and mountain.

The tale opens with theft, a chase, and a wild baby bear learning to live. Bruin meets hunters, traps, and a panther, and learns the ways of his kind. Hawkes tells it as a life, not a pet's romp, with real risk at each turn. Young readers who love true-feeling animal stories will find a full one here.
22100-slavery-and-four-years-of-war:
Joseph Warren Keifer, a Union general and later Speaker of the House, published Slavery and Four Years of War in 1900. His subtitle promises a political history of slavery and a personal history of the war of 1861 to 1865. Keifer opens with slavery's long past, older than written history itself. He traces it from barbaric times into the American republic he helped save.

The second half turns to his own service with Ohio troops. Keifer fought in the Shenandoah Valley and rose to command a corps. His verdicts on generals and campaigns carry a participant's weight. The book joins two subjects that shaped his life: the sin he opposed and the war he fought.
22464-the-last-of-the-chiefs-a-story-of-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Last of the Chiefs, a story of the Great Sioux War. Its young hero, Richard Howard, faces a terrible problem at the start. He feels no fear on his own account, Altsheler writes.

A boy in years, Richard is a man in self-reliance. His boyhood on an Illinois farm taught him wood and field. Where prairies slope up to forest, he learned their ways. He is full of courage, strength, and resource for the trail. The story sets him amid the Sioux wars of the plains. Altsheler's frontier tales were favorites with young readers. This one mixes history, danger, and a capable boy hero.
22537-mr-dooley-in-peace-and-in-war:
Mr. Dooley in Peace and in War, dated 1898, collects Finley Peter Dunne's famous sketches. Mr. Dooley is a Chicago bartender who comments on the news. His pub stands in Archey Road, an Irish-American neighborhood.

There one can see wakes and christenings in American dress. Marriages and funerals of the old country appear modified by usage. The Banshee has been heard many times in Archey Road itself. On All Saints' Eve, pookies play tricks in cabbage gardens there. Dooley's brogue carries sharp satire on politics and war. The Spanish-American War fills many of these pieces with bite. Readers get American humor that presidents themselves read and quoted.
2263-julius-caesar:
Brutus joins Cassius in murdering Julius Caesar on the Ides of March, believing tyranny must be stopped. Shakespeare's Roman tragedy then follows the consequences: Antony's funeral speech turns the crowd, civil war consumes the republic, and the conspirators die at Philippi haunted by Caesar's ghost. The play asks whether noble motives can excuse a killing.

Portia and Calpurnia, the wives, see the disaster coming and are ignored. Rhetoric is the true weapon here, and Antony's oration remains a masterclass in persuasion. The tragedy endures as a study of politics, honor, and unintended ruin.
2266-king-lear:
An aged king divides his realm among three daughters according to their flattery, and the honest youngest is cast out. King Lear follows Lear into madness on a stormy heath, while the subplot of Gloucester and his sons mirrors the main ruin with blinded eyes and forged letters. Shakespeare strips away court, clothes, and reason until only human need remains.

The Fool's bitter jokes and Edgar's disguise as Poor Tom give the horror its strange poetry. Lear's reunion with Cordelia, and her death, form one of literature's most devastating closes. The play is often called Shakespeare's greatest achievement.
22666-the-rainy-day-railroad-war:
Holman Day wrote The Rainy Day Railroad War, a novel of labor and timber country in Maine. The catalog record gives no year. Day, a Maine journalist and novelist, made his name with stories of lumber camps, ward politics, and the men who ran both.

In the sample, a troubled young man named Parker protests the broken promises made to the work crews. The food was to be free of weevils and spoilage. Instead the Italian laborers went half starved and did poor work, while their padrone pocketed the money meant to feed them. Crooked middlemen, hungry crews, and a railroad pushing through wet country set the conflict. Day writes with a reporter's ear for camps and a reformer's anger at graft.
22755-the-adventures-of-the-little-woman:
The Adventures of the Little Woman, Her Dog and the Pedlar is a children's chapbook in verse, with pictures, of the kind once sold for pennies. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its pages mix a comic rhyme story with short moral poems spelled out in syllables for beginning readers.

In the tale, a dog stops barking and the little woman cries out in comic surprise that now she knows who she is. The companion poem teaches that whatever brawls may disturb the street, peace should reign at home. Birds in their little nests agree, it sings, and it is a shameful sight when children of one family fall out and fight. Such chapbooks were the first books many children ever owned.
22816-the-adventures-of-buster-bear:
Buster Bear wakes up hungry in the Green Forest in Thornton Burgess's 1916 animal story book for children. He yawns on his bed of leaves, watches the first sunbeams chase out the shadows, and shakes himself awake. From that slow morning start, his day of wandering and mischief begins.

Each short chapter puts Buster among his neighbors, the rabbits, squirrels, and other forest folk Burgess made famous. The tales teach natural history through talk and teasing rather than lessons. Buster is strong, a bit greedy, and often outwitted, which keeps him likable. Generations of children met American wildlife through books like this one, and the gentle humor still carries the stories.
23036-dave-darrin-after-the-mine-layers-:
H. Irving Hancock lists the action in Dave Darrin After the Mine Layers. The chapter headings promise a renewed grapple, a mine-sweeper's daily round, and a captain lost overboard. Later comes the hour of despair, a vanishing destroyer, the meeting of searchlights, a cowboy Dane, and a German prisoner who talks at last.

Darrin, Hancock's naval cadet grown officer, fights the Great War at sea in this entry of a long boys' series. Mine warfare made unglamorous, deadly work, and the book sells it as high adventure. The pace is relentless, the patriotism open. Readers meet the war as American boys of 1919 were invited to imagine it, dangerous, technical, and winnable by nerve.
23241-my-daily-meditation-for-the-circli:
J. H. Jowett's My Daily Meditation for the Circling Year, published in 1914, offers a short devotional reading for each day. One entry reflects on Abraham. Abram began his journey, Jowett notes, with no knowledge of where he would end up. He obeyed a noble impulse without seeing what would come of it.

He took one step, without demanding a view of the road ahead. That, for Jowett, is faith: to do what God asks today, and leave the outcome to Him. Readers get brief, plain meditations meant for daily use across a full year.
23263-the-fugitives-the-tyrant-queen-of-:
The Fugitives is a tale of the tyrant queen of Madagascar. Its author warns readers, honestly, that he has shifted time and place a little. He has also mixed his characters and their deeds somewhat, to suit the conditions of his tale and the story he wants to tell.

Even so, he says he strove to avoid exaggeration. His aim was a true picture of affairs at the period treated. The island itself draws his highest praise, as one of the most interesting and progressive in the world. Readers get adventure under a feared queen, with a storyteller who admits where invention begins.
23338-the-rubaiyat-of-ohow-dryyam-with-a:
J. L. Duff wrote this nineteen twenty two parody of Omar Khayyam for the age of Prohibition, with pictures by Benjamin Franklin, noted as not of Philadelphia. Where Omar praised wine, Duff laments its loss, as the law scatters drink and moral reformers draft ever sterner rules.

Quatrain after quatrain, drinkers mourn taverns gone dry, toast coffee as all that is left, and curse the statutes that washed a free land dry. The verse copies the old Rubaiyat music while turning it to jokes about raids, dry agents, and thirsty nights. Readers who know the source will catch the play best, but the groans and laughs land even without it.
23487-tonio-son-of-the-sierras-a-story-o:
General Charles King wrote this nineteen hundred six tale of the Apache war, with pictures by Charles J. Post. Tonio, son of the Sierras, erect and slender, stands on the frontispiece, a figure shaped by mountains, raids, and the hard code of the frontier.

Chapters open with a dry land question, does it never rain here, then move to scrambling slopes, watches kept east and south east, and fire opened on Case and Clancy. King, himself a soldier author, writes campaigns, scouts, and skirmishes with first hand ease. Readers who like western military tales will find a vivid, if period bound, story of the Apache wars, told from the saddle with a soldier's eye for ground and men.
24053-the-little-lame-prince-rewritten-f:
Dinah Maria Mulock wrote the original fairy tale, and Margaret Waters rewrote it here for young readers, with pictures by Hugo von Hofsten. It tells of a royal baby whose mother, Queen Dolorez, dies soon after his birth, leaving the child to a court of guardians. Twenty-four godfathers and godmothers are chosen to watch over him, each giving him a name.

The story follows the lame prince as he grows up apart from other children, kept close by those who guard him. His godmother's care and his own courage carry him toward the day he must take up a prince's duties. Young readers get a gentle tale about loss, patience, and growing into responsibility.
24122-pushbutton-war:
Joseph P. Martino wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in August 1960, with pictures by Schoenherr. A crewman in a fur-lined parka steps through a hatch into Arctic air and takes over from Harry in the pilot's couch. Their ship's autopilot heading gyro still drifts, but the hangar is full of ships under periodic inspection, so a replacement must wait.

Martino frames his warriors as heirs of Vikings, Caesars, and Apaches, all riding machines their forebears never dreamed of. War here is fought at a distance, by crews tending instruments in cold and cramped ships. Readers get a tense service tale of modern war, where skill with machines matters more than strength of arm.
24307-the-twenty-fifth-regiment-connecti:
This regimental history, published at Rockville, Connecticut, in June 1913, gathers four pieces on the Twenty-fifth Regiment, Connecticut Volunteers, in the War of the Rebellion. Colonel George P. Bissell supplies a brief history. Samuel K. Ellis, who went out as a private in Company G, gives experiences and reminiscences. Major Thomas McManus tells the Battle of Irish Bend. First Lieutenant Henry Hill Goodell tells how the regiment's pay was carried to New Orleans.

The regiment was recruited in Hartford and Tolland Counties in the fall of 1862, almost wholly young men moved by patriotic motives. Adjutant-General Morse later called it one of the best nine months' regiments, conspicuous before the fall of Port Hudson. Readers get a Civil War unit's record, from enlistment to battle honors.
24442-report-on-the-department-of-ports-:
Queensland's Department of Ports and Harbours reported to both houses of Parliament on its work for 1890-91. The report is dated at Brisbane on 26 August 1891. Its new head took charge on 1 July 1890. He describes flood damage to dredged channels in the Brisbane, Mary, Burnett, and Fitzroy rivers, and the dredging that restored them.

Later sections cover lighthouses, harbour works, shipping channels, and wrecks along the Queensland coast. They include repairs at North Head and the stranded steamer Wentworth. The report gives a plain, detailed record of how a young colony kept its ports open and its coastal lights working. It remains a useful source for the history of Queensland's harbours.
2464-history-of-florence-and-of-the-affa:
Niccolo Machiavelli's History of Florence traces his city's story from its Roman roots through the rise of the Medici, with the affairs of Italy woven in. The history shows Machiavelli as a civic thinker, not just the author of The Prince, arguing about liberty, faction, and the corruption of republics. His prose is clear, hard, and unsentimental.

The work's value lies in its insider's view of Florentine politics, written by a man who served the republic. Readers of Renaissance history will find a foundational text. It complements Machiavelli's political theory.
24668-in-our-first-year-of-war:
Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States, gathered these messages and addresses to Congress and the people, from 5 March 1917 to 8 January 1918, published by Harper and Brothers. The volume covers America's first year of war, from neutrality to full belligerency, with a frontispiece from a drawing by Wilfrid Muir Evans.

Wilson's addresses include the war message to Congress, Flag Day and other speeches, and the Fourteen Points of January 1918. His words set out war aims, peace terms, and the hope of a League of Nations. Readers of American history will find here the president's own record of a fateful year, in his own voice.
24722-letters-from-port-royal-written-at:
Edited by Elizabeth Ware Pearson and printed in 1906, this volume gathers letters written from Port Royal, South Carolina, between 1862 and 1868. The writers were Northern teachers and agents who came south after Union forces took the Sea Islands. Their letters report on plantation work, schools, and the effort to raise Black regiments.

Read in order, the letters show how freedom took shape day by day: wages, cotton crops, church meetings, and the pride of men who took up arms for the Union. The writers also record songs, speech, and home life among the freed people. It stands as a firsthand record of the Port Royal experiment, told by the people who lived through it.
24765-a-treatise-on-the-tactical-use-of-:
Francis J. Lippitt, a former colonel of California volunteers, published this manual in New York in 1865, just as the Civil War ended. It teaches officers how to use infantry, artillery, and cavalry together on the field. Each arm gets its own section: attack, defense, formations, and the ground on which guns and horses should stand.

Lippitt draws on real battles, from Waterloo to the fights of his own war, to show why skirmishers screen a column and why squares hold off horsemen. The rules are short, numbered, and plain, meant to be learned by heart. Military readers still find it a clear window into how mid-1800s armies thought about battle.
24789-unto-caesar:
Baroness Orczy, best known for The Scarlet Pimpernel, published Unto Caesar in New York in 1914. Set in ancient Rome, the novel takes its title from Christ's words on rendering to Caesar what is Caesar's. Its hero, Taurus Antinor, brings a friendless, motherless girl to friends who will shelter her and teach her their faith.
