Around them move men of power, old loyalties, and new beliefs, with Rome's might pressing on private lives. Orczy writes in her usual brisk, romantic style, with sharp dialogue and high feeling. Readers who enjoy her tales of honor under pressure will find the same spirit here, set against the early Church in the capital of empire.
24980-william-pitt-and-the-great-war:
J. Holland Rose's study of William Pitt and the Great War opens with Napoleon's 1816 remark to Colonel Wilks. England and France, Napoleon said, have held the fate of the world, and of European civilization, in their hands. Rose traces Pitt's conduct of the war against revolutionary and Napoleonic France, weighing how much harm the two nations did one another and how much good they might have done. The narrative moves between London, Paris, Berlin, and Dublin, following cabinets and campaigns.

One episode shows Grenville, annoyed at Pitt's interference during his own absence, offering to retire from the Foreign Office over Earl Fitzwilliam's Irish Viceroyalty appointment. Pitt declined the offer, and order returned at Downing Street, though at Berlin the mischief proved irremediable, with Jacobi representing Pitt's words in the worst possible light. Rose's Pitt is a statesman managing allies as much as enemies.
25028-heist-job-on-thizar:
Randall Garrett's science fiction heist sends Anson Drake to Thizar, where influential Thizarians hold no love for him. He is known across fifty planets as a man who can take care of himself. Drake sits in the Flamebird Room of the Royal Gandyll Hotel, sipping a drink, though he has no business in public. Life is danger and danger is life to him, and only the braggart Viron Belgezad could have drawn him there.

Belgezad already suffered at Drake's hands, when a narcotics gang was smashed, three men died of their own thionite, and fifty thousand credits of illicit gain vanished. Each man knows the other's part, and each waits his chance. A newsfax headline gives Drake his opening: Belgezad has bought the Necklace of Algol, matched star diamonds worth more than a million credits. Drake books the first liner to Thizar, and the heist is on.
25049-my-reminiscences-of-the-anglo-boer:
General Ben Viljoen's My Reminiscences of the Anglo-Boer War, published in London in 1902, tells the Boer side of the South African war from a senior Transvaal commander. Viljoen served as assistant commandant-general of the Transvaal burgher forces and wrote while held as a prisoner of war on St. Helena.

His account follows marches, skirmishes, and retreats across the veld, with close attention to horses, wagons, supply, and the strain of guerrilla fighting against a larger army. Written soon after the events, it offers a commander's view of Boer tactics and morale, and remains a firsthand source for a war usually told from the British side.
25152-all-for-a-scrap-of-paper-a-romance:
Joseph Hocking's All for a Scrap of Paper, published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1918, takes its title from the German Chancellor's dismissal of Belgian neutrality as a mere scrap of paper. The phrase, quoted in the book's opening, frames a wartime romance about Britain's decision to honor its pledge.

In a Cornish setting, a young man named Bob faces a public meeting addressed by a captain bound for the front. Tension grows between him and his mother over what duty requires. Hocking writes for a home-front audience, mixing love, conscience, and patriotic argument in the popular style of the war years.
25244-aviation-in-peace-and-war:
Major-General Sir F. H. Sykes's Aviation in Peace and War, published in London in 1922, surveys flying from balloons to bombers. Sykes, late Chief of the Air Staff and Controller-General of Civil Aviation, writes from inside the service he helped build.

A pre-war chapter traces gliders, the Wright brothers, airships, and the birth of the Royal Flying Corps. War chapters cover reconnaissance, photography, bombing, and home defence by night. A final chapter looks to civil aviation and aerial defence in peace. The book is a pioneer's account of air power's first generation.
25449-the-young-castellan-a-tale-of-the-:
George Manville Fenn sets this boys' tale about 1640, as England slides toward civil war. Young Roy Royland becomes castellan of his father's castle while Sir Granby rides off to defend the king. Old Ben Martlet restores the defences, cleans the armour, and drills Roy in fencing. He also repairs the portcullis and drawbridge and trains farm men as soldiers.

Through treachery the Roundheads seize the castle and take Roy, his mother, and Ben prisoner. Sir Granby returns at last and drives the attackers away. Fenn closes with the monarchy restored and peace spreading through England. The book teaches loyalty and pluck through siege, drill, and a boy's command.
25666-the-boy-tar:
Captain Mayne Reid writes The Boy Tar, a sea tale unlike his usual Wild West books, though he wrote a few sea stories in the manner of other nautical authors. Most of this book plays inside the cargo hold of a merchant vessel, a setting that fits none of Reid's usual genres.

The young hero, no more than four feet high, outdoes village boys in escapades. One escapade means stowing away in a vessel bound for Peru, six months away. He thinks he boards just before sailing, but he misses a key fact about the ship's timing. Reid, a keen naturalist as well as a storyteller, keeps the hold adventure vivid.
25873-the-motor-girls-on-crystal-bay-or-:
Margaret Penrose sends the Motor Girls to Crystal Bay in this 1914 tale, where a worried girl, a red oar, and a night plot tangle the summer. Freda's story opens the trouble: she fears to speak her worry, glances over her shoulder, and says she can almost see the ending. Cora urges her to begin at the start, and the four girls settle in to hear her out.

Chapters move from the Chelton and the Motely Mote to frights and fancies, a merry time, a rescue, and a calm that does not last. An angry druggist, odd talk, a breakdown, and plotters at a cabin raise the stakes, and Cora's brave resolve leads to the red oar again. The discovery that closes the book ties the oar, the plot, and Freda's fear into one neat knot.
26516-the-log-of-the-sun-a-chronicle-of-:
William Beebe arranged this 1906 nature book month by month, from January to December. It follows birds, beasts, insects, and fish through a single year outdoors. Short chapters take up winter birds in snow, spring songsters, polliwogs, marsh life, ocean secrets, and autumn flocks. The seasons set the order and the pace of what the reader meets.

Beebe writes as a watcher, not a lecturer. He explains how grouse walk on snow and why a flycatcher weaves snakeskin into its nest. He also shows what animal voices and tracks reveal to a patient observer. The book suits a reader who wants close, plain observation of common wildlife across the year. It keeps returning to one theme: how animals adjust their habits, homes, and songs to each turn of the seasons.
26561-the-story-of-a-common-soldier-of-a:
Leander Stillwell, late of Company D, 61st Illinois Infantry, published this memoir in a second edition with Franklin Hudson in 1920. He wrote it at Erie, Kansas, in July 1916, at seventy-three, because his youngest son Jerry earnestly asked for an extended account of his Union service. The book runs from enlistment to veteran furlough, told in a plain soldier's voice.

Chapters move from Camp Carrollton and Benton Barracks at St. Louis to Shiloh, the siege of Corinth, and the siege of Vicksburg. Hospital life at Helena, winter at Little Rock, a furlough home to Jersey County, and an interview with General Sherman after the war fill the later pages. Stillwell notes how his Democratic regiment turned Republican under the war's hard teaching.
26867-john-jones-s-dollar:
Harry Stephen Keeler wrote this tale of compound interest run wild. On the year's 201st day in 3221, a history professor at the University of Terra seats himself before the Visaphone. He lectures pupils scattered across the earth, their faces appearing in frosted glass squares. His pupils are bald, toothless young men in immense horn spectacles, and one late scholar, B262H72476Male, pleads that wireless to the North Pole was cut off.

The lecture spans ten centuries ending three hundred years before the professor's day, tracing a single dollar deposited by John Jones in 1921. Jones left it to his fortieth descendant, through the oldest child of each generation, at three per cent compounded annually. Keeler's opening image says it all: double a grain of wheat across a chessboard's sixty-four squares, and the world holds too little wheat to fill the last.
26884-the-backwash-of-war:
Ellen N. La Motte, an American hospital nurse, published these sketches of the Great War with G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1916. Their subtitle names the subject plainly: the human wreckage of the battlefield, as seen from a field hospital in the zone of the armies. La Motte dedicates the book to Mary Borden-Turner, called the Little Boss, to whom she owed her experience at the front. Thirteen sketches follow, from Heroes to An Incident.

Heroes opens with a deserter who fired a revolver through the roof of his mouth and made a mess of it, losing his left eye. Rushed to hospital over rough Belgian roads, he must be nursed back to health. Then he can be stood against a wall and shot, since discipline must be maintained. Later sketches cover a Belgian civilian, women and wives, a surgical triumph, and a citation, all in the same unsparing key.
26892-chasing-an-iron-horse-or-a-boy-s-a:
Edward Robins published this boys' Civil War adventure with George W. Jacobs and Company of Philadelphia in 1902. It opens on a stormy April night in 1862, in woodland a mile east of Shelbyville, Tennessee. There a tall, full-bearded man named Andrews addresses twenty sturdy fellows in no uniform. They are loyal Union soldiers of General Mitchell's division, camped on Duck River, and Andrews warns them plainly that they take their lives in their hands.

The plan is to cut Chattanooga off from railroad communication to the south and east, while Confederates concentrate at Corinth and Grant and Buell advance by different routes. Ten chapters carry the party through hazardous plans, mingling with the enemy, plot and plotters, a turn on the rail, energetic pursuit, and greatest peril. The boy George, with Watson, Jenks, and Macgreggor, rides the iron horse northward through the final trials.
26917-zehru-of-xollar:
Hal K. Wells wrote this tale of three Earthlings whisked to the den of the scientist Zehru. It opens after midnight on a New York subway platform. Robert Blake, a bronze-tanned former All-Western tackle, waits there with Helen Lawton, a tiny blonde with his diamond on her slim left hand. A burly third passenger leans against a pillar, derby shoved back, a suspicious bulge under one arm.

Rolling thunder of infra-bass closes in from every side, a note below the lowest bass ever struck. Then the green net comes: quivering ribbons of blinding green flame spurting from walls and roof. Blake sweeps Helen into his arms as the tendrils lash about them. On the far side, ape-things close in on a thicket. Blake finds a dead branch that makes an excellent club, and Helen's rubberized topcoat guards her against attack.
2722-morning-star:
H. Rider Haggard dedicated this romance of old Egypt to his friend Budge. Budge was a master of the language and lore of the great people who rise from holy tombs to teach history and faith. Haggard, an amateur beside such learning, submits his tale with doubt and friendship.

Morning Star follows an Egyptian queen through love, war, and the gods of the Nile, in Haggard's grand manner. Tombs, priests, and battles fill a story of destiny and devotion. The novel offers Haggard's Egypt at its most romantic, where the past walks alive among the living.
27465-birds-in-the-calendar:
F. G. Aflalo published these monthly bird sketches in London with Martin Secker in 1914, after they first appeared in The Outlook, whose editor and proprietors allowed them to be reprinted in book form. Each sketch suits one month of the twelve, and Aflalo treats birds from any standpoint but that of sport.

January gives the pheasant, February the woodcock, March the woodpigeon, May the cuckoo, July swifts, swallows, and martins, August the seagull, October the moping owl, November waterfowl, and December the robin redbreast. April visits a high hall garden and June listens to voices of the night. Bird lovers get a pleasant year of observation, month by month.
27700-the-rose-jar:
Thomas S. Jones Jr. published this 1906 book of poems in a limited edition of three hundred copies printed at Clinton, New York. Many of the verses had first appeared in magazines such as Appleton's, Everybody's, and Lippincott's.

The poems move through memory, love, the sea, and old gardens, with the title poem comparing the heart to a rose-jar holding dried petals. Gentle and musical rather than bold, the collection preserves an early twentieth-century lyric voice at its most reflective. Contents include The Island, A Ballade of Old Romance, April, Violets, and The Little Ghosts.
27857-the-dominant-dollar:
Will Lillibridge published The Dominant Dollar in 1909 with A. C. McClurg and Company of Chicago, after the success of his Ben Blair. The novel's hero, Roberts, is accused of degrading every consideration in life to a dollar-and-cents basis.

In two books, from prophecy and rebellion to friendship, fulfillment, and decision, the story tests whether love and honor can stand against money's measure. Illustrations by Lester Ralph mark key scenes, including a lover's declaration that love outweighs the dominant dollar. The accuser tells Roberts that his little yardstick is always in evidence, measuring and measuring without rest.
27866-great-britain-at-war:
Jeffery Farnol, author of The Broad Highway and The Amateur Gentleman, published Great Britain at War in Boston with Little, Brown and Company in March 1918, after 1917 copyrights. Dedicated to all his American friends, the book reports Britain's war effort for American readers.

Chapters also visit cartridge works, Clydebank shipyards, battle cruisers, a hospital, the guns, a training camp, Arras, Ypres, and flying men. Farnol writes with admiration for workshops and for troops alike, and the book is a wartime portrait of a nation mobilized for a long and bloody war.
27897-the-kopje-garrison-a-story-of-the-:
George Manville Fenn wrote The Kopje Garrison, a story of the Boer War, opening with two men, Drew Lennox and Bob Dickenson, fishing with magazine rifles instead of rods on a river. The river banks rise like cliffs, cut by ages of swift water through soft earth.

The lads debate crocodiles and hippopotamuses taking the bait, with Drew coolly advising Bobby to let go if a great beast pulls. Fenn's tale of mounted infantry in South Africa mixes humor, comradeship, and campaign life, in the sturdy boys' adventure manner that made him popular.
2794-found-at-blazing-star:
Bret Harte set this California gold-camp story in the mining settlement of Blazing Star, where rain washes lost objects out of the dust before cabin doors. Early one morning a miner named Cass Beard finds a woman's ornament in the road, though no woman is known to live in camp. The glittering waif starts gossip, suspicion, and a search for its owner.

Harte follows the rough miners as pride, courtesy, and rough humor collide around the stranger the ornament seems to promise. The tale turns on mistaken ideas about who the owner must be and what the men owe her. It shows Harte's familiar mix of camp life, sentiment, and a twist that gently mocks the miners' hopes.
2805-with-lee-in-virginia-a-story-of-the:
G. A. Henty wrote With Lee in Virginia as a boys' adventure set during the American Civil War, told from the Southern side. His preface speaks directly to young readers, praising the courage of ill-fed and ill-equipped Confederate regiments against a stronger enemy with command of the sea. The hero serves under Robert E. Lee through campaigns, camps, and battles.

The story mixes fighting, scouting, and escapes with set pieces such as the ironclad duel between the Monitor and the Merrimac off Norfolk. Henty explains strategy in plain terms while keeping the pace quick. Modern readers meet it as a period adventure, valuable for its energy and for what it reveals about how the war was retold to British boys.
28257-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
The Story of the Great War, volume one, New York, 1916, edited by Francis J. Reynolds, gathers official records of the European war to date. Major General Leonard Wood prefaces the volume on what the war means to America, with naval lessons by Rear Admiral Austin M. Knight and theatre surveys by Frank H. Simonds. P. F. Collier and Son published the work, with drawings, maps, and photographs.

Introductions, special articles, causes of war, and diplomatic papers fill the volume. Arthur Ruhl writes on the war correspondent, and Allen L. Churchill aids the editing. The book offers a contemporary American record of the war's first years.
28326-aladdin-of-london-or-lodestar:
Max Pemberton wrote Aladdin of London, or Lodestar, in 1907 as a novel of a boy, a hall, and a promise. Alban Kennedy, in a hall by Union Street, makes a promise, passes without the gate, and enters caves where strangers, a house of five gables, and Anna Gessner await him. Frank Parker drew the pictures, including an orgy of blood and whips.

Chapters follow Alban to Warsaw, a prison yard, and a meeting, as Count Zamoyski sleeps and old friends return. Pemberton, author of The Hundred Days, writes with melodrama and pace. The novel offers a stirring, old-style tale of a London Aladdin finding his fortune.
28334-the-new-hudson-shakespeare-julius-:
The New Hudson Shakespeare: Julius Caesar, Boston, 1908, presents Shakespeare's play with introduction and notes by Henry Norman Hudson, revised by Ebenezer Charlton Black with Andrew Jackson George. Ginn and Company published the school edition, with a title page from North's Plutarch of 1603 reproduced inside. The contents treat sources, date, and famous cruxes.

Notes trace the main story to North's Plutarch and Appian's Roman Wars, and discuss the scene of the assassination and Brutus's speech. The edition aims at students, with clear help and no excess. It offers a solid classroom Caesar, from a time when Hudson's Shakespeare ruled American schools.
28393-china-japan-and-the-u-s-a-present-:
John Dewey's China, Japan and the U. S. A., published as New Republic Pamphlet Number One in 1921, reprints articles on present-day conditions in the Far East and their bearing on the Washington Conference. Dewey, professor of philosophy at Columbia University, kept the original dates of writing as a guide to the reader.

He contrasts Japan, where he senses uncertainty and nervous tension beneath liberal hopes, with China, where he finds a widespread feeling that Japan is working toward domination of Chinese politics and industry. Dewey records the mood on both sides of the Eastern seas without claiming to settle the facts, and the pamphlet now reads as a sharp contemporary witness to a turning point.
28440-the-dark-star:
Robert W. Chambers's 1917 novel The Dark Star opens with a strange cosmic prologue. A dying star grows dark, Prince Erlik laughs, and a brooding figure called Truth watches the heavens pass away. A prefatory section, Children of the Star, then sets up the human story that follows.

Chapters move from a wonder-box and a quiet home at Brookhollow through letters, a journey, and a locked house. Later scenes involve travel by radio and by sea aboard the Volhynia. Chambers blends romance, mystery, and wartime adventure, keeping the star prophecy hanging over his characters as their paths cross and separate.
28449-the-motor-boat-club-and-the-wirele:
H. Irving Hancock's The Motor Boat Club and the Wireless was copyrighted in 1909. It follows Captain Tom Halstead and the Motor Boat Club boys on the Dot, Dash and Dare cruise. Bored on a lonely island south of Long Island, Tom, Hank Butts, and Joe Dawson wait for word from Mr. Seaton.

Their bungalow holds a wireless set linked to a bell. A spark puts the boys and their boat on the jump, and chapters unravel a mystery of invisible hands at the wireless, a traitor at the aerials, and a drab boat. A distress call of C.Q.D. sounds in a northeaster. Hancock mixes motor boating, early radio, and detective adventure for young readers of the wireless age.
28595-the-man-who-drove-the-car:
Max Pemberton's The Man Who Drove the Car, published in London by Eveleigh Nash in 1910, is narrated by Lal Britten, a chauffeur. Britten drove Fauny Dartel of the Apollo, who earned thirty bob a week on stage in The Boys of Boulogne, yet paid him three pound ten each Saturday. His tale, though, centers on a man picked up outside the Carlton Hotel who said he did not know who he was.

Chapters titled The Room in Black, The Silver Wedding, In Account with Dolly St. John, and The Basket in the Boundary Road follow the mystery onward. The Countess and the lady who looked on add society intrigue to the motoring world. Readers get an Edwardian tale of identity, money, and life behind the wheel.
28766-elements-of-gaelic-grammar:
Alexander Stewart, minister of the gospel at Dingwall, wrote this grammar of Gaelic in four parts: pronunciation and spelling, the parts of speech, syntax, and derivation and composition. The Royal Celtic Society edition, fourth and revised, appeared in Edinburgh in 1892, with a preface by the Reverend Dr. McLauchlan. Stewart of Moulin had been out of print for years, to scholars' regret.

McLauchlan praises the grammar for simplicity, conciseness, and philosophical accuracy, calling its discussions of the article, noun, verb, and preposition ample proof of care. Students of Scottish Gaelic still value it as a clear, scholarly guide. Readers get a solid nineteenth-century grammar, written by a minister-scholar who knew the language from daily use.
29498-the-film-of-fear:
Arnold Fredericks, author of The Ivory Snuff Box, set this 1917 novel in the world of motion pictures. Its heroine Ruth Morton earns one thousand dollars a week as a film star. The book opens as Ruth, in an embroidered silk kimono, works through her morning mail, counting her time at nearly six dollars an hour, ten cents a minute. A note from a stranger waits among the letters, and fear enters her gilded life.

Fredericks builds a mystery of fame, money, and menace, with film sets and fan mail as its stage. The plot turns on who watches the watched, and what a star's fortune cannot buy. Readers who enjoy early Hollywood tales and period mysteries will find a brisk, glamorous story from the silent era's height.
29501-negro-migration-during-the-war:
Emmett J. Scott's study of Negro migration during the war traces the great movement of Black Americans from the South to the North in the World War I years. Its fourteen chapters run from introduction and causes, through stimulation and spread, to the call of the self-sufficient North and the draining of the Black Belt. Efforts to check the movement, effects on the South, and conditions in St. Louis, Chicago, the Middle West, and the East follow.

Scott, writing close to the events, grounds his account in numbers, testimony, and local reports, with a bibliography and index. The book remains a foundational source on the Great Migration. Students of American history will find a detailed, contemporary record of a movement that remade the nation's cities.
30199-mcilvaine-s-star:
August Derleth tells of Thaddeus McIlvaine, an eccentric old amateur astronomer who claimed a dark star for his own, in a short tale of queer people and cosmic messages. Reporter Tex Harrigan, the narrator, knows enough lost, strayed, and warped geniuses to fill a department, and McIlvaine heads his list. With a modest income, McIlvaine played cards and chess at Bixby's tavern on North Clark Street, watched the stars, and held a fixed idea.

He believed life existed beyond this planet and that talk with other beings was possible, so he rigged queer machinery and tried constantly to reach them. A trio of cronies at Bixby's heard his progress among the stars and made a great joke of it, while his machine flashed a message across the void. Derleth asks whether McIlvaine inherited a dark destiny, or something stranger still.
30679-the-trouble-with-telstar:
John Berryman wrote this short science fiction tale, printed in Analog in June 1963, around a plain but costly problem: fixing a satellite in orbit. Its opening joke says the real trouble with communications satellites is that even a small repair needs a very long screwdriver. The narrator, Mike, works in a lab that tests parts to destruction, and he is drawn into a fight over a faulty solenoid.

Doc Stone calls Mike in, and Paul Cleary, whose design the solenoid is, refuses to admit the test failures mean anything. Mike must weigh loyalty, proof, and his own job as the dispute grows. Berryman turns a small engineering quarrel into a wry story about pride, blame, and the gap between a design on paper and a machine that must work far above Earth.
3069-the-great-boer-war:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Great Boer War as a history of Britain's war in South Africa. It runs from the Boer nations and the cause of quarrel through negotiations and the eve of war to Talana Hill, Elandslaagte, Ladysmith, Magersfontein, Stormberg, Colenso, Spion Kop, and Paardeberg. Doyle, who served as a doctor in the war, writes with a participant's knowledge and a novelist's pace. A passage on the advance describes a small party of South African Horse under Lieutenant Carlisle.

Swimming a broad river under fire, they bring back a ferry boat, bloodless but coolly planned and gallantly carried out. The way then opens to the advance. The book remains a readable contemporary history, partisan for Britain yet detailed on both sides.
30951-the-boy-allies-with-the-cossacks-o:
Clair W. Hayes, author of The Boy Allies at Liège, On the Firing Line, and In the Trenches, wrote this 1915 boys' adventure, published by A. L. Burt in New York. Its full title promises a wild dash over the Carpathian Mountains with the Cossacks. The story opens in the air, in a chapter called Flying, with Chester Crawford, an American lad of some sixteen years, asking Hal Paine what is below.

Hal, at the steering wheel of the flying aeroplane, sees nothing at first, and neither does Chester, straining his eyes. Then the third occupant makes himself known: Marquis, a dog, barking twice. Hal slackens speed and glides closer to the earth, since something must be wrong, or Marquis would not bark like that. It is a fast, old-fashioned boys' tale of flight, friendship, and war.
31355-to-each-his-star:
Bryce Walton's story, printed in Space Science Fiction in May 1952, strands four men in space after a wreck, drifting together in bulbous pressure suits linked by a gravity-rope beam. Russell, the narrator, fears they cannot remain sane in the frosty blackness, not knowing within thousands of light years where they are or where they are going. Old Dunbar, burned by cosmic rays and distant suns, takes command.

The magazine's blurb gives Dunbar's counsel: nothing around those other suns but ashes and dried blood. Only one way lies open, straight ahead to the sun with the red rim, down through clouds to Paradise. Dunbar's eyes are old and uncertain, and every star in this forsaken section wears a beckoning red rim. Tense and bleak, the tale turns a choice of suns into a test of faith.
31414-bear-brownie-the-life-of-a-bear:
Bear Brownie tells the life of a bear in the bear's own voice, adapted from H. P. Robinson's Animal Autobiographies and revised by Jane Fielding, with copyright in 1913. Brownie begins by doubting that he was ever a cub, then recalls tumbling downhill, his enormous-seeming parents, and a smaller sister whose ears he could box when he pleased. The opening chapter sets the tone: comic, confiding, and close to animal life.

Later chapters follow Brownie through growth, trouble, and the wild world as he learns it. Written for young readers, the book uses a first-person animal narrator to teach observation and sympathy. Its charm lies in Brownie's plain talk and in the small, vivid incidents of a bear's youth, told without sentiment getting in the way of the story.
31572-rulers-of-india-akbar:
Colonel G. B. Malleson's Akbar, in the Rulers of India series edited by Sir William Wilson Hunter, was published at Oxford by the Clarendon Press in 1890. Its contents begin with the argument, then turn to the family and early days of Bábar, his conquest of Kábul, and his invasions of India, before reaching Akbar himself. A map of the Indian Empire illustrates the volume. Malleson, a soldier-historian of India, writes a short, clear life for general readers.

Akbar, the Mughal emperor, stands at the center of the book as the builder of an empire and a policy of tolerance. Malleson's narrative moves from Babar's conquests to Akbar's reign, showing how one dynasty made India. Readers of Indian history will find a compact Victorian biography, useful as an introduction to the Mughal age and to the British view of it.
31937-evil-out-of-onzar:
Mark Ganes's short story Evil Out of Onzar was printed in Planet Stories in September 1952. It is set in a spacefaring galaxy where the orphan system of Onzar fumes under its leader's driving, paranoid megalomania. The prize, as its headnote says, is vast: the major warp-lines of space crossing the galaxy between the Allied Worlds and the Darzent Empire.

Its hero Roger Thane watches an Onzar delegation through a one-way glass panel in a vast meeting hall. An illustration caption warns that Thane knows a crazy duel is just another of Candor's roadblocks, and he has to win. Readers get a pulpy space adventure of empires, warp routes, and duels.
31953-merchantmen-at-arms-the-british-me:
David W. Bone's 1919 book Merchantmen-at-Arms, with drawings by Muirhead Bone and published in London by Chatto and Windus, tells the British merchants' service in the Great War. Bone opens with the spell of ships and the romance of voyaging as older chroniclers felt it. He opens also with the fact that Britain's island gates are set fast on the tide-mark, leaving escape only by crossing the misty sea-line.

Its parts cover the merchants' service itself, its relations with the Navy, and its war staff, with a frontispiece of merchantmen at gun practice. Readers get a wartime tribute to civilian sailors who armed their ships and carried on trade under fire.
31957-lectures-on-horsemanship-wherein-i:
Lectures on Horsemanship, published in London in 1793 by T. S. , Professor of Horsemanship, explains every necessary instruction for both ladies and gentlemen in the useful and polite art of riding, with ease, elegance, and safety. Its opening address tells its audience that the horse is an animal destined from the earliest ages to the pleasure and services of man.

T. S. argues that mankind were not long before they learned the horse's noble qualities. They applied them to the purposes for which they were given, a truth apparent from the histories and traditions of almost all nations. Readers get a Georgian riding manual, direct and practical, for the polite equestrian.
31967-graded-poetry-third-year:
Graded Poetry, Third Year, edited by Katherine D. Blake, principal of the Girls' Department of Public School No. 6 in New York City. Georgia Alexander, supervising principal in Indianapolis, published in New York by Maynard, Merrill and Company in 1906 with copyright in 1905, collects poems for schoolchildren across two half years.

First-half poems include Edward Lear's Owl and the Pussy-cat, William Blake's Piper, Christina G. Rossetti's Year's Windfalls and Swallow, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's Hiawatha's Childhood and Hiawatha's Sailing. Readers get a classroom anthology of classic verse for third-year pupils, graded for reading and recitation.
32019-stone-s-river-the-turning-point-of:
Wilson J. Vance's history, published in New York in 1914, argues that the Battle of Stone's River was the turning point of the Civil War. Vance, writing from Newark, New Jersey, in July 1914, sets the battle inside the wider war of 1862, a year when Confederate hopes, in his account, stood at their height. Southern armies were at full strength, and their young soldiers had not yet been lost in battle.

His chapters move from North and South in 1862 and foreign relations that year, through the armies and their leaders, to the fighting itself. They cover the first day's battle, the night and the next day, and January 2, 1863, before a closing chapter on what might have been and what was. An appendix follows. Readers get a compact, argumentative battle study that claims a single river battle changed the war's course.
32106-dusty-star:
Olaf Baker's Dusty Star, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1936 with drawings by Paul Bransom, is a wilderness tale of animals and the people among them. Baker, author of Shasta of the Wolves, builds the book from short, titled chapters that read like campfire episodes. An illustration shows a mother making a long double journey five times more, hinting at the endurance the story celebrates.

The contents introduce Carboona's secret, Running Wolf, Kiopo, and Sitting-Always, with chapters on medicine-making, how the wolves sang, and how Kiopo came back. A silver fox called Baltook, yellow dogs, a grizzly, and a lynx all enter the tale, with a terror of the Carboona at its heart. Dusty Star meets that terror, dances with the wolves, and hears Carboona's call. Readers get an animal adventure in the tradition of wild-life fiction.
32254-world-without-war:
E. G. von Wald's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1954, imagines a future where cooperation itself is unlawful. The cover line says teaming up suited the dark ages, yet this age of high culture treats love as no joke. People who cooperated, even biologically, were unlawful, and worse follows.

Mark knows stopping is unwise, with Jennette's party already pressing, yet three folk in the open prove too tempting. He hovers over an undulating flow of magma, frozen toward the long, dry Potomac bed, with shallow caverns and mile-wide potholes. Under an overhanging cliff of half-vitrified soil stand two damaged cars and three men. Mark laughs out loud. It is not often one finds three people at once, so close together. Readers get a dystopia, where togetherness is crime.
32258-joseph-k-f-mansfield-brigadier-gen:
John Mead Gould's Joseph K. F. Mansfield, Brigadier General of the U.S. Army, a narrative of events connected with his mortal wounding at Antietam, Sharpsburg, Maryland, September 17, 1862, was printed in Portland by Stephen Berry in 1895. Gould, late acting adjutant of the Tenth Maine Volunteers and major of the Twenty-ninth Maine Veteran Volunteers, tells the general's life before his death in battle.

Mansfield was born in New Haven, Connecticut, on December 22, 1803, educated in his state's common schools, and entered West Point at fourteen, the youngest of a class of forty. During five years of study he distinguished himself especially in the sciences, graduating in 1822, second in his class. Promoted at once to the Corps of Engineers, he served throughout the Mexican War, becoming first lieutenant in 1832 and captain three years later. Readers get a Civil War general's life, ending at Antietam.
3272-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part two of Artemus Ward's complete works holds his Civil War humor. The show is confiscated first, with thrilling scenes in Dixie and a Fourth of July oration. The war fever in Baldinsville, a war meeting, and the draft in Baldinsville follow, with the surrender of Cornwallis thrown in for confusion. Things in New York and a touching letter from a gory member of the home guard keep the satire rolling.

Ward in Canada, the noble red man, and Ward in Richmond widen the tour, with a letter to the Prince of Wales to close. The misspelled dispatches mock both war fever and war profiteering. Readers get the Union's home front as Ward's showman saw it: blustering, tender, and ridiculous by turns, in prose that never spells quite right.
32780-asteroid-of-fear:
Raymond Z. Gallun tells of John Endlich, a homesteader on the asteroid Vesta, in this story from Planet Stories of March 1951. Endlich lands with his wife Rose and their children Bubs, seven, and Evelyn, nine, carrying a Homesteaders Office box that holds everything from a prefabricated house to toothbrushes.

Miners jeer him as a hydroponic pumpkin-head, and his hot temper has already cost him a farm and six months in an Illinois jail. On Vesta he raises a plastic dome, fits an airlock, and runs electrolysis from an atomic battery. His true trial is moral: to face brutal odds without serious violence, and without supine submission, by selling respect for himself.
3289-the-valley-of-fear:
Arthur Conan Doyle divides this Holmes novel into two parts. Part one holds the tragedy of Birlstone: a warning, Holmes discoursing, darkness, the people of the drama, and a dawning light toward the solution. A country house murder opens the case, with a secret society's mark upon it. Holmes reads the scene with his usual cold brilliance.

Part two, the Scowrers, rewinds to America: the man, the bodymaster, and Lodge 341 at Vermissa. The valley of fear itself, the darkest hour, and the trapping of Birdy Edwards close the tale. Readers get two novels in one: an English detective puzzle and a mining valley terror story, joined by a single avenging thread.
32896-tween-snow-and-fire-a-tale-of-the-:
Bertram Mitford sets a frontier tale in the last Kafir war, opening with a buck, a greyhound, and a Kafir runner on a grass slope. Watching hidden from a bush clump is Tom Carhayes, owner of a Kaffrarian stock run. He is furious: the runner, Goniwe, should be herding eleven hundred of his master's sheep three miles away.

The poaching quarrel widens into war, as Gcaleka raiders seize cattle and loyal men bring warnings. Jonas, a Bomvana mission-station man, reports a thousand Gcaleka cattle hidden in bushy kloofs below. Eustace, Tom's cousin, walks blindfold into a trap his enemies prepared. Eanswyth returns alone to her old home at Anta's Kloof, living her old life in shadow.
32910-with-wolseley-to-kumasi-a-tale-of-:
Captain F. S. Brereton follows Dick Stapleton from a Gold Coast trading store to war, in a tale of the first Ashanti war. Dick lies awake in stifling heat, listening to surf boom on the Fanti beach, with two hundred pounds in gold under his bed. His store is nearly empty of goods, his two houses unwanted, and his clerk James Langdon, he believes, has robbed him for years.

Dick joins Sir Garnet Wolseley's expedition toward Kumasi, scouting ahead of the column. He creeps past Ashanti sentries by hand signals and owl calls, learning how hard the task is. At the staff camp he studies star shells, hand grenades, rockets, and barrels labelled beads, meant to pay the way in some districts. If King Koffee meets the column in the open, Dick argues, rifles and gatlings will smash him; in the bush, it will be different.
32918-with-rifle-and-bayonet-a-story-of-:
Captain F. S. Brereton, R.A.M.C., opens in Redford, Surrey, where Captain Charles Somerton quarrels with his wife over their young son. The boy, about eleven, climbs the stairs sobbing while his parents argue below. His father pleads for gentler correction of a thin-skinned lad; his mother listens with passion nearly mastered.

The story carries the boy to the Boer War, where Jack and his comrades ride the veldt by night through thunder and lightning. A Boer hail of Wie gaat daar challenges their cart on the open road, and Wilfred whips his horses on rather than halt. Later, recovering in hospital, Jack and Guy plan an escape eastward through Komati Poort into Portuguese territory, aiming for Lorenzo Marques and a steamer to Durban. Disease, not only bullets, fills the hospitals they leave behind.
32930-a-gallant-grenadier-a-tale-of-the-:
Captain F. S. Brereton, R.A.M.C., follows Philip Western from a scolded schoolboy to a Crimean soldier. Chapter one finds Philip's father distressed after thirteen years of careful bringing-up, while jovial Joseph Sweetman defends the lad as generous and good-hearted, if a little wild. A practical joke on the odious Barrington sets the household quarrel.

In the Crimea, Philip prefers Russian guns to the disease filling the hospitals, where the young volunteers earn praise. By the middle of August the epidemic abates, though the fleet still suffers severely. Philip and Tony bivouac in a vineyard, hoping at dawn to dash for the British camp without stumbling on a French or Turkish outpost. On October 25th, fog over the Valley of the Shadow of Death lifts to the boom of Russian guns at Balaclava.
3305-ballads-of-peace-in-war:
Michael Earls writes ballads of war from the side of peace in this volume. His Light opens the set: gray mist on the sea, night coming down, and a woman waiting with sorrow in a far town. Her lover goes the sea-ways by dim channel lights, and her love watches for him like a true light. They would have wedded on a fair yesterday, but the quick regiment saw him away.

Gray mist fills her eyes as night falls, and he feels a prayer from a far town across the water. Earls, a Jesuit poet, gives war its home front in song form. The ballads suit readers who want the Great War in lyric rather than in report: lovers, mothers, and prayers, set against the noise of regiments marching away.
33467-narrative-of-a-second-expedition-t:
John Franklin's Narrative of a Second Expedition to the Shores of the Polar Sea, with John Richardson's natural history notes, tells of Arctic exploration by authority. Franklin, the famed polar explorer, leads a journey to the far north's shores, while Richardson, a doctor and fellow of the Royal Society, records its science. The narrative, with sidenotes kept inline, follows a hard road through ice and tundra.

The book's value lies in its first-hand Arctic detail, from native peoples to wildlife, told by men who lived it. Its tone is official yet vivid, suited to readers of exploration. For students of the polar regions, it is a classic account of a second voyage that added much to knowledge of the north.
33619-maori-and-settler-a-story-of-the-n:
G. A. Henty tells a boys' story of the New Zealand War, opening with a home broken up and a family's embarkation for the far side of the world. The voyage, a row on shore, a boat expedition, and the work of refitting carry young readers into a colony where settlers and Maori are at war. Henty's hero must learn soldiering, bushcraft, and the politics of a divided land.

Like Henty's other historical tales, the novel mixes adventure with instruction, explaining campaigns and colonial life as its characters live through them. Modern readers will note its period attitudes toward empire and indigenous peoples, and should read it as a document of its time as well as a story. It remains a vivid example of late Victorian boys' adventure fiction.
33769-the-harwich-naval-forces-their-par:
E. F. Knight records the Harwich naval forces' part in the Great War in this 1919 Hodder and Stoughton volume. Part One follows the Harwich Force of light cruisers and destroyers from the opening of the war. It covers the first shots of the naval war, the sinking of the Königin Luise, and the loss of the Amphion. It also covers the Heligoland Bight action, Arethusa's duel with the Frauenlob, the Dogger Bank battle, the Lowestoft raid, and the action off Texel.

Further chapters cover convoys, escorting seaplanes in the Cuxhaven and Sylt raids, and patrols of the Channel and mine-net barrages. Part Two covers the submarine flotilla, its composition, heavy losses, and humorous incidents. Knight writes with a sailor's attention to ships and actions. The book is a valuable contemporary history of a hard-worked force in the North Sea war.
34007-the-postage-stamp-in-war:
Fred J. Melville, editor of The Postage Stamp, wrote this book on stamps in wartime, published in London in 1915 by the author at Brixton. Melville thanks many collectors and dealers for lending stamps and envelopes for illustration, naming Bentley Wood, Harland, Holmes, Heywood, Ireland, and Wedmore among them.

A note tells of a new work on stamps of the new British Protectorate of Egypt, then on the press in the Melville Stamp Book series. The book shows how war reaches even the small world of the stamp album. It serves philatelists who collect the marks of conflict.
3402-the-parlor-car:
William Dean Howells sets this one act farce entirely inside a railway parlor car on the New York Central line. Late on a cloudy autumn afternoon, a gentleman dozes alone with his feet up and a newspaper across his lap. The conductor then brings in a heavily veiled young lady, followed by a porter with her wraps and bags, and the quiet car becomes a stage for awkward talk.

The comedy grows out of mistaken identity, polite evasion, and the forced closeness of train travel. Passengers cannot escape each other, so small courtesies and small lies pile up fast. Howells keeps the action to dialogue and entrances, which makes the piece easy to read aloud and a good sample of his light stage writing.
34360-roses-four-one-act-plays-streaks-o:
Hermann Sudermann wrote Roses, four one-act plays Englished from the German by Grace Frank and printed in New York in 1909. The four are Streaks of Light, Margot, The Last Visit, and The Far-Away Princess. A list of Sudermann's books names The Joy of Living, in Edith Wharton's rendering, and Morituri, three more one-act plays. Streaks of Light opens the volume, with three persons: Julia, Pierre, and Wittich.

The scene of that play is a small pavilion in the park of an old castle, in the present day. The room is eight-sided, of the Rococo age, its ceiling and walls cracked and spotted by rain. A glass door stands wide open at the back, its shutters closed. Sunbeams cut through the blinds in streaks of light across the half-dark room. A sofa and gilded chairs, a four-post bed, and a laid table fill the stage.
34522-the-secret-of-the-league-the-story:
Ernest Bramah wrote The Secret of the League, subtitled The Story of a Social War, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons. A frontispiece shows a woman unbuckling the frozen straps of a man's gear. The first chapter is named for Irene, and the second for the period and the coming of wings.

Contents promise a compact, the downtrodden, a schedule, secret history, and the effect of the bomb. Later chapters bring a great fiasco, a dark winter, the bargain of famine, and a closing cry of Poor England. Readers get a dystopian novel of class war and a secret league, from the writer who later created Kai Lung.
34579-bees-from-british-guiana-bulletin-:
T D A Cockerell names the bees of British Guiana in a short museum paper dated December 21, 1918. It stands as article twenty of volume thirty-eight of the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History. The pages run 685 to 690.

The bees came from the Bartica District. William Beebe's Tropical Research Station of the New York Zoological Society made the collection. John Tee Van sent the specimens on. Almost all were taken about a clump of flowering nightshades in thinned-out jungle. Cockerell gives an artificial key, so a non-specialist can separate each species. Bright green bodies start the key. One new small species is Augochlora callichlorura. Types of the new forms rest in the museum. Some came from the Penal Settlement, some from Kalacoon.
34826-the-rider-of-golden-bar:
The Rider of Golden Bar, a western novel by William Patterson White, was published in Toronto in 1922 with a front plate by Remington Schuyler. White also wrote Paradise Bend, Hidden Trails, and The Heart of the Range. The book is dedicated to his Point of Woods cousins Laura, Charlotte, Julia, and Dorothy.

The tale opens with Billy Wingo pressed by a rancher's daughter to show some ambition. Wingo jokes that he uses his ambition by asking her to marry him at every chance. Chapters name Hazel Walton, a district attorney, trappers, gunfighters, and a trap. A plate shows a girl clutching a rider's stirrup to save herself from a fall. Courtship, crime, and range honor drive the brisk plot.
34999-the-count-of-nideck-adapted-from-t:
The Count of Nideck, adapted from the French of Erckmann and Chatrian by Ralph Browning Fiske, appeared in 1897. Page and Company published it at Boston with illustrations by Victor Searles. A front plate shows the count standing upright on a window sill in alarm. Chapter one is called the summons to the castle in the contents.

Meeting the countess and a first night in Hugh tower follow in the contents. Knapwurst teaches the narrator the family tree of the Nidecks in a later chapter. The count unsheathes his claws, and a servant girl tells her own strange tale. A plague hunt, a midnight scene on the Altenberg, and a night lost in the dwarf lodge build the dread. Werewolf lore of the Vosges drives this French tale in English dress.
35211-war:
Pierre Loti wrote War, Englished from the French by Marjorie Laurie and printed at Philadelphia and London in 1917. Loti gives the book to his friend Louis Barthou. Contents open with a letter to the Minister of Marine, then two poor little nestlings of Belgium and a scene at the battle front. A letter to Enver Pasha, the phantom basilica, Tahiti, and an evening at Ypres stand in the list.

An appeal for the wounded in the East, Serbia in the Balkan war, Rheims, and the death-bearing gas fill the later heads. The first piece is Loti's letter of August 18, 1914, signed as a captain of the naval reserve. Recalled to active service, he writes, he had hoped for some duty less slight than the dock-yards gave him. He makes no reproaches: the Navy will not fill the chief role in this war.
35362-billy-barcroft-r-n-a-s-a-story-of-:
Percy F Westerman wrote Billy Barcroft, R N A S, a story of the Great War, issued in London by S W Partridge and Company. The book was first issued in December nineteen seventeen and reprinted in nineteen twenty eight, twenty nine, and thirty. A front plate shows flaming wreckage plunging earthwards. More than thirty chapters fill the tale. Billy serves in the Royal Naval Air Service.

Early chapters give Billy a price on his head and tell of his brother Peter. A Zeppelin raid, a kidnapping, and red ruin follow in fast order. Betty, a seaplane quest, and the terrors of the air fill the middle. Captives in a submarine, an ocean duel, and a hold up in the North Sea add sea peril. A bombing expedition and gas close the run. Boys got air and sea war in one brisk tale.
35392-a-woman-s-experiences-in-the-great:
Louise Mack, an Australian writer under her married name of Creed, published this account of her experiences in the Great War. Fisher Unwin published it at London in 1915, with eleven full-page illustrations including permits, passports, and a sketch map of Belgium. Fifty-three chapters take her from the Channel crossing to her return to London.

Mack opens on a burning August night at Folkestone quay, asking an old salt what is done about mines, and sails for Ostend under the flashes of English battleships. She travels toward Antwerp in the track of the invaders, through Aerschot and Ghent, meeting the grey-coats face to face. Chapters on Brussels under German occupation tell of Burgomaster Max, his arrest, and his influence on the city. She watches Antwerp shelled day by day until the city surrenders, then makes the flight into Holland and friendly shelter there.
35501-the-condition-of-catholics-under-j:
John Morris edited The Condition of Catholics under James the First, for Longmans in 1871. Morris was a priest of the Society of Jesus, the title says. The book holds Father Gerard's narrative of the Gunpowder Plot. Gerard's own life stands before the narrative in the volume. Contents open with the state of persecuted Catholics at the Queen's death.

Hopes of relaxation under the new king rose, and failed, the heads say. Persecution and all kinds of molestation then increased. The Puritan faction procured that increase, in this account. Diverse gentlemen conspired and concluded on some violent remedy. Scruples led them to ask learned men questions from afar, without opening the case. Father Garnett, suspecting somewhat, wrote letters to Rome against rebellion. The plot was discovered as Parliament drew near, and the prisoners were examined.
35726-the-united-states-and-the-war:
Gilbert Murray wrote The United States and the War, issued at London in 1916 by W Speaight and Sons. Murray warns that it is risky to judge the mind of a foreign folk too freely. He tells of a man who held that Americans cared only for comfort, money, and safety. That man told his view to two young Americans.

One of those men had worked fourteen hours a day for relief in Belgium. The other had passed as a Canadian to fight in the British Army. Murray tells of a man of letters who went at his own cost to aid Polish refugees. That man worked for months among folk starved and sick with typhus. Murray uses such tales to fault glib claims about America at war.
358-the-scarlet-car:
Richard Harding Davis tells four linked motoring tales in this brisk volume, all set among rich young New Yorkers and their cars. A Harvard-Yale game trip opens the book, and each later tale turns on a bold drive, a rescue, or a chase. The scarlet car itself becomes a mark of speed, nerve, and luck.

In one tale friends break a man out of jail by road; in another they foil kidnappers; in a third they race to save a romance. Davis writes fast dialogue and bright road scenes, with little time for doubt. The stories capture an early motoring age, when a car could still feel like a daring new machine.
36166-that-little-beggar:
That Little Beggar, a tale by King Hall, was published in London by Blackie and Son. A front plate shows Chris brought back by his friend the sergeant. Eight chapters follow the narrator, Jack the dog, and young Chris through a song and a story, eight flies, swimming lessons, a paste-man and a paint-box, and a golden farthing.

Chapter one, Jack and His Master, opens at a small country station. The narrator, tired from a long ride, asks the station-master for the carriage that Wyndham promised to send. None has come, and none is to be seen anywhere. A walk in July sun down a white road lies ahead, past gay flower-beds picked out in dazzling white stones. Hall sets a gentle country-house tale of a lady, her dog, and a beggar boy.
36499-rounding-up-the-raider-a-naval-sto:
Percy Westerman wrote a sea tale of the great war, printed at London and Glasgow in 1916 with drawings by Hodgson. A long list of his other boys' books stands at the front. The front picture shows Denbigh and his friends saved by a monitor warship. Contents open with a captured liner.

The last of a Japanese ship, life on board the raider, and a threat follow. The hunt for the Pelikan, a decoy, and a collier that foils the chase fill the middle. A midnight landing, a lagoon, and Denbigh's plan lead on. Westerman wrote scores of such tales of cadets, airmen and sea scouts for boys of the war years.
365-foreign-dishes-a-foreign-dish-for-ev: 365 Foreign Dishes gives one foreign dish for each day of the year. The recipes move across Austrian, East Indian, and other national kitchens, with clear steps for meat, fish, vegetables, sauces, and seasoning. Each entry names its ingredients and cooking time in plain order, so a home cook can follow it from start to finish. The year long sequence turns daily cooking into a tour of flavors from many countries.
36757-religion-and-the-war:
Yale religion faculty wrote these essays on religion and the war. Sneath edited the book for Yale University Press in 1918. The press issued it on the James Wesley Cooper fund. Cooper, Yale class of 1865, was a New Britain pastor long years.

His widow gift founded the fund in March 1918 memory. A poem up front lifts hands not in dumb resignation. Faith springs like an eagle to meet the sun, it cries. Tyrant feet trampling the common weal frame the war context here. The volume is the second work issued on that memorial fund by the Yale press.
36864-school-reading-by-grades-sixth-yea:
James Baldwin made a school reader for the sixth year of study. The American Book Company held the rights in 1897 for School Reading by Grades. Baldwin writes that a sixth-year pupil should read new words at sight with ease. Clear tones and faultless speech are the marks he sets for reading aloud.

Selections show nearly every kind of English writing at its best. Notes on authors' lives and on hard passages stand in an appendix. Portraits of authors and prints from famed paintings fill the book. Pupils gain a guided path into judging fine writing for themselves.
37088-john-pettie-r-a-h-r-s-a-sixteen-ex:
An art book fills this item: sixteen examples in colour of the work of John Pettie, printed at London in 1910 in a series on British artists. An introduction by Martin Hardie opens it. Bonnie Prince Charlie, one of the plates, stands on the cover. A portrait of the painter forms the first plate.

A list of plates names each picture and the owner of the original. The Vigil hangs in a national gallery; a drum-head court-martial in Sheffield; a sword-and-dagger fight in Glasgow; and a portrait of an actor as David Garrick is owned by its sitter. The introduction begins the life. Pettie, like many great painters, was of humble origin, born at Edinburgh in 1839. His father was a tradesman who bought a business in a village in 1852. The boy, Hardie says, was born with art in his blood.
37495-text-books-of-art-education-v-2-of:
Text Books of Art Education, Book Two, by Hugo B Froehlich and Bonnie E Snow, teaches drawing and colour to children in the second year of school. It is the second of seven books in the series, published by the Prang Educational Company in 1904.

The series was planned in meetings with leading art teachers, among them directors of art in Minneapolis, Indianapolis, and Providence. Froehlich had taught at Pratt Institute, and Snow had led drawing in the Minneapolis schools. The lessons borrow verses from Stevenson's A Child's Garden of Verses, lines by Christina Rossetti, and a stanza of Longfellow. The theory of colour relations used in the books is credited in the opening pages. The catalog title is clipped, but the title page gives the series and book plainly.
37682-heads-of-lectures-on-a-course-of-e:
Joseph Priestley's Heads of Lectures on a Course of Experimental Philosophy, particularly including chemistry, was printed at London in 1794 by Johnson of Paul's Church-Yard. The lectures were delivered at the New College in Hackney, the Dissenters' college open to all without distinction.

Priestley, connected with the tutors by friendship, undertook the course to help the college, and printed the heads to save students the trouble of writing them out. One lecture a week had to carry the whole subject, chemistry included. He tells beginners that a large outline serves best: no one subject wearies them, more ground is covered, and each may pursue any branch farther in later life as his ability allows.
3776-the-valley-of-fear:
Arthur Conan Doyle builds this Sherlock Holmes novel in two halves that fit like a lock and key. The first half opens at Birlstone, where a warning in Porlock's handwriting reaches Holmes, and a murder in a moated manor sets Watson, Inspector MacDonald, and Holmes to work. A bundle weighted with a dumb-bell, raised from the moat by Barker, proves one of the clues that turns the case.

The second half travels back to America, to the mining valley of Vermissa and Lodge 341 of the Scowrers, where a detective named Birdy Edwards infiltrates a terror gang. The two stories join at the close, as the Birlstone victim's past catches him at last. Readers who like Holmes at his most dramatic will find a novel of secret societies, revenge, and careful deduction.
3779-the-world-war:
Logan Marshall wrote this early American history of the Great War for readers stunned by the guns of 1914. The book opens with the Sarajevo murders of Archduke Francis Ferdinand and his wife. Then it steps back a century to trace how the French Revolution, the fall of feudalism, and rival empires led Europe to war. Battles, sieges, and diplomacy follow in plain narrative, with the Italian campaigns of an earlier age sketched as background.

One passage follows Austrian troops back to the Quadrilateral fortresses of Peschiera, Mantua, Verona, and Legnago, while French and Italian forces bivouac on the Chiese. Marshall writes for a popular audience, with maps of motive rather than fine military detail. Readers who want a first history of the war as its own age saw it will find a brisk and earnest volume.
37792-england-canada-and-the-great-war:
England, Canada and the Great War is a war tract by Desjardins, a past law man of a French state of the north land and of its chief house. It came out at that state town in October of nineteen eighteen. Its front note tells the book first came out in his own tongue the year past. A next form had to be struck past weeks to meet the press calls of its hands.

Men of weight have since urged an English form of the work on him, he says. He wrote the book to prove the right of the friends cause in the great war and to rout the false views of a chief of his own folk. He first meant to write but a short form of his French book. At work the book grew past twice the size he had set.
38154-text-books-of-art-education-v-4-of:
Book Four of the Text Books of Art Education, for the fourth year of school, was written by Hugo Froehlich and Bonnie Snow. The Prang Educational Company published the series in 1904. Froehlich had taught at Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, and Snow had supervised drawing in the Minneapolis public schools.

The preface explains that the series grew from conferences with leading art teachers. Its plan joined drawing to the child's growth, year by year, rather than treating art as copying alone. Advisers named in the front matter include art directors from Indianapolis, Providence, and St. Louis, and the Harvard psychologist Hugo Münsterberg. The fourth-year book carries graded lessons in drawing and design for classroom use. Prang's series helped set the pattern of art teaching in American public schools.
38454-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, volume twelve, slice eight, runs from Haller to Harmonium. The articles in the slice are set out in a two column list at the front. They open with Albrecht von Haller and close with the harmonium itself. A transcriber's note explains the signs used for roots, accents, and Greek letters.

Lives in the slice include Berthold Haller, Edmund Halley, and Marcus Hanna. Places range from Hamburg and Hanover to Hang Chow Fu in China. Hallstatt, Hallowe'en, hallucination, and haloes stand among the general topics treated. The Hanseatic League and the battle honours of Hannibal both appear in the list. Handsel, handicap, handwriting, and hanging fill out the run of entries. The slice forms one part of the great eleventh edition's twelfth volume.
38610-frank-merriwell-s-new-comedian-or-:
Frank Merriwell's New Comedian stands in the Merriwell series of boys' tales. Burt Standish wrote the long line of Frank and Dick Merriwell stories. The series sold at fifteen cents a book for young men readers. A half million followers attest the tales' unfailing interest, the list boasts. Fun and thrills in all branches of sports fill the adventures told.

School days, chums, foes, and a trip west open the long series list. Down south, bravery, a hunting tour, and Europe follow in order. At Yale, sports afield, races, and a bicycle tour come next. Courage, daring, loyalty, and camp stand among the later titles named. The brothers play fair with themselves and the world in all tales. High moral tone and fired ambition stand as the series' promise. All titles stay always in print, the publisher assures boy readers.
38793-south-america-and-the-war:
Kirkpatrick gave these lectures at King's College, London, in the Lent term of 1918. Cambridge University Press published them that year under the Tooke Trust. General conditions in Latin America fill his introduction, on the book's contents page at the front.

Political currents and forces in the republics form the first chapter. The German outlook on Latin America and the economic war with its propaganda follow in the list. The recognition of Latin America, effects of the war on the republics and Pan-Americanism close the lectures, with a map of the former Spanish and Portuguese possessions at the end.
38938-through-east-anglia-in-a-motor-car:
J E Vincent wrote a motoring travel book published in 1907, with sixteen color illustrations by Frank Southgate. A frontispiece shows Ely at eventide. Chapter one runs in winter from Oxford to Cambridge, Newmarket, and Ipswich. Chapter two continues from Ipswich to Norwich by Woodbridge, Beccles, Lowestoft, and Yarmouth.

Spring chapters cross the heart of East Anglia and return to Norwich, Ely, and Cambridge. Summer chapters start from Colchester and visit Gainsborough's country. One chapter promises troubles made easy for motorists. Great houses, the fens, and a priory fill later pages. King's Lynn forms a center for the final chapter. Vincent writes for the new class of car tourists.
38969-ralph-the-train-dispatcher-or-the-:
Ralph, the Train Dispatcher, or The Mystery of the Pay Car, by Allen Chapman, was published in nineteen eleven by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. The tale is the fifth volume of Chapman's Railroad Series. Earlier volumes followed Ralph from the roundhouse through the switch tower and the engine cab.

The contents promise a wreck on the Overland Express, wire tappers, and trouble in a tunnel. Ralph makes a schedule, holds the Limited Mail, and chases a runaway. A strange message and the Slump secret build toward the mystery of the pay car. The chapters end with a battle of wits and one minute after twelve. Like its companions, the book sold railroad work to boys as adventure with a trade attached.
39150-a-hero-of-lie-ge-a-story-of-the-gr:
A Hero of Liege is a boys' war story by Herbert Strang. Its subtitle calls it a story of the Great War. Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton published it in London. It was first printed in 1914, the year the war began. Cyrus Cuneo illustrated the volume. A cover picture shows a spy unmasked. The contents open with card game titles, The Opening of the Game. Tricks, neutral territory, and a close call follow in sequence.

Later chapters bring an old mill fight and life in the trenches. A fight with a Zeppelin and the great guns raise the scale. Strang wrote a shelf of war stories for boys. The list inside includes tales of India, Canada, and the Russo-Japanese War. This one turns to Belgium's stand at the war's opening. Liege gives the tale its hero and its setting.
39487-erasmus-against-war:
Erasmus Against War holds the great scholar’s famed plea for peace. Lewis Einstein shaped the book as the Humanists’ Library’s second part. J W Mackail wrote the front words for the Boston issue. The Merrymount Press printed it in nineteen hundred seven.

War is sweet to them that know it not: the old saw heads the plea. Love of great men and love of maids share that blind sweet trap. Youth rushes bold where age, taught by grief, hangs back in fear. If one thing must be fled with prayer, it is war, Erasmus cries. None is more foul, more sad, more wide in ruin, he argues here. Yet men take it up for each light cause, in each land, each year. Priests and bishops bless the sword that laymen lift in haste. The plea stands in the grave English of a far off age of print.
39540-the-revolutionary-movement-of-1848:
The Revolutionary Movement of 1848-9 in Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Germany, by C Edmund Maurice. G P Putnam's Sons published the work at New York and George Bell and Sons at London in 1887. An engraved frontispiece shows Giuseppe Mazzini. Maurice also wrote The Lives of English Popular Leaders in the Middle Ages.

Schiller's lines on man's hope of better days stand as epigraph. The preface calls the book the result of many years' work. It aims to show the links that connected the movements together, with some examination of the previous thirty-three years.
40219-the-border-rifles-a-tale-of-the-te:
Gustave Aimard, the French writer of frontier tales, set this romance in the Texan war. Ward and Lock printed The Border Rifles in London in 1861. Aimard had roamed the Americas, and his books trade on that wild schooling.

The Runaway opens the tale, on a land where great woods fall before the axes of squatters and pioneers. Towns and tilled fields now stand where thick forest rose ten years back, he notes. Quoniam, Black and White, and Black-Deer fill the first list. The Snake Pawnees and the battle bring the war in. Carmela, love and jealousy, and the conducta de plata — the silver train — mix love with gold. The White Scalper and the ambuscade close the thirty chapters.
40567-the-mercenary-a-tale-of-the-thirty:
Eccott wrote The Mercenary, a tale of the Thirty Years' War published by Blackwood in Edinburgh and London in 1913. His other novels, listed at the front, include His Indolence of Arras and The Red Neighbour. The hero is Nigel, a soldier of fortune. The first chapter sends him in search of booty, and the second has him collecting his dues. War in seventeenth-century Germany was a trade, and Nigel plies it.

The contents sweep across the war's great stage. Tilly, the imperial general, appears early. The castle of Hradschin at Prague and the emperor's circle follow. Wallenstein and an archduchess enter the story, with a Jesuit confessor weaving through the plot. Lost despatches are found, a devil is cast out, and the battle of Breitenfeld fills the twenty-fifth chapter. Eccott builds a swashbuckling romance on the war that ruined Germany.
40581-the-secret-service-submarine-a-sto:
Guy Thorne wrote The Secret Service Submarine, a story of the present war, issued in New York in 1915. A poem, The Song of the Submarine by William Booth, opens the book. The submarine sings of roaming from Scapa Flow to the Bight of Heligoland, lying in wait like a sleeping whale. Its name in the poem is Sudden Death.

The tale is told by John Carey, whose brother Bernard commands submarines in the Navy. John dates the strange affairs from the day he tried to enlist and was rejected. His father ran a small foundry at Derby, and John idled at Exeter College, Oxford. Contents promise a murder, a fight with a German giant, and a submarine fighting for England in the North Sea.
40602-the-freebooters-a-story-of-the-tex:
Gustave Aimard wrote a tale of the Texan War and its wild border men. The book came out in London in 1861. Aimard also wrote Border Rifles and The Indian Scout. A front note claims the tale's core facts are true in full. It is the second link in a set of three tales.

The White Scalper, the third book, tells how Texas was freed. San Jacinto's famed fight stands in that close, the note says. This book shows the South's bent on the eve of civil war. That war then loomed as North and South drew apart. Border fights and bold rides fill the tale at hand. Young and old took Aimard's west tales up fast.
40652-a-guide-to-the-scientific-knowledg:
Ebenezer Brewer wrote A Guide to the Scientific Knowledge of Things Familiar. Jarrold and Sons issued it at London. Brewer headed King's College School at Norwich. He held a post at Trinity Hall, Cambridge. Salt and snow are both white, his preface opens. A rose is red and leaves are green, he notes.

Few persons ask the reason why, he says. A flute sounds sweet and a cracked bell jars. Fire is hot, ice cold, a candle bright. Water boils with heat and freezes with cold. A child asks why and gets a frown, he laments. Silly questions get the child called foolish, he adds. Some two thousand such questions fill the book. Each stands answered in a child's plain words. Sheet by sheet, two scholars checked his facts. Brewer's famed why-book taught parlors and schools that common things hide deep science.
40660-the-interpreter-a-tale-of-the-war:
Whyte-Melville wrote this tale of the Crimean War, illustrated by Kemp-Welch and published by Longmans. A frontispiece shows a man saying his heart sank within him, at page 172. The old desk opens the contents, and the deserter follows in the second chapter.

Father and son, a Romany camp in the tale's old spelling and school days fill the early list. Ropsley, Beverley Manor and Alton Grange carry the home story forward in turn. Omar Pasha, a figure called Skender Bey, a Beloochee and Zuleika swing the tale east to the war, where the interpreter earns the title at the Golden Horn.
40774-brooks-s-readers-third-year:
Brooks's Readers, Third Year is a school reader put together by Stratton D. Brooks, superintendent of schools at Boston. The American Book Company printed it, with copyright entries of 1906 and 1907. It is the third step in a graded set for young pupils.

The contents mix tales, poems, and nature pieces at a gentle climb of skill. Robert Louis Stevenson gives The Land of Story Books, and Christina Rossetti gives The Sky Bridge. Other pieces treat flowers that tell time, the dandelion, the farmer's wheat field, and the song of the mill wheel. An old legend, The Diamond Dipper, stands among them, and pieces on my country close the patriotic side. The first tale, The Magic Windows, promises that readers who look through them will see strange and beautiful sights.
40931-the-early-history-of-the-scottish-:
Omond wrote this early history of the Scottish Union question, here in a bi-centenary edition printed at Edinburgh and London in 1906. Omond had written on Fletcher of Saltoun for the Famous Scots series. Press notices from the first edition fill the front pages. They praise a brief, bright, and even-handed account of a long dispute.

The story runs from the time of Edward the First to the Act of Union in 1707. Reviews say Omond is at home in the struggles that led up to that act. One calls the book a genuine gift to British history, and one thanks him on behalf of students. A portrait of John Hamilton, Lord Belhaven, fronts the volume.
40945-the-shadow-of-the-czar:
John Carling wrote a romance printed at Boston in 1902. The coronation duel stands as frontispiece. A prologue gives a meeting in a forest, a castle by the sea, fever and recovery, a sealed chamber, and the return of the master. The story proper starts two years afterwards, amid Czernovese politics and a menace from the Czar.

The princess and the cardinal, the Russian frontier, and Katina the patriot follow. What happened in Russograd, Paul and the princess, and a display of swordsmanship fill the middle. The deed of Michael the guardsman, the envoy of the Czar, and a Polish conspiracy drive the close. Carling's hero wanders late at night in a deep pine forest of Dalmatia as the tale opens. Thrones and swords rule this old Poland plot.
41172-the-white-scalper-a-story-of-the-t:
Gustave Aimard wrote The White Scalper, a story of the Texan war put out in London in 1861. Aimard had told tales of scouts, free bands, and a tribe chief of the plains. A note at the front sets out the right order to read his eleven books. The White Scalper stands third in the first set of three.

Border Rifles and Freebooters come first in that set, by that list. A next set of six runs from Trail Hunter to Indian Chief. A last set holds Prairie Flower and Indian Scout. The firm says a rich form with twelve plates is in train. Each plate was drawn and cut by the best hands of the day. Care for the dress and scenes of each tribe came from the great work of Catlin.
41243-brooks-s-readers-first-year:
Stratton Brooks, head of schools at Boston, wrote a first year reader for young children, held under copyright in 1906. Brooks says the one aim of the book is to help children learn to read. Its lessons use things each child knows and words children use in talk each day.

New words come in slow steps and are used again and again so their shapes grow known. Brooks says skill in reading comes best from much practice, so the book gives a large store of tales a child can master. Sentences stay short, each tale ends on one leaf, and no pictures break into the text in the first hundred pages.
41264-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, volume XV, slice II, runs from Jacobites to Japan, part only. The slice forms part of the 1911 dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Its article list opens with the Jacobites and Jacobus de Voragine. Jacobs Cavern, Jacob's Well, and the Jacquard loom follow in the alphabet. The Jacquerie and jade, both the estuary and the stone, appear.

A long run of Jameses fills the middle columns. Kings of Scotland and England stand beside James of Hereford. Henry James and William James, the American philosopher, both appear. Anna Brownell Jameson and Leander Starr Jameson close the family. The editor's corrections touch the Jamaica article. Compensation there ran at 19 pounds per slave against a market value of 35 pounds. Another note prices a trained Japanese dwarf tree at as much as 200 pounds. Jameson's fifteen months in Holloway after the raid are corrected too.
41278-pastoral-days-or-memories-of-a-new:
Pastoral Days is a nature book by Hamilton Gibson, published in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1881. Its sub-title calls it memories of a New England year. The book is inscribed to a close companion, to whom each page recalls a shared past. The contents follow the cycle of the seasons. Spring is The Awakening and summer The Consummation. Autumn and winter close the round. A long list of plates names the artists who drew the country scenes. Hoskin, Morse, and Marsh stand among them.

Birds, brooks, and orchards fill the text. The phoebe's nest, the columbine, and the meadow brook get their sketches. Little plunderers in the apple orchard and a marvel of nature stand in the run. Gibson was a naturalist and artist of Connecticut. His book is a year in the fields, kept as a diary of sights.
41435-british-secret-service-during-the-:
Nicholas Everitt's British Secret Service during the Great War was published in London by Hutchinson, and this copy is the third edition. Everitt dedicates the book to Viscount Northcliffe, praised as the greatest of living Englishmen in the national crisis. The first chapter recalls the calm of 1914 and the multitude of German spies said to be undermining England.

Contents chapters compare secret services old and new, and note that the modern British service was founded in 1910. Later chapters teach the reader temporary codes, from grammatical and geometrical codes to a knot code. Others hunt German mine-layers, recall the loss of the Audacious and introduce the agent Jim to active work.
41455-the-lady-in-the-car:
William Le Queux wrote The Lady in the Car, published in Philadelphia by Lippincott in an edition of 1908. The preface, headed An Apology, explains the book's game.
