These are curious chronicles of an adventurous motorist, Le Queux writes, and of his actions toward certain female acquaintances. With the law of libel looming, real names had to go, and assumed ones stand in their place.

The hero, called the Prince, has been Le Queux's friend since they played cricket at Cheltenham as lads. Le Queux has met him in unexpected places all over Europe, especially beyond the Danube. For the friend's actions no apology is offered. While the game of mug-hunting stays so easy and profitable, there will always be hunters and hunted. The first chapter opens His Highness's love affair. Riviera readers got the gentleman adventurer at the wheel.
41588-europe-from-a-motor-car:
Russell Richardson wrote this motor tour of Europe, copyrighted in 1914 by Rand McNally. A photo of the approach to the Stelvio pass fronts the book as its first plate. Richardson dedicates the volume to his mother in a short note at the front.

Berlin to Marienbad opens the contents, and Marienbad to Trafoi follows on the road. Crossing the Stelvio into Italy, a visit to Lyons and runs through Nîmes, Carcassonne and Tarbes fill the middle. A day in Spain, the châteaux of Touraine and a run from Orléans to Dieppe close the tour, with expenses and suggestions at the end.
41709-a-girl-s-life-in-virginia-before-t:
Letitia Burwell wrote A Girl's Life in Virginia Before the War, copyrighted in 1895, with sixteen full-page illustrations. A dedication to her nieces states the book's purpose plainly. They will find their ancestors called cruel slave-owners, inhuman wretches, southern taskmasters, and dealers in human souls in English and American publications.

From such names they will recoil, she writes. Her own life would have been embittered had she believed herself descended from such monsters. So she leaves a record of plantation life as it was, that the truth be preserved among a few. Readers get an unrepentant planter-class memoir, valuable now chiefly as evidence of how the slaveholding world wished to be remembered.
41779-the-human-boy-and-the-war:
Macmillan printed this set of school tales at New York in June 1916, and reprinted it by October. The Human Boy and the War shows the Great War through the eyes of boys at an English school. Fortescue, a knowing lad, does much of the explaining.

The Battle of the Sand-Pit leads the set. Fortescue holds that two great ideas of the soul stand behind the war of guns. A good idea at your back, he says, often wins the fight. The Mystery of Fortescue, Travers Minor the scout, and the Fight follow. Percy Minimus and his Tommy, the prize poem, and the revenge fill the list. War games and war work mix in a boy's world turned grave.
41855-the-marne-a-tale-of-the-war:
Edith Wharton writes a boy at war in The Marne, a tale of the war, printed in London in 1918. Macmillan made the book. Chapter one builds its hero out of crossings. Ever since the age of six Troy Belknap of New York had embarked for Europe every June, on the fastest steamer of one of the most expensive lines.

With his family he descended at the dock from a large noiseless motor. He kissed his father good bye, and shook hands with the chauffeur, a particular friend. He trotted up the gang plank behind his mother's maid. One steward captured his mother's bag, and another led away her miniature French bulldog, also a friend of Troy's. For six golden days Troy ranged the decks, splashed in the salt water of his huge porcelain tub, and dined with the grown ups. War will end this charmed round, the title warns.
42127-the-german-war:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The German War, issued by Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto in MCMXIV. Doyle had earlier written The Great Boer War. Nine chapters fill the short book. The first treats the causes of the war. Later chapters treat plots, creeds, and the small British army in the field.

Doyle states the British case in plain terms for home and foreign readers. A note says the first piece ran as a call for recruits in Great Britain. It also ran in full in fifty top journals in the United States and in Dutch and Danish forms. Doyle holds that Britain fights for its life and for all that is fair and sacred. The book is a wartime plea from its first months.
42144-the-spring-of-the-year:
Dallas Lore Sharp walks the season in The Spring of the Year, a volume of the Dallas Lore Sharp Nature Series from Houghton Mifflin, with pictures by Robert Bruce Horsfall. Sharp had written The Lay of the Land and The Fall of the Year. He dedicates this one to his sister Jennie, best of companions in the woods and fields.

The contents promise The Spring Running, an old apple tree, and chapters of things to see, to do, and to hear this spring. Turtle Eggs for Agassiz and Woods Medicine close the set. The first chapter asks who your spring messenger is, and votes for the frogs.
42232-a-child-s-dream-of-a-star:
Charles Dickens wrote this short tale, issued at Boston in 1871 with illustrations by Hammatt Billings, engraved by W J Linton. A brother and sister spend their days wondering at the flowers, the sky, and the bright water.

One clear shining star comes out before the rest, near the church-spire above the graves, and the two watch for it hand in hand and bid it good night. Then the sister droops, and the boy looks out alone and reports the star to the pale face on the bed. The plate list follows her little grave, and the man with graying hair who still sees the star above it. Readers get Dickens at his most tender and grave.
42280-popery-the-accommodation-of-christ:
The Reverend Edward Hoare attacks Roman Catholic doctrine in a lecture given at Islington on Monday, June 26, 1848. The Islington Protestant Institute published it at London for one shilling. J H Jackson of Islington Green handled the printing.

Hoare's title states his charge. Popery, he argues, bends Christianity to suit the natural heart. The front pages list the institute's officers and rules. Its stated aims are to wake Protestants to the progress of popery and to rally their energies against it. The body also defends the Protestant principles of the constitution. Such lectures fed the fierce church debates of the 1840s. Hoare was incumbent of Christ Church, Ramsgate. The pamphlet shows popular Protestant polemic at full voice.
42451-heroines-of-service-mary-lyon-alic:
Heroines of Service is a collective biography by Mary Parkman, published by the Century Company. The book was copyrighted in 1916 and 1917 and reprinted several times, a sign of its welcome in schools and libraries. Parkman dedicates it to her mother and to all true mothers, whom she calls heroines of service.

Eleven lives fill the contents. They begin with Mary Lyon, founder of a college for women, and Alice Freeman Palmer. Clara Barton of the Red Cross and Frances Willard of the temperance cause follow. Julia Ward Howe and Anna Howard Shaw stand for letters and suffrage. Mary Antin, Alice Fletcher, and Mary Slessor of Calabar carry the story to immigrants, Native peoples, and Africa. The book closes with Marie Curie and Jane Addams. Each life is told as a record of service to others.
42826-austria-containing-a-description-o:
Frederick Shoberl wrote Austria, a survey of its peoples. C S Williams issued it at Philadelphia in 1828. Twelve colored engravings aid the text. Women of Slavonia front the book. Pope's line on man's study heads the title. The preface warns of a seeming imbalance. Most plates show Hungary, not Austria proper.

High culture smooths out dress and manners, Shoberl argues. German states show few odd traits for the pencil. Hungary holds tribes of many nations instead. Their habits stand unmelted by refinement there. Such lands give the artist far richer matter. Provinces and their extent open the contents. An early costume book, the work sells wonder at an empire's mix of peoples to readers who would never ride its roads.
42850-the-pied-piper-of-hamelin-and-othe: The Pied Piper of Hamelin and Other Poems was a volume in Every Boy's Library, a cheap series of story and verse books for young readers. The hosted pages open with the series list for the 1910 edition, which runs from The Man Without a Country and a Christmas Carol to The Gold Bug. A rhymed bookplate begs borrowers to return the book. The Pied Piper volume gave a boy the famous rat-catcher poem with other poems beside it, in a binding made to be lent and handed on.
43077-a-clerk-of-oxford-and-his-adventur:
A Clerk of Oxford, by Everett-Green, is a tale of the Barons' War in old England. Nelson and Sons printed the book in London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1898. A view of Oxford from an old print fronts the tale.

The first chapter opens on a youth of fifteen or sixteen face down on a fresh grave. A gentle voice behind a moss-grown wall tells him not to mourn as those without hope. The chapters take the young clerk to Oxford by river, into the new life of a student. A mad parliament, a fair, and a magician's tower fill the early terms. Kenilworth Castle, the great earl, and Prince Edward draw him into the war. The field of Lewes, a captive who conquers, and Leofric's reward close the tale.
43083-a-young-man-s-year:
A Young Man's Year is a novel by Anthony Hope, author of Phroso and The Dolly Dialogues, first published in 1915. Its hero, Arthur Lisle, is a young barrister of the Middle Temple with a hundred and fifty pounds a year and no interest to push him. Thirty-six chapters follow his year among Miss Sarradet's circle, household politics and the law.

The novel opens on a dark, drizzly Monday morning in March, with mist over the Temple garden. He curses the small income that tempted him into the fatal ambition of the Bar. The comedy is gentle and exact: a young man with every advantage but momentum, measuring his life against the briefless terms. The chapter titles promise flutter, complications and a new vision before spring.
43469-a-counterfeit-presentment-and-the-:
William Howells published two short plays in one volume with David Douglas at Edinburgh in 1882. A Counterfeit Presentment, a comedy, fills the first and longer half. The Parlour Car, a farce, follows it at page 191 in the contents. The comedy never leaves the parlour of the Ponkwasset Hotel in its scenes.

Bartlett the painter and Cummings enter at noon on a fine September day. Easel, camp stool, colour box, and canvas pile around the piano legs at rest. Bartlett is bearded, quick eyed, and stubborn, with arrogance in his very step. Cummings is pale, dreaming, and gentle, a foil in temper and in build. A striking likeness drives the plot, as four part titles promise in turn.
43519-commentary-on-the-maya-manuscript-:
Commentary on the Maya Manuscript is a scholarly paper from Harvard. The Peabody Museum issued it in October 1906 as its Papers, volume four. Ernst Forstemann wrote the commentary on the Dresden Codex in German. Selma Wesselhoeft and Parker translated it into English for the museum. Forstemann himself revised their translation before it went to press.

A note explains the museum plan to translate key Maya studies. Charles Bowditch of the museum committee directed the work in Cambridge. The Dresden Codex is the famed Maya manuscript in the Royal Library there. Forstemann used Arabic numerals for the days in his German text. Glyph by glyph, the commentary unlocks calendar signs in that old book.
43536-none-so-deaf-as-those-who-won-t-he: None So Deaf as Those Who Won't Hear is a comedietta in one act from Baker's Edition of Plays, sold by the Walter H Baker Company of Boston for twenty-five cents. The front pages are a publisher's catalogue of plays for colleges and high schools, with cast sizes, running times, prices, and royalty terms for dozens of titles. The play itself begins after that catalogue, under its proverb title about wilful deafness. No author is named in the pages shown, and no cast list appears before the text starts.
44202-the-red-cross-in-peace-and-war:
The Red Cross in Peace and War is a history of that aid group. Notes at the front own that plates can not be shown in plain text form. Signed notes in the first book are here set out in type in their place. No year is shown in the front notes of the hosted text.

Parts trace the cross from its birth on fields of war to home aid work. A fresh charter of the group earns its own head out of place in the list. That slip in the list is owned and set right in the front notes. Sick care, wreck aid, and war nurse work fill the kind deed tale. The book stands as the groups own claim to a vast field of good.
44212-italian-highways-and-byways-from-a:
Francis Miltoun wrote this motor tour of Italian highways and byways. Page printed it at Boston in 1909, McManus drew pictures. Miltoun past books rambled the Riviera, Normandy, and Brittany roads. Contents open with the way about Italy as first chapter.

Italian men and manners, chianti and macaroni, and roads follow. In Liguria takes the tour onward in the fifth chapter. A Bologna scene fronts the volume among its travel plates. Page lists his cathedral and chateaux books at two fifty each. The Automobilist Abroad stands last in the Miltoun works list on the front leaf.
44256-brown-of-moukden-a-story-of-the-ru:
Brown of Moukden is a boys' war adventure novel by Herbert Strang, published by Putnam in 1906 with illustrations by William Rainey. The subtitle calls it a story of the Russo-Japanese War. A preface letter explains that his earlier Kobo showed the war from the Japanese side. This book places the reader among the Russians. It is not a sequel, and it leaves the naval battle of Tsushima aside.

The contents follow the hero, Jack Brown, through the later incidents of the war. Chapter titles run from Ivan Ivanovitch Brown to the battle of Moukden and Sakhalin. A glossary at the back serves young readers meeting Russian and Manchurian terms. The Tennyson motto on the title page, to strive, to seek, to find and not to yield, states the book's heroic temper.
44316-kobo-a-story-of-the-russo-japanese:
Herbert Strang's Kobo, a story of the Russo-Japanese War, was published in New York by Putnam's Sons in 1905. William Rainey supplied the pictures, and Strang dedicated the book to Lilliput, with all due respect to Brobdingnag. A letter to Ralph, dated Michaelmas Day 1904, prefaces the tale.

Strang recalls watching a battalion of the Imperial Guards march through Osaka toward the China war ten years before. He argues that Japan was then only measuring her strength for the struggle with Russia. The contents follow Rokuro Kobo from a samurai's home through a fleet action and the battle of the destroyers, to a chase by Cossacks and a night reconnaissance.
44441-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Grenville Kleiser gathered great sermons from famous pulpits into ten volumes. Volume seven runs from Hale to Farrar. Funk and Wagnalls issued the set in 1908.

Each preacher gets a short life sketch, then one strong sermon. Edward Everett Hale opens with The Colonization of the Desert. Magee preaches on Christ stilling the storm. Seiss gives The Wonderful Testimonies, and Maclaren The Pattern of Service. Crosby's odd title, The Prepared Worm, sits beside Dale on the argument from experience. Liddon treats the Holy Spirit's sway. Taylor sets Christ before Pilate, then Pilate before Christ. Farrar closes with work in a groaning creation. The set served ministers hunting models and lay readers who liked strong pulpit prose.
44448-the-queen-of-the-savannah-a-story-:
Gustave Aimard wrote a tale of the Mexican war printed in London in 1862 by Ward and Lock. The tale starts on May 5, 1805, in wild New Spain, in lands now held by Coahuila. A troop of lancers in yellow garb, nicknamed for a sweet fruit, rides out of a gorge at a gallop.

Those lance men were loathed for their cruelty by the folk of the land, the first pages warn. A hacienda, a count, and fair Leona Vicario stand in the roll of names to come. Councils, alarms, dungeons, ambush, and chase crowd the long list of parts in the war tale.
44579-slavery-in-pennsylvania-a-disserta:
Slavery in Pennsylvania, a dissertation by Edward Raymond Turner, was submitted for the doctorate at Johns Hopkins University in 1910 and printed by the Lord Baltimore Press at Baltimore in 1911. Turner was professor of history at the University of Michigan. The work of Johns Hopkins scholars in southern history stands behind the book.

The first chapter treats Negroes about the Delaware before Pennsylvania existed. Dutch and Swedes held the valley first, and blacks appear among them early. An African convict was imported in 1639. In 1644 a Negro spent many years in Governor Printz's service at Tinicum. The colony that William Penn founded inherited slavery from its neighbours. Turner follows the institution through its long decline to its legal end, working from records, laws, and newspapers.
44649-the-last-boer-war:
The Last Boer War, by Rider Haggard, was published in London in 1900, in its thirty fifth thousand. The front pages quote speeches by Sir Garnet Wolseley at Pretoria in 1879, and by Lord Kimberley in 1880. Both insist that no British government would dare give back the Transvaal.

In his author note Haggard says students of South African history might now gladly read an account of the Boer rebellion of 1881. So he reprints parts of a book he wrote in 1882. He grants the matter may seem stale. Its value, he argues, is just that it was written at the time, by a man who took an active part in those sad and stirring events. Readers get a first hand history, revived as a new Boer war began.
44889-the-story-of-a-confederate-boy-in-:
David Johnston of the Seventh Virginia Infantry published his story of a Confederate boy in the Civil War in 1914. An introduction by a Methodist minister and loyal legion chaplain fronts it. The contents open with the presidential election of November 1860, and a schoolboy's fear and anxiety in Giles County.

Virginia's part as peacemaker, the failed peace conference, and the ordinance of secession fill the early chapters. A company organizes at Pearisburg, the ladies present a Bible and a flag, and the boys march to Manassas Junction. Johnston is careful to say what will not be attempted here: his is a soldier's record, from school desk to regiment, in his own county's words.
44964-battles-of-the-civil-war:
Vineyard of Spencer, West Virginia, published this battle-by-battle history of the Civil War in 1914. His preface makes the claim plainly: no conflict in any nation's history was so terrible. Napoleon and his dream of universal empire would not compare with it. The veterans, he notes, are fast passing away. The book is written so that all walks of life may know the great battles in detail.

Twenty-five chapters run from First Bull Run to the surrender at Appomattox. Shiloh, Antietam, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, and Gettysburg get their full tellings, with Chickamauga, the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor after them. Sherman's march to the sea and the siege of Petersburg close the campaigns. Portraits of Lee and Grant and a picture of John Brown on his way to the gallows illustrate the text. Vineyard aimed the book at teachers and students, as a supplement to the school histories.
45023-the-pictorial-grammar:
The Pictorial Grammar is a picture book of English grammar by Alfred Crowquill. William Tegg and Company published this edition in London in 1876. Crowquill was the pen name of Alfred Henry Forrester. A short life of the author opens the volume. Forrester was born in London in 1806. He practised as a notary, his family's trade for years.

Early in life Forrester began writing for the magazines. He soon became the illustrator of his own works. He contributed to Punch from its first commencement and to the Illustrated London News. His books include the Comic English Grammar and the Comic Arithmetic. The Wanderings of a Pen and Pencil is also named. Forrester died on May 26, 1872. The Pictorial Grammar itself teaches through pictures: page after page of numbered illustrations carries the lessons, with the drawings doing the explaining that rules do in drier grammars.
45269-inventions-of-the-great-war:
Russell Bond, managing editor of Scientific American, wrote this account of the new tools of war. The Century Company printed it in New York in 1919, with many plates. Bond had earlier written On the Battle-Front of Engineering.

War in and under the ground opens the book, then hand grenades and trench mortars. Guns that fire themselves, great guns and super-guns, and the chemists' war follow in turn. Tanks get a full chapter, then war in the air and ships that sail the skies. Finding the range and talking in the sky close the part of the list shown here. A front plate shows oil-tempering the lining of a big gun.
45493-on-yacht-sailing-a-simple-treatise:
On Yacht Sailing by Thomas Fleming Day, editor of The Rudder, is a primer on handling small yachts and boats, published in New York and London in 1904. Day says in his preface that writing for the learned is easy, but writing for the ignorant is hard, and sailing's language is wholly technical. He promises to explain terms as he uses them and to load the book with explanations of explanations.

Chapters cover the boat and rig, the helm, the names of rigging and sail, sailing on and off the wind, reefing and jibing, and rules of the road. A glossary and diagrams close a book Day calls almost absurdly simple, on purpose.
45568-the-song-of-the-rappahannock-sketc:
The Song of the Rappahannock, by Ira Seymour Dodd, holds sketches of the Civil War, printed in New York in 1898. Dodd gives the book to his comrades, the living and the dead. Contents list six pieces, from the title sketch to one called Sacrifice. Others treat the making of a regiment and a little battle. Dodd served as a young soldier in the Army of the Potomac.

The Song of his title is the sound of shells in flight. He wore the white cross of the Second Division of the Sixth Army Corps. He recalls trips to a clear spring under fire, with open fields to cross. Half his regiment lay sick from bad camp water at the time. His sketches keep the feel of camp and field as men lived it.
45577-betty-s-happy-year:
Betty's Happy Year, by Carolyn Wells, was copyrighted in 1909 and published in New York in September 1910, with drawings by Reginald Birch. Wells was known for The Story of Betty. Twelve chapters follow Betty month by month through a full year of holidays and school life.

The year starts with a Thanksgiving guest and a Christmas party, then moves to boarding school and a valentine. Later chapters bring a practical joke, a green paper doll, an Independence Day party, and a Labor Day lunch. A front plate shows Betty close to her mother before a bright tree. Light verse, family fun, and small scrapes keep the tone gay for young readers.
45745-the-heart-of-the-wild-nature-studi:
The Heart of the Wild, nature studies from near and far, was written by S L Bensusan and published in London in nineteen eight by John Milne. Bensusan had written A Countryside Chronicle and Wild Life Stories. Actual wild life photographs illustrate the sketches. The first study pairs two unlikely neighbours in the Scottish highlands.

A golden eagle holds his eyrie on a rocky ledge above a fox's earth. The king of the air surveys his hunting grounds from Ben Hope to Ben Loyal. The fox below lives dejected, vermin in the eyes of gamekeepers. The contents range widely from that highland pair. Badger, camel, red grouse, roebuck, flamingo, fighting bull, seal, giraffe, and wild boar each get a study. Bensusan writes observed natural history with a storyteller's warmth.
46034-gibraltar:
Gibraltar is a travel and history book by Henry Field, published by Chapman and Hall at London in 1889. Field sent it as a Christmas present to his friend Joseph Choate, calling it a story of fortress and siege to beguile a winter evening hour. The preface owns that the common tour of Spain leaves Gibraltar out.

Field notes the Rock is not part of Spain, though tied to the Spanish shore, for it belongs to England. No railroad touches it, and steamers call only at gaps of days. Easy travelers with round tickets give it the go-by. Yet Field calls it unique in the world, in place, in beauty, and in story, standing out of the water between two seas.
4611-where-no-fear-was-a-book-about-fear:
Arthur Christopher Benson published Where No Fear Was in 1914, as a book about fear in all its shapes. He opens with the shadow, shapes of fear, and the darkest doubt, then moves through vulnerability and the use of fear, and through fears of childhood, boyhood, youth, middle age, and age. A passage from Pilgrim's Progress stands at the head, where Christiana sees an ugly thing on the road that she cannot name.

Later chapters turn to Dr. Johnson, Tennyson, Ruskin, Carlyle, Charlotte Bronte, and John Sterling, asking how famous minds met fear, then to instinctive fear, fear of life, simplicity, affection, sin, and serenity. Benson writes as a thoughtful companion, not a doctor, and his aim is courage without denial. Readers get a reflective Edwardian meditation, still useful for anyone who wants to name their fears and live with them more calmly.
46122-the-story-of-the-pullman-car:
Joseph Husband wrote this tale of the Pullman car. A plate at its front shows George Mortimer Pullman, with his years, 1831 to 1897. The book tells how the car that bears his name came to be, and how it grew to a place in the life of the road of rails. The name of Pullman is bound to the car in which men sleep as they ride, a home on wheels for the long trip.

Such a book has two threads: the man and the thing. The man is the maker whose face stands at the front, a chief of the trade of his day. The thing is the car of sleep, with its berths that fold by day to seats, its staff, and its fine trim. The tale of the two is the tale of how the long ride in America was made soft.
46166-history-of-the-zulu-war:
Wilmot wrote this short history of the Zulu War, printed in London in 1880. A front note says long dull detail has been cut on purpose. The aim was a fair, readable view of cause and course. Blue Books and letters from the front gave the chief facts.

Wilmot links the war with King Cetywayo to past Cape wars. He names Dingaan, Kreli, and Sandilli from those past fights. He argues the same clash of rule drove each campaign in turn. The book shows how British readers then framed South African wars.
46188-elsie-s-young-folks-in-peace-and-w:
Martha Finley brought her Elsie family back in this volume of the series, copyrighted in 1900 by Dodd, Mead. The young folks are aboard the yacht Dolphin at Bar Harbor, on the coast of Maine. Elsie Raymond and her brother Ned have spent a fortnight at a villa on shore. Now they are glad to be in their own dear sea home again, and the anchor is coming up.

Brother Max has promised them places where sea fights happened in the two wars with England. The children beg their grandma to tell the stories instead, and she begins with the earliest Maine. West Quoddy Head, the Penobscot, and the French settlement of St Saviour on Mount Desert Island follow. Captain Argal drove those colonists away as trespassers. Finley's method is family talk as history lesson, with Revolutionary times promised for the next sitting.
46283-the-motor-bus-in-war:
A M Beatson, a temporary lieutenant in the Army Service Corps, wrote The Motor-Bus in War. T Fisher Unwin published it at London in 1918. The book gives the impressions of an A S C officer during two and a half years at the front. Beatson dedicated it to Lieutenant-Colonel Gerald Charles Gordon Blunt. The contents open with an au revoir to England. Railhead, supply columns and rations, and the motor-lorry convoy follow.

The workshops and life behind the line fill the middle chapters. The road runs from Bethune to Ypres, then along the Somme valley. Between the Ancre and the Somme, from Arras to Albert, and to Bapaume and Peronne close the route. Beatson owns that most war books treat the fighting itself. His buses and lorries did the carrying that kept the trenches fed.
46313-jones-of-the-64th-a-tale-of-the-ba:
Colonel Brereton wrote Jones of the 64th for Blackie and Son, with illustrations by Rainey and a plan of Assaye. The subtitle names the battles of Assaye and Laswaree in India. A long list of Brereton's earlier boys' books fills the front pages. Contents open with Benjamin Halbut, a protege, and a hunting trip before sailing east.

An East Indiaman under attack, the city of palaces, and John Company follow in turn. A Mahratta stronghold, a first assault, and special service lead toward a glorious victory. Holkar the treacherous and a dangerous Frenchman keep the plot hot to the close. A plan marks the battle of Assaye on September 23, 1803. Young readers get Wellesley era war as stirring schoolboy adventure.
46322-punch-cartoons-of-the-great-war:
Punch Cartoons of the Great War was published in New York in 1915 by the George Doran Company. The book gathers the magazine's war pictures into nine groups, from The Days Preceding the War to The Struggle, Uncle Sam, and Italia. Captions and verses under each cartoon are kept with the drawings.

The days before the war reach back decades: a cartoon of October 6, 1888, shows Bismarck as Daedalus warning his son Wilhelm, the Icarus of the piece. The dropping of the pilot returns as a ghost in March 1915, twenty-five years on, asking if he would be dropped now. Fidgety Wilhelm, the imperial jack-in-the-box, and the Kaiser as the new rake fill out the early shelf.
46361-springfield-in-the-spanish-america:
Walter Ward wrote Springfield in the Spanish-American War, printed at Easthampton, Massachusetts, in 1899. Ward gives the book to the officers and men of three companies of the Second Regiment, Massachusetts Infantry, and to a naval brigade company.

Springfield men fought at El Caney and drew the lines tight round Santiago till it gave up. Others served at sea and helped sink a Spanish transport and a gunboat. Ward names the dead, Bowen, the Vesper brothers, Bearse, and more, whose names a new monument will carry. His aim is to show the town what its sons went through.
46377-a-practical-handbook-on-the-distil:
Wright wrote A Practical Handbook on the Distillation of Alcohol from Farm Products, here in a second edition, revised and enlarged, printed at New York in 1907. The book teaches malting, mashing, fermenting, and distilling in plain steps.

Alcohol can be made from grain, beets, potatoes, and molasses, Wright shows. Chapters treat alcoholometry and the denaturing of alcohol, with the government's own formulas. The fuel serves farm engines, automobiles, launch motors, and heating and lighting. A summary of the new Free Alcohol law and its rules closes the volume. French and German practice, the most advanced, informs the methods throughout.
47044-stories-about-general-warren-in-re:
A Lady of Boston wrote Stories About General Warren for young readers of the Revolution. James Loring issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred thirty five. Its tales tie Warren to the Fifth of March Massacre and Bunker Hill. Plain words aim the lessons at each child who can read.

What did Warren do to earn his fame, folk ask her. Bravery and death in one fight were not his whole worth, she says. Years of toil for the cause came before blood was shed. His love of land was a life rule, not a flash of heat. Mary Montague and her son William frame the telling at home. A hoop tired boy rests by the fire to hear the tales. Warren’s mother begs him not to risk his dear life once more. Where danger is, her son must be, he tells her with tears near.
47705-a-sister-of-the-red-cross-a-tale-o:
A Sister of the Red Cross, a tale of the South African War by Meade, was published in London, Edinburgh, and New York by Thomas Nelson and Sons. A frontispiece shows a woman calling to a wounded man by name: Gavon, I am here, I have come. Twenty-eight chapters run from Consecration through Kitty's Dream and A Legacy to Away to the Wars, In the Hospital, and Dark Days.

Chapter one, Consecration, presents Sister Mollie Hepworth, twenty-five years old. She has just finished a long, exhaustive training as a nurse, rising from probationer to ward sister at the London Hospital. Six months at Netley followed, for her dream was to nurse soldiers in their hours of danger and death. Mollie is bright, handsome, and self-controlled. Meade sends her to the Boer War as heroine of a hospital romance.
47844-the-young-collector-s-handbook-of-:
The Young Collector's Handbook of Ants, Bees, Dragon Flies, Earwigs, Crickets, and Flies, by W Harcourt Bath, reached a second edition with Swan Sonnenschein and Company at London in 1890. The groups named carry their Latin orders: Hymenoptera, Neuroptera, Orthoptera, Hemiptera, and Diptera.

Bath's preface argues that collecting natural objects beats stamps, crests, and coins as a boy's hobby. Insect collecting trains the observant and intellectual faculties, gives healthful recreation in fields and woods, and costs almost nothing. He points deeper students to Kirby's illustrated Text-Book of Entomology. A frontispiece shows the great stick insect Cyphocrania Goliath, reduced in size.
48029-best-stories-of-the-1914-european-:
Best Stories of the 1914 European War was drawn from all sources that year. J S Ogilvie Publishing Company held the rights in New York in 1914. A news photo shows two Belgian soldiers chatting with a sailor at Ostend. One of the pair came from the Congo, the caption notes.

The book came out while the war's first shock still rang in the papers. Tales and reports from the front were rushed into print for eager readers. Such quick books froze the mood of the war's opening months. Students gain a raw slice of how the home front first heard the guns.
48118-the-british-state-telegraphs-a-stu:
The British State Telegraphs, published in 1907, is Hugo Richard Meyer's study of state-run telegraphs and their staff. Meyer had taught political economy at the University of Chicago. His question is wide: what happens when a democracy employs a huge body of civil servants? The British telegraph purchase gives him his case.

The contents read like an indictment of the official forecasts. The cost of buying the companies rose from early guesses of $15,000,000 to sums past $30,000,000. The railway companies' rights, valued at $3,500,000, cost the state $10,000,000 to $11,000,000. Working expenses ate over nine tenths of earnings. Meyer holds that Scudamore's bright promises of profit and growth all failed.
48147-bennie-ben-cree-being-the-story-of:
Arthur Colton wrote Bennie Ben Cree, the story of an adventure to southward in the year 1862. Doubleday and McClure put it out at New York in 1900. Colton gives the book to the memory of his mother. It opens with the Commodore Inn and the great wharves as a playground. Ben, the narrator, says no neat door-yard or inland street could match that world. Warehouses crowd down to Doty's Slip, with piles leaning awry and slick with damp.

The stores change each week: cotton, tobacco, slabs of crude rubber, and boxes of unknown goods. Each stock leaves its queer smell in the old rooms for fifty years of trade. Uncle Benson states a point that frames the tale to come. Colton gives a port boyhood in rich, fond detail, before the southward trip begins.
48237-the-lady-of-north-star:
The Lady of North Star is a novel by Ottwell Binns, printed in New York by Alfred A Knopf in 1922. Binns had also written A Mating in the Wilds. Twenty five chapters carry a tale of the Canadian north.

The tale opens at the end of a trail, with the smell of burning spruce in sharp air. Corporal Bracknell of the North West Mounted Police sniffs it with thanks as his dog team rests. Heads that follow name a strange vanishing, a letter found by the corporal, and a puzzling scent. A woman named Joy makes a request, and a man called Koona Dick steps in. Later heads bring a dastardly deed, a rescue by night, and a snow blind man. North fans get police grit, love, and snow.
48330-ferdinand-of-bulgaria-the-amazing-:
The author of The Real Kaiser wrote a hostile life of Ferdinand of Bulgaria, printed in London in 1916 with cartoons by Will Dyson. Ferdinand gazes from his palace across the Black Sea toward Constantinople in the front cartoon. Who is that evil looking man, an Australian asked at the funeral procession of King Edward the Seventh.

Chapter heads run from a pot house prince and the training of a traitor to Ferdinand the ambitious, the faithless, and the Hun. The broken hearted princess, Ferdinand and his creatures, and Kultur in Bulgaria fill the mid book. Ferdinand as war lord and in extremis close the tale. Wartime British scorn drives every page of the shoddy czar story.
48339-mr-punch-in-wig-and-gown-the-light:
Mr Punch in Wig and Gown gathers the law humor of Punch magazine, with one hundred and twenty plates. J A Hammerton shaped the Punch Library of Humour, which aimed to give the cream of Punch wit from 1841 to the present day. Each book in the line stands alone.

Artists named on the title run from H Stacy Marks and Sir John Tenniel to George du Maurier, Charles Keene, and Phil May. The theme here is the lighter side of bench and bar, judges and lawyers in court and out. One plate shows a man up before the beak. A lead note grants that Punch could bite hard on light sentences for rich swindlers. Humor fans get court jokes in word and line from the masters of Punch.
48347-amiens-before-and-during-the-war:
One of Michelin's illustrated guides to the battle-fields of 1914 to 1918, covering Amiens before and during the war. The front matter serves the motor tourist directly: hotels and motor agents at Amiens, drawn from the Michelin Guide of 1919.

A key explains the signs for central heating, electric light, bathrooms, garages by car count, inspection pits, and petrol. The du Rhin and the Belfort-Hôtel head the hotel list on the rue de Noyon, with telephone numbers given. The Grand Garage de Picardie stocks Michelin and agents Panhard, Peugeot, and Delage. The guide dates its facts to March 1, 1919, and warns tourists to check the latest edition. Battlefield pilgrims get practical help first.
48349-the-religious-and-loyal-subject-s-:
The Religious and Loyal Subject's Duty is a church talk by Isaac Terry, once of a great hall at Oxford. It was spoke in the great church of Canterbury on a fast day of seventeen twenty three. That day is kept each year for the death of King Charles the First. The church men who heard it asked that it be put in print. It came out at London that same year.

Its text is a charge from the wise book of the old faith. My son, fear thou the Lord and the king, it says. And meddle not with them that are given to change. The talk opens with the sad cause of the day's meet. There is no need, it says, to tell those here what that cause is.
48422-air-men-o-war:
Air Men o' War, by Boyd Cable, was published at New York in 1919. Dutton issued the tales under copyright that year. Cable had written Between the Lines and Action Front before. He gives the book to the air men of the Western Front. Their hospitality, he writes, taught him these stories. The dedication is dated in the field, September 1918. Silver Wings opens the contents. Bring Home the Bus and A Tender Subject follow. A Good Day, A Rotten Formation, and Quick Work come next. The titles speak the slang of the flying service.

Cable writes of the men who flew and fought over the trenches. Patrols, forced landings, and the daily hazard of the air fill the tales. He means them as a tribute, and says so plainly.
48525-a-concise-chronicle-of-events-of-t:
A Concise Chronicle of Events of the Great War is a day-by-day record by Rowe, printed in London in 1920. Rowe was a captain late of the Royal West Kent Regiment and of the Military Intelligence Directorate. He thanks the librarians of the Royal United Service Institution and of the Admiralty for records and dates not readily accessible.

The chronicle opens in the July crisis of 1914. On July 27 France and Italy accept England's proposal for an international conference. On July 28 Germany rejects it. From those dry lines the book marches through four years of war, date by date and front by front. Submarines and Zeppelins are indexed by their numbers in the text. Rowe's aim is a reference a reader can trust: no argument, only the order of events, set down by a staff officer who had lived by such lists.
48572-germany-before-the-war:
Baron Beyens, late Belgian minister at the court of Berlin, wrote this study of Germany before the war, turned into English by Paul V Cohn. Thomas Nelson and Sons first published it in March 1916. Contents open with the Emperor William, then the imperial family, court, and government. The army and navy, and the war party, fill the third chapter.

The Reichstag and its parties, public opinion, and the economic causes of the war follow. Morocco and the Eastern Question lead to the week of tragedy. Belgian neutrality and the invasion of Belgium close the account. Beyens's introduction recalls the Hague peace conferences and the treaties meant to put law in place of brute force between nations.
48811-from-makin-to-bougainville-marine-:
From Makin to Bougainville is a war past of the sea raider bands of the United States in the war past the wide sea. Major Jon Hoffman of that corps wrote it, as part of a set of such tracts. Shots from the war desks grace its pages, with notes on the arms and gear of those bands. A list of its parts stands at the front.

In February of nineteen forty-two the head of the corps bid a new band of that name be made. That band and its three kin won great fame for fight craft in the war. The tract holds that their tale shows more than brave deeds. Their birth, growth, and swift end teach much on how sea borne war grew, and on the strain of a corps swelled from a small host to near half a vast host.
49113-is-the-vicar-of-brompton-a-tractar:
A layman wrote a sixpenny tract asking if the vicar of Brompton was a Tractarian, printed in London in 1855. Gains from the sale were to go to a dispensary serving Chelsea, Brompton, and Belgravia. The vicar, Dr Irons, is quoted at the front saying he was no Tractarian in any sense.

The writer states he bears the vicar no ill will as a man and means only to show, by the vicars own words and deeds, that he stands with that party. Wise Tractarians, he warns, hold back from the hot heads and win folk little by little. That plan, he says, explains much that goes on in the parish.
49123-lille-before-and-during-the-war:
Michelin issued an illustrated guide to the battle-fields of 1914-1918, this one covering Lille before and during the war. The hosted text opens with practical matter drawn from the Michelin Guide of 1919: hotels and motor agents at Lille. A key explains the firm's signs for comfort, heating, baths, garages, and petrol.

The Bellevue on the Grande Place and the Hôtel de l'Europe on the rue Basse head the hotel list, each with its telephone number and garage room. Stockists follow, from the Garage Dulieux to the Grand Garage Farcot, with notes on repair shops and agents. Motorists touring the war zone with a need for beds and benzine were the readers served.
49155-marion-harland-s-cookery-for-begin:
Marion Harland's Cookery for Beginners is a set of plain lessons for young housekeepers. It is by the author of Common Sense in the Household, The Dinner Year Book, and The Cottage Kitchen. The book came out in Boston from the D. Lothrop Company, with copyright dates of 1884 and 1893. The contents run from first bread to cake.

Home-Made Yeast and the First Loaf stands first. Bread Sponge and Breakfast Breads and more breakfast breads stand next. Eggs, Broiled Meats, and Fried Meats stand in the list. What to Do with Left-Overs and Other Dinner Dishes stand there too. Meats and Vegetables stand later, then Desserts and Cake-Making. The book is a first cook book for the new keeper of a house, in the voice of a famed teacher of the home arts of her day.
49215-recollections-of-the-civil-war:
Recollections of the Civil War, by Maud Morrow, tells war days from a child view. John Morrow of Lockland, Ohio, issued the small book in nineteen o one. Morrow gives the pages to the Forty Third Ohio regiment with respect. She also honours all who fought at Corinth and every boy in blue.

Her preface calls the book a simple true tale in the first person. She grants it is dearer to her than it can be to others. Writing it, she lived those days over again in full force. Hospital walls and faces from the past rose up around her. Her mother name runs like a gold thread through the whole story.
49267-a-watch-dog-of-the-north-sea-a-nav:
Percy Westerman wrote A Watch Dog of the North Sea, a naval tale of the Great War first issued in London in December 1916. Westerman had written of air dreadnoughts and Royal Navy men before. Here a boy named Eric Greenwood serves in a warship on cold North Sea watch as the tale opens with a shrill bugle call to action stations.

Thirty five parts bring in a secret petrol store, spies and super spies, a foiled raid, and one Zeppelin brought down. A sea duel, a wreck adrift, a stay as a prisoner of war, and a dash for freedom raise the pace. Trawlers that fight back, monitors in action, and a shell torn hospital fill the last third.
4931-won-by-the-sword-a-tale-of-the-thir:
G. A. Henty's tale of the Thirty Years' War opens in October 1639, as a mounted officer rides from Paris to St. Denis and finds boys playing at war with sticks. Their leader, Hector Campbell, commands a make-believe regiment of Turenne against a hilltop fortress, and the officer's questions reveal a Scottish boy with a soldier's future.

Hector's play becomes real campaigning as the novel follows him through the wars of religion that tore Europe apart. Henty mixes battles, sieges, and personal courage in his usual brisk style. Young readers get both an adventure story and a plain introduction to a war that shaped modern Europe.
49444-five-years-in-texas-or-what-you-di:
Thomas North wrote this account of his years in Texas and Mexico through the Civil War. Five Years in Texas runs from January 1861 to January 1866. The Elm Street Printing Company of Cincinnati put it out in 1871.

His subtitle makes the pitch: what you did not hear during the war. North owns in his preface that making a book feels a bold thing for a modest man. Many run to and fro, he says, and knowledge grows; the runners make books for the million. His tale is no voyage round the world with Captain Cook, he jokes. It treats of stirring events at home: travel, hardship, and sharp sights in a Texas torn by war, and a Mexico in its own storms.
49540-days-to-remember-the-british-empir:
Days to Remember: The British Empire in the Great War is a history by John Buchan and Henry Newbolt. It was printed by Thomas Nelson and Sons, with London, Edinburgh, New York, Toronto and Paris on the title page. The first impression was in 1922, and the book was reprinted again and again into the 1930s. Portraits of the commanders and maps of the battles fill it.

Thirty two chapters in six parts tell the war. The third part, The Side Shows, tells of the landing at Gallipoli and the capture of Jerusalem. The fourth, The Silent Service, is the war at sea: Coronel, the Falklands, Jutland, the submarine service and Zeebrugge. It is the war told for the empire's school and home readers, while memory of it was still fresh.
49629-beadle-s-dime-song-book-no-3-a-col:
Beadle and Company of New York put out Beadle Dime Song Book Number Three, a cheap song book. Rights were held from the year 1860 by Irwin P Beadle and his firm. The title page calls the songs new and sought after, both comic and full of feeling. A dime book like this one was sold at news stands for a low price.

Ads in front push lives of great chiefs of war at ten cents each. Scott, Wayne, and Garibaldi are the men named in those ads. The song book itself gives words to sing, not the tunes in notes. Such books let folks at home or in camp sing the hits of the day. The mix of fun songs and sad songs shows the taste of the crowd it served.
49772-hagar:
Mary Johnston published her novel Hagar with Houghton Mifflin in October 1913 at Boston and New York. Thirty-four chapters trace one woman from childhood to Brittany at the close. Chapter one, The Packet-Boat, floats a canal boat under low bridges at sunset. A dark girl of twelve sits aft with her hat upon her knees.

Young Hagar asks her Aunt Serena what evolution means, to her aunt's blank dismay. Grandfather blamed Darwin, and his dreadful book stays banned at Gilead Balm. Gilead Balm chapters recur as a refrain through the table of contents in full. New York, a socialist meeting, Alexandria, London, and Denny Gayde widen her world in turn. A Southern girl grows into new womanhood.
49782-the-czar:
Told as a tale of the time of the first Napoleon, this novel appeared from Nelson and Sons in an 1895 edition. Its author is named only as the writer of 'The Spanish Brothers.' The story opens in a sleeping village on the plain near Moscow. There Russian serfs till the fields of their lords much as their fathers did before them.

The hero Ivan moves from village life toward a wider world. Schooling, lots drawn for service and the storm of war carry him onward. Chapters take him to Moscow, the Beresina and Versailles, and past Alexander himself. Serf and boyar, camp and court, give the tale its broad Russian sweep.
49833-directions-for-cooking-by-troops-i:
Directions for Cooking by Troops, in Camp and Hospital is a Confederate army cookbook of 1861. J W Randolph published it at 121 Main Street, Richmond, Virginia. The directions were prepared for the Army of Virginia. They appeared by order of the Surgeon General. Two essays by Florence Nightingale, Taking Food and What Food, accompany the recipes.

Every recipe is scaled for one hundred men. Coffee for a hundred takes 12 gallons of water, 3 lbs of ground coffee, and 6 lbs of sugar. Fresh beef soup uses 75 lbs of beef and 15 gallons of water. Soyer's stew simmers 50 lbs of beef with onions and potatoes for about two hours. Suet dumplings divide their dough into about 150 pieces. Plain directions cover frying meat and cooking salt beef or pork. The book taught camp cooks to feed companies from kettles, with weights and times stated exactly.
49848-the-man-who-ended-war:
The Man Who Ended War is a novel by Hollis Godfrey, issued at Boston in 1908, with drawings by Charles Grunwald. A front picture shows a man crying out as he points at a window, crying a name. Other pictures give an officer raising a lantern twice, a warship's search light playing on the heroes, and a man counting aloud.

The first chapter opens in the office of the Secretary of War. That is all there is to tell, the secretary says, about the building of a new transport. From such a start the tale builds its wonder: a means found to end war itself, and the powers of the earth closing in to seize or crush it. Godfrey wrote tales of invention and statecraft, and this is his best known.
50041-beadle-s-dime-song-book-no-4-a-col:
Beadle's Dime Song Book No. 4 gathers new and popular comic and touching songs for ten-cent sale. Beadle and Company of New York, general dime book publishers, issued it. The front pages carry house notices for the firm's dime lives of great soldiers, among them Winfield Scott, Anthony Wayne, and Garibaldi of Italy.

The song book itself belongs to the cheap print trade of the Civil War years. Its copyright was entered in 1860 by Irwin Beadle and Company. Such books gave singers and families a pocket store of the day's songs, comic and sad alike, at a price any soldier or worker could pay.
50312-john-stevens-courtship-a-story-of-:
John Stevens Courtship: A Story of the Echo Canyon War, by Susa Young Gates, was published at Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1909. A dedication names three friends who made the book possible. A preface states the theme plainly: a story of love, in the rugged setting of pioneer days.

The characters, Gates says, move among the stirring incidents of the Echo Canyon War. That affair was absolutely unique in the history of the land. Scenes depict the conditions of Utah Territory in that war. Much information also came from a church magazine and from numerous pioneers. They recall vividly the intensity of feeling in the days of Johnston Army and the Move. The characters are mainly fictitious: John Stevens is a composite, and Diantha was modeled on a woman yet living. Readers get a Mormon pioneer romance of 1857.
50406-operation-interstellar:
George Smith wrote a science fiction novel published at Chicago in 1950, with a cover by Malcolm Smith. Its hero, Paul Grayson, walks slowly toward the spaceport, in no hurry. He savours the fresh spring air and the sounds of his fellow men, knowing what waits ahead.

Soon he will breathe canned air, tangy with compressor oil, in a capsule of the Bureau of Astrogation. His goal is a stinking, overheated mote of a planet circling Proxima Centauri, unfit for human life. Man keeps it only as a place to stand and survey the galaxy. Ten days cooped in the ship lie between Grayson and that station.
50578-a-sub-of-the-r-n-r-a-story-of-the-:
A Sub of the RNR, a story of the Great War, is a naval tale by Percy Westerman, printed at London by Partridge. Westerman also wrote The Rival Submarines and The Dreadnought of the Air, and Wigfull drew the pictures. The contents run to twenty-nine chapters of sea action, from foul play in an engine room to a last honour for Lieutenant Aubyn.

The tale opens aboard the steamer Saraband, a Red Band Line boat of 5260 tons out of Cape Town. Her chief engineer, Jock McBride, reports engine trouble to Captain Ramshaw in his slow, stolid way. Two hundred miles from Las Palmas the breakdown peaks, and the ship lies helpless in the Atlantic rollers.
50595-bohemian-grammar:
Jaroslav Victor Nigrin wrote a grammar of the Bohemian tongue for English speakers. The book came out in Chicago in 1918. Nigrin taught at Harrison Technical High School in Chicago. He gave the book to Charles Crane, a friend of the Slavs. The Bohemian Literary Society put it out.

Nigrin says few such books in English were then in print. One was out of print and one was made for scholars, not home use. His book gives rules in a new, clear way with drills to fix them. Sound, form, and word order build step by step. New learners get a full, workman-like path.
50750-the-officer-s-manual-napoleon-s-ma:
The Officer's Manual, Napoleon's Maxims of War, was printed at Richmond, Virginia, in 1862 by West and Johnston, in the second year of the Civil War. A letter from Winfield Scott, the old American commander, recommends the reprint to regular and volunteer officers alike. The publisher calls the little volume timely for the occasion.

The maxims distill Napoleon's campaigns into rules, with cases drawn from Gustavus Adolphus, Turenne, and Frederick. The translator D'Aguilar added matter from Montecuccoli and Frederick's own instructions to his generals. Confederate officers carried such books in their pockets, learning modern war from the last age's master.
50759-grocers-goods-a-family-guide-to-th:
Grocers Goods is a family buying guide by Goddard, copyrighted in 1888. The Tradesmen Publishing Company of the Tribune Building, New York, issued the book. Its price was twenty cents for housekeepers who bought the family stores. Flour, sugar, tea, coffee, spices, canned goods, cigars, and wines head the title bill.

An index list helps housekeepers make up orders and find pages for each article. Adulterations get a chapter early, at page six of the guide contents. Butter and butterine, baking powders, chicory in coffee, and canned goods all come under test. Consumer protection begins in such plain guides to honest weight and purity.
50781-the-mystery-ship-a-story-of-the-q-:
Percy Westerman wrote The Mystery Ship, a story of the Q ships during the Great War, first printed in London in 1920. Pictures by Morrow go with the book. A plate shows the mystery boat moving slowly, her triple torpedo tubes ready. Contents run to thirty-five chapters. The two sub-lieutenants open the tale.

On patrol, sunk in action, and the spy follow. Picked up, a U-boat of sorts, and prisoners of war come next. A struggle for life, a double decoy, and mutiny fill the middle. The tables turned and the end of U 247 stand late. Trapped, battered but undaunted, and the homecoming lead to the great surrender. The scuttling and what they fought for close the book. The first chapter opens below decks. Kenneth Meredith, second in command of a motor launch, is writing his weekly letter home when a hail comes from above.
50878-beadle-s-dime-song-book-no-5-a-col:
Beadle's Dime Song Book Number Five gathers new and popular comic and sentimental songs. Beadle and Company, the New York dime book publishers, issued it from William Street. The copyright was entered in 1860. The firm sold it cheaply for soldiers, travelers, and home singers who wanted words without music.

The contents run from Auld Lang Syne and A Man's a Man for A' That to Camptown Races. There are parlor pieces like Call Me Pet Names and Ever of Thee. A Yankee Ship and a Yankee Crew supplies the salt air. Cheer, Boys, Cheer and Comin' Thro' the Rye are here too. The little book is a pocket songster of the Civil War years, the kind carried in a coat and sung from at camp or cottage piano.
50956-russia-s-part-in-the-world-war:
Colonel Shumsky-Solomonov wrote this plea for Russia's war record, sent out by the Russian Information Bureau in New York in 1920. Sack, the bureau's chief, dated his note May 25, 1920. Russia's part in the World War had by then been dimmed by her fall into chaos.

Was it possible for Germany to win the war asks the opening head. Talk of Russia's role, the colonel says, starts with her losses, counted in many millions. Her gifts were great, he grants, and then sets out her claim in full. A Russian officer in exile pleads his old army's case to America, lest her dead be forgot in the tale of the war.
51000-school-reading-by-grades-fifth-yea:
James Baldwin made a school reader for the fifth year, printed in New York in 1897. The preface tells teachers what to aim at now. Pupils who read the earlier books are ready to study style with care. Spelling, defining, and pronouncing still matter, but story craft matters more.

Children should watch how a writer narrates a story, describes an action, or portrays emotion. They should hunt the passages prized for beauty, truth, or aptness. Baldwin wants the habit of enjoying fine qualities in any literary work, above all in works held classic by common consent. Lessons in the book were chosen and ordered to build that habit step by step through the school year.
5102-the-path-of-a-star:
Mrs. Everard Cotes's Path of a Star opens on an actress entering a room, pushing the portiere aside with a curved hand and gracefully separated fingers. Her body follows after an instant's poised hesitation, head thrust forward, eyes inquiring, a tentative smile on her face, though she knows precisely who waits there.

She crosses quickly, the train of her luxurious morning gown folding with audacity as she bends over Laura Filbert on a bamboo sofa and cries, You poor thing. The novel follows an actress's career and loves with theatrical immediacy. Readers get a story of the stage, where performance and private feeling constantly trade places.
51055-frenzied-liberty-the-myth-of-a-ric:
Otto Kahn's Frenzied Liberty prints extracts from his address at the University of Wisconsin on January 14, 1918, under the subtitle The Myth of a Rich Man's War. Kahn, himself of German birth, calls the war a just and righteous one and the nation's purpose single and unshakeable.

He refuses to grade towns by a loyalty thermometer. Dreamers and old-style politicians may lag, he says, and a small, shrinking minority of German-born Americans stand irresolute. But the vast majority have acted as loyal Americans and deserve trust and sympathy for their heartache. One element alone, he argues, truly challenges national unity: the militant Bolsheviki, preachers of liberty run amuck.
51064-ruba-iya-t-of-a-motor-car:
Carolyn Wells wrote these jest verses on the motor car, printed in 1906 with cuts by Frederick Strothmann. The book is sent forth to the crank that makes the machine go. Its form apes the famed Rubaiyat, the quatrains of Omar. The first verse bids the sleeper wake. The honk of the car has scared the hens to flight, and the car stands at the door.

It bids the man come out for an hour of sheer joy in the dawn. Fill the tank, tune the valve and the spring, and fling your garb of the road round you, the verse goes on. The bird of time is on the wing, in the words of the old poem made new for the road. The book is a light, fond jest on the new craze of its day, the tour by car.
51070-raiders-of-the-sarhad-being-an-acc:
Dyer wrote Raiders of the Sarhad, printed in London in 1921 with many photographs and two maps. The subtitle calls it an account of a campaign of arms and bluff against the brigands of the Persian-Baluchi border during the Great War. Dyer was a brigadier-general. A plate shows a typical gorge in the Sarhad. Contents open with orders for the west. Its heads run from German agents and India to petrol in the desert.

The road to Robat follows, with Idu of the Chagai Levies, called Idu the invaluable. A plan of campaign weighs the tribes and a summons to the chiefs. Bluff and arms then tells of Ladis and its fort, a force without arms, and a first sight of the enemy. Bluff succeeds, though bad news comes from the north. Khwash and more bluff follows, with chiefs coming in one by one.
51072-shamar-s-war:
Shamar's War is a tale of the stars by Kris Neville. Guinta made its plates. The host text was made from a sheet of tale writ of the year past the mid age. A sword with two edges is its bill word for its hero: he was the hid arm of Earth, as keen as a sword, and two edged. The tale starts in the year past two mints of years from now.

Earth, at that time, was a state of the crowd's rule, the tale says. The crowd was ruled by a high board, and past it by boards and town boards. Each was made of men chose by the vote of the crowd from two foe bands. Chiefs of work were chose by the vote of the fit board. A free court kept the laws in force.
51075-a-stone-and-a-spear:
A Stone and a Spear is a tale by Raymond Jones from Galaxy magazine. John Bunch drew the pictures for the December 1950 printing of it. The tale opens with a given and a proposition about the future. Can probabilities be made improbable so a certainty fails, it asks. Doctor Curtis Johnson drives through green Maryland toward Baltimore that day.

His wife Louise holds her blowing hair and laughs in the warm air. Curt muses on a crack about the weapons of the next war. The war after next, someone said, will be fought with stones and spears. Men at Detrick and a lieutenant at Bikini both get the credit. Louise asks if any of them ever thinks of anything but war. Doctor Dell had quit Detrick rather than make toxins and aerosols. His walking out stood as a futile gesture to his old friends.
51153-the-semantic-war:
The Semantic War is a science fiction story by Bill Clothier, taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for November 1955. Its epigraph sets the tone: perhaps there have been causes for slaughter just as silly as this one, but try to find one. The narrator is a lone survivor picking his way through a ruined Oregon. Rain pours from a sullen sky as he hurries back to his cavern.

He cannot afford to catch a cold. Alone, without medicine, a cold could open the way for some worse disease to strike him down for good. The skies still hold traces of nameless sickness in their clouds. Inside the cave he wraps himself in a cow-hide from a peg and waits to get warm. He wonders why he bothers to put off the end.
51256-the-cool-war:
Andrew Fetler wrote this spy tale, The Cool War, taken from a science fiction magazine of June 1963, with pictures by Nodel. A headnote gives its shape: what happens when two master spies tangle, and stay that way.

Pashkov comes out of a villa forty miles from Moscow with his friend Medvedev, soothing him. Erase the man's memory, give him a new name, feed him more love of country; very simple. The villa has grown famous since a book named in the tale was published from it, and soldiers now guard it against visitors. Medvedev growls that all will guess the man is a robot. Pashkov answers that men are suspected when they are not like robots. Then a question slips out that Medvedev is told not to ask: who smuggled the manuscript out of Russia?
51347-submarines-mines-and-torpedoes-in-:
Charles W Domville Fife wrote an illustrated account of submarines, mines, and torpedoes in the first World War, issued by Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto. A photograph shows the British submarine E 2. The caption gives her displacement as eight hundred tons and speed as sixteen knots. She carried four torpedo tubes and two quick firing guns.

Seventeen vessels of her class were completed between 1912 and 1914. Domville Fife had written on the submarines of the world's navies. His war book explained undersea weapons to a public alarmed by them. The E boat photograph anchors the technical detail in a real vessel.
51368-a-queen-of-tears-vol-1-of-2-caroli:
W H Wilkins writes the life of an ill-fated queen in A Queen of Tears, the first of two volumes published by Longmans, Green and Company in 1904. His subject is Caroline Matilda, Queen of Denmark and Norway and Princess of Great Britain and Ireland, whose portrait by Sir Joshua Reynolds forms the frontispiece. Chapters cover her birth, childhood, betrothal and arrival in Denmark to marry Christian the Seventh.

The volume then follows the marriage, the birth of a prince, the king's visit to England and the rise of Struensee. Later chapters name the tempter, the queen's folly and the fall of Bernstorff, ending with Struensee as reformer and dictator.
51369-a-queen-of-tears-vol-2-of-2-caroli:
A Queen of Tears, volume two of two, is Wilkins's life of Caroline Matilda, Queen of Denmark and Norway and sister of George the Third. Longmans published it in London in 1904, with portraits and illustrations. Wilkins had already written The Love of an Uncrowned Queen. The frontispiece shows Matilda in the uniform of colonel of the Holstein Regiment of Guards.

This volume takes up the turn of the tide. A masked ball leads to a palace revolution and the triumph of the queen-dowager. The imprisoned queen is divorced, and Struensee and Brandt go on trial and to execution. Her release follows, then refuge at Celle, a restoration plot, and her early death. A final chapter is named retribution. Wilkins writes royal biography in the full Victorian manner, documents and pathos together.
51427-glorious-deeds-of-australasians-in:
E C Buley wrote Glorious Deeds of Australasians in the Great War for Andrew Melrose at London, first printed in October 1915. The fifth, enlarged edition came out in January 1916. A front plate shows General Birdwood in charge of operations at Anzac. Buley also wrote Australian Life in Town and Country.

The opening chapter, The Long Black Ships, follows troops to war. Ads at the front list war books on Russia, the Balkans, and the Dardanelles, a sign of the market in 1915. Buley's aim is plain from his title: to record brave acts by Australian and New Zealand men. Pride at home and news from the front drive the volume.
51487-othmar:
Othmar is a novel by Ouida, shown here in a new edition issued at London in 1886. A line from Lytton stands at its head: a fear of life's many changes, not of death's changelessness. The contents run past forty chapters, in the long manner of the three volume novel of its day. Page numbers climb past three hundred within the list alone.

Ouida, the pen name of a prolific English novelist, set her tales among the rich and titled of Europe. Her heroes move through ballrooms, spas, and country houses, carrying grand passions in a high style. Othmar, named for its hero, belongs to that glittering line of her work. The long chapter list, without a single descriptive head, was the fashion of its first readers, who took their fiction in bulk.
51664-palace-and-mosque-at-ukhaidir-a-st:
Gertrude Lowthian Bell wrote Palace and Mosque at Ukhaidir, a study in early Mohammadan building, issued by the Clarendon Press in nineteen fourteen. Bell gave the book to Walther Andrae, in thanks for days spent in the first capital of Assyria. Her study opens with past travellers' tales of the desert ruin. An unnamed Englishman's journal, quoted by Niebuhr, tells of a deserted city with walls fifty feet high.

Major John Taylor saw the ruin in June, seventeen ninety, and passed it by in a few lines. Massignon, Bell notes, was the first to make any real record, with a plan and photos. The site lies hours from Meshed Ali, left dry for want of water. Bell's own survey gives the palace and mosque their first full account.
51665-tippoo-sultaun-a-tale-of-the-mysor:
Colonel Meadows Taylor wrote Tippoo Sultaun, a tale of the Mysore War, and this second edition came from Kegan Paul and Company of London in 1880. Taylor dedicated it to William Newnham, his best and earliest friend in India. A front picture looks ahead to page 397 of the tale.

The publisher's list at the front shows the shelf this book sat on. Taylor's Confessions of a Thug drew praise from the Daily News for its grip on the imagination. Tara, a Mahratta tale, was praised by the Spectator for showing native life in India on its nobler side. Seeta and A Noble Queen stood beside them. The present tale turns to Tipu Sultan and the British wars in Mysore. Readers of Anglo-Indian fiction get war, court, and camp from a man who served in India.
51717-tekla-a-romance-of-love-and-war:
Tekla, a romance of love and war by Robert Barr, was copyrighted in 1898 and published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Barr also wrote A Chicago Princess and The Mutable Many. The dedication is to the Countess Laura. The scene is the medieval empire, at Treves and at Castle Thuron.

The Emperor enters Treves in the first chapter, then vanishes. An archer steps forward, and love leads the way. The Countess flees an unwanted marriage, and pursuers hunt a wife with a troop of horse. Two archbishops fall out, and the Black Count is talked out of hanging his Emperor. Attacks on Castle Thuron build to a siege of two years. A night escape and a traitor's price close the tale.
51807-poems-of-peace-and-war:
Poems of Peace and War is a book of verse by Elizabeth Connor, printed at the Record Press in Haverhill, Massachusetts, in 1917. The title places the volume in the Great War years, and its poems mix devotion with patriotic hope. The first poem, Simplicity, calls simplicity the essence in all God's wondrous work. It prays that all that is base will fade away and evil be suppressed.

A later poem, A World Republic Is Arising, looks across the war. A torn sunset of purple and crimson floats over the warring breeze, while a new light forms far over the seas. The day of dynasties is fading into the darkest night, the poem says. Faith in God will light the vision through grim despair, and reveal the dawn of a brighter day in fair democracy.
51888-the-new-eschatology-showing-the-in:
J G Broughton Pegg wrote The New Eschatology, showing the indestructibility of the earth. J B Lippincott published it at Philadelphia in 1872, years after its English appearance. The subtitle adds a second claim: the wide difference between letter and spirit in Scripture. The publisher's note states the argument plainly.

Certain texts have been read as foretelling the destruction of the material universe, the note says. Rightly interpreted, they refer to nothing in the outer realm of matter. They concern the inner realm of mind: the church's condition, lost charity, and eclipsed faith. That fall was foreseen for the close of the first Christian dispensation. Swedenborg's name never occurs in the book, the note owns, yet the author writes from the Swedenborgian standpoint. The little work argues scripture by correspondences.
52141-under-the-white-ensign-a-naval-sto:
Percy Westerman wrote this naval story of the Great War, as its title page announces. Review lines at the front promise no boy will read his pages without quickened pulses. The Outlook supplies that praise, printed above short notices of his other tales in the front matter.

The Dispatch-Riders, the Sea-girt Fortress and Rounding up the Raider show their notices there. The Fight for Constantinople and Captured at Tripoli join the list of his gift books. Under the white ensign means under the Royal Navy's flag, and Westerman's young sailors fight the war at sea in his brisk manner.
52148-dorothy-south-a-love-story-of-virg:
George Cary Eggleston wrote Dorothy South, a love story of Virginia just before the war, first issued in March, nineteen two. Print runs listed in the front climb from the twelfth thousand to the forty-second in a year. Drawings are by Williams, and the front plate asks for an old time horseback ride soon in the morning. The tale opens on a perfect June day in south side Virginia.

A young man of about twenty-seven walks a narrow road with a swinging stick. Chapter heads bring Wyanoke, the home place, and Arthur Brent, a doctor who is puzzled by Dorothy's case. A duel under the code, Aunt Polly's advice, and letters fill the middle parts. The birth of war and the old Dorothy and the new close a tale of love on the edge of civil war.
52157-craven-s-part-in-the-great-war:
Craven's Part in the Great War is a memorial volume compiled and edited by John T Clayton, editor of a Skipton newspaper. It was presented to each man from the Skipton parliamentary division who joined the forces in the war of nineteen fourteen to nineteen, or to his next of kin. A local landowner bore the whole cost, the presentation page states. Each copy was a memento of service.

Inside, rolls of honour, unit accounts, and local loss record what one Yorkshire district gave to the war. Craven's part is praised as noble, in the formal words of the time. Such town and district war books are now prime sources for family and local history. Names come first.
52201-soldiers-stories-of-the-war:
Soldiers' Stories of the War is an edited volume of first hand accounts, published in London in 1915. Walter Wood edited it; he had written on North Sea fishers and survivors' tales. Twenty full page illustrations by Michael accompany the text. Each chapter is one soldier's own story, named with his rank and unit. The frontispiece shows a battery making a heroic stand.

Mons and the great retreat open the book, told by a Gordon Highlander. A driver of the Royal Field Artillery treats alleged German atrocities. Greenjackets in the firing line and the struggle on the Aisne follow. A corporal who won the Victoria Cross tells of the most critical day. Life in the trenches, sapping and mining, and despatch riding fill the middle. The tellers are privates, gunners, and sappers, not generals.
52229-adventures-of-sonny-bear:
Frances Margaret Fox wrote Adventures of Sonny Bear, copyrighted in 1916. Warner Carr drew the pictures. Fox had written Doings of Little Bear. The book is given to her little friend Helen Margaret Parsons.

Eleven tales follow Little Bear and his parents. In the first, Mother Bear steps out for rain water while the porridge cools, and a man with a gun finds the sleeping baby in his cradle. He means to carry the cub home as a pet for his children. Later tales give Grandfather Grizzly, Baby Bear's party, and maple sugar time. Sonny Bear visits Goldilocks' camp, and the three bears reach an enchanted land.
52886-my-year-of-the-great-war:
Frederick Palmer wrote My Year of the Great War, held in 1915 and rushed through five editions by December. Palmer had writ The Last Shot and With Kuroki in Manchuria. A note to the reader links the war to his past novel. That novel had sought to show a war between two great land powers in Europe.

A friend tells Palmer he was wrong in some ways and right in more. Guns did play the great part he foresaw, the friend says. Trenches did lock the vast hosts in a stale line. Palmer was wrong on how long the war would last and how bitter it would be. The book then gives his own year at the front as a witness for the press.
52934-war-dogs-of-the-world-war:
John Anderson published War Dogs of the World War at New York with copyright in 1919. The book opens not with battle but with a poem called My Dog, by John Kendrick Bangs. The speaker has no dog, yet insists somewhere there is one that belongs to him.

The poem's dog has a wagging tail, dark brown eyes, and a cold black nose that sniffs out hidden things. He chews shoes, sits up and begs, and waits by a garden gate with yelps of delight for his master's homecoming. Against that tender frame, the book takes up dogs in the Great War. Readers get the war's working dogs honoured through a pet lover's lens.
52964-patty-s-motor-car:
Pattys Motor Car is a girls tale by Carolyn Wells, of the Marjorie books. Patty stands in her own long line of tales for young readers. A gift page sends the book with love to a named friend of the author. Rights date the work to the year nineteen eleven.

Tea at home opens the tale as Patty plans a new car of her own. A talk on road craft and the hard quiz of rules fill early parts. A prize, a new near home, and a swift guest named Camilla mark turns. Moon rides, a swim, and a dance chart the gay summer of the set. A close escape late in the list lends spice to the bright tale.
53453-instincts-of-the-herd-in-peace-and:
Instincts of the Herd in Peace and War is a work of social psychology by W Trotter, first published in London in February 1916. Its first two essays had seen print in the Sociological Review in 1908 and 1909. Trotter's aim, stated in his preface, is to show that psychology can be a guide in the acts of life. It need not be a mass of dreary general terms. Read beside biology, it can give a grip on the mind of man in the mass.

The herd instinct is the core of the book. Men, like herd beasts, answer to the voice and mood of the group. That pull explains crowds, parties, and nations at war. Trotter notes that his core thoughts were formed before the great war.
53732-standard-catholic-readers-by-grade:
Mary Doyle made a fifth-year reader for Catholic schools in grades. The book came out with the American Book Company. Doyle had led a normal school at Seattle and taught at Superior. A Raphael plate, the Madonna of the Chair, fronts the book. It is book five in a set of eight such readers.

Whittier, Longfellow, Lowell, and Burroughs stand in its pages. Helen Hunt Jackson's work stands there by a set deal as well. Poems by Father Tabb come from a Boston house's leave. Tales, verse, and prose bits build the year's school reads. Each piece is picked to suit faith and home at once. Young readers get a rich, grave store.
53869-how-to-become-a-public-speaker-sho:
How to Become a Public Speaker, by William Pittenger, was published at Philadelphia in 1903. Its copyright dates to 1886.
