The subtitle promises the best manner of arranging thought for ease and fluency. Chapter one asks if the art of speech can be learned. Pittenger notes a common scorn for the study of oratory. A minister he knew hid his elocution lessons from his flock, he says.

He grants the scorn a grain of reason, since fake oratory exists. Yet any sound power, he argues, grows with wise training. Chapters treat the four methods of speech, fear at the start, and debating societies. Voice, gesture, confidence, and plan building follow. A model embryo speech gives practice matter for the student.
53887-armenia-and-the-war:
Armenia and the War is a plea by Hacobian, an Armenian writer, published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1917 with a preface by Viscount Bryce. Its subtitle states the purpose: an Armenian's point of view, with an appeal to Britain and the coming peace conference. Bryce had compiled the official report on the Armenian massacres.

Hacobian stresses that he speaks for no organisation. The views are one individual's, offered because the Armenian blood shed in the war lays a duty on every living Armenian to seek justice and reparation for the survivors. The introductory note argues that Britain, arbiter of the peace, cannot judge fairly without hearing all sides. The front matter quotes Gladstone that to serve Armenia is to serve civilization, and prints the Allies' description of the Ottoman government as barbarous and corrupt. The book is wartime advocacy at its most urgent.
54226-servetus-and-calvin-a-study-of-an-:
Servetus and Calvin is R Willis's study of an important epoch in the early history of the Reformation. Henry S King and Company of London published it in 1877, with a portrait of Michel Servetus. Willis had already written on Spinoza and edited the works of Harvey for the Sydenham Society.

His preface traces the road to the subject: Spinoza led him to Giordano Bruno. The renewed debate among medical men over Harvey's discovery of the circulation then turned him to another sufferer in the cause of human progress. The book sets the Spanish thinker Servetus against Calvin, the two names carrying the tragedy of the title. A saying of Melanchthon on the Trinity stands at the head as motto: what tragedies, he asks, will this question stir up for those who come after?
54230-the-gates-ajar:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps's Gates Ajar was entered for copyright in 1868 and issued by Osgood at Boston in 1873. The dedication, dated at Andover on October 22, 1868, is to her father. An epigraph from Madame de Gasparin asks for a little definite happiness over grand words. The narrator opens a diary one week after the blow: her brother Roy is dead. His last letter, bright with jokes and pet names, lies laid away by itself.

The mourner walks the house like a prison while children snowball outside, their voices hurting like knives. Well-meaning voices tell her a soldier's life always hangs by a hair, and that she should have been prepared. The book became the famous Civil War consolation story of its generation. It imagines heaven as a place of continued, homelike life beyond the gates.
54275-the-fleets-at-war:
Archibald Hurd wrote a handbook on the navies of the Great War as the second volume of a newspaper's war books, published at London in 1914. Admiral Sir John Jellicoe, supreme admiral of the British home fleet, fronts the volume in a photograph. An introduction surveys the opening phase: the peaceful victories of British sea power.

Chapters then weigh the relative standing of the British and German fleets, treat each navy in turn, and profile Jellicoe and the German commander in chief. Officers and men, German naval bases, and the Kiel canal follow. A tabular statement of the great fleets engaged closes the survey. A shilling bought the key book to the naval situation, its series promised.
54859-organization-how-armies-are-formed:
Organization: How Armies Are Formed for War is a manual by Colonel Hubert Foster of the Royal Engineers, printed in London in 1911. Foster sets out to explain how an army is built, led, and kept supplied in the field. His contents run from the object of organization to the chain of command.

Part one treats the fighting troops arm by arm: cavalry, artillery, engineers, and infantry, then new arms like machine guns and cyclists. Divisions, corps, staff work, and war establishments follow. Part two turns to British practice, the expeditionary force, its transport, supply, medical, and postal services, and the lines that link an army to home.
54871-the-great-push-an-episode-of-the-g:
Great Push is a war book by Patrick MacGill, published by Herbert Jenkins in 1916. Its subtitle calls the work an episode of the Great War in plain words. MacGill had written Children of the Dead End and The Rat Pit before enlisting. A dedication verse to Margaret warns that if we forget the fairies, God may forget us.

MacGill served as a rifleman and stretcher bearer in the London Irish at Loos. The push of the title is the great attack his battalion made in 1915. Mud, fear, humour, and comradeship fill his prose from the trench line. War literature holds MacGill among the true voices of the ranks.
55021-through-swamp-and-glade-a-tale-of-:
Kirk Munroe wrote a boys' tale of the Seminole War in Florida. The book came out in New York in 1896. Victor Perard drew its pictures. Munroe wrote to his readers in a front note of care. He says the chief deeds of Coacoochee in the tale are true.

That war ran from 1835 to 1842, he tells the young. Most of the tribe were then shipped to the far west. Three hundred and one souls still held out in the Big Cypress. Flame by a road side blazes in the front plate. Swamp and glade give the hunt its hard, wet stage.
55148-the-drums-of-war:
Stacpoole's novel, published by Duffield at New York in 1910, opens on the road to Frankfort on the first of September, 1860. The narrator, aged nine, rides in the family carriage with his father, General Count Mahon, and Joubert.

The boy presses his cheek against the hot blue cushions and dreams of being a soldier like his father, with white moustaches, cigars, and a sword. Chapters promise Von Lichtenberg, Eloise, a man in armour, a duel in the woods, and a fall into disgrace. Paris nights, remorse, the marriage of Eloise, and a second duel fill the later parts. Stacpoole wrote The Blue Lagoon.
55186-cassell-s-history-of-england-vol-4:
Volume four of Cassell's Illustrated History of England, the King's Edition of 1909, runs from the fall of Marlborough to the Peninsular War. The first chapter concludes Queen Anne's reign: the Utrecht negotiations, Bolingbroke's visit to Paris, the break-up of the Grand Alliance, and the intrigues with the Pretender at Saint Germains. Steele is expelled from the House, the Schism Bill passes, Oxford falls, and Anne's death brings the proclamation of George the First.

The second chapter opens the new reign: the impeachment of the late ministers, the flight of Bolingbroke and Ormonde, the Riot Act, and the rebellion of 1715. Sheriffmuir, the Pretender's landing and flight, and the Septennial Act follow. The volume carries numerous illustrations, including coloured and Rembrandt plates. Cassell's was the popular illustrated history of its day, written in full narrative chapters with detailed contents summaries.
55583-the-life-story-of-a-black-bear:
The Life Story of a Black Bear, by Perry Robinson, tells a wild life in the voice of the bear himself, and it was issued at London in 1913. The first chapter is called How I Tumbled Downhill. Cubhood days and the coming of man follow in the tale. A forest fire and the loss of a sister mark the young years.

Life in camp and the parting of the ways carry the bear to manhood. Alone in the world, he finds a companion and visits the old home. The troubles of a father and the wiping out of old scores fill the later chapters. A trap and a fall into the hands of man close the list. The book gives young readers the woods as a bear might know them. Danger and kinship shape the story.
55779-to-herat-and-cabul-a-story-of-the-:
To Herat and Cabul is a story of the First Afghan War by Henty, printed at New York in 1901. Sheldon drew its eight illustrations. Scribner issued it, and a map of Afghanistan and the north-west frontier stands inside. Nineteen chapters run from Alone in the World to The British Captives.

The tale opens on September 20, 1837. A lad stands before M'Neill, the British minister at the Persian court, at the turning point of his life. The front picture shows Angus and Pottinger watching the fight from the walls of Herat. Chapters ahead give the siege of Herat, the murder of Burnes, and the annihilation of the army. Henty tells the war through one boy's service.
55910-social-life-in-old-virginia-before:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote Social Life in Old Virginia Before the War, copyrighted in 1897 and published at New York in 1898 with illustrations by the Misses Cowles. A frontispiece caption sighs over tall lilies, white as angels' wings and stately as the maidens that walked among them.

The illustration list sketches the whole world of the book: the plantation house, shining tables with brass-tipped legs, the room where the guns were kept, and bookcases of brown-backed, much-read books. Tobacco, a typical mammy, little girls in great sun-bonnets, and an old Virginia sideboard follow. Readers get the plantation legend in its most lyrical form, written by its most famous maker as elegy for a lost order.
55926-the-commentaries-of-c-sar:
Anthony Trollope wrote a short life and guide to the Commentaries of Caesar for English readers. The book came out in Edinburgh and London in 1870. It stands in a set of short books on old Greek and Roman writers. Trollope calls the Commentaries the start of modern history, since Caesar wrote of deeds done under his own eyes.

Chapters walk through each book of the war in Gaul and the civil war in order. Readers meet the drives against the Swiss and the Germans, the fights in Britain, the revolt of Vercingetorix, and the crossing of the Rubicon. A last chapter sums up Caesar as a writer and a man of war.
56027-the-achievement-of-the-british-nav:
The Achievement of the British Navy in the World War, by John Leyland, was issued at London by Hodder and Stoughton in 1917. A New York edition came from George H. Doran the same year. A front picture shows the king in talk with Admiral Beatty. The book was sold for a shilling, for wide reading in war time.

Chapters take up the duties of the sea service and the centre of sea power. Leyland tells how the enemy was swept from the oceans. He treats the grip on the Mediterranean, by sea power and land power joined. A chapter deals with the submarine peril, the great fear of that year. The book is a wartime survey for the home reader. It sets out what the navy did, and why that work held the fate of the war.
56143-with-roberts-to-pretoria-a-tale-of:
With Roberts to Pretoria is a boys' war tale by Henty. Scribner's Sons published it in New York in 1901. Its subtitle calls it a tale of the South African War. Twelve illustrations by Rainey and a map accompany the text. Henty also wrote With Buller in Natal among many war tales. The contents list twenty one chapters of campaign adventure. A Change of Fortune opens with a sad morning at an English rectory. The rector's private income rests on shares in a Midlands bank.

On a Dutch Farm and A Quarrel bring the hero to South Africa. The Ultimatum and Scouting start the war story proper. Belmont, Graspan, and the Modder give real battles as chapters. Kimberley, Magersfontein, and Paardeberg follow in the advance. The Relief of Kimberley and Mafeking near the close. Johannesburg and Settled end the march to Pretoria.
56162-the-illustrated-dictionary-of-gard:
The Illustrated Dictionary of Gardening, a practical and scientific encyclopaedia of horticulture for gardeners and botanists, opens with Division I, running from A to Car. Upcott Gill of the Strand published it at London in 1887, with James Penman as agent for the United States and Canada. George Nicholson of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew edited the work.

Trail assisted on the parts touching insects and fungi, and Garrett on fruit, vegetables and general garden work. The preface aims high: the best and most complete work on gardening and garden plants yet published. Bentham and Hooker's Genera Plantarum is followed for generic names, tangled synonymy is revised, and figures and references point readers to fuller accounts elsewhere.
56256-a-probable-italian-source-of-shake:
Alexander Boecker wrote a doctoral thesis, printed at New York in 1913, arguing that an Italian tragedy stands behind Shakespeare's Julius Caesar. The play in question is Il Cesare by Orlando Pescetti, printed at Verona in 1594. Boecker gives its prologue, its plot, and its Senecan traits.

He then sets the two plays side by side, scene by scene and speech by speech. Brutus and Antony speak in both, the mob cries out in both, and ghosts and portents work alike. Much, he claims, comes through Appian, Pescetti's main source, and some matter in Shakespeare that Plutarch cannot explain may come from Pescetti. Scholars of sources are his readers.
56312-rules-and-examples-of-perspective-:
Rules and Examples of Perspective Proper for Painters and Architects is the English edition of Andrea Pozzo's famous treatise on perspective drawing. Pozzo, a Jesuit master of the art, first printed the work at Rome in 1693 in Latin and Italian. John James of Greenwich translated it, and John Sturt engraved it. The London edition shown here appeared in 1707 from Benjamin Motte.

The title promises a most easy and speedy method to draw in perspective all designs relating to architecture. It works after a new manner, wholly free from the confusion of hidden lines. The book is engraved in 105 large folio plates, with 200 initial letters to the explanatory discourses. Pozzo's system taught painters and architects to construct convincing depth on flat surfaces. Its plates of arches, vaults, and stage-like interiors made it the standard perspective manual of its age across Europe.
56323-motor-transports-in-war:
Motor Transports in War is a war craft book by Horace Wyatt, out in nineteen fourteen. A Hodder and Stoughton house brought it out in the Telegraph war set. Wyatt told the Autocar on heavy motors and led a realm motor board. Part one takes up the scope of the motor cart in war use. Part two weighs how key the war motor is to hosts at war.

Trials and war games fill part three of the scheme in rank. True war use tales of motors fill part four in its heads. Sick cart work, shot and gun haul, and steel cars fill mid parts. How to raise war motor fleets and realm match heads stand next. Grant type motors and far host carts close the scheme of parts.
56360-how-the-nations-waged-war-a-compan:
The Daily Telegraph issued this war book as a mate to its How the War Began. How the Nations Waged War tells how the world faced Armageddon, in the list's own words. It tells as well how the British Army answered the call.

The Telegraph line sold at a shilling in cloth, in the first years of the Great War. Mate volumes treat the fleets at war, the campaign of Sedan, and the fight round Liege. Other titles cover the Red Cross, great battles, and the inner tale of German statecraft. Stephen Crane's name stands on one. This volume takes the wide view: nation by nation, the means and the will to wage a world war.
56495-our-women-in-the-war:
Our Women in the War is an address by Captain Francis Dawson, delivered on February 22, 1887. He spoke at the fifth annual reunion of the Association of the Maryland Line, at the Academy of Music in Baltimore. The address was printed by order of the association, at Charleston.

Dawson opens with a passage from Count Montholon. On great occasions, it says, women have almost always given the strongest proofs of virtue and devotion. Macaulay is quoted on perfect self devotion, of which man seems incapable. That virtue, Dawson says, was shown on every side by southern women during the Confederate war. Their constancy, fidelity, tenderness, courage, cheer, and patience have, he claims, no parallel. Readers get a veteran tribute to Confederate women, in the memory culture of the post war South.
566-the-history-of-the-thirty-years-war:
Friedrich Schiller narrates the Thirty Years' War in this history, translated by A. J. W. Morrison. Schiller traces the Reformation's effects, the revolt of Matthias, the Bohemian rising, and the clash of Union and League, with lucidity and impartial judgment. His preface praises his own gift for history as well as drama.

Chapters move from emperors and electors to armies and treaties, showing how faith and power tore Europe apart. Schiller writes as a dramatist turned historian, keen on character and cause. The work endures as a classic popular history, clear, grave, and humane.
56603-a-boy-in-the-peninsular-war:
Julian Sturgis edited the autobiography of Robert Blakeney, a subaltern in the 28th Regiment, published at London in 1899 in a second impression with a map. Sturgis dedicates the memoirs to his wife. Blakeney was her mother's father, and the editor owes her yet another debt for knowing him. An introduction quotes Othello's plea that he cannot grace his cause with studied eloquence.

Blakeney served as a boy officer in the Peninsular War against Napoleon. His services, adventures, and experiences fill the memoir. Such subaltern accounts give the war from below the generals. John Murray published it at Albemarle Street. The book joined a shelf of Napoleonic reminiscence.
56670-our-lady-of-the-pillar:
Eça de Queiroz wrote Our Lady of the Pillar, done into English by Edgar Prestage and published at London in 1906. The book is dedicated, by permission, to D Amelia, Queen of Portugal. A motto from the author heads it: over the strong nakedness of truth, the diaphanous mantle of fantasy.

Prestage's address to the reader begins in Lisbon. Sauntering one October evening into the Livraria Bertrand, the recognised meeting-place of men of letters in the Chiado, he fell into talk of Eça with a Rio newspaper proprietor. Readers get a short tale by Portugal's great novelist in the translation of his English champion.
56862-market-harborough-and-inside-the-b:
Market Harborough and Inside the Bar are two hunting tales by Whyte Melville, issued together in one illustrated volume. The author of other novels named on the title page, he is shown here in his sporting vein. Pictures by John Charlton run through the book. The contents of the first tale start with one of the old sort.

Quoted speech makes up many chapter heads, in the manner of talk at the stable door. Marching orders, boots and saddles, and hazy weather lead into a Leicestershire lark. Four o'clock at the stables and a merry go round keep the hunting pace. The paired second tale, Inside the Bar, shares the volume's world of horses, fields, and country houses. Together they give a full day of the author's best known country.
56889-the-blue-star:
The Blue Star is a novel by Fletcher Pratt. It came out in New York from Twayne Publishers, with a copyright date of 1952. The contents show a tale told in named scenes of time and place. A prologue stands first, then a chapter set in Netznegon City in March rain. April night, an escape, and a stretch of day and night at a place of refuge follow in the list.

Later chapters bear heads of night and day, of masks, and of high politic. A chapter called Sedad Vix: A New Life stands in the middle of the list as shown. The front matter is spare: it gives the plan of the tale by its chapter heads and no more. The novel is a work of fancy whose scene names, such as Netznegon City, are of the author's own making.
56956-great-poems-of-the-world-war:
Great Poems of the World War is an anthology of war verse edited by Eaton, printed at Chicago. Denison published it in nineteen twenty two, from an earlier war collection of nineteen eighteen. Eaton adds an introduction, notes, and matter of his own to the poems. The contents run in alphabet order from Lincoln poems to songs of the ranks.

Vachel Lindsay's Abraham Lincoln Walks at Midnight leads the long list here. McCrae, Sassoon, Service, and Guest stand among the named poets of the set. Pieces mark Edith Cavell, Captain Fryatt's murder, and the graves of Gallipoli. Guest's Battle of Belleau Wood and Do Your All speak for the home front. An epitaph for the unknown soldier and a gold star poem close the roll. Soldiers, chaplains, and mothers all find voices in the gathering.
5713-tales-of-war:
Lord Dunsany's Tales of War, published in 1918, gathers short pieces written during the First World War, many in the voice of soldiers and villagers. The opening prayer of the men of Daleswood tells of a hill village with only twenty houses. Thirty men between sixteen and forty-five lived there. All of them went to war together in the same battalion. That small scale gives the book its power.

Dunsany writes with a poet's brevity, letting a single image or farewell carry the weight of loss. Readers meet trenches, home villages, and the strange quiet between battles, rendered without long battle scenes. The collection suits readers of war literature who prefer short, haunting sketches to full novels, and it preserves how one well-known fantasist faced a real war.
57133-the-motor-routes-of-france-to-the-:
The Motor Routes of France, by Gordon Home, was printed in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1910. Sixteen full page plates in color, sixteen in black and white, and sixty maps and plans fill the book. The routes run to the great houses of Touraine, Biarritz, the Pyrenees, the Riviera, and the Rhone Valley.

A review from the Pall Mall Gazette, quoted at the front, calls Home just the companion to add to the pleasure of a day run. All along the main roads he chats brightly of history, building, and old remains. He conveys much fact without being a heavy teacher. A twin book treats the motor routes of England south of the Thames. Early motorists got a road guide with culture mixed in, town by town.
57336-ancient-britain-and-the-invasions-:
Ancient Britain and the Invasions of Julius Caesar is a historical work by Rice Holmes, published at the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1907. Holmes had written a history of the Indian Mutiny and Caesar's Conquest of Gaul. His motto, from Tylor, holds that no human thought is so primitive as to have lost its bearing on our own. Part One of the book is an introduction and a long chapter on the Palaeolithic age.

The contents ask why a whole chapter goes to the stone age. They treat Tertiary man, the Ice Age, and continental Britain, when the island was still joined to Europe. Palaeolithic skeletons, artists, workshops, and tools follow. A list preserved in the copy runs to river-drift implements, handles, and the uses of tools. Then come the culture and religion of the inhabitants, totemism, and magic.
57458-sacred-mysteries-among-the-mayas-a:
Augustus Le Plongeon wrote Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches, set eleven thousand five hundred years back. Robert Macoy issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred eighty six. Le Plongeon gave it to Pierre Lorillard for his aid. Pictures show ruins and carved stones of Yucatan.

Le Plongeon says Yucatan woods still hide lost towns from most eyes. Tour books by Stephens and others gave but a dim hint, he argues. He links Maya rites to old cults of Egypt and Greece. Chaldea and India join the chain in his scheme. Free Mason rites, he claims, predate the Temple of Solomon. His claims are bold and were much fought in his day.
57481-the-war-that-will-end-war:
H G Wells wrote essays on the great war, issued by Duffield and Company in 1914. Wells had written Tono-Bungay and The New Machiavelli, as the title page notes. Eleven pieces run from why Britain went to war to the war of the mind. A plea to the American people stands near the heart of the set.

Wells says Britain fought since treaty vows bound her to shield Belgium. The attack on Luxemburg and Belgium, he holds, forced her hand at once. He then asks what end the war must serve, past mere revenge. Maps, food, and a new Europe all get sharp, plain argument.
57559-buster-the-big-brown-bear:
Buster the Big Brown Bear, by George Ethelbert Walsh, was published in 1922, with coloured pictures by Edwin Prittie. The book belongs to a Twilight Animal Series for boys and girls from four to ten years of age. Walsh also wrote the Bumper the White Rabbit books, and the Bobby Gray Squirrel books.

A front picture carries the cry: No you wont, Mister Loup, for my mother will kill you first. Other titles in the set include White Tail the Deer and Washer the Raccoon. Each volume was issued in a uniform style, at sixty five cents postpaid. Readers get a short animal tale for young children, built round a big brown bear, his kin, and his foes in the woods.
57642-the-black-bear:
The Black Bear, by William Wright, was issued at New York by Scribner in 1910. Pictures from photographs by the author and by Kerfoot illustrate the book. A plate shows a bear called Ben with the author himself. Wright had written The Grizzly Bear before this volume.

His two bear books grew from years of hunting and watching in the west. The black bear is smaller than the grizzly, but sly and strong. Wright treats its habits, food, cubs, and temper from his own camps. He writes against tall tales, from notes made on the spot. Sportsmen and naturalists both took his word on bears. The book stands as a sober life history of a famed American animal.
58073-secrets-of-radar:
Roy J Snell wrote Secrets of Radar, a war novel for young readers. The Goldsmith Publishing Company issued it in Chicago with a nineteen hundred forty four copyright. Twenty nine chapters carry the action from India toward Japan. Chapter names name Burma, night bombers, and a zero hour.

A young woman in a WAC uniform runs the first scene. She carts odd radio gear to a big anti-aircraft gun in India. Her orders come straight from the colonel. She plans to send small balloons with hollow steel balls aloft. The gun crew will track them as drill for real raids. Radar stays a guarded secret in the tale. The heroine, Gale, must guard it and use it well.
58212-the-noble-and-gentle-men-of-englan:
The Noble and Gentle Men of England is a book of notes on the arms and descents of the ancient knightly and gentle houses of England. Shirley attempted it, arranging the families in their counties. The third edition, corrected, was printed at Westminster in 1866. Shirley had sat in Parliament as a knight of the shire for Warwickshire.

His preface quotes a 1691 account of the Bruce family: long succession in wealth, honour, and repute is among the most valuable of worldly blessings. Shirley confines himself first to families still existing, and set up as knightly or gentle houses before the fifteen hundreds began. He takes no notice of families who merely took a name. Where a family's whole landed estate has been spent away, he omits it too, though the male line remains. The book is a county roll of old landed stock, part heraldry, part family history.
58358-cassell-s-history-of-england-vol-5:
Cassell History of England, volume five of eight, runs from the Peninsular War to the death of Sir Robert Peel. The King Edition was published in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne in 1909, with many illustrations, including coloured plates. The reign of George the Third is continued in chapter one.

Heads there name Napoleon desire for an heir, and the Archduchess Maria Louisa. A divorce was determined upon, and a marriage followed. Napoleon quarrelled with his family, and Louis Buonaparte abdicated. Bernadotte was chosen king of Sweden, and formed an alliance with Russia and Britain, then broke with Napoleon. George the Third insanity, plans for a regency, and the currency question fill the British side. Wellington difficulties and Massena retreat close the opening heads. Readers get a popular illustrated national history at the Napoleonic climax.
58419-an-address-given-in-to-the-late-ki:
An Address Given in to the Late King James was printed in London in 1690 for Baldwin in the Old Bailey. The pamphlet purports to print a memorial from the titular Archbishop of Dublin. The address came from a general meeting of the Catholic bishops and clergy of Ireland, held the May before by the king's order. The pamphlet adds reflections on each paragraph.

The title page says the original was found in King James's closet in Dublin Castle as he left the city. A copy, it adds, was found in the archbishop's lodgings. The editor argues that emissaries of Rome led James to trample the laws and liberties of the three kingdoms. The tract is a piece of post-revolution polemic, printed as evidence in the paper war of 1690. Its charges belong to that heated moment.
58480-perry-s-saints-or-the-fighting-par:
James Nichols wrote this war record of Perry's Saints regiment. Lothrop printed it at Boston, copyright 1885, with portraits. A memorial sketch of the author opens the volume here. Nichols died just after placing his finished copy with publishers.

Nichols was born at Haverhill, Massachusetts, in the year 1835. Public schools of his native town gave his early schooling. The sketch calls his record faithful and full of army life. To the rising generation the war already seems romance, it says. He finished and revised the work himself before his sudden call, the sketch records with pride.
58523-reminiscences-of-peace-and-war:
Sara Pryor wrote these reminiscences, copyrighted in 1904 and issued in a revised edition by Grosset. A photograph shows General Lee on Traveller, taken by Miley at Lexington, at the front. Pryor had written a life of the mother of Washington before this book of her own memories.

Her husband Roger Pryor served the Confederacy as a general through the war. Sara followed camps and capitals, kept a famous salon and watched the old Virginia world vanish. Peace brings her back to a New York life of letters, and the memories move between ballrooms and battlefields with a hostess's eye.
58549-the-civil-war:
James Robertson wrote this short history of the American Civil War for the Civil War Centennial Commission. The Commission published it at Washington in 1963, midway through the centennial years of 1961 to 1965. A board of teachers, librarians and historians from many states advised on the text.

Names on that board include Coulter of Georgia, Hesseltine of Wisconsin and Hollis of South Carolina. The mix shows an aim to serve schools across the country, North and South alike. Robertson gives young readers a clear, brief account of the war, its causes and its course, in a form fit for classroom use.
58700-crimes-and-punishments-including-a:
James Anson Farrer gives a fresh English version of Beccaria's famed book on crimes and punishments, issued in London in 1880. Farrer argues that the work is a classic whose interest is still living, not merely past. Older English versions, he says, follow a different order of chapters and so make a different book.

Opening chapters set Beccaria's life and the state of criminal law in Lombardy, where torture still held a place. Farrer traces the sway of Montesquieu and Helvetius on the young writer and the fame of the book in Paris, with Voltaire's praise. He adds no notes of his own, holding that readers should comment for themselves. Students of law get the great reform text with its setting plainly told.
58813-cartoons-on-the-war:
Cartoons on the War is a set of drawings by Boardman Robinson, published at New York in 1915. Dutton and Company issued the book, copyrighted in that year. Thanks are given to the New York Tribune and to Harper Weekly for leave to reprint. A prefatory note explains the making of the cartoons for the reader.

These drawings, the note says, are selections from cartoons published for the most part in a daily newspaper. They represent the emotions evoked by the news from day to day in that paper. They do seek to express a deep conviction that Germany is chiefly to blame for the war. Robinson, who had seen the Balkan wars as an artist, drew the Kaiser and the empires for an America still neutral in 1915. His bold line made the book a piece of Allied persuasion in the year before America chose its side.
58921-landmarks-of-charleston-including-:
Thomas Petigru Lesesne, author of a History of Charleston County, wrote this guide to the landmarks of Charleston. Garrett and Massie published it at Richmond in 1939, with a frontispiece of Saint Michael's Episcopal Church at Broad and Meeting streets. Its second part describes a walk the author calls an incomparable stroll.

The foreword promises the visitor the people and places of Charles Town under the Lords Proprietors, Charlestown under the royal government, and Charleston under the republic. Lesesne sends garden lovers by highway to Middleton Place and Magnolia-on-the-Ashley on the Ashley River Road, Cypress off the Coastal Highway, and Belle Isle Gardens on Winyah Bay toward Georgetown. The guide section runs past a hundred pages with a careful index, covering churches, houses, gardens, and sites from the colonial powder magazine to the Cooper River Bridge.
59293-my-spanish-year:
My Spanish Year is Mrs Bernhard Whishaw's record of a year in Spain, published by Mills and Boon of London in 1914 with twenty illustrations. With her husband she had already written Arabic Spain, a study of the country's Moorish past. The frontispiece portrait is titled Doña Elena.

Her introduction hands the new arrival one piece of advice. So much in Spain seems topsy-turvy that the temper suffers, unless the visitor views every discomfort from the standpoint of comic opera. Travellers arrive expecting an enlarged Carmen, then rage at tough beef, bad butter, and unpunctual trains. Whishaw chose to laugh instead, since Spain, to her mind, kept the last stronghold of romance in western Europe. The year's notes follow that comic-operatic rule.
59679-the-rumble-and-the-roar:
The Rumble and the Roar is a science fiction story by Stephen Bartholomew, taken from Worlds of If for February 1957. A short blurb says the noise was too much for the hero, who wanted quiet at any price. His name is Joseph, and he works on defense contracts.

Joseph gets to the office with ears aching from copter noise and from his ear plugs. His stomach churns, his feet hurt, and his drafting team lags on its work. Most days the clatter of typewriters soothes him, yet today a hit song on the speakers, Slam Bang Boom, grates on him. All folk wear ear plugs in his loud world. Readers get a sharp tale of noise as a plague of modern life.
59793-collections-of-the-minnesota-histo:
Collections of the Minnesota Historical Society for the year 1867 was printed in Saint Paul by the Pioneer Printing Company. The society's officers that year included president H H Sibley and secretary J F Williams. Its contents mix the secretary's annual report with studies of early Minnesota and the upper lakes region.

Articles cover the mineral regions of Lake Superior, the traveller Constantine Beltrami, and historical notes from the United States Land Office. Other pieces treat the geography of Perrot and Dakota superstitions. Readers get a young state historical society preserving frontier records, travel accounts, and Native lore within two decades of statehood.
59795-a-finnish-grammar:
A Finnish Grammar, by Eliot, a fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, was printed at the Clarendon Press in 1890. Eliot states his aim plainly in the preface. He seeks to give an account of Finnish clear enough for any reader to grasp the structure of the written language. He also places the chief facts of the tongue before students of language science.

He owns that his treatment falls short on the many dialects of the countryside, whose weight for the language's history he rates high. Still, he believes his book the only grammar of Finnish in English, and the only syntax beyond brief sketches in any language. His examples come chiefly from the Kalevala and the Bible. Others come from proverb collections, modern works, and the dictionaries of his day. The grammar opened a hard, rich language to English students for the first time in full.
5981-the-boy-scouts-in-front-of-warsaw-o:
Colonel George Durston opens on 5 August with Warsaw fallen, brilliant and beautiful, now torn by bombs, wrecked by shells, and left in ruins. Her people seem to have vanished in the two days since the city was taken, while wealthy citizens shelter in the lower town and invaders take the grand houses.

Warsaw lies on a plain by the Vistula, its streets twisted like snakes, its houses very old. Into this wreckage come the Boy Scouts, in the twentieth volume of the series. Durston sets a boys' adventure against real war damage, where courage must serve amid deserted streets and broken palaces.
59901-fear:
Angelo Mosso, a Turin physiologist, wrote a study of fear translated from the fifth Italian edition by E Lough and F Kiesow, published by Longmans in 1896. The translators dedicate their work to Mosso himself. They thank him for personal kindnesses and for furthering one of them in scientific research. Translating the splendid little work, they say, was an agreeable duty.

Mosso studied fear's bodily signs: trembling, blushing, the heart's action, and fatigue. His laboratory used new instruments to record the emotions. The book brought Italian experimental psychology to English readers. Mosso also wrote on fatigue and mountain sickness. Fear made his name with the general public.
60123-the-wonderful-year:
The Wonderful Year, a novel by William Locke, author of Jaffery and The Belovèd Vagabond, was copyrighted in 1915 and 1916 and printed by John Lane. Chapter one opens in Paris, at the Hôtel du Soleil et de l'Ecosse near the Halles Centrales, where a concierge hands an Englishman a letter.

Martin Overshaw reads it on a worn cane seat. Corinna Hastings writes: she is delighted he is in the city, though what brought him in August heaven only knows. She cannot ask him to her abode: one room, one chair, and a bed, and nothing to offer but a cigarette and the fag end of a bottle of grenadine. They will dine instead at the Petit Cornichon in the Rue Baret, where she takes such meals as she can afford. Meet me there at seven, she says. Overshaw asks the concierge whether to wear evening dress.
605-pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs returns to the hollow Earth in this sequel to At the Earth's Core. A letter from Algiers lures the narrator from lion hunting in Africa back to Pellucidar, where David Innes fights Hooja's cutthroats, cave prisons, and raids. Chapters race from lost wanderings to conquest and peace.

Burroughs writes at his usual gallop, with chutes, captures, kidnappings, and escapes. The inner world's eternal sun and strange beasts frame each peril. The book charms as a brisk continuation, where a modern hero must win a stone-age world by nerve and friendship.
60936-the-church-year-and-kalendar:
The Church Year and Kalendar is a hand book of the study of church rite by John Dowden, late head church man of Edinburgh. It was put out at the great press of Cambridge in nineteen ten. It stands in a set of such hand books, whose aim is set out at the front.

The set treats the past lore and the ground sense of the rites and forms that hold a place in the praise of the church. It gives as well some tale of the old books of rite in which those forms are kept. Care is laid on the weight that set forms of praise hold as speech of what the church holds true.
61130-ritual-of-the-order-of-the-eastern:
The Ritual of the Order of the Eastern Star was published by authority of the General Grand Chapter at Chicago in a revised edition of January 1890. A preface traces the text. Representatives met at Indianapolis on November 16, 1876, and organized the General Grand Chapter, which adopted a ritual in 1878. A committee received amendments through the eighties and presented the revised work in 1889.

Contents give general regulations, then opening, closing, initiation, installations for subordinate and grand chapters, and funeral ceremonies. The regulations open the book. Membership is open to Master Masons in good standing and to their wives, daughters, mothers, widows, and sisters over eighteen. Government rests in three bodies in rank: the General Grand Chapter, the Grand Chapter, and the subordinate chapter. The landmarks begin with belief in a Supreme Being, and the order has five degrees, named for Adah, Ruth, Esther, and Martha.
61272-the-woman-in-the-bazaar:
Alice Perrin wrote the Woman in the Bazaar, first published 1914. Cassell put the novel out in four cities that year. Mills drew its frontispiece. Coventry guessed that this was the woman, the caption says. The Vicar's Daughter opens the contents of the novel.

In the Garden follows in the list. A hostess and the Lie take the next two chapters. The Bachelors stand as a chapter head in the contents. Perrin had written East of Suez and the Anglo-Indians before. The Charm, Idolatry, and the Spell of the Jungle stand listed. Summertime at a lonely English house opens the tale's weather. Winter could be grim and cruel in that isolated place, it owns. Summer compensated in a measure for those severities each year. Perrin gives India and England one woman between them.
61622-the-discovery-of-radium-address-by:
The Discovery of Radium is an address by Madame Curie, printed by Vassar College. She gave it in the college chapel on the fourteenth of May, 1921. It was the only long address she made in America. The pamphlet is number two of a monograph series. That series honours Ellen Richards, a worker for public health. A note by a department chairman opens the piece.

The note tells how simply she told her story. She faced great difficulties with small means, it says. Her find bore on the great question of what matter is. Hope of healing by its rays spread the fame worldwide. Curie urges some hearers to carry the work on. Make a lasting gift to science, she tells them. Radium was then more than twenty years old. Her short account keeps the drama of its finding.
61709-revolt-on-the-earth-star:
Carl Selwyn wrote Revolt on the Earth-Star, printed in Planet Stories for the spring of 1940. The head note names the hero: Carver, a lonely derelict from a happier earth-age. He raises the revolt-cry, Down with the Capeks. The luxurious human stockyards discharge their men of no hope behind him. The tale opens on Rod Carver climbing a glacier. Sweat freezes on his brow as he chops shallow holes with his ax.

He wedges trembling fingers into the cuts and pulls himself up inch by inch. His toes kick into the niches below, and ice splinters fly into his face. A patch of gray lichen marks his goal, a few yards up. The ax sticks in a crack, then tears loose at a jerk. His feet slip, his face bangs the ice, and he dangles by one arm.
61769-the-thirteenth-hussars-in-the-grea:
Mortimer Durand wrote the war record of the Thirteenth Hussars, printed in 1921 with maps and prints. Opening chapters sketch horse troops before the war and the early past of the unit. The book then follows the men to France in 1915 and into hard fighting in 1916.

Most of the tale lies in Mesopotamia, in heat, dust, and long marches up the Tigris. Pages cover the retaking of Kut, the fight at Lajj, and the fall of Baghdad in 1917. Later moves at Ramadie and Tekrit lead to the last fight with the Turks and the trip home. The front pages honor the officers and men of the unit who died in the war years.
61869-satellite-of-fear:
Fred A Kummer Jr wrote a tale of a crippled space ship on Ceres. Satellite of Fear ran in Planet Stories in the spring of 1941. The Comet lies broke on Ceres' Darkside, where cold sits near five above absolute zero. Pitchblend ore in lead chests would yield over a million in radium.

Ken Grant paces the control room as air runs low and hope thins. Two men, Allers and Kennerly, walked for Bowman's Crater and vanished in the gloom. Miss Conway, the ship's commander, holds a firm chin amid the dread. Pulp fans get a taut tale of dark, cold, and things unseen.
62129-a-history-of-story-telling-studies:
Arthur Ransome's A History of Story-Telling, studies in the development of narrative, was published in London in 1909 by Jack, with twenty-seven portraits by Gavin. Ransome had edited the World's Story-Tellers series, whose volumes stand listed at the front. Jean de Meung's portrait opens the plates.

Part one runs from origins through the Romance of the Rose to Chaucer and Boccaccio. The rogue novel, the Elizabethans, the pastoral, and Cervantes follow. Bunyan and Defoe mark a turn, then Richardson and the feminine novel against Fielding, Smollett, and the masculine. Part two takes romanticism: Chateaubriand, Scott, the men of 1830, Balzac, and Gautier, then Poe and the new technique, Hawthorne, Flaubert, and a note on Maupassant to close.
62310-the-two-kinds-of-fear:
The Two Kinds of Fear is a farthing picture book for children, number forty-four in Dean's Illustrated Farthing Books, published by Dean and Son of Ludgate Hill, London. Its whole lesson fits in its title. The tract opens by asking what keeps some wicked people back from the evil things they wish to do.

The answer divides the world in two. Some are held back only because they are afraid of being punished, and that fear fades whenever a child escapes being found out. Good children are held back by the fear of sin itself, since God forbids it. A story makes the point concrete: Robert Wright, a rich gentleman's clever son, receives a shilling from his mother for the missionary box. What he does with that shilling on his way home is the tale.
63123-the-eyes-of-thar:
The Eyes of Thar is a science fiction story by Henry Kuttner, printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1944. Its hero, Dantan of Earth stock, returns warily to Klanvahr, an ancient Martian fortress, though a price hangs on his head. There a girl speaks a tongue dead a thousand years and knows him not, though she died in his arms from an assassin's wounds years before.

Kuttner builds the tale from Martian ruins, shamans hoarding scraps of forgotten knowledge, raids by the Redhelm Tribe, and the mystery of the girl's return. The story blends swordplay with lost science in the pulp manner. It shows Kuttner, one of the most skilled pulp writers of his day, working the romantic Mars that magazine readers loved.
63320-when-i-was-czar:
When I Was Czar is a romance by Arthur Marchmont, published in New York in nineteen o three. Burt issued it, and Marchmont had written By Wit of Woman before it. Thirty two chapters follow an Englishman who bears a strong likeness to the Czar. A letter home from the palace at Saint Petersburg opens the tale.

Years before, the Czar saved the narrator's life at a pig sticking in Germany. The two men found their strange resemblance on that day of danger. Now the narrator visits Russia as the Czar's guest, bound for Khiva. Prince Kalkov makes him an offer that turns the trip into a plot. Chapters promise a czar defied, a majesty made prisoner, and a death trap. Helga, a queenly woman met on the train, speaks and rages through the tale.
63342-the-white-czar-a-story-of-a-polar-:
Clarence Hawkes wrote The White Czar, a story of a polar bear, printed at Springfield in 1923 with pictures by Charles Livingston Bull. Hawkes had written Pep, the story of a brave dog. A front picture shows the bear greeting Eiseeyou with an angry snarl. The book is given to the memory of Rear Admiral Peary, who first planted the flag at the North Pole.

A long poem, The Lash of the Northland, stands before the tale. It sings of the land of frozen sea, where half the year is sun and half is night. Dog teams race over the floes past Melville Sound, and bergs sail in slow parade. A white bear at the headland and a walrus on the floe belong to that world. The tale itself then tells the bear's own story in the far north.
63392-doorway-to-kal-jmar:
Doorway to Kal-Jmar is a science fiction story by Stuart Fleming, printed in the magazine Planet Stories in the winter of 1944. Its blurb gives the plot in one breath. Two men had died before Syme Rector's guns to give him the key to the ancient city of Kal-Jmar. The city holds untold wealth, and robots that make desires instant commands.

The story opens under a dome. A tall man with a space-burned face loiters before a garish window display while a Lillis patrolman passes. Then he pulls his sand cape round his chin and follows the dark figure ahead. Above, the city's coloured lights reflect from the translucent dome, through which the stars shine dimly. He had posed as a wandering prospector after his ship crashed in the Mare Cimmerium. The rest, he knows, will not be so simple.
63419-death-star:
Death Star is a science fiction novelette by Tom Pace. It appeared in Planet Stories in the spring of 1945. The hero is Starrett Blade, a hunter of space pirates. His foe is Devil Garrett, the most feared pirate of the void. A cover note sets the stakes in brief. Blade is weaponless, his ship gone, and his hope a girl who wants him dead.

The tale opens on a barren world of Alpha Centauri. Blade crouches by a small, deep lake. His ship has just spun into its waters. He waits for Garrett to come down and search. A strange energy beam had struck his ship. Blade puzzles over its power source while he hides. Pulp tales of the forties ran on such hooks. Speed and peril fill every page here.
63596-our-navy-at-war:
Josephus Daniels, Secretary of the Navy from 1913 to 1921, wrote this account of the United States Navy in the World War. The Pictorial Bureau published it at Washington in 1922 with official photographs. He dedicates it to the six hundred thousand men who served in the Navy and Marine Corps, manning more than two thousand vessels.

Thirty-six chapters run from the day of decision and the sending of Admiral Sims to Europe through the convoy system, Gibraltar, and the shutting up of the submarine hornets in their nests. Daniels treats President Wilson as a strategist, the ferry of troops to France, the navy that flies, and the building of a thousand ships. He boasts in his dedication that of all the vast army sent overseas, not one soldier on an American troop-ship lost his life on the way to France.
63597-the-aeroplane-in-war:
The Aeroplane in War is a book on military aviation by Claude Grahame-White and Harry Harper. Lippincott published it at Philadelphia. A portrait shows Grahame-White, winner of the Gordon Bennett aviation cup of 1910. The authors also wrote The Aeroplane: Past, Present, and Future. The first section reviews progress before the first military tests of aeroplanes.

The book was written when armies were only beginning to try the flying machine. It weighs scouting, bombing, and fighting from the air as new arts. Grahame-White, a pioneer pilot, speaks with the authority of the airfield. The work shows how completely the aeroplane had entered war planning even before the First World War.
6386-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Suetonius himself was son of a Roman knight who commanded a legion for Otho at the battle that gave Vitellius the empire. He was born near the close of Vespasian's reign, his translator's preface notes. His first life, Caius Julius Caesar the Divine, loses his father at sixteen. Named high priest of Jupiter the next year, he repudiates a wealthy equestrian bride, Cossutia, contracted as a boy. He marries Cornelia, daughter of four times consul Cinna, and has a daughter Julia.

Resisting dictator Sylla's efforts to make him divorce Cornelia, Caesar suffers penalty and exile's shadow before his rise. Later he reforms the calendar to three hundred and sixty-five days, with an intercalary day every fourth year. Inserting two months so the year begins on January's calends, he makes a fifteen month year. Suetonius writes Caesar as ambition, law, and family honour in one life, from priesthood to calendar.
63886-the-seven-jewels-of-chamar:
Raymond F Jones spins a space adventure in The Seven Jewels of Chamar, printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1946. Scattered, the seven jewels flame like distant suns; united, they promise godlike power and mastery of the Solar System. The story's young hero, Nathan Ormondy, learns from his dying father what that power costs in blood.

The tale opens in a Venusian cave, where the bearded giant Thymar Ormondy lies shot in the back amid the eternal rains. With his charred arm he warns his son against the Firebird, who will kill a thousand men for every jewel, yet bequeaths him two of the stones.
63910-a-woman-and-the-war:
A Woman and the War, by the Countess of Warwick, was published at New York in 1916. Doran issued the book in the third year of the Great War. A portrait of Frances Evelyn Warwick fronts the volume as a plate. Chapter one treats King Edward and the Kaiser as a pair.

The greatest fight of all, drink legislation in England, and war and marriage follow in the contents. Nursing in war time gets a chapter from a woman view of the conflict. Two years of war, with woman loss and gain, forms the sixth chapter of the book. Child labour on the land in wartime is the next theme in the list. Aristocratic voice and social concern mix in this wartime survey by a famed hostess.
64101-nova-scotia-s-part-in-the-great-wa:
Nova Scotia's Part in the Great War was compiled and edited by Captain Hunt and printed by the Nova Scotia Veteran Publishing Company at Halifax in 1920. It is dedicated to the immortal memory of fallen comrades. Portraits of the lieutenant governor and of the premiers of Canada and Nova Scotia stand at the front.

Forty seven chapters, by the contents, record the province's units one by one. Headquarters of Military District Number 6 opens the book, then the mounted rifles, the siege batteries and field batteries, and the Royal Canadian Regiment. A long roll of numbered battalions follows, the 25th and 85th among them, with the construction battalion and the Forestry Corps. Service corps chapters cover the medical, dental, pay, ordnance, and engineer arms. College chapters treat Acadia, Dalhousie, King's, and Saint Francis Xavier, and the book closes toward recruiting and ocean transport.
64198-captives-of-the-thieve-star:
Captives of the Thieve-Star is a science fiction novelet by Schmitz. It appeared in a magazine called Planet Stories in May 1951. A cover blurb promises a haunted derelict ship. Two salvors grapple it and win a death-prize. The Yomm and the Mysterious Nine stalk them.

The story opens at a wedding in space. Peer, a voyageur girl, marries Channok in a moon crater. Solidograph banners fake an outdoor banquet hall. Eighty-four small ships of her space-rat tribe line the crater's edge. Police boats from Irrek cut the feast short. Her father gives the couple six minutes to flee. Channok, an honest licensed trader, must now run from the law. His bride's people rarely stray far from their ships.
64217-death-star:
James McKimmey wrote this space tale for Planet Stories' September 1953 issue. Its blurb gives the germ: for twenty long unholy years Hurtz the pilot dreamed of giving up the ships. He found his acre of heaven on a death star.

Hurtz goes through the set motions of landing on a small, unnamed planet. Each thing he does is wasted, for the boy Jones will put the rocket down. Hurtz rubs his rough cheek and swears in silence. His hard, aging muscles stay taut. His blue eyes keep their old fire, but his brows have gone near grey. Why did he ever try to help the boy, he asks himself, as the ship turns its blazing fins to the strange globe.
64342-vassals-of-the-lode-star:
Vassals of the Lode-Star is a science fiction tale by Gardner Fox. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Planet Stories for the summer of 1947. Its headnote shows outlawed man-beasts making a last stand against a horde of androids. Thor Masterson of Earth fights instead a strange green flame.

The tale opens before time itself, with a Rebel that was a cancer of space. Seventeen hundred billion years ago its streams flowed from unfathomable errors. Then the scene cuts to a library on Earth. A purple light tints the rugs and the bookshelves. The mansion rocks and tilts, torn loose from its base, and Thor Masterson comes up from his chair. A woman with long yellow hair stands on the rug, a slim dagger in her hand, as a club-wielding dwarf leaps at her.
64633-the-ways-of-war:
The Ways of War is a book of war thought by Kettle, a chair man of lore and a young chief in a Dublin corps. It was put out at New York in nineteen seventeen. A tale of his life by his wife stands with the work. The book is sworn to that wife and mate. A Latin line on truth past shades stands past the sworn leaf.

A first note sorts the parts of the book. They are the words of an Irish man of pens on why he felt the call to give his life. That call was for the free state of the world in the great war. He was one of the most bright men of the young Ireland and young Europe of his time.
64763-the-irish-war:
The staff of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County prepared this pamphlet in 1953. It is one of a historical series published under the library boards' direction. Trustees of the school city and the county library board are named at the front of the pamphlet.

Such library pamphlets gathered documents and reading lists on a single episode for citizens. The Irish war, from rebellion to treaty and civil war in this series' scope, gets the treatment here. A House of Representatives document of December 1835, referred to the Committee on Claims, stands among the papers the staff assembled for readers.
64933-the-arnold-bennett-calendar:
Frank Bennett compiled The Arnold Bennett Calendar, issued in New York with copyright in 1912. A sketch of Arnold Bennett's life opens the book, signed F C B. Enoch Arnold Bennett was born at Hanley in the Potteries on May 27, 1867. He was educated at the Middle School, Newcastle-under-Lyme, and worked in his father's solicitor's office.

In 1889 Bennett took a post in a London solicitor's office, leaving law in 1893 to help edit Woman. He became editor in 1896 and left in 1900 to write full time. His first novel, A Man from the North, came out in 1898. Major works listed include The Old Wives' Tale, Clayhanger, and How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day.
65138-revolt-of-the-devil-star:
Ross Rocklynne wrote Revolt of the Devil Star, first printed in Imagination in February 1951. The tale is the last in a line about Darkness, a vast being of pure force. Darkness crossed the void between two worlds to seek the sense of life. His child Sun Destroyer sought wise Oldster and died, still yearning for her son. That son, Vanguard, was mocked as Yellow Light for a flaw at his core. Oldster led him to mate, to make life, and so to die.

Now the lead is Devil Star, a purple light born of that line. A law of all worlds says each life must create and die. Devil Star defies that law, armed with a dread secret of his birth. The tale asks if any life can break the one rule that binds all.
65262-the-fritz-strafers-a-story-of-the-:
Percy Westerman's Fritz Strafers, a story of the Great War, was published by Partridge at London. Westerman had written Billy Barcroft and A Sub of the RNR before it. Thirty-four chapters carry the naval war against the U-boats. Hugh Holcombe opens the tale in a muggy railway carriage, blaming a young brother who wrecked his motor-bike. The contents promise an ober-leutnant's jaunt, a torpedoed ship, and the strafing of U 254.

The blimp comes to the rescue in one chapter; a burning munition ship fills another. Billy's flying-boat, a rammed vessel, and the last voyage of the Andromeda mark the middle. Prisoners of war, a fight to a finish, and a dash for freedom close the book. The frontispiece shows a flag defiantly displayed as the emblem of freedom. Westerman wrote the war as boys' adventure, with British pluck against the Huns throughout.
65464-charles-peace-or-the-adventures-of:
Charles Peace, or The Adventures of a Notorious Burglar is a life of crime in parts. It first ran in one hundred week prints, each with a drawn plate at its head. Peace, who went by a false name too, won a name to match the famed house break men of old tales. The book calls him a mix of parts in one man.

He was born in a steel town and was wild from his first years, first in bold games past his mates. At ten he had to help his father, a small file made man of faith, earn the bread of the house. That father played the great bass at the church hall and taught the boy the small string box. The boy grew skilled and set out as a string man of note, past the crook path the book traces.
65761-a-merchant-fleet-at-war:
Archibald Hurd's A Merchant Fleet at War, from Cassell in 1920, tells what the great passenger liners did in the Great War. A map at the front marks the incidents the text describes, and colour plates show the Aquitania leading the transports.

Chapters cover the mobilisation of the fleet, the combatant Cunarders, and the work of carrying on under attack. Hurd then gives the ordeal of the Lusitania a chapter of its own, followed by the toll of the submarines and the shore work done for the services. The plates show the Carmania sinking the Cap Trafalgar and the torpedoing of the Ivernia, Ausonia, Thracia, and Volodia, among others. The book honours merchant crews who sailed war routes in peace-built ships.
65773-playing-with-fire-a-story-of-the-s:
James Grant wrote Playing with Fire, a tale of the Soudan war put out in London in 1887. Grant had told a vast shelf of war tales, from The Romance of War to The Cameronians. A long list of those tales fills the front of the book. The war in the Soudan, in Africa, gives this tale its ground.

Parts name a man called Hawkey Sharpe who seeks advice in his straits. A Scots song of a lass, a call of love made to Hester, and a slip by Sharpe mark the home thread. The town of the caliphs and a fall month in the land of the pharaohs set the war scenes. Jack Elliot falls in peril, and Annot feels dark doubts of what may come.
65827-frederick-the-great-and-the-seven-:
Ferdinand Schrader wrote this life of Frederick the Great in German, as one of a set of life tales for young folk. George P. Upton put it in English dress, and it was printed at Chicago in 1905. The book deals with seven years of the king's life alone. But those years were some of the most famed in the tale of Austria and Prussia, as the man who did the work in English notes.

That span is the Seven Years' War. It gave Frederick firm hold of Silesia, and raised Prussia to the first rank of the states of Europe. Three times the king went to war for that prize. The first time, in 1740 to 1742, he had Saxony, Bavaria, and France at his side, against Austria and Great Britain. The next time, in 1744 to 1745, Austria had the aid of Saxony.
65983-the-harroun-site-a-fulton-aspect-c:
The Harroun Site is a dig report by Edward B. Jelks and Curtis D. Tunnell, issued in 1959 by the University of Texas at Austin. The work was done under a pact with the National Park Service. Crews dug at the site in Upshur County, Texas, ahead of dam work at Ferrell's Bridge Reservoir.

The report first sets out the land, the soil, and the dig methods used on the ground. It then treats four mounds in turn, with their floors, houses, and burials. A long part describes the finds, chiefly pots of brushed, incised, and engraved ware. The site is classed as a Fulton Aspect part of the old Caddoan area, and the finds help date that phase.
6604-two-months-in-the-camp-of-big-bear:
Theresa Gowanlock and Theresa Delaney tell, in their own words, two months spent in the camp of Big Bear during the North-West troubles. Their chapters run from leaving Ontario and the fight at Battleford to the massacre, the fall of Fort Pitt, and life as captives cooking for a large family. Hope almost deferred gives way, at last, to rescue and the road home.

A second part adds Gowanlock's youth, marriage, and later life, with notes on Father Fafard and the Saskatchewan stream. The tone is plain and direct, with no polish to hide fear or grief. Two Months in the Camp of Big Bear is a stark, first-hand account of war, captivity, and survival on the Canadian plains.
66442-the-minor-horrors-of-war:
The Minor Horrors of War is a natural history of the pests that plague armies. Shipley wrote the study. He was a Cambridge zoologist and master of a college there. Smith, Elder published it in London in 1915. An enlarged model of the house-fly forms the frontispiece. Twelve chapters treat the creatures in turn.

The louse opens the parade. The bed-bug and the flea follow. A flour-moth that infests biscuits earns a chapter. Flies take two chapters between them. Mites and ticks come next. Leeches close the book in three chapters. One leech chapter treats the medicinal kind. Others treat leeches of the Nile and Ceylon. Each pest is pictured at several stages of life. The war of 1914 made such knowledge urgent for soldiers.
66585-the-boy-s-king-arthur-sir-thomas-m:
Lanier edited the Boy's King Arthur from Malory's history. Scribner at New York keeps the classic in print. Wyeth illustrated this schoolroom edition of the romance. Copyright pages run back to 1880 for Lanier's own editing. Some minor passages are omitted in this newer printing, it notes.

All the greater tales are retained, it says. Arthur and Launcelot stand in its contents. Galahad, Percival, and the Holy Grail stand in the list too. The fair maid of Astolat and the death of Arthur close it. It befell in the days of Utherpendragon, Malory begins the tale. A son born to him was king in after time, it says. Launcelot names himself a knight of the Round Table within. King Mark slew Tristram as he sat harping, the captions tell. Lanier gives boys the Round Table in seven books.
6673-young-knights-of-the-empire-their-c:
Robert Baden-Powell, founder of the scouts, offers further yarns for boy-men, with the scout code at their heart. His foreword warns that yarns alone are of little worth unless the ideas in them are put into daily, habitual practice. Boys, he says, need encouragement to live the code, not just to hear it.

The tales that follow show self-education in character and good citizenship, step by step as in Scouting for Boys. Courage, loyalty, thrift, and service run through each story. Young Knights of the Empire is a plain, earnest scout book from 1917, made to turn reading into doing.
66762-the-life-of-the-caterpillar:
The Life of the Caterpillar, by Henri Fabre, was turned into English by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and issued at New York in 1916. The table opens with the pine processionary and the laying of its eggs. The nest and the community of that caterpillar follow. The procession itself, in its strange single file, takes a long chapter.

Weather lore of insects, the moth, and the stinging power come next. The arbutus caterpillar and an insect virus widen the field of the book. The psyches and their cases get two chapters of close watching. The great peacock moth and the banded monk close the main list. Fabre watches small lives with endless patience, and makes philosophy of a garden path.
66872-the-beneficent-burglar:
Charles Neville Buck's novel The Beneficent Burglar opens with a chapter called A Call for Help. Lewis Copewell bursts through the anteroom of Alexander Hamilton Burrow like a comet run amuck. The room is already full of waiting men, weary from delay, all eyes fixed on the door that shuts the great man in his sanctum behind a placard reading Private.

A young woman at a typewriter guards the door with calm contempt, silently telling the crowd to wait, since the great do not hurry. Copewell alone ignores the rule. He and her employer are old intimates, and he demands to know where Aleck is, quick. Several hopeful men, eager to serve the city in its police and fire departments, rise as the great man himself appears.
66918-report-of-the-twentieth-national-a:
This report of the twentieth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar was printed at Boston in 1854. It opens not with accounts but with weather: a storm on December 28 and 29, unprecedented in severity for many years, brought bereavement to some homes and loss to many more.

For days the mails stopped and communication with Boston's environs was cut off, while every hour brought fresh tidings of shipwreck. Against that gloom, the bazaar of 1853 had closed with what the writers call brilliant success. Receipts are given at four thousand two hundred and fifty-six dollars. Readers get an abolitionist fundraising report where the cause's bookkeeping starts with a New England storm.
66919-fairy-tales-from-far-and-near:
Fairy Tales from Far and Near holds tales retold by Katharine Pyle. Both text and prints come from the hand of the teller. Past books by her tell of angels, geese, and green woods in like mode. The book came out in Boston in the year nineteen twenty two.

Twelve tales span the globe, each tagged with the land of its birth. A Hindu tale leads, then Lithuanian, French, and Irish tales in turn. Norse, Korean, Scotch, and Greek tales fill the wide back half. A front print shows two old eagles in flight on the wing. Bright art and clear prose suit the set to read aloud at home.
67071-the-star:
Wells wrote a famous short tale of a star that comes near the earth, prefaced here by a note that explains its science. A new body is seen drawing close, and one astronomer works out what its pull will do. He warns the people, but they discount his words and call him mad.

The tale itself opens on the first day of a new year, with word from three observatories that Neptune's motion has gone erratic. Ogilvy had already marked a slowing in December. A faint speck of light in that region grows larger and brighter, moving unlike any planet. Though the star never touches the earth, the wreck it works is, the note promises, complete and horrible.
67512-the-irish-nuns-at-ypres-an-episode:
A member of an Irish nuns' house at Ypres wrote the tale of their war, printed at London in 1915. Barry O'Brien edited the book, and John Redmond adds a first word. The prioress vouches for its truth in a note of April 1915. The notes were first kept for the house alone.

Newspaper tales of their fate ran wild, she says, and friends begged for the true account. Contents trace the coming of the Germans and the allies in Ypres. Life in the cellars and the shelling follow. Flight, care of the wounded, and two tries to go back fill the middle. The trip to England and a new home at Oulton close the book.
67590-a-son-of-the-ages-the-reincarnatio:
A Son of the Ages tells the reincarnations and adventures of Scar, the Link, in what its subtitle calls a story of man from the beginning. Stanley Waterloo, author of The Story of Ab, wrote it, and Doubleday and Page printed it at Garden City in 1914, with illustrations by Craig Johns.

Chapter one is told by an ape among the treetop people. He has fallen fighting the Brown One, the biggest ape in the forest, over a female both wanted. His broken thumb and crushed fingers leave him unable to climb back and renew the fight. Fourteen chapters then march the same soul forward: axemen, bowmen, clansmen, boatmen, sowers, and tamers. A deluge, kitchen midden dwellers, lake dwellers, armourers, and sailors follow, ending at Alesia.
67593-alkibiades-a-tale-of-the-great-ath:
Charles Hamilton Bromby wrote this tale of the great war of Athens. A word from Lord Byron stands at its head: of all the names of old time, none comes down with such charm as that of Alkibiades. Why that is, Byron owns he cannot say. The list of parts maps the life of that man and the war that broke his town. Perikles and Sokrates stand at the start, his guides in peace and in thought.

War and the plague at Athens come next, then the feast of Kleon and the great meet of the town. The games at Olympia and a fight in Arkadia fill the first book. The next book turns to the dark acts: the maim of the statues of the gods, the sail to Sicily, and the call home. Death is his lot from Athens and from Sparta in turn.
67642-the-cruise-of-the-gyro-car: Herbert Strang made this tale of a tour by gyro-car, one of his set of Romances for boys. The front of the book gives praise for the past books of that set. King of the Air is called the best of its kind by a great sheet. The Bookman says few men know as well as Strang the right mix of fun and fact for boys. In that set and vein, this cruise takes its place.
67840-essay-on-the-literature-of-the-mex:
Lawson surveys a war's books in an Essay on the Literature of the Mexican War. Lawson writes as a man of the class of 1882 at Columbia College, New York. The essay opens with the scale of the prize the war won.

The annexation of Texas and the consequent war with Mexico added more than eight hundred thousand square miles of land to the United States, he states. That is much greater than all the states east of the Mississippi, and almost equal to the Louisiana purchase of 1803. Those events have been obscured by the magnitude of the recent civil war, he holds. They seem almost as remote as the romantic incidents in the campaigns of Cortez. A fresh interest wakes as mines and herds develop the won lands, he notes.
67854-reminiscences-of-the-civil-war:
Cora Mitchel's reminiscences, printed at Providence by Snow and Farnham, recall her girlhood in Apalachicola, Florida. Her father, Thomas Leeds Mitchel of Groton, Connecticut, was a cotton merchant at the mouth of the Chattahoochie River, shipping the interior's cotton down to the bay. Her mother, Sophia Brownell of Providence, Rhode Island, helped him build a home in an almost new country.

The elder Mitchel, Northern in sentiment, did not believe in slavery and owned only three enslaved people, who had begged him to buy them rather than face sale in the open market. In the spring of 1861 the town felt the first gun at Fort Sumter: companies drilled, sandbag batteries rose along the bay, and ladies met to embroider banners. Young Cora was allowed to a mass meeting and felt the thrill of it.
68333-the-history-of-company-b-311th-inf:
Colonna put in shape a short war history of Company B of the 311th Infantry. The book came out in Freehold, New Jersey, in 1922. David Gardenier, Charles Peter, and Tracy White gave parts. Bert Stiles built the lists of names and counts. A photo shows Colonna and Foulkes at Camp Dix in 1918.

Chapters run from Madison Barracks and Camp Dix to the trip to France. The men serve in English and home zones, then at Saint Mihiel and the Meuse-Argonne. Lists name each man, the hurt and dead, and the awards won. Kin and vets can trace a man's whole war here.
68391-round-the-year-with-the-stars-the-:
Round the Year with the Stars is a guide to the sky for the plain eye. Garrett Serviss wrote it, known for books on the sky for all. It came out in New York and London in the year 1910. No glass is called for to use the book in the field.

Maps show the sky at the four turns of the year in the book. Charts trace the star groups and name the chief stars in each. The dusk sky at the spring turn is the first part of the work. The sky at the high sun, the fall turn, and the cold turn come next. The worlds that roam the sky get a part of their own at the end. A list tells how to say the names of the stars in the right way. The book makes the dome of night a ground a man can learn.
68459-the-rambler-club-s-motor-car:
The Rambler Club's Motor Car is a boys' adventure by Sheppard, printed at Philadelphia in 1913. Sheppard wrote a shelf of Rambler Club books: afloat, in winter camp, in the mountains, on a ranch, among lumberjacks, and in an aeroplane. He illustrated this volume himself. A chorus of good-byes fronts the tale.

The front matter introduces the club. Bob Somers is strong and athletic. Stout Dave Brandon loves his ease but can be remarkably active when circumstances demand. Tom Clifton is a trifle self-conscious, his enthusiasm apt to carry him away. The three have reached Chicago, homeward bound after a trip up the Hudson. On the steps of a house on Michigan Avenue stands Victor Collins, gazing up and down the wide street. The motor car of the title waits to carry the club out again.
68676-the-passionate-year:
The Passionate Year, a novel by James Hilton, was published at Boston in 1924. Its plan follows a school year: the summer term, the winter term, a Christmas interlude, and the Lent term. Kenneth Speed, a tall young man in his early twenties, arrives at Millstead School to take up his post. The head welcomes him with a warm, moist hand, which Speed grips so hard the man winces.

Speed does things vigorously when nervous, the narrator says, to hide his secret fear. His nerves are not about the interview or about feeling lesser. They are the keen sense of life turning a fresh corner, which may or may not lead into a blind alley. A month before, he was an undergraduate at Cambridge. Now he is an arts master at Millstead. Hilton, later famed for tales of school and loss, writes here of a young teacher's first year.
68679-the-unseen-ear:
Unseen Ear is a detective novel by Natalie Sumner Lincoln, issued by Burt at New York. The copyright is of 1920 by Street and Smith and of 1921 by Appleton. Lincoln is named as author of I Spy, The Moving Finger, and The Red Seal. A frontispiece shows a woman on her knees turning a dial at page 249.

She dedicates the book to her mother, whose unflagging interest stimulated her literary work, in its front. Contents open with Through the Portieres and Identified for the mystery of the tale. Theories and Lost: A Memorandum follow in the list of chapters of the book. More Theories, Speculation, and The Knave of Hearts fill the middle of the contents. Lincoln wrote Washington society mysteries by the dozen. Her unseen ear, the listener behind the portieres, is the first fact of a plot of memoranda, threats, and drawing room detection.
6870-why-we-are-at-war:
Woodrow Wilson's Why We Are at War gathers his messages to Congress from January to April 1917. It adds his war proclamation of April 6 and his message to the American people of April 15. Harper published the book in May 1917. It runs from a world league for peace and the severance of ties with Germany. Then it moves to a request for power and the stark message that war must be accepted.

Publishers note they sought approval for the title and captions, and present these historic documents in collected form as a service of lasting worth. Wilson's prose is grave, idealistic, and direct. Why We Are at War is a key primary source on America's entry into the Great War.
68723-memories-of-the-civil-war:
Henry B James, of Company B, 32nd Massachusetts Volunteers, recalls his service in Memories of the Civil War, published at New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 1898. He dedicates the book to his boys, who delighted in hearing their father tell stories of the war. Twenty-nine chapters run from enlistment through Antietam, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville and Gettysburg to the Wilderness, Cold Harbor and Petersburg.

James writes thirty-three years after the close, answering the question of what the privates did. Born of Quaker stock in New Bedford, he traces his leaning to adventure to a grandfather imprisoned by the English in the War of 1812.
68798-strange-stories-of-the-civil-war:
