Strange Stories of the Civil War was published in 1907 by Harper and Brothers at New York and London. Its authors include Robert Shackleton, John Habberton, William Henderson, and Chittenden. Captain Howard Patterson and General Forsyth also contribute. Twelve illustrated tales make the volume, each by a hand that knew the war or its records.

Contents open with a boy's impressions of the Civil War and the captain of Company Q, the tale of an unenlisted soldier. Midshipman Jack tells the action of Apalachicola, and Captain Billy gives aid and comfort to the enemy. Two days with Mosby and a blockade-runner follow. Later tales tell how Cushing destroyed the Albemarle, Lincoln and the sleeping sentinel, and the battle between the Monitor and the Merrimac. Sheridan's ride and Lee's surrender at Appomattox, told by men present, close the book.
69107-international-cartoons-of-the-war:
H Pearl Adam picked and introduced International Cartoons of the War, a book of press drawings. E P Dutton and Company issued the book in New York. A Rheims Cathedral plate by Marcel Gaillard clothes the cover. Punch of August twelfth, nineteen hundred fourteen leads the set.

Bravo, Belgium, by F H Townsend, stands as frontispiece in the book. Will Dyson of The Nation mocks German honour in two sharp plates. A burglar with his swag but no food jeers at blockade hunger. W Heath Robinson offers mad war machines for pure fun. The Sketch and the Daily Mirror lend English laughs to the set. An Auckland paper weighs sea mines from far New Zealand. War mirth from many lands shows one fight in many keys.
69190-troubled-star:
Troubled Star is a science fiction novel by George Smith, printed in the magazine Startling Stories in February 1953. Smith wrote engineering-flavoured tales of space. His foreword, styled en saga, lays down the theme before the story starts.

At least once in every generation, the foreword says, a person turns up who embarrasses the custodians of history. With neither talent nor ambition nor admirable character, this person succeeds where the bright and honest would have failed. Stubborn, vain, and often stupid, he blunders in where the wise would not dare. His hide is thicker than a rhinoceros's. He tells the surgeon where to cut and instructs the statesman in diplomacy. His success, Smith argues, is due to the law of averages: there are more bums than geniuses, and more laziness than ambition in the world. The novel gives that lucky blunderer a troubled star to steer by.
69207-tibetan-grammar:
Tibetan Grammar is a language manual first written by Jaschke, a Moravian missionary. Trubner published the second edition at London in 1883, prepared by Wenzel. The first edition had been printed by stone plate at Kyelang in 1865, in few copies, and was long out of print. Ill health kept Jaschke from revising the work himself.

Wenzel explains in his preface that he used the author's own notes with care. He added remarks from old Tibetan books and from the speech of western Tibet. That dialect gets special weight through the book. It was the speech Jaschke knew best from long residence at Kyelang. It is also the one English workers in India were most likely to meet. Rules, examples, and a guide to sounds fit the book for learners of the written tongue.
69289-little-comrade-a-tale-of-the-great:
Burton Stevenson wrote this tale of the Great War, Little Comrade. Holt printed it in New York in March 1915. Contents open on the thirty first of July, 1914, war eve. First rumblings, a state of war, and satin slippers mystery follow.

A snare, a trap, the frontier, and a night attack fill the middle. The passage of the Meuse and a last dash lead to disaster. Bloem and Stewart, friends from a Vienna congress, open the tale. Coffee on a terrace marks their last meal together in peace. A trust fulfilled closes the contents list of the war tale at its end.
69318-youthful-folly-detected-written-fo:
Youthful Folly Detected is a conduct tract written for the benefit of youth, particularly the female sex. David Newhall printed it at the Observatory Press in Walpole, New Hampshire, in 1804. A verse on the title page warns the maid who walks in folly's path that misery waits at the end of it.

The advertisement explains the tract's origin. The hints were first designed for a few individuals the author felt obliged to guide. Since all young people stand in one predicament, the advice was printed for all. The virtuous girl who minds instruction young earns a name sung on harps of gold. The tract belongs to the stern moral literature of the early republic. Parents and ministers bought such pamphlets to steer daughters away from the vices that ruined women.
69349-a-story-of-the-sawdust-the-patheti:
A Story of the Sawdust tells the pathetic history of Old Props' darling, a circus child. It ran as number twenty five of the Multum in Parvo Library, a Boston monthly. The pamphlet sold for five cents in January eighteen ninety six. Its heroine, Patty, was born in a circus dressing room behind a canvas strip.

Her mother, a slack wire performer, fell in her act and died years later. The fall came two hours before Patty's birth amid the roaring of lions. Old Props, the gruff property man, took the fatherless baby as his own charge. Patty grew up in the sawdust ring as a true daughter of the arena. She rode bareback as an infant prodigy billed in every town they played. The title warns she died for her love, meeting her fate in New Zealand.
69461-rondah-or-thirty-three-years-in-a-:
Florence Carpenter Dieudonne wrote Rondah, or Thirty Three Years in a Star, held in 1887 at Philadelphia. Front praise calls it a bright and odd novel with a strong plot. Four folk, three men and one woman, sit at the heart of the tale. A storm casts them from Earth to a small star.

The star is still hot and half cooled when they land. They stay there for more than thirty three years. For twenty years of cold they sleep, as the star folk do. The star folk are bird folk with wings who grow in large pods. Love, envy, and strange trips fill the tale. Rondah, the lead woman, is left behind at first and joins them later.
69487-the-complete-servant-being-a-pract:
Samuel and Sarah Adams, servants for fifty years in different families, wrote this guide, published in London in 1825. Its price was seven shillings and sixpence. The book speaks to every grade of service, from the housekeeper to the servant of all-work, and from the land steward down to the foot-boy, with useful receipts and tables.

In their preface the Adamses argue that no bond in society is as wide as that of masters and servants. Yet no book, they say, had yet set out those duties as they are done in daily practice. Sermons on duty existed; a working manual did not.
69681-the-southern-war-poetry-of-the-civ:
The Southern War Poetry of the Civil War is a doctoral thesis. Esther Ellinger presented it at the University of Pennsylvania in 1918. The Hershey Press printed it at Philadelphia that year. Two chapters carry the argument. The first weighs the meaning of the South's war verse. The second traces its growth through the war years. Bibliographies and an index of poems fill the back. Chapter one opens with Simms on the emotional literature of a people. Facts alone, Simms wrote, do not show a nation's true spirit. Poetry speaks without reserve, and so betrays the heart.

Stedman is quoted to the same end. A people's verse may be the voice of its time, he held. Ellinger applies both tests to Confederate song. Her index lets a reader find the poems themselves.
69691-the-west-riding-territorials-in-th:
The West Riding Territorials in the Great War, by Laurie Magnus, was published in London in 1920, fully illustrated, with a foreword by Field Marshal Earl Haig. A portrait of Major General Baldock fronts the book. Contents divide into three books: before war, war, and war end.

Book one treats the West Riding Association, the West Riding troops, and mobilization. Book two opens with a French song title, then the day work. Serving in reserve, preparations on the Somme, and operations on the Somme follow. With the 62nd in France, the northern ridges, and the battle of Cambrai in two phases come next. Book three opens with fateful days in 1918. The two divisions were the West Riding own. Readers get a county regiment history of citizen soldiers.
70113-thirty-years-in-madagascar:
Matthews, of the London Missionary Society, wrote thirty years in Madagascar, in a second edition published at London in 1904 with sixty-two illustrations from photographs and sketches. His portrait fronts the volume, and the contents tell the island's church history as a drama in acts: a land of darkness first.

The killing times follow, the persecution under the old monarchy, with plates of the fosse where martyrs were speared and the cave where the Bible was hid for twenty years. From darkness to dawn, the morning breaking, and progress all along the line carry the missions forward. Gathering clouds, the conquest of Madagascar, the end of the monarchy, and the triumph of the gospel close the record. A missionary's lifetime, told as national conversion, is the book.
70125-mexican-letters-written-during-the:
Mexican Letters, written during the progress of the late war between the United States and Mexico, by B H M Brackenridge, was printed at Washington by Robert A Waters in 1850. The letters are collected and republished, with notes and corrections, to be completed in two numbers.

In his preface Brackenridge says one who thinks for himself is very apt to think alone, or with a minority. In a free republic, opinion runs into party. The individual is restrained by party trammels from asserting his independence. Although agreeing with the Whigs generally, he could not agree with them in the late war with Mexico. He could not hold that justice was on the side of that republic. He holds the letters may serve as materials for history. War fans get a Whig defense of the Mexican War.
70128-max-havelaar:
Max Havelaar, or The Coffee Auctions of the Dutch Trading Company is a novel of protest by Multatuli, turned into English by Baron Alphonse Nahuijs. It was published at Edinburgh in 1868. The preface tells the book's strange birth. Multatuli was the pen name of Eduard Douwes Dekker. He had served seventeen years as a Dutch official in Java. His book caused a sensation in Holland such as no book had made before. Not one fact in it was ever contested, the preface says.

Dekker tells of the extortions and tyranny laid on the natives of the Dutch Indies. The great men of the colony would not answer him in parliament. The tale is told through Havelaar, an honest resident who fights the system and is broken by it. The book is set beside Uncle Tom's Cabin in its aim and its fire.
70199-tanar-of-pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote a novel of Pellucidar, the world inside the hollow earth, first issued in book form in 1929. The prologue turns on Jason Gridley, a radio enthusiast of twenty-three who lives at Tarzana. The narrator met him when Jason bought land there after Stanford.

Jason's experiments with a new principle of radio make the tale possible, though the narrator owns he knows nothing of the science. The story proper belongs to Tanar, and chapters promise a disaster, a tandor hunter, and an island of love. Korsars attack, prisoners are taken, and two suns appear. Burroughs keeps his inner world savage, strange, and swift.
70378-twelve-months-in-madagascar:
Joseph Mullens, foreign secretary of the London Missionary Society, wrote a book dated 1875 on a year in Madagascar. Sent with a colleague to visit the rulers and the churches, he was met with warmth at each stop. The pair saw the two central provinces in full, in length and breadth, and left by the north west route.

Mullens states that a great change in faith on the isle is a real thing, felt most at the capital. Church life is shown at its best and at its least taught, from town to far coast. Talks with staff of the Norwegian, Friends, and Medical missions fill out the wide tour.
70486-the-lurking-fear:
The Lurking Fear, by Lovecraft, is a tale of horror from Weird Tales of June 1928. Its first part is named The Shadow on the Chimney. The narrator tells it, as a confession he can no longer hold back.

Thunder was in the air the night he climbed Tempest Mountain. His goal was the deserted mansion on its top, and the fear that lurked there. He took two faithful, muscular men, partners in his explorations of horror. Reporters still lingered in the village after the panic of a month before. That creeping death, he says, was nightmare made real. The party slipped out quietly by motor-car, through primeval forest. The country looked more than sinister by night. No wild creatures stirred, for animals are wise when death leers close. He alone knows what manner of fear haunted that mountain.
70595-a-visit-to-the-bazaar:
A Visit to the Bazaar, by the author of Juliet, or The Reward of Filial Affection, was printed for Harris and Son in London in 1820, in a third edition. A frame story sends a family to the Bazaar in Soho Square, where Susan Boscawen, grateful for past kindness, keeps a stall supporting her aged mother and two helpless brothers.

The visit becomes a tour of trades, chapter by chapter. The jeweller, the linen draper, the toy shop, and the pastry cook come first. Then the hatter, the lace man, and the optician. Umbrellas, work baskets, artificial flowers, and singing birds follow, with English china, a hair merchant, a shoe maker, and a gun smith. Green houses, a milliner, a chemist, prints, a grocer, a furrier, a bookseller, a watch maker, and a sculptor complete the walk. Theodore, aged ten, asks what bazaar means.
70782-the-united-states-marine-corps-in-:
The United States Marine Corps in the World War is the corps' own brief history of its part in the Great War. Edwin McClellan, a major in charge of the corps' history office, prepared the book. The Government Printing Office issued it at Washington in 1920. A note explains that orders of 1919 called for such a history.

McClellan states that facts and figures are given as exactly as they could then be had. He avoids praise, blame, and large conclusions by design. A fuller, detailed history was still in preparation, the note adds. Tables carry much of the record, with notes tied to their figures. The book told marines and the public what the corps had done overseas. Belleau Wood and the great drives stand behind its dry tables.
71105-the-story-of-a-border-city-during-:
The Story of a Border City During the Civil War, by Galusha Anderson, was printed at Boston by Little, Brown in 1908, with twelve portraits and views. A bird's-eye plate shows Saint Louis in 1860 as the front of the book. Anderson taught at the University of Chicago, but his ground here is first hand: he lived in Saint Louis from 1858 to 1866. His opening note says men from all parts had long urged him to write the tale out.

The book is given to those who, by wit, tact, and cost, helped keep Missouri in the Union. Its motto is Milton's: on the perilous edge of battle. War fans get a slave-state city held for the North, told by a man who walked its streets through the whole storm.
71736-aircraft-in-war:
Eric Stuart Bruce wrote a war book on flying craft in war, printed at London in 1914, with a picture of a Farman scouting biplane and its gun. Bruce had long served the flying society of Great Britain and the Aerial League, and gives the book to his wife for her years of help in that cause.

Early chapters trace the first air scouts, the growth of the airship, and the types flown by each great power. A full chapter covers the German airship fleet. Later parts cover the coming of the aeroplane and its first use in war in Tripoli and the Balkans. They end with its faults and future in the great war then raging.
71866-war:
War is a poem in blank verse, out at London in seventeen forty-five. A Latin line at the front asks who will lift foul slay and rage from the world. The poem opens with a plea to a blest teacher to spare the weak voice of the bard. That voice is spent, and was at best a childs, it says.

Yet the bard speaks once more, in trust of a high power. War is named man slayer and town waster, fell and hell born. The bard means to curse it, not to sing it, since tune and song ill fit its din. First of the cursed is the first slayer of a brother in the old book. Sin is named the first mover of all war, and the forge of the first sword takes its curse in turn.
7189-a-short-history-of-the-great-war:
A. F. Pollard, professor of English history at the University of London, tells the Great War in one short volume with nineteen maps, first published in 1920. His chapters run from the breach of the peace and the German invasion through Russia's moves and war on and beyond the seas. Then comes the fixing of the Western Front, two winters of war, and the failure of the Allied offensive.

Pollard carries the tale on to the defeat of Russia and the climax of German success. A second German offensive in the west meets the Allied counter-offensive, with the Balkans and politics alongside the fighting. The book aims at a clear, compact account for readers who want the whole war in view without a shelf of volumes. Maps help the reader hold each front in mind.
72085-women-of-the-war:
Barbara McLaren wrote Women of the War, published in nineteen eighteen with a foreword by H H Asquith. The book profiles women who took on hard new work during the First World War. Each chapter gives a short life and a plain account of the job.

Early pages honour two women doctors who ran a military hospital staffed by women. Later pages cover hospital work in Serbia, welfare work in arms plants, and land work with stock. Readers also meet the founder of the Scottish Women's Hospitals and a woman who ran a large filling plant. Canteen work in France rounds out the set.
72195-a-woman-s-wanderings-and-trials-du:
A Woman's Wanderings and Trials during the Anglo-Boer War is the memoir of the wife of General de la Rey, turned into English by Lucy Hotz. It was published in London by Fisher Unwin in 1903. Plates show the general, the waggon, and the children of the wandering life.

Her husband left for the western border on October 4, 1899. She visited him in the great laager and found all going well. That same day came the order to move on Kraaipan with twelve hundred men. She spent the night in camp and went home to wait. Next day came word of the first fight, and of prisoners brought in by train. The frontispiece is named The Wanderers, and the book tells what the war cost a Boer household on the move.
72394-home-made-cider-vinegar:
Home-Made Cider Vinegar, by Walter Sackett, is Bulletin 192 of the Colorado Agricultural Experiment Station. The station at Fort Collins issued it in November 1913. Sackett served the station as its bacteriologist.

The bulletin opens on waste in the fruit-growing country. Thousands of bushels of apples and other fruit rot yearly, Sackett writes. In fat seasons of low prices, growers will not trouble to gather the crop. Any business house, he argues, would call such waste extravagant. The largest profits, captains of industry say, come from using waste products whole. Indifference and ignorance of what second-grade fruit can do blind the grower. He forgets the ninety-three million others who might use what he throws away. The bulletin then teaches the making of vinegar from that wasted fruit.
72554-a-short-introduction-to-english-gr:
A short introduction to English grammar, with critical notes, was printed in London in 1762. Its preface argues that English has been much polished in two hundred years, in verse and prose on all subjects. Yet in grammatical accuracy, the writer says, it has made no advances at all.

Swift had made the same complaint some fifty years before, in a public letter to the Earl of Oxford. The grammarian holds that the charge is true of even polite speakers and approved authors. But the language itself, he insists, is not irregular by nature; of all modern tongues it is perhaps the simplest in form. Rules, rightly drawn, can set the matter straight.
73323-soissons-before-and-during-the-war:
Soissons Before and During the War belongs to the Michelin Illustrated Guides to the Battlefields, issued after the war in Clermont-Ferrand, London, and New Jersey. The hosted pages open with practical help for motorists. Hotels and motor-agents at Soissons are drawn from the Michelin Guide of nineteen nineteen, and a key explains the arbitrary signs: central heating, electric light, bathrooms, modern water closets, and telephone numbers.

Garage signs promise shelter for twenty or thirty cars, petrol, repair shops, inspection pits, and depots of bottled compressed air for tyres. The Croix d'Or hotel stands on the rue Saint-Christophe and the Lion Rouge near the station. A closing note warns that the facts date from the first of March, nineteen nineteen, and may no longer be exact, so tourists should consult the latest guide.
73709-next-year:
Harry Pick, himself a Barr colonist, published this historical account with the Ryerson Press of Toronto in nineteen twenty eight, twenty five years after the adventure it describes. In April nineteen three nearly two thousand English emigrants sailed on the Lake Manitoba for Canada's northwest. Their leader was the Reverend Barr, a Church of England parson Pick calls unscrupulous in his subtitle.

The colonists, lawyers, doctors, clergymen, farmers, clerks, and babies, carried half a million pounds and a ship rated for eight hundred passengers. Pick follows them through Saskatoon, buying transport and machinery, on to Battleford through snowstorms, prairie fires, and alkali flats, and into choosing land and planning for next year. The title is the pioneers' refrain. Pick writes as an insider settling accounts, proud of the colonists who stayed and blunt about the management that misled them.
73887-modern-ships-of-war:
Modern Ships of War pairs two naval men: Sir Edward J Reed, late chief constructor of the British Navy, and Edward Simpson, rear-admiral in the United States Navy. Harper and Brothers issued the illustrated book in 1888, with supplementary chapters and notes by Lieutenant J D Jerrold Kelley. A drawing of the Battle of Trafalgar fronts it.

The preface is an American warning. After many years of neglect, it says, the people have awakened to the need of a modern fleet, having let the Navy sink almost to dissolution. Congress bestirred itself at last, ordering three unarmored cruisers and a despatch-boat.
7411-an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-expositi:
Sheldon Cheney wrote this guide for visitors to San Francisco's great exposition of 1915, the Panama-Pacific fair that celebrated the city rebuilt after the earthquake. He explains the architecture, sculpture, and mural paintings court by court: the Court of the Universe, the Court of the Four Seasons, the Tower of Jewels, and the palaces facing the Marina. The Palace of Machinery and the Festival Hall get their own chapters.

Cheney writes for the less practiced eye, praising and criticizing in terms a lay visitor can use. He admits he claims no special power of artistic judgment, only the wish to help others see new beauties. A final guide for study in the art gallery turns a day's visit into a course. The book now doubles as a souvenir of a vanished fair.
74144-jackie-sees-a-star:
Marion Zimmer Bradley wrote this short story, printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1954. It is told by Jackie's aunt Dorothy, who at first turns away a man who comes asking about the boy. She has had her fill of reporters, mind doctors, and cranks, and she says the fuss is spoiling the child. When she learns the man is from the university, she softens and tells the tale.

Jackie's father died a week after the boy was born, worn out by the Big Bombings of 1964, and his mother works at the Tax Bureau. Jackie keeps a secret of his own: a star he found, one that in time draws even Doctor Milliken into the stir.
74180-stories-of-the-war-of-1812-and-the:
Stories of the War of 1812 was published at Philadelphia in 1854. Leary issued the story book, with many engravings. Mexican War stories share the volume. A preface explains the aim for young readers. The war of 1812, it argues, finished the work of independence. Britain had treated Americans as revolted subjects still. Free trade and sailors' rights were the watchwords. After that war, the flag stood respected by all nations. The Mexican war taught a second lesson, the preface says. A republic with a small standing army raised great ones. Its militia beat a military republic of vast resources. Such wars deserve the attention of the country's youth.

The first story is the surrender of Detroit. Hull held it with twenty five hundred men. Brock, with thirteen hundred, summoned him to yield.
7435-springhaven-a-tale-of-the-great-war:
R. D. Blackmore published Springhaven in 1887, and its great war is not the war of his own century's end but the Napoleonic struggle. In the days when England trusted mainly to the vigor of one man against a world of enemies, the quiet village of Springhaven lay on a coast in great peril. Yet the village, sheltered by a bold point called Haven-head, kept its tranquil ways.

The novel opens when the ship comes home, and follows the village as war presses on its fishermen, smugglers, and families. Blackmore, author of Lorna Doone, writes with the same love of the West Country coast and its people. Springhaven is a tale of a small place holding its character while history storms offshore, with the sea itself as a constant presence.
74494-helmet-and-spear:
Helmet and Spear is a retelling of the wars of the Greeks and Romans by Church, formerly professor of Latin at University College, London, published by Macmillan in New York in 1900. Church had made his name with Stories from Homer. Six books carry the story from Marathon to the fall of Rome, each in short dramatic chapters.

The first book opens with the grounds of the feud between Greeks and barbarians, as Herodotus recorded them. Then come the men of Marathon, the lion king at Thermopylae, and the wooden walls. Later books take up Syracuse and Carthage, Hannibal's avalanche from the Alps, Caesar's conquests, and three deadly blows at the end. Church writes classical history as story, for readers who want the wars vivid and in order.
74812-reminiscences-of-an-army-nurse-dur:
Adelaide Smith, an independent volunteer nurse, wrote her Reminiscences of an Army Nurse During the Civil War, published in New York in 1911. Her portrait carries the dates 1831 to 1911. She dedicates the book to the Boys in Blue and to the women who sent them out, and to the nurses who died in hospital service.

The contents start at home: the Long Island College Hospital in Brooklyn and the post on Bedloe's Island. Then comes the great Manhattan fair of the Sanitary Commission. Smith starts for the front, and the war takes over. She serves at Point of Rocks and at the depot field hospital at City Point in Virginia. Dorothea Dix appears, and a Thanksgiving of 1864 passes under fire at Dutch Gap. Union readers get the woman's war, ward by ward.
75218-secret-of-the-earth-star:
Secret of the Earth Star is a science fiction story by Henry Kuttner. It appeared in Amazing Stories for August 1942. A jewel theft opens the action, in an air conditioned palace room in India. Three Europeans produce a Gladstone bag before a Rajah. Inside a metal case rests the Earth Star itself. The great gem flames on black velvet, lens shaped and alive with shifting colour.

The magazine's own line promises death along the jewel's trail. A weird city under the Sahara waits at the trail's end. The stone is no diamond, though it outshines one. Its secretary calls it carbon, born of a tree fern a million years back. Pressure at unthinkable depths made it harder than diamond. Kuttner's tale mixes jewel crime with lost world adventure.
75281-dorset-dear:
M E Francis, also known as Mrs Francis Blundell, wrote Dorset Dear, idylls of country life, issued by Longmans, Green, and Company in New York, London, and Bombay in nineteen oh five. The tales first ran in Country Life, The Graphic, Longman Magazine, and The Illustrated London News. Francis gave the book to the memory of Lady Smith Marriott, a kind neighbour and true friend. Some seventeen tales fill the volume.

Witch Ann stands first, followed by A Runaway Couple, Postman Chris, and Keeper Guppy. Ann Kerley had lived in great peace for more than seventy three years at the start. Neighbours held her a good plain woman with a kind word for all. Later tales treat a worm that turned, a woodland idyll, and the majesty of the law. A line from William Barnes in Dorset dialect heads the book. Readers get warm tales of Dorset folk and fields.
75678-his-vanished-star:
Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name of Mary N Murfree, wrote this novel, printed by Houghton, Mifflin of Boston and New York in 1894. The copyright stands in Murfree's own name. Kenneth Kenniston owns a great property, a day's journey across, in leagues of mountain wilderness. Yet the land bears only a nominal price, with an abandoned mine in the depths of its gorge.

Kenniston's eye is a speculator's, not a poet's. He appraises the pure mountain air for summer sojourners and plans a great hotel on a level space over the crags. He is an architect by trade, and the world shows him building sites. Science is set to work on his schemes as the tale opens, in Craddock's high, ornate Tennessee manner.
75855-the-smear:
Smear is a Yukon tale by John Beames, set in the Malamute Saloon at Dawson. Lights blaze in the saloon with noisy music, whisky, and gambling for the sourdoughs. Outside it is dark, with the first breath of Yukon winter in the wind. Finn Charley lugs out a heavy poke and pours gold dust into the scales.

Two Mounted Police enter as Finn celebrates his sudden prosperity at the bar. The corporal keen eyes search the company, missing no man in the room. Finn flinches, gulps raw whisky, and straightens, knowing the man is dead. Guilt under a calm police gaze drives this Dawson murder tale.
76109-a-photographic-record-of-the-russo:
A Photographic Record of the Russo Japanese War was edited and arranged by James Hare, a war photographer, and printed by Collier in New York in 1905. Photographs come from Bulla, Dunn, Archibald, Barry, Bartlett, and Ricalton, and Captain Mahan contributes an account of the battle of the Sea of Japan.

The list of illustrations reads as the war in sequence. Portraits of the two emperors, of Russia and of Japan, precede street scenes in both capitals. Japanese troops train at the Tokio barracks, mobilize, and march through cheering streets to the stations. The destruction of the Variag and Korietz at Chemulpo, the night landing of Japanese troops, and the occupation of Seoul follow. Russian scenes answer from the other side: ladies sewing for the Red Cross, and the army on its march to the front.
76219-deductions-from-the-world-war:
Deductions from the World War was written by Baron von Freytag Loringhoven, lieutenant general and deputy chief of the German imperial staff. Putnam published it in New York and London in 1918. An introductory note presents the author as the most distinguished soldier writer of Prussia, the leading living writer on militarism in theory and practice.

Freytag, the note explains, was born in Russia, the son of a Russian diplomatist, and served in the Russian army before joining a Prussian guard regiment at twenty one. On the outbreak of war he represented Germany on the Austro Hungarian general staff, became quartermaster general in the field, and in September 1916 took the deputy chief's post. He received the peace class of the order Pour le Mérite. The book was written for German readers; its chapters on the army in the future and still ready for war drew notice.
76299-a-dictionary-of-men-s-wear:
A Dictionary of Men's Wear is a trade dictionary by William Henry Baker, published at Cleveland in 1908. Baker had written a dictionary of engraving. This one gathers, so far as he could gather them, all the terms used in the men's wear trades.

The scope is wide. Terms cover raw and finished products, the stages and items of production, and selling terms. Trade and popular slang and cant are included, with many other things curious, pertinent, and impertinent. An appendix holds useful tables, the uniforms of old independent military companies, and charts of correct dress and livery. Baker dedicates the book to those most likely to be benefited: some fifteen thousand retail clothiers, as many custom tailors, twelve hundred clothing makers, and twenty-two thousand shoe dealers. A trade's whole language, priced and defined.
76613-nature-s-year:
Nature's Year, subtitled The Seasons of Cape Cod, by John Hay, was published by Doubleday in 1961. Hay follows the narrow peninsula month by month, from a July arrival among the summer crowds through the quiet of winter and back to June. David Grose illustrated the book.

Each month brings essays on birds, tides, gardens, and weather: a walk with an oven bird, the sea in the ground, restless March days, April light, and the binding rain of June. Hay writes as a resident naturalist, watching how people and wild life share the same ground. The book is a gentle classic of Cape Cod nature writing, valued for close observation and for its sense of the year as a single turning whole.
76725-hungarian-grammar:
Hungarian Grammar, by Arthur and Ilona Ginever, was published at London in 1909 by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company. The book belongs to Trubner's Simplified Grammars of the principal Asiatic and European languages, a series whose list runs from Hindustani, Persian, and Arabic to Basque, Malagasy, and modern Greek.

The series list prices its volumes in shillings: Palmer's Hindustani at five shillings, Redhouse's Ottoman Turkish at ten shillings and sixpence, Morfill's Serbian at four shillings and sixpence. The Ginevers' grammar gives the English learner the forms and rules of Hungarian in that plain series style. Their book was printed at the Ballantyne Press in Edinburgh, with the rights of translation and reproduction reserved.
76768-english-grammar:
Lillian Kimball, once head of English at a teacher training school at Oshkosh in Wisconsin, wrote a school grammar printed in 1912. Kimball had earlier written on the build of the English sentence and two books of basic English for younger pupils. Lessons run past fifty in the part of the book shown in the contents.

Early lessons treat telling sentences, subject and verb parts, nouns, verbs, and words that stand for nouns. Asking sentences, describing words, and joining words come in their turn. Later lessons sort sentences as simple, joined, or complex, and treat noun number, sex, case, and the forms of verbs in time.
77049-the-adventures-of-twinkly-eyes-the:
Allen Chaffee wrote The Adventures of Twinkly Eyes, the Little Black Bear, for Milton Bradley in 1919. Peter Daru drew the plates for the book, printed at Springfield, Massachusetts. It is given to Howard Folsom Brock, whose great heart had room for furred and feathered folk. Chapter one gives Twinkly a ducking in an icy lake, bump, slide, and splash. Mother Black Bear comes to the rescue, and a stern lesson follows.

More than forty short chapters trace the cub through the wild year. Mrs Porcupine shows fight, a black snake named Writho appears, and a bee tree tempts him. Twinkly gives first aid, meets Bobby Lynx, and goes to a bunny ball. Chaffee teaches wild ways to children through one small bear's mishaps and growth.
77148-mission-of-fear:
George Harmon Coxe wrote Mission of Fear, a Borzoi book printed in New York. A list of his books at the front runs from Murder with Pictures of 1935 to this tale of 1962. A jacket note sets the case. Sam Adler appeared one afternoon at Marion Hayden's door, trying for the big payoff: blackmail. The next day he was dead, paid off with a knife in the back. For the Haydens the nightmare had just begun.

Now, with Lieutenant Garvey pushing hard, it could mean a murder charge for both of them. Garvey kept the questions coming fast, and they all shrank to one: was Ted Corbin alive? Corbin is Marion Hayden's former husband, and by every sign dead two years in an airplane crash. Doris Lamar knew some of the answers, the note says, but she had her own good reasons for silence.
77177-bear-and-forbear:
Bear and Forbear, by Oliver Optic, is a boys tale in the Lake Shore Series. Lee and Shepard of Boston issued the book, entered in eighteen sixty nine. Optic, whose true name was William Adams, wrote many boys series. The Boat Club, Starry Flag, and Young America Abroad sets are named.

Optic gives the book to a band of Bangor boys and girls. They had sent him a black bear as a token of love and esteem. He did not eat the bear, and its life was too short for lessons. The beast is kept at the Society of Natural History rooms now. Its tale frames a young skipper story on Lake Ucayga waters.
77356-a-lady-s-cruise-in-a-french-man-of:
Gordon Cumming wrote A Lady's Cruise in a French Man-of-War, issued in a new one volume edition at Edinburgh in 1882. She had written At Home in Fiji and From the Hebrides to the Himalayas. A map and illustrations go with the tale.

In 1875 the author sailed to Fiji with the party of Sir Arthur Gordon, its first governor. Two happy years passed among the isles. Then a French warship, lent to the Bishop of Samoa for his rounds, called at Fiji. Its commander and the bishop urged her to join the cruise and sketch the scenes. The best cabin was made ready for her.
77800-old-house-of-fear:
Old House of Fear, by Russell Kirk, was copyrighted by Fleet Publishing Corporation of New York in 1961. Kirk inscribes his Gothic tale to Abigail Fay, in direct descent from The Castle of Otranto. Fifteen chapters carry the story.

Something is wrong on Carnglass, the heap of gray stones beyond the Outer Hebrides. Lady MacAskival, the proprietress, has brought a queer lot of people from England, and strangers who try to land may be fired on. Five MacAskivals from Daldour saw a pillar of flame rise by Askival Harbor on a black night, and heard gunfire. In Michigan, Duncan MacAskival of the MacAskival Iron Works wants to buy the home of his ancestors, and meets stony silence. Then an unsigned, water stained note begs for confidential agents and immediate action. He sends Hugh Logan, his legal counsel, to investigate. Chapter one opens on that night of fog and flame.
77982-the-war-trail-of-big-bear:
The War Trail of Big Bear is an account by William Bleasdell Cameron of the Canadian North-West Rebellion of 1885. Its subtitle states its scope: the part of Big Bear and other Cree chiefs and their followers in that rising, the Frog Lake Massacre, and the events before and after it. It tells as well of two months spent as a prisoner in the camp of the hostiles. The book came out in Boston in 1927.

A portrait of Big Bear, chief of the Plains Crees, stands at its front. The contents open with The Frog Lake Settlement, then The Annuity Payments at Fort Pitt. When Poundmaker Defied— breaks the list in the part shown. A note states that italics are marked by underscores and small capitals by uppercase. The work is a first-hand tale of the last armed rising in the Canadian west.
7803-the-story-of-sugar:
Sara Ware Bassett's The Story of Sugar, pictured by C. P. Gray, follows boys at Colversham through sugaring off, a refinery visit, and a family tangle. Bobbie is called from algebra to play, Van springs a surprise, mutinies, bears punishment, and performs a great deed, while Mr. Carlton wins a wager.

Like Bassett's stories of lumber, wool, leather, and glass, the book teaches an industry through adventure, with thanks to the American Sugar Refining Company and Senator Truman G. Palmer. Chapters end with a new year dawning, after lessons in work, fairness, and pluck.
78106-things-near-far:
Arthur Machen wrote a book of memories printed at London in 1923. Machen had written The Terror, The Bowmen, The Great Return, and The Hill of Dreams. The road from Newport to Caerleon on Usk winds, as it comes near to the old Roman, fabulous city, with the winding of the tawny river, he begins.

The new road was made early in the nineteenth century when stage coaching came to perfection, he says. The old road passed over the Roman bridge, blown down the river by a great storm in the seventeen nineties, and climbed the break neck hill to Christchurch. Saint Julian's Wood rose east of the road, a vast wood of some fame as a ghostly place in 1870. It was cut down long ago by an owner who thought timber better than ghosts. Welsh boyhood, London years, and wonders near and far fill Machen's tale.
7826-l-p-m-the-end-of-the-great-war:
J. Stewart Barney's L. P. M., The End of the Great War, published in 1915, imagines one man with a secret that could stop the fighting. Chapters run from the man and the hour, a one-man secret, and crossing with royalty through rebuffs, echoes from the Wilhelmstrasse, and a rusty cannon ball.

Diplomacy wins, a spy-driven taxi follows, Buckingham Palace opens, the hero meets the king, and a deionizer shows force. Later come a royal tea table, soldiers all around, a dinner at the Britz, and a voice in the telephone. It is a bold wartime fantasy of invention ending war.
78467-the-lovable-liar:
The Lovable Liar, a western story by Tuttle, opens in the two house town of Tecoma. The town holds a depot, a saloon, and a restaurant. The saloon and restaurant share one building between them. Trains stop there on a flag signal, at five thousand feet of elevation.

A wagon road of sorts runs from Tecoma down to the Moolock cattle country. The same road winds back to the mines of the Bearpaw district. That road serves as the main street of the town. A long hitch rack stands in front of the saloon. Horses there stand at a steep angle on the slope. From that spare scene the tale of its lovable liar unfolds. Tuttle was a steady hand at the western yarn, and place comes first here.
78520-the-rise-of-a-star:
Edith Ayrton Zangwill wrote The Rise of a Star, a novel of the stage. John Murray issued the book in London in nineteen hundred eighteen. Frances West, a touring actress, takes her first true hit as the tale opens. She plays Biddy, an old Irish orange woman, in the hit piece.

Nine calls bring the cast back in a frenzy of joy. West wires her daughter Imogen in New York at once. Twenty five years of third rate tours led to this night. She had begun at barely fourteen on one night stands. Imogen, now at a New York school, is her one fixed star. Manager Hobson wants the piece held in Chicago a month. Parks, her road chief, warns of hard one night towns instead.
78551-magpie-s-night-bear:
W C Tuttle's Magpie's Night-Bear is told by a prospector who bunked with Magpie Peters in a cabin on Plenty Stone Creek in western Montana. The pair dug holes from Nome to Mexico and as far east as Butte, and the tale turns on their prize possession, a phonograph that sourdoughs came for miles to hear.

Magpie, the narrator says, had read books on hypnotism and tried it on a bob-cat, and music is said to soothe savage beasts. Between them the partners made do with a bent iron bed and a rocking chair losing its stuffing. A baby's high chair stood there too, left behind by some high-toned family that summered in the hills.
79026-the-enterprising-burglar:
The Enterprising Burglar is a comic novel by Hearnden Balfour. Balfour also wrote A Gentleman from Texas. The book was printed at Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in 1928. It is inscribed to all the shareholders in New Bells, Unlimited.

The chapter titles run in a playful line: A Policeman's Lot, Vive le Sport, Fog, and The Meeting of the Fraternity. Then come Twinkling William, An Ultimatum, and The Feminine Element. A late chapter is Twinkling William's Diary, and another is Bobby's Theory. Sir Toby is amused. The titles promise a light tale of crime as sport, where burglary is a trade with its own club and its own code. Balfour writes in the comic line of the English club story, with the police and the burglars on oddly friendly terms.
79095-hagar:
James Arthur Macknight wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1889 and dedicated to the friend who encouraged him in a dark hour. It opens in Ohio in the autumn of 1862, with the Civil War stripping the countryside of its young men.

Ohio had sent her sons freely and suffered at Shiloh and Donelson, yet battle itself stayed far away. Around Cleveland the crops stood unharvested in places, while the city buzzed with speculation, politics, and war work. The first chapter rides out along a turnpiked lane past corn shocks and golden wheat on a bright Sunday. Readers get a home-front novel of the war's second year.
79204-tar:
Tar is a tale of a midwest childhood by Sherwood Anderson. Parts of the book first ran as short bits in home magazines. A gift page sends the work to Elizabeth Anderson by name. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty six.

Poor folk have their young with no great joy, the first page owns in flat terms. A new boy is no great cost: cast off garb and work will serve in time. Work is mans plain fate, the text holds, set from the first tale of man. A school sheet print of Cain and his slain kin frames that hard creed. Small town want and boy dreams fill the famed prose tale.
79271-brown-eyes-and-brown-bear:
Brown Eyes and Brown Bear is an Alaska tale by Frank Richardson Pierce. It first appeared in North-West Stories magazine in 1925, and this edition keeps the story's light punctuation. A line at the front warns that Alaska has bear and bear, but brown ones do not come tame. The tale opens in an argument between partners.

Sam tells Dave Sloan he would knock his block off for two cents. Dave hands him a nickel and tells him to keep the change. Sam's real grievance is a lie Dave told a tourist girl. Dave claimed to be the best bear shot in Alaska, and to have killed a bear the colour of a girl's eyes. Bill Halsey did that, Sam says. Dave answers that tourists expect to be lied to.
793-aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot wrote this account of flying machines in war, at a time when their use was still new and much debated. He traces the dirigible balloon and the aeroplane from early trials to their first service, weighing what each could do for scouting, bombing, and naval work. Theories, he notes, outran proof for years.

Talbot gathers reports from the first air war, with details on types, crews, and raids. His prose is clear and factual, aimed at readers who want to grasp a fast-changing art. The book is a valuable record of how war in the air looked while it was still being invented, before later histories tidied the story.
8101-bertram-cope-s-year:
Henry Blake Fuller followed a year in the life of Bertram Cope, a young man at a college tea. Through Sunday calls, dinners, excursions, a house party, sailing, cross-purposes, and a distressful Christmas. The chapter headings trace Cope under scrutiny, considered and considered further, entertained by several ladies, committed, rescued, and in danger anew. The setting is university and small-town society, where reputation is watched closely.

Fuller's novel is a comedy of manners with a serious undercurrent, about a young instructor navigating admirers, patrons, and his own uncertain desires. Published in an era that could not name its subject plainly, it has since been recognised as an early American novel of same-sex affection. It remains a subtle, witty portrait of social life and private feeling.
8222-early-letters-of-george-wm-curtis-t:
George Willis Cooke edited these early letters of George William Curtis to John S. Dwight, covering Brook Farm and Concord. Curtis was born in Providence on February 24, 1824, schooled at Jamaica Plain and Providence, and inseparable from his brother Burrill. About 1835 he came under Ralph Waldo Emerson's influence, hearing him in Providence, and the letters that follow show a young man entering the Transcendentalist circle at Brook Farm and Concord.

The letters are fresh, idealistic, and observant, recording communal experiments, conversations, and the hopes of youth. They give a ground-level view of Brook Farm from inside, by a participant who later became a famous editor and reformer. For students of American Transcendentalism, the volume is a delightful primary source.
8385-the-short-line-war:
Samuel Merwin's novel turns on a railroad war, with Jim Weeks at its center and a struggle for possession of a short line. Chapters move through Tillman City politics, judges Black and Grey, and a matter of possession. Later chapters bring somebody losing the books, a politician, Katherine, train number 14, and a capture at Brushingham. Rival interests fight for control of the line throughout.

Merwin, writing in the age of railroad trusts, uses the short line as a picture of American business and politics: courts, promoters, and townsfolk all pulled into the fight. The novel reads as both adventure and commentary on how railroads shaped towns. Readers of business fiction will find a brisk, plot-driven tale from the railroad era.
8440-men-in-war:
Andreas Latzko wrote Men in War from the Austro-Hungarian side of the First World War. Its contents tell the arc: Off to War, Baptism of Fire, The Victor, My Comrade, A Hero's Death, and Home Again. The opening story sets a war hospital garden in late autumn of the war's second year, where soldiers wait between battles.

Latzko, himself an officer wounded in the war, writes against glorification, showing fear, friendship, and the gap between home and front. Dedicated to friend and foe, the book was banned in some countries for its pacifist force. Readers get short, intense stories that rank among the war's most humane fiction, unsparing and compassionate at once.
8576-by-sheer-pluck-a-tale-of-the-ashant:
G. A. Henty tells this boys' adventure through Frank Hargate, a schoolboy first seen fishing and watching a chaffinch nest threatened by a snake. School rivalries, house matches, and country walks fill the opening, before Frank's courage and quick thinking carry him toward West Africa and the Ashanti War. Henty builds his hero the usual way: decent, observant, and steady when danger arrives.

The war chapters put Frank among soldiers, marches, and fighting in unfamiliar country, where pluck, in Henty's phrase, matters more than polish. The book belongs to the late Victorian school of empire adventure, written to stir and instruct young readers at once. Modern readers will notice its period attitudes, but its pace, clear action, and school-to-battlefield arc explain why Henty stayed popular with boys for decades.
92-tarzan-and-the-jewels-of-opar:
Gold from the lost city of Opar draws Tarzan back to its vaults, and trouble follows. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar opens with Belgian and Arab rivals on the road to the city. The priestess La still guards the altar of the Flaming God.

Tarzan steals jewels, loses his reason, and leads the apes again as a beast. Werper the Belgian steals the treasure in turn, and Jane Clayton faces capture and peril. The novel weaves two thefts and a rescue into one chase. Opar's gold keeps pulling Tarzan between man and ape.
9542-graded-poetry-seventh-year:
Katherine D. Blake and Georgia Alexander edited Graded Poetry: Seventh Year in 1906, a school reader of verse for young pupils. The book splits the year in halves, moving from Shakespeare and Milton through Burns, Wordsworth, Scott, and Byron. Poems include The Star-Spangled Banner, Lochinvar, John Gilpin, and The Solitary Reaper. Each piece was picked to suit a child's ear and mind.

First-half poems stress good name, noble nature, and brave deeds, while later poems widen to nature, war, and home. Notes and order guide a teacher through the school year. A reader gets a fine old school anthology, and a view of what American children once learned by heart.
9617-echoes-of-the-war:
J. M. Barrie, famed for Peter Pan, wrote Echoes of the War in 1918, four short plays of wartime London. The Old Lady Shows Her Medals opens, as three charwomen and a hostess talk war over tea. The New Word, Barbara's Wedding, and A Well-Remembered Voice complete the set. Barrie's people are plain folk, and his war is felt at home, not on the front.

Medals, weddings, and remembered voices carry grief, pride, and hope in small rooms. Barrie's humor stays gentle, even as loss shadows each play. A reader gets a tender, humane view of war's home front, from a master of sentiment who knew how to make small scenes ache.
9868-the-united-states-since-the-civil-w:
Charles Ramsdell Lingley, Dartmouth history professor, wrote The United States Since the Civil War in 1920, a survey from Reconstruction to the World War. Chapters follow Grant's time, the new era's economic roots, and the politics of the early eighties. The overturn of 1884, transportation, industry, and laissez faire follow, with diplomacy, wage earners, and money problems.

Later chapters treat 1896, war with Spain, imperialism, Roosevelt, and Wilson, closing with America and the World War. Maps and an index aid study. A reader gets a clear, compact national history, fit for students of modern America.
9944-the-conquest-of-fear:
Basil King's book, with a new introduction by Henry C. Link, argues that fear, not circumstance, rules most unhappy lives. King, writing from his own experience, traces fear from a life-principle through ideas about God, the mind of today, and the world as it is.

Later chapters name the false god of fear, face the fear of death, and point toward abundance of life. The tone is personal and earnest, closer to a friend's counsel than a lecture. Readers looking for early twentieth-century spiritual self-help will find a sincere, plainspoken attempt to answer worry with faith.
a-school-history-of-the-great-war: Albert Edward McKinley, with Charles Coulomb and Armand Gerson, writes this school history of the Great War, copyrighted in 1918. The chapters move from Europe before the war through German militarism, the Hague conferences, alliances, and the Balkan states into the war years from 1914 to 1918. A final section treats the United States in the war, giving pupils a complete arc from causes to American entry.
a-short-history-of-the-great-war:
A. F. Pollard, professor of English history in the University of London, published A Short History of the Great War in 1920, as the title page records. In twenty chapters with nineteen maps he tells the whole First World War in one volume, from the breach of the peace to the foundations of the peace settlement.

The narrative follows the German invasion, the making of the Western Front, the failure of offensives, and the defeat of Russia. Sea war, the Balkans, and political reactions at home get their own chapters before the tide turns in 1918. Pollard writes as a professional historian close to the events, and the book served a generation that wanted the war explained whole.
a-short-view-of-the-frauds-and-abuses-co: Christopher Merret, doctor in physic and fellow of the College of Physicians and the Royal Society, exposes the frauds and abuses of apothecaries toward patients and physicians alike. Licensed for print in November 1669, the tract argues that the only remedy is for physicians to make their own medicines. Its Latin epigraph mocks the crowd who call themselves doctors: the uneducated, the priest, the nurse, the barber, the apothecary, and the old woman.
aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot explains, in plain language, how aircraft were being used in the great war then raging in Europe. His preface says the book draws on official reports and men who took part, from British, French, Russian, and German sources. Captive balloons, airships, and aeroplanes all get full treatment.

Chapters cover Germany's airship fleet, scouting from the skies, guiding artillery fire, dropping bombs, armored planes, fights in the air, and guns built to shoot aircraft down. Later chapters take up wireless, naval use, and fleets of the air. The book shows how fast flight changed war while the change was still new.
an-apologie-for-the-royal-party-1659-and: John Evelyn defends the royal party in his Apologie of 1659 and praises Charles the Second in a panegyric of 1661. The two pieces show a royalist writer arguing for monarchy through civil war and Restoration. Together they record how loyalist hopes turned, within two years, from plea to celebration. The pairing lets readers watch a political cause move from defence to triumph.
an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-exposition-ex:
Sheldon Cheney wrote An Art-Lover's Guide to the Exposition as a handbook to the art of the San Francisco exposition, printed at Berkeley in 1915 as its title page shows. He promises two things: to explain the symbolism of the architecture, sculpture, and mural painting, and to point out the special qualities that give each work its appeal.

Chapters walk the grounds court by court — Abundance, the Universe, the Four Seasons, Palms and Flowers. Then take up the Tower of Jewels, the machine and fine arts palaces, and the outdoor sculpture. A closing section guides study inside the fine arts galleries themselves. For a visitor then, or a reader now, it preserves how the fair's art was meant to be read.
an-unpardonable-liar: Gilbert Parker writes An Unpardonable Liar, a novel that opens with an echo and moves to a meeting that sets its drama in motion. The story turns on a lie that cannot be taken back, and on the honour, love, and pride entangled with it. Parker's Canadian and English scenes give the tale its colour, while character keeps the plot taut.
ballads-of-peace-in-war:
Michael Earls gathered his verse in Ballads of Peace in War, a book of poems shaped by the First World War and by older American wars. Earls, a Jesuit priest and teacher, writes in ballad stanzas meant to be read aloud. His first poem watches a woman keeping vigil for a sailor at sea. Love and prayer, in his telling, guard the absent man.

Other ballads retell brave deeds and narrow escapes. One poem follows a rider sent to fetch the countersign before a Civil War regiment can advance toward Manassas. Soldiers, mothers, and sweethearts share the pages. Earls favors clear stories, strong rhythm, and Catholic faith over modern experiment. Readers find wartime verse that seeks consolation and courage rather than bitterness about the fighting.
battle-pieces-and-aspects-of-the-war:
Herman Melville published this book of Civil War poems in 1866, dedicating it to the memory of the three hundred thousand who fell devotedly under the flag of their fathers. Most pieces, he says, sprang from an impulse given by the fall of Richmond. They were written without a collective plan, then fell into order when reviewed together, battle answering battle across the war's whole geography.

Portraits, battle lyrics, and aspects follow: Donelson, Shiloh, Malvern Hill, and the Monitor share the volume with meditations on the slain at Gettysburg. One visionary piece sees a pastoral field convulse into a goblin-mountain of marl and slag, then sink, leaving the fear that solidity is only a crust over fire. Melville the whaler turned poet laureate of a divided house, writing grief before the nation had words for it.
beechenbrook-a-rhyme-of-the-war:
Margaret Junkin Preston published this long war poem at Baltimore in 1866, with Kelly and Piet. She dedicates the rhyme to every Southern woman widowed by the war. First printed while the struggle ran, it is reissued as a faint memorial of sufferings of which there can be no forgetfulness. Beechenbrook Cottage, her Virginia home, gives the poem its name and its sorrow.

May sunshine opens over a house of grief: birdsong and tender blue sky against the news the cottage waits for. Later stanzas exhort the soldiers of the Cross to bear toil, reproach, and loss, lest the despot sin wrest away the rights Christ died to win. A wife apostrophises her Douglass, recalling when love seemed a perfect sufficiency. Preston writes the Confederate home front in verse: waiting, praying, and burying, in the war's own idiom.
before-the-war:
Viscount Haldane wrote this memoir of the years before the Great War, defending his record as War Secretary and his missions to Berlin. Haldane, a German-reading statesman, had worked for an understanding with the Kaiser and stood accused of failure when war came. His chapters reconstruct cabinets, armies, and conversations from inside the machine.

The July crisis gets the closest reading. The ex-Chancellor Bethmann-Hollweg, Haldane reports, had learned the tenor of Austria's documents early, though the ultimatum to Serbia was not seen until late July. Berlin judged it no part of Germany's duty to advise her ally on the Sarajevo murder. Yet every effort was to localise the quarrel. Haldane writes a lawyer's brief for himself and for pre-war diplomacy, in the first person, with the telegrams still warm.
bertram-cope-s-year:
Henry Blake Fuller's novel follows a young instructor through one year in a university town, in thirty-odd short chapters that read like a log of sieges. Cope at a college tea, Cope considered, Cope under scrutiny, Cope at his house party: the headings chart a handsome, obtuse young man being appraised by every hostess in town. Widows, students, and faculty wives compete for him while Cope stays courteously blank.

A sailing accident gives the sampled scene: a capsized sloop righted by the station boat, no damage done, and Cope relieved to learn no charge awaits him. The station rigs him a dry outfit from here and there and telephones Mrs. Phillips for fresh clothes. Later headings promise evasions, snares escaped, and freedom regained. Fuller writes the campus comedy dry and sad: a man everyone wants, who wants his rooms, his friend, and his quiet.
bleek-comparative-grammar:
Wilhelm Bleek published his Comparative Grammar of South African Languages in 1862. The German scholar worked in Cape Town among speakers of many tongues. His book founded the true study of the Bantu language family.

Bleek showed that the Bantu tongues form one great linked family. He worked out their sound laws as Grimm had for Europe's tongues. Noun classes and shared roots lock his case into firm order. The feat ranks among the age's great wins in language science. Scholars still cite his Cape Town work as the field's true start point. Bleek gave African tongues the same respect long given to Europe's.
britannica-1911-aasen-ivar:
Ivar Aasen receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by Edmund Gosse. Aasen, a Norwegian student of language, was born a peasant's son in Söndmöre in 1813 and raised to farm work. Reading filled his spare hours, and at eighteen he kept a parish school.

Latin picked up in a writer's household opened the path to many tongues. Folk songs of his district came first in print, in 1843. His Grammar of the Norwegian Dialects in 1848 and Dictionary in 1850 built, from scattered peasant speech, one common folk tongue for Norway. Verse and a play, The Heir, showed the new language at work. Gosse calls him the one man who made a language his country took for school, sermon, and song.
britannica-1911-abana-and-pharpar:
Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, receive a joint entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Naaman's scorn in the Second Book of Kings made the pair famous. Abana, also Amanah and Chrysorrhoas of old, is now the Barada; Pharpar is likely the A'waj, or the Taura if the city alone counts.

Both streams run west to east across the Damascus plain and die in marshes at the desert edge. Their canals fan out from a gorge below the mountains, one keeping a trace of Abana in the name Nahr Banias. John M'Gregor, of Rob Roy fame, praised the canal works as among the most complete and extensive in the world. The plain owes its fertility to these two modest rivers.
britannica-1911-abgar:
Abgar receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abgar names a line of twenty-nine kings or toparchs of Osrhoene, with their capital at Edessa near the Christian era's turn. One king, likely Abgar the Fifth, called the Black, anchors a famous legend.

Leprosy, in the tale, drove him to write to Jesus for healing, offering asylum at Edessa. Jesus declined in a letter yet promised a disciple after his ascension. Eusebius prints both letters from the Edessa archives, and a portrait joins later forms of the story. Augustine and Jerome deny Christ wrote at all, and Pope Gelasius ruled the letters false about 495. Lipsius found time errors that sink the tale. A wish to trace Edessa's faith to apostolic days likely bred it.
britannica-1911-abiathar: Abiathar is the subject of a short Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names the son of Ahimelech, priest at Nob, sole priest to escape Saul's massacre there. He fled to David at Keilah carrying the ephod, and served David well in Absalom's revolt. Under Solomon he first shares the priesthood with Zadok. Then he backs Adonijah's claim, and Solomon deposes him, banishing him to Anathoth.
britannica-1911-adabazar:
Adabazar is a commercial town in Asia Minor. It stands on the old military road east from Constantinople. A branch line joins it to the Anatolian railway. About eighteen thousand people lived there. Moslems formed the larger half of the population. Christians numbered about eight thousand inhabitants. Armenians founded part of the town's growth. The town was founded in 1540. An Armenian colony enlarged it greatly in 1608.

Trade figures dominate the short entry. Silk and linen industries employ local workers. Exports run six times the value of imports. Tobacco heads the goods sent to Constantinople. Walnut-wood, cocoons, and vegetables follow behind. That imbalance marks a producing town. It sells far more than it buys abroad.
britannica-1911-adrar:
Adrar is a Berber word for uplands and names more than one district of the Sahara. A 1911 Britannica entry sorts out the several places that share the name. One Adrar forms the south part of the Rio de Oro protectorate. Another is a plateau north east of Timbuktu and a base for Tuareg groups.

The Adrar most often meant lies in the west Sahara, north of the Senegal river. It is mostly barren land, yet it holds oases with about ten thousand people in all. Atar, Shingeti, Wadan, and Ujeft are its chief centres of trade and life. Caravans from Shingeti carry gold dust, feathers, and dates to the coast.
britannica-1911-afium-kara-hissar:
Afium-Kara-Hissar is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a city in Asiatic Turkey. Its short name means opium, and the full name is Kara-hissar Sahib. The count given is 18,000 folk, most of them Moslems. A steep rock with a ruined castle rises above the town.

The city sat on the caravan road from Smyrna toward Armenia and Georgia. That spot made it a place of wide trade, with well stocked bazaars. Opium grown near the town was its chief good for sale. Black felts, carpets, arms, and saddlery were also made there. Rail lines linked it to Smyrna, Konia, Angora, and the capital.
britannica-1911-aguilar:
Aguilar de la Frontera took its second name from a border: the southern Spanish town stood in medieval times at the edge of Moorish lands. The castle of Anzur, by 1911 a ruin, once guarded that line. The town lies in Cordova province near the small river Cabra, on the rail line between Cordova and Malaga, and it counted 13,236 people in 1900.

Wide squares and new houses leave scant trace of Moorish rule. Two goods made Aguilar's fame across Spain: its olives and its white wine, much like sherry, though the wine sells as Montilla, after a town nearby. Salt springs bubble close at hand. South of town sit two small lakes, Zonar and Rincon, both thick with fish.
britannica-1911-alamos-de-barrientos-bal:
Baltasar Alamos de Barrientos was a Spanish scholar who lived from fifteen fifty-five to sixteen forty. He was born at Medina del Campo. His close tie to Antonio Perez led to his arrest in fifteen ninety and near thirteen years in prison. The entry is a brief life sketch from the nineteen eleven reference work.

The sketch names his one signed book, a work on Tacitus with short wise sayings, printed in Madrid in sixteen fourteen. He may also have writ the discourse on rule that bears the name of Perez. With help from great lords he later rose to high office.
britannica-1911-albumazar:
Albumazar, more properly Abu-Maaschar, an Arab astronomer of 805 to 885, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Balkh, flourished at Baghdad, and died at Wasid in Central Asia. His career belongs to the great age of Arabic astronomy, when Baghdad's scholars preserved and extended Greek learning about the heavens.

Three principal works are named: De Magnis Conjunctionibus, on great conjunctions of the planets, an introduction to astronomy, and Flores Astrologici, flowers of astrology. In the first he argued a striking doctrine of the world's span. The world, he held, was created when the seven planets stood together in the first degree of Aries. It will end when they conjoin again in the last degree of Pisces. The entry closes with references to the standard bibliographies of astronomy for readers tracing his books.
britannica-1911-alkmaar:
Alkmaar is a town in the province of North Holland, in the kingdom of Holland, lying north-west of Amsterdam on the North Holland canal. Its population in 1900 was 18,373. The entry pictures a typical North Holland town of tree-lined canals and brightly coloured seventeenth-century houses, with gardens and walks where the old city walls once stood.

Landmarks include the Groote Kerk, built between 1470 and 1498, the town hall of 1507, and the picturesque weigh-house of 1582. Alkmaar's real importance comes from trade: it centres the butter and cheese business of its region and markets horses, cattle, and grain. Its history holds a successful seven-week resistance to a Spanish siege in 1573 and the convention of 1799 that ended a Russo-British campaign in Holland.
britannica-1911-almacantar: Almacantar is an astronomical term, taken from an Arabic word for a sun-dial, for a small circle of the sky parallel to the horizon. Two stars lying in the same almacantar have the same altitude, the same height above the horizon. The word was also given, in 1880, to an instrument invented by S. C. Chandler for finding the latitude or correcting a timepiece. The entry stresses the instrument's great value, which came from its freedom from instrumental errors that troubled other observing tools.
britannica-1911-anjar:
Anjar is a fortified town of India. It is capital of a district of the same name. That district lies in the native state of Cutch. Cutch belongs to the Bombay presidency. The country around is dry and sandy. Wells alone supply its irrigation water. The town stands ten miles from the Gulf of Cutch. Its population in 1901 was 18,014.

An earthquake struck Anjar severely in 1819. It destroyed many houses there. Several lives were lost. Political transfers fill the rest of the entry. Britain received town and district in 1816. The Cutch government regained them in 1822. An annual money payment was the price. That obligation pressed heavily on the state. Britain wholly remitted it in 1832. The remission covered arrears as well.
britannica-1911-aquila-caspar:
Caspar Aquila, a German reformer who lived from 1488 to 1560, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Augsburg, he studied there and in Italy, Bern, Leipzig, and Wittenberg. He met Erasmus in Rome during his youth. He entered the ministry in 1514 and served for a time as an army chaplain.

Aquila spoke openly for the teaching of Luther and paid for it. He was jailed for half a year and first sentenced to death. That sentence was changed to exile through help from a royal patron. Back in Wittenberg he taught Hebrew and helped Luther with the Old Testament. He later led the church at Saalfeld for many years. His fierce stand against the Augsburg Interim forced him to flee for a time. Sermons and tracts by him are noted.
britannica-1911-avatar:
Avatar, from a Sanskrit word meaning descent, is used in Hindu belief for a god coming down to earth in bodily form for some purpose. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives the idea in English usage as the incarnation of a deity visiting the earth.

Best known are the ten avatars of Vishnu. The list runs through a fish, a tortoise, a hog, and a half-man, half-lion form, then a dwarf and two appearances as Rama. Krishna and Buddha follow as the eighth and ninth. The tenth, Kalki, had yet to come in the belief reported here: a white-winged horse who will destroy the earth.
britannica-1911-avenzoar:
Avenzoar, also called Abumeron, was an Arabian physician of Seville who flourished at the start of the 12th century. His family had been famed as physicians for generations, and his son was later held even more eminent. Averroes, his contemporary, is said to have heard his lectures and learned physic from him.

A follower of Galen and the rational school, Avenzoar attacked quackery and the superstitious cures of astrologers. He described inflammation and abscess of the chest wall lining from his own case, telling it apart from pleurisy and other chest ills. For a blocked or palsied gullet he set out feeding by a silver tube and by nutritive enemata, that is, food given through the bowel. His book on preparing medicines and diet reached Latin through a Hebrew version.
britannica-1911-avocado-pear:
Avocado Pear is the fruit of the tree Persea gratissima, which grows in the West Indies and elsewhere. Its flesh is soft and buttery in texture and highly esteemed as food. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry is brief, centered on the fruit, its tree, and the puzzle of its name.

Avocado, Spanish for advocate, is a sound-substitute for the Aztec word ahuacatl, the name the fruit carried before Spanish speakers reshaped it. A further corruption gave alligator-pear, a name still known in English. Variants listed include avocato, avigato, and abbogada. So one short entry joins botany, taste, and word history: a prized buttery fruit whose names record its path from Aztec speech into Spanish and English.
britannica-1911-baronius-caesar:
Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was an Italian cardinal and church historian, born at Sora and educated at Veroli and Naples. At Rome he joined the Oratory in 1557 under St Philip Neri and succeeded him as its superior in 1593. Clement VIII, whose confessor he was, made him cardinal in 1596 and librarian of the Vatican.

Twice Baronius came near to election as pope, and twice Spain blocked him over his work on the monarchy of Sicily, which backed papal claims against Madrid. His fame rests on the Annales Ecclesiastici, twelve folios printed in 1588–1607 as an answer to the Protestant Magdeburg Centuries. The 1911 Britannica entry praises the work, for all its errors in Greek history, as an honest attempt at history, in strict year order, with a sincere love of truth.
britannica-1911-bastar:
Bastar was a feudatory state of British India, in the Chattisgarh division of the Central Provinces, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covered 13,062 square miles and held 306,501 people in 1901, a slight decrease on the decade before. The east is a flat plateau 1800 to 2000 feet up. The centre and north-west are very mountainous, and the south mixes hills and plains, crossed by the Indravati, Sabari, and Tal.

Farming in the jungle shapes the human picture. Plateau streams run slowly through dense sál forests, and the soil of light clay mixed with sand suits rice and wet crops. The Marias, an aboriginal people of Gond origin, grow millet-like kosra by shifting tillage: clearing a patch, cropping it for two or three years, then moving on. They use no plough and keep no cattle, working only with a long-handled iron hoe.
britannica-1911-bazaar:
Bazaar, from the Persian bazar, means a standing market, a street of shops, or stalls grouped under one roof. The word spread west into Arabic and Turkish and then into European tongues. Eastward it reached India, where it is now in general use for markets.

In southern India and Ceylon a bazaar can mean a single shop or stall. The Genoese writer Pegolotti used “bazarra” for a market-place as early as about 1340, and Malay peoples took the word in as pazar. English later stretched it further, to any mixed sale of goods, whether for charity or for trade.
britannica-1911-behar:
Behar, a town of British India, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the Patna district of Bengal, on the right bank of the river Panchana, and lends its name to an old province. Its people numbered 45,063 in 1901. Some making of silk and muslin went on, but trade had left it for Patna and other places better placed on the Ganges and the rail line.

The article says the old province stretched wide across the Ganges valley, from the border of Nepal to the hills of Chota Nagpur. It covered more than 44,000 square miles and held more than twenty-four million people. That made it the most thickly peopled tract in India, and so always at risk of famine. Rail lines now guarded it well. The tongue there is a form of Hindi, not Bengali.
britannica-1911-belshazzar:
Belshazzar, placed in the sixth century B.C., was long known only from the book of Daniel. There he appears as son of Nebuchadrezzar and last king of Babylon. Yet Greek lists of Babylon’s kings omit him, and scholars guessed he might be Evil-Merodach, Nabonidos or Neriglissor.

Cuneiform writing settled the puzzle. In 1854 Rawlinson found the name Bel-sarra-uzur, “O Bel, defend the king,” in a text of Nabonidos from Ur, calling Belshazzar his first-born son. Contracts likewise call him simply “the son of the king.” So he was never king himself, nor Nebuchadrezzar’s son; Daniel’s feast and the fall of Babylon belong to legend built on his name.
britannica-1911-bentley-richard-scholar:
Richard Bentley (1662–1742) was an English scholar and critic born at Oulton near Wakefield in Yorkshire. His royalist grandfather’s losses left the family poor, and his mother, a stonemason’s daughter, gave him his first Latin. Wakefield grammar school and St John’s College, Cambridge, followed, then a headmastership at Spalding before he was twenty-one.

As tutor in Dean Stillingfleet’s house, Bentley gained the best private library in England and six years of deep study. His Dissertation on the Epistles of Phalaris, proving those letters false, made his scholarly fame. In 1700 he became master of Trinity College, a post the entry calls both his reward and his scourge. Posterity ranks him with the great heroes of classical learning.
britannica-1911-berar:
Berar, also called the Hyderabad Assigned Districts, was a province of India long run by the British for the nizam of Hyderabad. Since October 1903 it has been governed with the Central Provinces. Its name may be a worn form of Vidarbha, a Deccan kingdom of Mahabharata times to which Berar likely belonged.

Berar’s history follows the Deccan’s: Andhra kings, Chalukyas, then the Yadavas of Deogiri until Muslim invasions ended their rule.
