The Bahmani kings made it one of their four provinces in 1348, then split it between Gawil and Mahur. Wellesley’s wins at Assaye and Argaon in 1803 reshaped its fate, and under British control its cotton trade boomed and the province grew rich and settled.
britannica-1911-bernhard-of-saxe-weimar:
Bernhard, Duke of Saxe-Weimar (1604–1639), was a leading Protestant general in the Thirty Years' War. He was the eleventh son of Duke John of Saxe-Weimar. He studied at Jena, then took the field in 1622. He served under Mansfeld at Wiesloch and under Baden at Wimpfen. Defeats did not drive him from the war. He later fought for the king of Denmark and in Holland.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows his rise under Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. At Lützen, when Gustavus fell, Bernhard took command at once. He later won ground in Alsace and hoped to make Breisach his capital. His health broke before the plan matured. He died in July 1639, and Breisach passed to France.
britannica-1911-biggar:
Biggar is a police burgh in Lanarkshire, Scotland, with 1,366 people in 1901. It lies on Biggar Water, near the Clyde, in upland country. Carstairs Junction stands about ten miles north-west of the town. The bracing, picturesque setting made Biggar a health and holiday resort. Dr John Brown, author of Rab and his Friends, was born there. His father was the secession minister of the town.

Biggar became a burgh of barony in 1451 and a police burgh in 1863. St Mary's church was founded in 1545 by Lord Fleming. His seat, Boghall Castle, is now a ruin nearby. The 1911 Britannica entry ties the town to William Wallace lore. A rock called Wallace's Chair crowns Quothquan Law west of the town. At Lamington nearby, Wallace avenged the killing of Marion Bradfute, sheriff Heselrig's victim, the entry recounts.
britannica-1911-bijawar:
Bijawar is a native state of central India, in the Bundelkhand agency. Its area is 973 square miles, and its 1901 population was 110,500. Revenue came to about £10,000 a year. Forests cover nearly half the state's ground. The land is believed rich in minerals, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Poor transport has held back any working of those resources. The chief town, also called Bijawar, held 5,220 people in 1901.

Bijai Singh, a Gond chief of Garha Mandla, founded the town in the 17th century. Chhatarsal, the Bundela founder of Panna, conquered the state in the 18th century. His descendants still held it when the article was written. Britain confirmed Ratan Singh in 1811 under the usual deed of allegiance. In 1857 Bhan Pratap Singh aided the British during the Mutiny. He won an eleven-gun hereditary salute and the title of maharaja in 1866.
britannica-1911-browning-oscar:
Oscar Browning (born 1837) was an English writer born in London on 17 January 1837, son of the merchant William Shipton Browning. Educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, where he became fellow and tutor after graduating fourth in the classical tripos of 1860. He spent fifteen years as a master at Eton before returning to Cambridge in 1876 as university lecturer in history.

There he became a prominent figure in college and university life, pushing the study of political science and modern political history. The extension of university teaching and the training of teachers. Dante students know him by his Dante: Life and Works of 1891, and Italian history by his Guelphs and Ghibellines of 1903. Modern history works crowd the list: England and Napoleon in 1803, a four-volume History of England, Wars of the Nineteenth Century, and Napoleon, the First Phase of 1905.
britannica-1911-buckner-simon-bolivar:
Simon Bolivar Buckner (1823–) was an American soldier and political leader. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born in Hart county, Kentucky, on 1 April 1823. He graduated at West Point in 1844. He taught geography, history and ethics there. He fought in the Mexican War with gallantry. He was wounded at Churubusco and brevetted for his conduct. He resigned from the army in 1855.

When the Civil War came, Kentucky tried to stay neutral. Buckner commanded the state guard for Governor Magoffin. In September 1861 he openly joined the Confederate cause. He rose to lieutenant-general in that service. At Fort Donelson in February 1862 the duty of surrender fell to him. Generals Floyd and Pillow had escaped, leaving him in charge. He later served under Bragg in Kentucky and at Chickamauga. After the war he was governor of Kentucky, from 1887 to 1891. In 1896 the Gold Democrats ran him for vice-president.
britannica-1911-calabar:
Calabar, or Old Calabar, is a seaport of West Africa in the British protectorate of Southern Nigeria. It stands on the left bank of the Calabar river, five miles above where the river meets the Calabar estuary of the Gulf of Guinea. It has about 15,000 people. It is the chief town of the eastern province of the protectorate. Ships and wires keep it in steady touch with Europe.

Business houses and the customs office stand by the beach. Cliffs of fair height rise behind them. On the hills stand the main buildings: Government House, the European hospital, and the church of the Presbyterian mission. The native quarter, called Duke Town, fills the vale between the hills. Its chiefs live in fine bungalow-style houses there. A tramway runs along the river front from Duke Town to Queen Beach.
britannica-1911-car:
A car was first a small two-wheeled vehicle for transport. The word comes from the late Latin carra. This 1911 Britannica article traces its widening use. It now covers almost anything like a carriage or chariot. It even names the carrying part of a balloon. With qualifiers it forms a whole family of words. Tram-car, railway-car, sleeping-car and motor-car are examples.

The article then takes up the Irish jaunting-car in detail. That vehicle is the common public carriage of Ireland. It also carries the mails in country districts. Gentry and farmers use it as a private carriage. It has two wheels and carries four besides the driver. A deep well in the centre holds parcels and luggage. Wing seats hang over each wheel. Hinged footboards fold up to narrow the car on tight roads. The description gives the car's working parts one by one.
britannica-1911-cedar:
Cedar is the name of more than one tree of the pine order, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The famed sort is the cedar of Lebanon, praised by poets and painters for its grace and strength. In the Bible it stands as a sign of power, plenty, and long life. It grows high on the hills, some six thousand feet above the sea.

The tree climbs to a height of fifty to eighty feet. Its boughs spread out flat, tier on tier, till the crown is wider than the trunk is tall. Its leaves are short dark needles in tufts of about thirty. Male and female blooms grow apart on the same tree. The cones take two full years to ripen and weep resin as they grow. Its root runs strong and wide in the ground.
britannica-1911-central-provinces-and-be:
Central Provinces and Berar is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a province of British India. The province was formed in October 1903. It joined the Central Provinces with the Hyderabad Assigned Districts. Its total area is given as 113,281 square miles. A count from 1901 puts its people at 10,847,325. As its name shows, it sits at the centre of India. It covers much of the hill and plateau belt of the peninsula.

That belt splits the plains of Hindustan from the Deccan. Bombay lands lie along its western side. Hyderabad and Madras estates bound it on the south. Bengal tributary states stand along the east. In October 1905 most of Sambalpur moved out of it. Five Oriya speaking hill states moved with it then. The entry fixes the young province in place and time. Its bounds and peoples shifted even as it formed.
britannica-1911-char:
Char, a fish of the salmon family, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chars are found in Europe, Asia, and North America. The best known kind is Salvelinus alpinus, the char of British and Irish lakes. It is a graceful and fine eating fish, covered with very small scales.

Above, it is dark olive, bluish, or purplish black, with or without round orange or red spots. Below, its colour runs from pinkish white to scarlet or claret red. When chars go to sea, they take on a silvery coat like salmon and sea trout. The young are silvery on the sides, with bars or parr marks. The fish varies much from place to place, and many local forms were once named as separate kinds. In some English lakes it stays dwarfed, while elsewhere it grows to two feet or more.
britannica-1911-cheddar:
Cheddar is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small town in Somersetshire, England, in the Wells parliamentary division. It stands 22 miles south west of Bristol by rail. Its population in 1901 was 1975. The town, with its Perpendicular church and picturesque market cross, lies below the south western face of the Mendip Hills. The hills rise sharply from 600 to 800 feet above it.

A fine gorge opens from the hills right at the town. Its sheer walls give it the name Cheddar cliffs. Falls of a small stream and rich growth make it a scene many visitors admire. Several stalactite caverns open nearby. Cox's and Gough's caves are the two most visited, for their strange and beautiful formations. Relics of British and Roman settlement found in the caves are kept in a small museum. The manor was a royal demesne in Saxon times.
britannica-1911-chile-peruvian-war:
Chile-Peruvian War (1879–1882) began, the entry says, when Bolivian authorities seized the effects of the Chilean Nitrate Company at Antofagasta. Chilean troops landed there and routed militia at Calama on 23 March 1879, while warships took Cobija and Tocapilla. Bolivia declared war on 1 March and Peru on 5 April that year. At Iquique the Peruvian ironclad Huascar sank the Esmeralda, but the Covadonga drove the Independencia aground as a wreck.

Off Angamos on 8 October 1879 Chilean ships captured the Huascar after Admiral Grau and most of her turret crew were killed, ending the Peruvian navy. Land fighting took Pisagua and Iquique, though the allies beat the Chileans at Tarapacá on 27 November. A second campaign drove inland through Moquegua toward Tacna and Arica, with 12,000 men landed at Pacocha. Sea power, desert marches and heavy losses shape the whole account.
britannica-1911-chilean-civil-war:
Chilean Civil War of 1891 grew out of dissension between President J M Balmaceda and his congress, and it began in January that year. At Valparaiso the Congressional leaders boarded the ironclad Blanco Encalada, and Captain Jorge Montt took command of a Congressional fleet. Most of the navy joined congress, while the army rank and file stayed with the president. Each side thus held one arm of war and lacked the other at the start.

Congressional forces landed at Pisagua, lost early actions, then retook the port and won at San Francisco on 15 February. Iquique fell to their fleet, and at Pozo Almonte on 7 March Colonel Del Canto beat and killed Robles and scattered his army. Northern Balmacedist troops then gave up, some fleeing into Peru or Bolivia. A Junta at Iquique raised a trained army under Del Canto and Emil Körner for a direct blow at the president.
britannica-1911-chino-japanese-war:
Chino-Japanese War names the conflict of 1894 and 1895 in east Asia. The 1911 Britannica entry traces its cause to a long rivalry. China and Japan each sought the chief sway in Korea. In the 1500s a long war there had ended in failure for Japan. Lack of sea power had cost Japan its footing on the mainland then.

In 1875, 1882, and 1884 Japan sent fresh forces to Korea. It backed a party of progress at the court in Seoul. The Tientsin pact of the 1880s bound each side to warn the other. Each had to tell the other before it sent troops to Korea. In 1894 a revolt led Korea to call on China for aid.
britannica-1911-choiseul-cesar:
Cesar Choiseul, duke and marshal of France, lived from sixteen o two to sixteen seventy five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Men knew him for most of his life as marshal du Plessis Praslin. His old family rose in the upper Marne valley in the tenth century.

Choiseul joined the army at age fourteen as head of a foot regiment. He fought at the siege of La Rochelle under Louis the Thirteenth. He helped defend the isle of Re against English attacks led by Buckingham. In sixteen thirty he served as envoy at the Savoy court in Italy. War with Spain then gave him fresh fame in battles round Turin.
britannica-1911-chunar:
Chunar, or Chunarghur, is a town and old fortress of India, in the district of Mirzapur, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It stands on the south bank of the Ganges, and had 9,926 people in 1901. The fort sits on top of a steep rock that commands the river, and was once a place of great strength.

Inside the old citadel, the remains of a Hindu palace with fine carvings show the former weight of the place. The town itself is one or two straggling streets, with a handsome English church. The article traces its past from the 1500s, through its taking by the emperor Akbar after a siege of six months. It fell to the English under General Carnac in 1763, and a treaty with the nawab of Oudh was signed there in 1781.
britannica-1911-cigar:
Cigar is the common term for tobacco leaf prepared for smoking by being rolled into a short cylinder. The roll tapers to a point at the end placed in the mouth. The other end, which is lighted, is usually cut square, the entry notes. Spanish cigarro gives the word, though its own origin is doubtful and two possible sources are discussed.

One source may be cigarra, a cicada, from a likeness to that insect's body, and the other cigarral, an Arabic word for a pleasure garden. A claimed Cuban word for a kind of tobacco is judged probably wrong, since no such native word is known. Cigarette, the diminutive, denotes a roll of cut tobacco usually in thin paper. It may also sit in tobacco leaf or in the husk of Indian corn.
britannica-1911-cinnabar:
Cinnabar, in the 1911 Britannica, is a mineral entry on red mercuric sulphide, the common ore of mercury. The name comes from a Greek word used by Theophrastus, perhaps for more than one stuff. The mineral is most often found in heavy, grainy, or earthy masses of bright red. At times it forms crystals with a bright metallic shine, in the six sided system.

Cinnabar bends light more than any other known mineral, past even diamond. Its hardness is 3 and its weight near nine times that of water. It occurs at every place that yields quicksilver, from Almaden in Spain to Huancavelica in Peru. Fine crystals come from Kweichow in China, and the stone is still forming from hot waters in California.
britannica-1911-circar:
Circar is an Indian term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the parts that make up a subah or province, each run by a deputy governor. In English the word lives on chiefly in the name of the Northern Circars. That name marked a strip of land in the Madras presidency along the west side of the Bay of Bengal.

The Northern Circars were five in number, and their joint area was about thirty thousand square miles. The land matches much of the modern districts of Kistna, Godavari, Vizagapatam, and Ganjam. Muslim armies first came in 1471 and held the land in part for a time. The article then traces later rule, gifts to the French company, and the British gain of the coast by war in 1759.
britannica-1911-ciudad-bolivar:
Ciudad Bolívar is an inland city and river port of Venezuela, capital of the state of Bolívar, on the right bank of the Orinoco 240 miles above its mouth. Its people numbered 11,686 in 1891, and it stands on a small hill 187 feet above sea level. There the river narrows to less than half a mile wide, a fact that gave the town its old name. It is the seat of the bishopric of Guayana and the commercial centre of the Orinoco basin.

Cathedral, federal college, theatre, market, custom house and hospital mark the town, which has water supply, tramway and telephones. Steamship links run up and down the river from its port. Exports include cattle, horses, tobacco, cacao, rubber, tonka beans, hides and timber from the basin. Mendoza founded it in 1764 as San Tomás de la Nueva Guayana. It was called Angostura, the narrows, until 1849.
britannica-1911-colcothar: Colcothar is a brown red powder made of ferric oxide. The brief 1911 Britannica note links its name to an Arabic word for copper bloom. The stuff forms when ferrous sulphate is heated to make fuming sulphuric acid. Workers use it to polish fine goods, and it serves as the rouge of jewellers. As a paint tint it is known as Indian red, and some call it Crocus Martis.
britannica-1911-colmar:
Colmar is a town of Germany in Alsace-Lorraine, once capital of the French department of Haut-Rhin. It stands on the Logelbach and Lauch streams, 40 miles south-west of Strassburg on the rail line to Basel. Its people numbered 41,582 in 1905. It seats the government of Upper Alsace and the high court of appeal for the province.

Old walls gave way to pleasant walks round the town. Narrow, quaint streets fill the centre. Saint Martin's church, from the 1200s and 1300s, heads the list of sights. A former Dominican house now serves as a museum. The Kaufhaus, or trade hall, dates from the 1400s. Cloth work rules the town's trade. Wool, cotton and silk weaving lead, with thread, starch and sugar works beside them. The entry adds a civic past. Colmar became an imperial city in 1226.
britannica-1911-crimean-war:
Crimean War, the war of 1853 to 1856, is introduced in a war history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Turkey declared war on Russia in October 1853 after a spell of uneven fighting. Britain and France, later joined by Sardinia, stepped in. At first their help was just a fleet in the Bosporus.

Anger in Britain and France at the sinking of the Turkish fleet at Sinope forced stronger action. Both states declared war on the tsar in January 1854. On the Danube, Turkish troops had held their own well. Omar Pasha checked the Russian push and won a run of fights. A later Russian drive laid siege to Silistria, which held firm. The siege was lifted when Austria massed troops nearby and the balance of power shifted.
britannica-1911-cupar:
Cupar is a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cupar is a royal and municipal burgh and the capital of the county of Fife in Scotland. It stands on the left bank of the Eden, in the east of the Howe of Fife. The count of 1901 put its people at about four thousand five hundred. Among its chief buildings are the town hall, the county buildings, the corn exchange and the Bell Baxter school.

The Mercat Cross stands at the main street cross, set there in 1897. The town got its charter in 1356 from David the Second. Set between Falkland and St Andrews, it was often visited by Scottish kings. James the Sixth held his court there for a time in 1583. Cupar is a farm and law centre, and its chief trade is the making of linen.
britannica-1911-familiar:
The word familiar is pulled apart in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At root it means what belongs to the family or household. That plain sense, the entry says, is now rare in use. The word more often means close, friendly, or well known. From close talk it can slide to conduct that is too free.

As a noun, a familiar is a spirit that serves a wizard. Such a spirit was called up to do its master's will. The thought sits near the guardian angel and the Roman genius. In the Church the name marks men tied to a pope's or bishop's house. Familiars of the Holy Office were lay men who made arrests for the Inquisition.
britannica-1911-farid-ud-din-attar:
Farīd ud-Dīn 'Attār (1119–1229) was a Persian poet and mystic born at Nishapur. His real name was Abu Talib, or Abu Hamid, Mahommed ben Ibrahim. Farīd ud-Dīn, Pearl of Religion, was an honorary title. He followed his father's trade of druggist or perfumer, and 'Attār, dealer in otto of roses, became his pen name. Dawlatshah tells how a wandering fakir's words turned him from the shop to the Sufi path.

He studied under Sheik Rukneddin, travelled to Mecca, Egypt, Damascus and India, and took the Sufi mantle from Sheik Majd-ud-din of Bagdad. Most of his life passed at Shadyakh. Captured by a soldier of Jenghiz Khan, he talked his captor out of a good price and was slain for it. He left some 120,000 couplets. His famous Mantiq uttair, the Language of Birds, is an allegorical poem.
britannica-1911-felspar:
Felspar is a name for a group of rock forming minerals. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats them as key parts of many rocks. The word came from the German Feldspath. Kirwan respelled it as felspar in 1794. He thought it named a rock mineral, not a field mineral. The odd spelling stuck in England.

The group splits in two by the shape of its crystals. Each kind shows two clear split planes. In one branch the planes meet at a right angle. That branch takes the name orthoclase. In the other branch the angle is never quite square. That branch is called plagioclase. Twin crystals are common in all felspars. The entry adds that the two branches split again by what they are made of. A French view is noted too: all felspars may be one shape, twinned to look like two.
britannica-1911-friar:
Friar, from the Latin frater through the French frère, is the English general name for members of the mendicant religious orders. Once used as a title for single men of those orders, it later named the orders men as a class. In England the chief orders were told apart by the colour of the habit they wore.

The Franciscans or Minors were the Grey Friars, the Dominicans or Preachers the Black Friars, and the Carmelites the White Friars. With the Austin Friars or Hermits they formed the four great mendicant orders, Chaucer ordres foure. The Trinitarians were called Red Friars though really canons, and the Crutched Friars were a separate order again. Many lesser orders of friars were ended by the second council of Lyons in 1274. The entry points elsewhere for the line between friars and monks.
britannica-1911-gaekwar: Gaekwar, or Guicowar, is the family name of the Mahratta rulers of Baroda in western India. The English turned it into a dynastic title. The name derives from the vernacular word for cow, but the family is not of the cowherd caste. It belongs to the upper Mahrattas and sometimes claims Rajput origin. Three warriors, Damaji I, Pilaji and Damaji II, founded the dynasty. They established Mahratta rule across Gujarat in the first half of the 18th century.
britannica-1911-gahanbar: Gahanbar is the name of six festivals in the ancient Avesta calendar. The Parsees still keep them at six seasons of the year. The seasons match the six periods of creation in the old faith. The feasts are Maidhyozaremaya at mid spring and Maidhyoshema at midsummer. Then come Paitishahya in the corn season and Ayathrema in the season of flocks. Maidhyarya falls at the winter solstice. Last comes Hamaspathmaedha, the festival of sacrifices.
britannica-1911-gear:
Gear, in the 1911 Britannica, is a short word entry with a wide spread of senses. At root it means an outfit: a person's clothing, a horse's harness and trappings, or household goods. Phrases such as riding-gear and hunting-gear show that first sense, and 'out of gear' began as being out of harness, not ready to work.

The word then covers apparatus in general. In machines it names the parts that pass motion from one part to another, by cog-wheels, bands and the like. A special bicycle sense closes the entry: the gear is the diameter of an imaginary wheel whose rim equals the distance one turn of the pedals carries the machine. The entry links the word to garb and to an old Teutonic root meaning to make ready.
britannica-1911-girnar:
Girnar is a sacred hill in western India, in the peninsula of Kathiawar, ten miles east of Junagarh town. The 1911 Britannica entry describes five peaks rising about 3,500 feet above the sea. On them stand numerous old Jain temples, much frequented by pilgrims.

At the foot of the hill lies a rock carrying an inscription of Asoka, dated by the entry to the 2nd century B.C. Two other inscriptions stand with it, dated A.D. 150 and A.D. 455, and the entry calls them of great historical importance. The notice is very short: the hill, its temples and pilgrims, and the three carved records at its base. Those inscriptions are its chief claim on a reader's attention.
britannica-1911-gjallar: Gjallar, in Scandinavian mythology, is the horn of Heimdall, guardian of the rainbow bridge. The 1911 Britannica entry is only two sentences long. The bridge is the road by which the gods pass and repass between earth and heaven. Heimdall's duty was to blow the Gjallar whenever a stranger approached the bridge, sounding the warning to the gods above. Nothing more is given: the whole entry is the horn, its keeper, the bridge it guards, and the blast that had to greet any stranger's approach.
britannica-1911-goslar:
Goslar is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Germany. It lies in the Prussian province of Hanover. It stands on the Gose, a feeder of the Oker. The Harz hills rise at its northern foot. Hildesheim and Brunswick lie at rail distance from it. A count from 1905 gives the town 17,817 people. Walls surround it, and it has an antique look. Its old buildings draw the eye of visitors.

One tower, the Zwinger, has walls twenty three feet thick. The market church is built in Romanesque style. It was restored after fire damage in 1844. It holds the town archives and a library. Manuscripts of Luther are kept in that library. The old town hall holds many interesting antiquities. The Kaiserworth shows statues of eight German emperors. The Kaiserhaus is the oldest secular building in Germany. Henry the Third built it before the year 1050.
britannica-1911-gracian-y-morales-baltas:
Baltasar Gracián, a Jesuit prose master of Spain, is set down in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Calatayud in Aragon in the year 1601. At eighteen he joined the Society of Jesus as a novice. He rose to head the Jesuit college at Tarrazona in time. He died there in December of the year 1658.

His chief works teach wit, poise, and the conduct of life. The Hero sets out the marks of the ideal man in brief saws. The Oracle, a hand book of prudence, gives rules for living. The Criticón spins a tale of man's life as a moral fable. Most of his books came out under a false name, the entry notes. That breach of rule drew a rebuke from his chiefs.
britannica-1911-grammar:
Grammar, the study of how words join to make sense, opens a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through Latin from a Greek term for a letter. Grammar can mean the links that words bear to each other in a sentence. It can also mean the set book that lays those links out in order.

The piece holds that the aim of speech is to carry thought. If the thought gets across, the gear that moves it counts for little. A phrase is right or wrong by the use of its own tongue, the entry argues. What folk cannot grasp is what counts as a fault. That is why the grammar of a fine dialect and of a local one can clash. Each is right in its own sphere, by its own custom and consent.
britannica-1911-grosse-julius-waldemar:
Julius Waldemar Grosse (1828–1902) was a German poet. He was born at Erfurt, a military chaplain's son. He was educated at Magdeburg. He briefly entered an architect's office. From 1849 he studied at Halle. He nominally read law there. In practice he devoted himself to letters. His tragedy Cola di Rienzi appeared in 1851. A comedy of his reached the stage that same year.

Success turned him toward literature as a profession. In Munich he joined the circle around Paul Heyse. Hermann Lingg belonged to that circle too. He worked as a dramatic critic and newspaper editor. From 1869 he served as secretary of the Schiller-Stiftung. He settled finally at Weimar in 1890. He wrote prolifically across novels, drama and verse. His lyric collections show him at his best. Gedichte appeared in 1857 and Aus bewegten Tagen in 1869. His collected dramatic works fill seven volumes.
britannica-1911-hamar:
Hamar, or Storehammer, is a town of Norway. It lies in Hedemarken county, 78 miles by rail north of Christiania. Its population in 1900 was 6,003. It sits between two bays of great Lake Mjösen. Railways branch from it to Trondhjem and to Otta. The present town was laid out in 1849. It became a bishop's see in 1864.

An older town stood near the same site. Nicholas Breakspeare founded it, with a bishop's see, in 1152. Breakspeare was an Englishman who became Pope Adrian IV. Swedes destroyed town and cathedral in 1567. A nave-arcade with rounded arches survives from the cathedral. The modern town centres local farming trade. Timber trade passes through it as well. The entry is short, pairing the new town with its destroyed medieval predecessor.
britannica-1911-hardwar:
Hardwar, or Hurdwar, an old town of British India, is given a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands in the Saharanpur district on the right bank of the Ganges, where the Ganges canal takes off. A branch railway to Dehra opened in 1900, and its count in 1901 was 25,597. The town is a Hindu place of pilgrimage of great age.

It first bore the name Kapila, from the sage of that name, and ruins of an older city stand at Mayapur to the south. The great draw is the bathing ghat with the foot mark of Vishnu set in its wall. A fair each year at the start of the Hindu solar year draws about 100,000 pilgrims. Every twelfth year the Kumbh-mela draws far more, some 400,000 in 1903. The meeting is also a chief horse fair of Upper India, with brisk trade in grain.
britannica-1911-hincmar:
Hincmar, who lived from about 805 to 882, was archbishop of Reims. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica counts him a giant of French church history. Born to a noble house of Gaul, he was raised at Saint Denis. Its abbot took him to the emperor's court in 822. When the abbot fell from grace in 830, Hincmar shared his exile. He stayed loyal to the emperor Louis in the wars with his sons.

After Louis died in 840, Hincmar backed Charles the Bald. The king gave him abbeys, then the see of Reims in 845. The old archbishop, Ebbo, had been cast out for breaking his oath. Hincmar's first care was the return of church lands held by laymen as grants from Ebbo's time. Fights with clerks ordained by Ebbo dogged him from the start.
britannica-1911-holkar: Holkar is the family name of the Mahratta ruler of Indore, taken up as a dynastic title. The ending -kar carries a clue to the family's start: it implies that the founder of the family came from the village of Hol, near Poona. The whole entry is two sentences long, giving the name, the house it belongs to, and that village origin, with a pointer to the Indore article for the state's fuller history.
britannica-1911-honavar:
Honavar, also called Onore, is the subject of a short place entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a seaport of British India in the North Kanara district of Bombay. The entry gives its count of people in nineteen hundred one as six thousand nine hundred twenty nine. Trade there was noted as far back as the sixteen hundreds.

Most of the entry tells two tales from its past. In sixteen seventy, English traders there were killed by a mob after their dog killed a sacred bull. In seventeen eighty four, Captain Torriano held the port for three months. He and a small force of sepoys held out against the army of Tippoo Sultan.
britannica-1911-hundred-years-war:
The Hundred Years War is the subject of a past entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name is given to a long clash of France and England. It ran from 1337 to 1453 in all. Six French kings and five English kings held thrones in that span. Fights over French lands of English kings lit the war. A claim by Edward the Third to the French throne fed it too.

In the first reign the English had the best of it. Their fleet won a great sea fight at Sluys in 1340. Edward won a land fight at Crecy in 1346. Calais fell to him the next year after a siege. A truce then paused the war for some years. Later notes cover Poitiers, where the French king was seized. A pact at Bretigny gave France a rest in 1360.
britannica-1911-idar:
Idar, also spelled Edar, a native state of India in the Mahi Kantha agency, is described in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its area was near seventeen hundred square miles, and its people in 1901 numbered about one hundred and sixty eight thousand. That count was down sharply on the decade, a fall the entry lays to famine.

Much of the land was held by kin of the raja on feudal terms. Its crops were grain, oil seeds and sugar cane, and a rail line from Ahmedabad ran through the state. The town of Idar, once the capital, held about seven thousand people, while Ahmednagar served as the seat of rule by then. In 1901 both the raja and his posthumous son died, and the succession passed to Sir Pertab Singh of Jodhpur.
britannica-1911-isobar:
Isobar, from Greek words for equal and weight, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a line on a weather map that joins points with the same air pressure. The pressure is taken at sea level or at the ground. Broad maps use such lines to show mean pressure for a month or season over large areas.

Daily weather charts for smaller regions use the same lines in a tighter way. They mark all places that share one barometric reading at one time. Closed rings of lines reveal a cyclonic or anticyclonic system at a glance. The entry adds a fine point of form. Isobaric lines are where sloped surfaces of equal pressure cut the surface of the earth.
britannica-1911-issachar:
Issachar is the subject of a Bible entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name is Hebrew and seems to mean there is a hire or reward. It was the name of a son of Jacob. He was the ninth son and the fifth by Leah. The name was also borne by a tribe of Israel. Two parts of Genesis give slightly different accounts of the name.

The land of the tribe lay south of four other tribes. It took in the whole great plain of Esdraelon. It also took in the hills east of that plain. A main trade road ran through the rich land. Some key towns stayed in Canaanite hands for a long time. The tribe took some part in a war under Deborah. Yet the blessing of Jacob hints at a taxed and bound state. Farm life and hill shrines close the notes on the tribe.
britannica-1911-jacamar: Jacamar is a bird name taken from Jacameri, the Brazilian name given by Marcgrave. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the word was formed by Brisson from that source. It passed into most European tongues for that first species and its kin. Together those birds form the family Galbulidae. The hosted head gives only this naming account, with no further detail on form or habits.
britannica-1911-janssen-pierre-jules-ces:
Pierre Jules Cesar Janssen, a French star watcher born in eighteen twenty four, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, he studied number work and the laws of nature at the faculty of sciences. He taught at a Paris school and then at the school for building design.

His real work lay in trips sent by the state. He went to Peru to fix the line of the magnetic equator. He studied how the air dims the sun spectrum in Italy and Switzerland. He watched both passings of Venus across the sun, one in Japan and one at Oran. He also joined a long run of trips to watch the sun go dark. The entry shows a life spent chasing light round the world.
britannica-1911-jawhar: Jawhar is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a native state of India. It lies in the Konkan part of Bombay among the Ghat hills. Its area is three hundred and ten square miles. The folk count for 1901 is 47,538 in the state. Its chief is a Koli by caste, the entry states. His line is traced back to the year 1343. Teak and rice are its chief goods for trade.
britannica-1911-jubilee-year:
The jubilee year, in the Roman Catholic Church, is a special year kept every twenty fifth year, from Christmas to Christmas. During it, full pardon of sins can be gained by all the faithful. The terms are a penitent confession and visits to set churches a stated number of times, or an equal amount of good work.

The practice dates from Boniface VIII, whose bull of the 22nd of February 1300 set it up. A rumour at the close of 1299 held that all who visited St Peter's on the 1st of January 1300 would gain full pardon, and crowds poured into Rome. An old man of 107 years told how his father had gained the same grace a century before. At first only St Peter's and St Paul's counted as jubilee churches. The Lateran and Sta Maria Maggiore were added later.
britannica-1911-jucar:
The Júcar is a river of eastern Spain. It rises in the north of the province of Cuenca, at the foot of the Cerro de San Felipe, 5906 feet high, and flows south past Cuenca to the borders of Albacete. There it bends east and holds that course for most of its remaining length.

A canal, the Maria Cristina, links it on the right with the city of Albacete. After it enters Valencia it receives on the left its chief feeder, the Cabriel, which also rises near the Cerro de San Felipe in the Montes Universales. Near Alcira the river turns south-east, then sharply north, then curves south-east again. It reaches the Mediterranean at Cullera after a course of 314 miles. Its mouth forms the harbour of Cullera, and its lower waters are much used for watering the fields.
britannica-1911-karasu-bazar:
Karasu Bazar is a town of Russia, in the Crimea and government of Taurida, 25 miles east northeast of Simferopol. Its people in 1897 numbered 12,961: Tatars, Armenians, Greeks, and Qaraite Jews. About 200 Krymchaki, Jews in Tatar language and dress, live by making leather goods, knives, and embroidery. The site is low, but hills ring the town and shield it from the north wind.

Its dirty streets of petty traders, its gloomy bazaar of tiny shops, its market squares and blind alleys stamp it as a Tatar or Turkish town. Set on the high road between Simferopol and Kerch, amid corn land, vineyards, and gardens, it was once a chief seat of trade in the Crimea. It is slowly losing that rank, though it is still a fair centre for the export of fruit. The caves of Akkaya near by give proof of early settlement on the spot.
britannica-1911-kashgar:
Kashgar is a weighty city of Chinese Turkestan, 4043 feet above the sea. It consists of two towns, Kuhna Shahr, the old city, and Yangi Shahr, the new city, about five miles apart, split by the Kyzyl Su, a feeder of the Tarim. The Chinese call it Su leh, a name that seems older than Kashgar, which is said to mean variegated houses.

Routes meet at Kashgar from the Oxus valley, from Khokand and Samarkand, and from Aksu and Khotan. It has been a centre of rule and trade from very early times. Like all cities of Central Asia it has changed hands again and again. From 1864 to 1887 it was the seat of the Amir Yakub Beg, who built a Muslim state of the chief Tarim cities and ruled it with rare success.
britannica-1911-kathiawar:
Kathiawar, or Kattywar, is a peninsula of India within the Gujarat division of Bombay, and it gives its name to a political agency. Its total area is about 23,400 square miles, and its people numbered 2,645,805 in 1901. Those figures count a part of the British district of Ahmedabad, a part of the state of Baroda, and the small Portuguese settlement of Diu.

The Runn of Cutch bounds it on the north, Ahmedabad and the Gulf of Cambay on the east, and the Arabian Sea on the south and west. Its greatest length is 220 miles and its breadth about 165. The surface is mostly rolling, with low ranges running in varied directions. The north is flat, but in the south the Gir range runs near the coast, with the solitary Osam hill set against it.
britannica-1911-keonjhar: Keonjhar is a tributary state of India, within the Orissa division of Bengal. It covers 3096 square miles and held 285,758 people in 1901, with a revenue put at £20,000. The state is an offshoot from Mayurbhanj. Part of it is rugged hills, rising to more than 3000 feet above the sea. The raja lives at the town of Keonjhar, which held 4532 people. The entry is a few lines only: size, people, revenue, parent state, hills, and the raja's seat.
britannica-1911-krishnagar: Krishnagar is a town of British India, headquarters of Nadia district in Bengal, standing on the left bank of the river Jalangi. A light railway links it with Ranaghat, on the Eastern Bengal railway. In 1901 it held 24,547 people. It is the seat of the raja of Nadia and has a government college, and coloured clay figures are made there. The hosted text for this record is a segment inside a shared file that also holds parts of neighbouring entries, and the segment itself is the whole of this brief entry.
britannica-1911-kuch-behar:
Kuch Behar, or Cooch Behar, is a native state of India in Bengal. It is a tract at the foot of the hills, not far from Darjeeling, ringed round by British territory. Its area is 1307 square miles, and in 1901 it held 566,974 people. Its revenue is put at £140,000. The state is a level plain of triangular shape, cut by many rivers that run south to the Brahmaputra. Most of it is rich and well farmed.

Rice grows on three-fourths of the farmed land, and jute and tobacco are raised for export. The one special craft is the weaving of a strong silk from worms fed on the castor-oil plant. The state takes its name from the Koch or Rajbansi tribe. Its greatest king was Nar Narayan, who came to power about 1550. He conquered the whole of Kamrup and built temples in Assam.
britannica-1911-lacunar: Lacunar is the Latin name in architecture for a panelled or coffered ceiling or soffit. The word derives from lacuna, a cavity or hollow, a blank or gap. The panels or coffers of such a ceiling are called lacunaria by Vitruvius. The hosted file runs on from this short article into the neighbouring article on Lacuzon; the account here rests on the Lacunar article alone.
britannica-1911-macassar:
Macassar is the chief town of Dutch rule in Celebes. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its people and trade. It stands on the west coast of the south peninsula. The strait by its name parts Celebes from Borneo.

The town splits into a Dutch port part and a Malay part inland. About eighteen thousand people lived there at the count given. Europeans numbered under a thousand of that total. Chinese and Arab traders made up much of the rest. Yearly trade ran to about one and a quarter million pounds. Coffee, sea slugs, copra, gums, and spices led the exports. Fine timber also shipped from its wharves. The entry warns that macassar oil is a trade name only.
britannica-1911-maihar: Maihar was a native state of Central India in the Baghelkhand agency, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covered 407 square miles, held 63,702 people in 1901, and drew an estimated revenue of 4,700 pounds. Watered by the Tons river, its soil was mostly rich alluvial land over sandstone, fertile except in the hilly south, with much forest that fed a small export trade. Its raja claimed descent from the Kachwaha Rajput clan, and the state had suffered badly in the famine of 1896-1897.
britannica-1911-malabar:
Malabar is a district of British India, in the Madras Presidency, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry fixes the reach of the name. In geography the name is sometimes stretched to the whole west coast of India. Properly it belongs to the strip of land below the Ghāts. That strip is home to people who speak the Malayalam language.

Malayalam is a branch of the Dravidian stock of tongues. Its speakers form a distinct people, with castes and customs of their own. The district so defined matches the old kingdom of Chera. It takes in the modern states of Travancore and Cochin, and part of Kanara. In 1901 the count of Malayalam speakers in all India was 6,029,304. The district runs 145 miles along the coast. It runs inland to the Ghāts, with a breadth of twenty five to seventy miles.
britannica-1911-malan-solomon-caesar:
Solomon Caesar Malan, a British divine and student of eastern tongues who lived from 1812 to 1894, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was Swiss by birth, of an exiled French family, and was born at Geneva. His father was a famed Protestant divine there. From his youth Malan showed a rare gift for languages.

At eighteen he came to Scotland as tutor in a marquis's family, already advanced in Sanskrit, Arabic, and Hebrew. He entered Saint Edmund Hall, Oxford, in 1833, with English almost unknown to him. He asked leave to write his exam papers in French, German, or other tongues, and was refused. He still won scholarships and graduated in 1837. He then went to India as a lecturer at Bishop's College, Calcutta. Illness forced him home in 1840, but he had laid the base of a knowledge of Tibetan and Chinese.
britannica-1911-malar:
Malar is a lake study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a great lake of Sweden. The lake runs seventy three miles west from Stockholm, where it meets an arm of the Baltic Sea. Its surface sits barely above sea level, and its outflow at times runs backward.

The article gives the lake an area of 449 square miles. Its floor is a chain of basins split by ridges, from which many islands rise. The deepest sounding is 210 feet. One long arm reaches north for thirty miles, close to the city of Upsala. Canals join the lake to a second lake and to the Baltic by three routes. Towns on its shores hold royal palaces and an old cathedral town. The lake serves the people of the capital as a field for rest and sport.
britannica-1911-medlar:
Medlar is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small fruit tree. Its Latin name is given as Mespilus germanica. The tree belongs to the rose order, Rosaceae. It is closely allied to the pear genus, Pyrus. It is a native of European woods in the main. Its range runs from Holland southward, and into western Asia. In England it occurs in hedges but is not native.

The tree is small, much branched, and spinous. It sheds its leaves each year in season. The fruit was well known to the ancients. Greek and Roman writers name it in their works. Old French forms of the name became medle and medlier. The German word Mispel keeps the Latin form most closely. The fruit is round but flattened on top. Leafy sepals stay fixed to the ripe fruit. Inside sit stones of a half round shape.
britannica-1911-michael-tsar:
Michael (1596-1645) was tsar of Russia and first tsar of the Romanov house. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how a national assembly chose him in 1613. Envoys found the youth with his mother at a monastery near Kostroma. She at first refused the crown for him as too hard a burden.

He was crowned in July after weeks of delay for lodgings in Moscow. Peace with Sweden and a truce with Poland cleared the land in time. His father Philaret then ran the state until his death in 1633. Michael is shown as gentle and pious, content to stand behind his advisers.
britannica-1911-mortar:
Mortar is a word with two chief senses, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a vessel in which stuff is crushed or pounded. It also names the mixes used in building, made of lime and cement with sand or other fine stuff, worked with clean water. The Latin name for the vessel and for the mix in it is the same word.

As a vessel the mortar serves in the making of drugs, ground with a pestle. The name passed, from likeness of shape, to a short thick gun used for high-angle fire. Its barrel was short, at times shorter than wide, like a bowl. The howitzer has since taken its place. The article then gives the craft of building mortar, how sand and lime are laid in a ring, sprinkled, left to slake, and turned.
britannica-1911-mortara-edgar:
Edgar Mortara was an Italian Jew of a Bologna family whose seizure as a small child stirred Europe. The 1911 Britannica article tells the tale in full. In 1858 the boy, aged five or six, fell ill. His Catholic nurse had him baptized in secret, with the help of her priest. Both child and nurse then vanished at once. The case set off protests in near every land of Europe.

England and France pressed the Vatican to act, but Pope Pius the Ninth refused. He held the matter to be one of faith, beyond his earthly power. He made the boy his ward instead. Italy later sought to charge the nurse, but she had entered a nunnery. When Italian troops took Rome in 1870, Mortara could have gone back to his old faith. He chose not to, and in time became an Augustinian friar.
britannica-1911-mullingar:
Mullingar is a market town and county town of Westmeath, Ireland, near the river Brosna and on the Royal Canal. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 4,500 people in 1901 and a place 50 miles from Dublin. It is a railway junction where the branch for Longford, Sligo, and Cavan leaves the main line.

The parish church of 1813 has a tower and spire, and the Roman Catholic cathedral serves the diocese of Meath. Tanning, brewing, and coarse woollens employ the town, which trades for the farms around it. An Augustine convent of 1227 and a Dominican one of 1239 both fell under Elizabeth. William the Third made the town his headquarters before the siege of Athlone. Anglers use it as a base for trout fishing on Loughs Ennell and Owel.
britannica-1911-nayar:
Nayar is a people entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a caste group on the west coast of south India. They form the lead group in the Malabar region by old rank. By old tale they are a soldier folk, but many now hold high office.

The entry gives their count in India as just over a million souls. Two odd customs mark the group out from all their neighbours. Lands and goods pass down through the line of sisters and their children. Their unions take a loose form with no set duty for the husband. A new law let such unions be writ down as true wedlock, but few used it.
britannica-1911-o-shaughnessy-arthur-wil:
Arthur William Edgar O'Shaughnessy is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English poet. He lived from 1844 to 1881. He was born in London on the fourteenth of March 1844. At seventeen he gained a post through Lord Lytton. That post was transcriber in the British Museum library. Two years later he moved to natural history work. There he made fish study his special field.

His true bent, the entry says, was toward literature. He published his Epic of Women in 1870. Lays of France, drawn from Marie de France, came in 1872. Music and Moonlight followed two years after that. At thirty he married a daughter of John Westland Marston. He printed no new volume in his last seven years. Songs of a Worker came out after his death. He died in January 1881 from a chill's effects. The entry calls him a true singer in verse.
britannica-1911-par: Par is a term of trade and banking, from a Latin word for equal. When stocks or shares can be bought at the price first paid for them, they are said to be at par. That price is their face value. When the price stands higher, they are above par, or at a premium. When it stands below, they are below par, or at a discount. Par of exchange names the sum in the coin of one land that is worth the same sum in the coin of another land.
britannica-1911-pear:
Pear is a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a fruit tree of the rose kin, close to the apple tree. What men call the fruit is in truth the swelled top of the flower stalk. The true fruit sits hid as the core at its heart.

The entry tells how to tell a pear from an apple with care. Shape alone can fool the eye, since some pears look like apples. The sure mark is grit, hard woody cells set in the pear flesh. No such grit forms in the flesh of a true apple. Bark, leaf, and bloom also help to part the two trees at a glance.
britannica-1911-pindar:
Pindar was born about 522 and died about 443 before Christ, a great lyric poet. The 1911 Britannica life hails him as the top song poet of old Greece. He was born at Cynoscephalae in Boeotia at the Pythian games. His father was Daiphantus, and his mother was Cleodice by name. Family lore left a deep mark on his verse and thought.

His clan, the Aegidae, traced its line back to the hero Aegeus. That clan formed part of the old noble stock of Thebes. Its roots were said to reach to Cadmus, the founder of Thebes. A branch of the clan had settled of old at Amyclae. Spartans took that branch into one of their Dorian tribes in time.
britannica-1911-quinet-edgar:
Edgar Quinet was a French writer on the past and on books who lived from eighteen three to eighteen seventy-five. He was born in a small town in the Ain tract. His father had been a stores man in the host but quit in disgust at the rise of the great chief. The son was an sole child and much alone.

His mother, a woman of deep thought and strong faith views, shaped his mind in those lone years. He spurned posts in the host and in trade and held out for books. A turn of a famed German work on the past made his name. Posts and a chair of books in the south, then at Paris, came in time.
britannica-1911-rear:
Rear is a word for the back part of a thing, and a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica untangles its forms. In military and naval use, the rear is the part of a force placed last in order. It stands in contrast to the van, the front part. The word van is itself a short form of vanguard, from French words for in front.

Rear is likewise a worn down form of an older word, arrear. That word came from Old French and Medieval Latin terms for to the back. The entry is careful to split rear from the verb to rear. That verb has two main senses in modern use. A horse rears when it stands up on its hind legs. To rear can also mean to raise up, whether a building, an animal, or a child.
britannica-1911-regular:
Regular means orderly, done by rule, steady, and formally correct. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its older church sense. The word comes from a Latin term for a rule. Through Old French that root also gave English the word rule.

For centuries the word named clergy bound by a rule. A regular was a monk or friar under an order rule. Secular clergy, who lived in the world, stood apart from them. The word later took a second set sense in war. Regulars are troops kept on a standing paid footing. Irregulars are levies raised for one campaign and then let go. Britain split its forces into regular and territorial parts in 1906.
britannica-1911-saar:
Saar is a river article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Saar is a river of Germany that flows into the Mosel. It rises in the Vosges, near the Franco-German frontier. From there it runs north and north-west to its meeting with the Mosel at Konz.

The entry notes that the river is 143 miles long. Its middle valley was a busy district of coal mines and varied trades. Saar wines were also well known at the time. The article lists the main towns on its banks, such as Saarbrucken and Saarlouis. Boats could travel up the river as far as Saargemund. A canal linked the valley with the Rhine-Marne canal, and the piece gives its length and date.
britannica-1911-sabzawar:
Sabzawar is a town of Afghanistan, set 3,550 feet high on the left bank of the river Harud. It lies 93 miles south of Herat. Sabzawar was once a city of fair size. It still holds a fort with sides of about 200 to 250 yards, though that fort has been left empty. The town is now the centre of a group of villages and does well. Its bazaar has about 800 shops, and it trades with Seistan.

The plains round Sabzawar are farmed with care by the Nurzai Duranis. Each village has its own small mud fort. The article is brief and gives the town's place, height, old fort, shops, and trade as its main points. It notes the busy flow of goods with Seistan as a sign of the town's present health.
britannica-1911-sabzevar:
Sabzevar is a district article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Sabzevar is a district of the province of Khorasan in Persia. It was once called Baihak, and it lies between Nishapur and Shahrud. The district runs about eighty miles long and fifty broad.

Some 60,000 people lived there, and the district paid a yearly revenue to the government. Flourishing villages and much farmed land marked the country. Its produce included wool and excellent cotton, with some silk besides. Fruit was dried in large amounts for export, and a few Russian Armenian merchants ran that trade. The town of Sabzevar itself held about 15,000 people. That number had fallen by half since a famine in 1871. The entry gives a plain account of a Persian district and its shrunken capital.
britannica-1911-sagar: Sagar, or Saugor Island, sits at the mouth of the Hugli river in Bengal. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that its name means sea. Hindus hold it as the spot where the holy Ganges meets the ocean. That belief makes it one of the most sought sites of pilgrimage in India. The great yearly gathering falls in January. A lighthouse stands on the side that faces the sea. Farther out lie the Sandheads, where the Calcutta pilots cruise.
britannica-1911-san-lucar:
San Lucar, a fortified seaport in southern Spain, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the Guadalquivir estuary, in the province of Cadiz. About twenty four thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. The town splits into an upper part and a lower part.

The upper town is the older, topped by the ruins of a Moorish citadel. Villas ringed by pine and orange groves fill the outskirts. Seville families come in summer for the fine sea bathing there. A church from the fourteenth century and a ducal palace hold many valued pictures. The estuary is deep and sheltered, lit by four lighthouses. Ruins prove that Romans settled the site, though their town names are lost. From this port Columbus sailed in 1498, and Magellan set out in 1519 to circle the world.
britannica-1911-schoppe-caspar:
Caspar Schoppe, German writer of controversy and scholar, was born at Neumarkt in the upper Palatinate on 27 May 1576 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at several German universities in his youth. At about 1599 he became a convert to the Roman Catholic faith. That step won him the favour of Pope Clement the Eighth.

Even in an age of harsh religious polemic, his pen stood out for its venom against Protestants. He fell into a fight in print with Scaliger, once his close friend. One work of his attacked James the First of England in sharp terms. In another he urged Catholic princes to wage war on the Protestant states. At about 1607 he entered the service of Ferdinand, archduke of Styria. That prince used him to rebut Protestant claims and sent him on errands of state.
britannica-1911-secular:
Secular is a word from the Latin saecularis, tied to an age or generation, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica splits it into two main branches of meaning. The first is that which lasts or takes place over a long, open ended stretch of time. That sense, taken straight from classical Latin, is found chiefly in science, for slow changes that are not regular or repeating.

The entry gives the slow cooling of the earth as a case of this use. The second branch means non spiritual, with no concern for religious matters. In medieval Latin it marked what belongs to this world. It set the parish priests, the seculars who lived in the world, apart from the regular clergy bound by the rule of an order. In the wide sense it covers all that stands apart from religion. Property passed to temporal hands is thus secularized.
britannica-1911-seven-weeks-war:
Seven Weeks War is the name for the war of eighteen sixty six in Germany. Its war entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Prussia fought Austria, Bavaria, Hanover, Saxony, and allied German states in that war. A linked war in Venetia pitted Italians against the Austrian south army.

The entry traces roots to the Olmutz surrender of eighteen fifty. Prussia saw that clash made a later war with Austria a must. King William chose Bismarck, Moltke, and Roon to prepare for that war. They recast call up plans and near doubled field battalions in six years. New breech load guns for foot and guns tested well against Denmark.
britannica-1911-smith-william-farrar:
William Farrar Smith, an American general who lived from 1824 to 1903, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Saint Albans in Vermont, he graduated from West Point in 1845. He was assigned to the engineer branch of the army on leaving. Twice he served as assistant professor of mathematics at West Point, in the 1840s and again in the 1850s.

In the first campaign of the Civil War Smith served on the staff. In August 1861 he became a brigadier general of volunteers. He won a brevet for bravery at the action of White Oak Swamp. In July 1862 he rose to major general of volunteers. The head breaks off as it turns to his lead of a division in the field, a role in which his work was said to stand out in clear view of all.
britannica-1911-solar: Solar, also spelled soller, is a building term explained in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In building use it names a room in a high place, a loft or a garret. It can also name a raised chamber in a church. From such a chamber a watcher could tend the lamps that burnt before the altars. The Latin word solarium was used most of all for a sundial. It was also used for a sunny part of a house, which helps explain the shift in sense.
britannica-1911-szekesfehervar:
Székesfehérvár is a town in Hungary, capital of Fejer county, south west of Budapest. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its German name as Stuhlweissenburg and its Latin name as Alba Regia. It stands in a marshy plain as a well built town. A Catholic bishopric among the oldest in Hungary sits there.

For ages the town crowned and buried the kings of Hungary. Saint Stephen built its first church for that royal use. Some fifteen kings were laid to rest in that church. Turks held the town from 1543 to 1686 and wrecked the tombs. Dug remains of royal coffins were found below the cathedral.
britannica-1911-tar:
Tar is a thick product made by heating organic matter without full burning. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses that its makeup shifts with its source. Heat level during the process changes the result as well. Two main trade forms are wood tar and coal tar, it notes.

Wood tar came chiefly from pine roots in Russia, Finland, and Sweden. In the American south it came from swamp pine roots instead. Two ways of making it are compared in the entry. Stack burning wastes useful byproducts, while retort work saves them. Layers that form on settling, and the oils drawn from them, are described in turn.
britannica-1911-temesvar:
Temesvar is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the capital of the county of Temes in Hungary. The town lies 188 miles south east of Budapest by rail, on the navigable Bega canal and the river Bega, and held 53,033 people in 1900. It joins a once strongly walled inner town to four outlying suburbs, with parks now laid on the broad glacis that once parted them.

In the main square a Gothic column 40 feet high marks the town's stand against a siege of 107 days in 1849. The emperor Francis Joseph set it up in 1851. The town is the chief trade and industry centre of south Hungary, dealing in grain, flour, spirits, and horses.
britannica-1911-tredegar:
Tredegar is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an urban district in Monmouthshire, in the west of England's border country. It stands on the Sirhowy River, twenty-four miles north of Cardiff, at about a thousand feet above the sea. The count of 1901 gave it 18,497 people.

The town owes its birth to the works of the Tredegar Iron and Coal Company, set up at the start of the nineteenth century. Those works employ most of its large working population. The place also gave a title, Baron Tredegar, to Sir Charles Morgan, whose line came in by marriage to the Morgan heiress of Tredegar. His son Godfrey, made a viscount in 1905, had served in the Crimea. He had ridden in the famed charge at Balaclava. The entry ties a coal town's rise to one landed family.
britannica-1911-weimar:
Weimar, a city of Germany and capital of the grand-duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in a rich vale on the Ilm, a small stream that feeds the Saale. Rail lines link it to Leipzig, Berlin, and Jena. Its people grew from about twenty-one thousand in 1885 to about thirty-one thousand in 1905.

Weimar owes its fame not to trade but to books. Its tie to the great age of German letters won it the names of poets' city and German Athens. That golden age ran with the reign of Charles Augustus from 1775 to 1828. The old town still keeps its narrow lanes and its market square ringed by steep-roofed houses. The parish church holds the tombs of the ducal house.
britannica-1911-wetzlar:
Wetzlar is a town of Germany, in the Prussian Rhine province. It stands where the Dill meets the Lahn, sixty-four miles north-east of Coblenz by the rail line to Giessen. It had 12,276 people in 1905. The chief building is the cathedral, which dates in part from the 1000s and in part from the 1300s to the 1500s. The town archives hold papers of the old imperial chamber.

The town keeps strong ties to Goethe. He lived there in 1772 as a legal official and wrote The Sorrows of Young Werther out of that stay. Charlotte Buff, the Lotte of that tale, is tied to the town as well. The ruins of the castle of Kalsmunt look down on Wetzlar. The town has iron mines and foundries and works that make optical instruments. It became a free imperial town in the twelfth century.
by-sheer-pluck-a-tale-of-the-ashanti-war:
G. A. Henty's Ashanti war tale stands here in a second full copy, with its title page in full dress. A fishing trip gives the first chapter its name. Frank Hargate skips a school cricket match for a bush by the water. A chaffinch nest, new-hatched, fills his eye.

A small black snake threats the brood, and the mother bird fights back with spread wings. Frank keeps still, set to help if the snake gains. A school mate comes at a run and scares both snake and bird off. The match had slipped Frank's mind clean. Boy pluck of the school sort is the stock the war tale builds on. This copy and its twin in the same slice hold the same tale; the heads and first pages match line for line in the parts checked.
camp-fire-and-cotton-field-southern-adve:
Thomas W. Knox, a Herald man with the Union armies, wrote a war book dated 1865. Its two halves match its title: camp life with the armies, then home life on a Louisiana cotton farm. Press men who rode with the armies get the book, in a warm front word. No plea opens the text, Knox owns.

The book came to be when a publisher turned up, he says in plain words. Stuff came from notes of the march and from his own mind's store. Worth or lack of it is left to the reader's test, with no vow on the front page. New York, September 1865 signs that word. The rebel ram Arkansas, shown in a plate running the Union fleet, gives the war half its stamp. South seen by a north pen in war years forms the whole.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abiathar:
Abiathar was a high priest descended through Achimelech, Achitob, Phinees, Heli, and Ithamar from Aaron, whose name means father of plenty. He alone escaped the slaughter at Nob, fled to David during his banishment, and advised him through his campaigns. With the high priest Sadoc he helped carry the ark to Jerusalem, and he stayed close to David in flight, giving counsel at key moments.

His fortunes turned when he backed Adonias for the throne. Solomon's banishment of him to Anathoth finished the ruin of Ithamar's house foretold in Samuel. The entry tracks his career passage by passage through Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, and points readers to commentaries for the puzzle of 2 Samuel 8:17.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adar:
Adar is four things at once, and this entry separates them. First, a frontier town in Chanaan's south, named in Numbers 34:4 and Joshua 15:3, which has not been identified. Second, it is a king of Edom in Genesis 36:39, called Adad, or Hadad in the Revised Version, at 1 Chronicles 1:50.

Third, Adar is the twelfth month of the Jewish year, matching roughly late February to mid-March. Fourth, Adar is a Chaldean god, whose name appears in the compound Adramelech, meaning Adar is King (2 Kings 17:31). The short entry thus serves as a sorting of one name across place, person, calendar, and god.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-anton-:
Albert Anton von Muchar was an Austrian historian born at Linz in Tyrol in 1781 and dead at Graz in 1849. Descended from the old noble Muchar family, he studied at Graz and joined the Benedictine order at Admont. He was ordained a priest soon after taking his vows in 1808. He later became librarian and keeper of the archives at his monastery, then professor of Greek and eastern languages there.

Muchar's tastes ran to history rather than pure language study. His historical works rest on close reading of original sources in libraries across Austria, Bavaria, and northern Italy. Vienna's Academy of Sciences elected him a member in 1829, and he helped found the Historical Society for Inner Austria. His chief works include Roman Noricum in two volumes and his nine-volume History of the Duchy of Styria, the first four volumes edited by himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avatar:
Avatar comes from the Sanskrit avatara, meaning descent, and names a god's descent to earth in Hindu religion. A portion of the god's essence then takes a coarser form, animal, monster, or man. Vishnu's descents matter most, falling in different ages and measures of his essence. Their number runs from ten to twenty-eight, at last countless.

Any man may be hailed as a more or less perfect avatar of Vishnu. The entry counts that homage to men, above all to sect founders, among Hinduism's worst features. The ten most famous avatars open with the Fish, which saved Manu from the Deluge. Next come the Tortoise, bearing Mount Mandara in the churning of the ocean of milk, and the Boar, lifting the earth from flood. Later avatars adopt the cults of Rama, Krsna, and Buddha, yet their likeness to the Incarnation is most superficial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldachium-of:
A baldachium is a dome-like canopy over the high altar of larger churches. It usually stands on four columns, though sometimes it hangs by chains from the roof. Its late medieval name, baldacchino, comes from Baghdad, source of the precious cloths for such canopies. Earlier it was called ciborium, from Greek kiborion, the lotus seed-pod used as a drinking cup.

It likely arose from the wish to give the plain altar table a dignified architectural setting. By the fourth century it formed the church's architectural center, marking the altar as a throne of honor. Altar curtains hung between its columns, and lamps and crowns hung from its roof. Use ran general until the twelfth century, when the reliquary displaced it, though Italy kept the older form. The most magnificent baldachium is Bernini's in St Peter's, Rome, made for Urban VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltasar:
Baltasar is the Greek and Latin form of Belshazzar, Hebrew Bel-sarra-usur, meaning 'May Bel protect the king.' Bel was Babylon's chief and titular god. In Daniel chapter five, Baltasar appears as son of Nabuchodonosor and last King of Babylon. While he feasted his nobles, the Medes under Darius invaded the town, and the king was slain.

At the feast he defiled vessels taken from Jerusalem, and his wives and concubines drank from them. A hand then wrote Mane, Thecel, Phares on the wall, which no counsellor or magician could explain. The Queen urged calling Daniel, who read the doom: the kingdom was numbered, the king weighed and found wanting. Its rule would pass to the Medes and the Persians. Herodotus names Labynitus II as Babylon's last king, commonly read as a corruption of Nabonidus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boso-breakspe:
Boso Breakspear, third English cardinal, rose as nephew of Adrian IV and steered the papacy through the schism of 1159. A Benedictine of Saint Albans famed for piety and learning, he wrote lives of eleventh- and twelfth-century popes, including his uncle, and versified saints' lives now in the Cotton manuscripts. Adrian made him cardinal-deacon in December 1155 and camerlengo, and sent him to Portugal.

On Adrian's death, four imperial cardinals chose Octavian as Victor IV, but Boso led twenty-three cardinals into Sant'Angelo on burial day, 5 September 1159, and elected Rolando as Alexander III. Alexander raised him to cardinal-priest in 1163 and took him to Venice for the Peace of 1177 with Frederick. Boso died at Rome about 1181.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buenaventura-:
Buenaventura Sitjar, a Majorcan Franciscan, spent his life at California's San Antonio mission and preserved its Telame language. Born at Porrera, Majorca, on 9 December 1739, he took the habit of Saint Francis in April 1758 and joined the College of San Fernando in Mexico after ordination. Assigned to California in 1770, he landed at San Diego on 21 May 1771.

Present at San Antonio's founding, he served as its first missionary under Junipero Serra until his death on 3 September 1808. By then 3,400 Indians had been baptized there. He mastered Telame, the mission's tongue, and put together a vocabulary with Spanish explanations, issued at New York in 1861. Shorter than Arroyo's Mutsun dictionary, his work gives pronunciation and fuller notes, and he also left a journal of a 1795 exploring expedition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bye-altar: A bye-altar is an altar that ranks below the central or high altar of a church. The name is most often given to altars set in the bays of the nave, the transepts, or other side spaces. Such altars stand apart from the high altar yet within the same church, giving each bay or transept its own place of worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canons-and-ca:
Canons regular are religious clerics who live under a rule while serving the Church's sacramental and pastoral work. The entry sets them apart from monks, for whom clerical status is incidental rather than essential. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, it argues that their order exists precisely for work tied to the divine mysteries. Erasmus himself, a canon regular, called it a middle path between monastic life and the secular clergy.

From origins in the early Church the entry follows their growth, reforms, and congregations across the centuries. It contrasts their choral duties, discipline, dress, and diet with those of Benedictines and Cistercians. English houses get close attention, with dozens founded between the Conquest and the death of Henry II. The account closes with the canonesses regular, the women's branch of the same life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-vica:
The cardinal vicar is the pope's vicar-general for the spiritual government of Rome and its surrounding district, properly called Vicarius Urbis. The entry opens with a critical list of vicars from 1100 to 1600, built from earlier lists by Ponzetti, Moroni, Crostarosa, and Eubel with new manuscript finds. Names before 1100, it warns, must count as uncertain, with Bovo of Tusculum about 1106 the first clearly attested holder.

Until 1260 vicars came from the cardinals, and the first drawn from nearby bishops followed after that date. Later sections set out nomination and oath, authority, the vicegerent, and the organization of the vicariate. Departments covered include ordinations, religious orders, preaching, parochial clergy, the court, and the secretariate. A reform by Pius X, published after the entry's main source, gets a closing note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-cal:
A vast entry on the Christian calendar, the Church's reckoning of time and feasts. It opens with the calendars of Egypt, Babylon, China, India, and the Aztecs, the Celtic calendar stones found at Coligny in 1897, and the verse Fasti of Ovid. It then turns to the Jewish calendar of Leviticus, with lunar months of 29 and 30 days corrected to keep pace with the moon and the sun.

The main body covers the Easter cycle, the Nativity, and saints' days. It goes on to the earliest calendars and feasts of Our Lady and the apostles. Later developments and the modern calendar imposed by authority follow, ending with the churches of the East. Greek movable feasts get close attention, from Sexagesima, the Sunday of abstinence from flesh, to All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost, our Trinity Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
Clerks regular join the religious state's perfection to the priestly office. Essentially clerics, they devote themselves to preaching, sacraments, education of youth, and works of mercy. At the same time they are religious in the strictest sense, professing solemn vows and living community life under a rule approved by the sovereign pontiff. Canon law often uses the term for canons regular, and authors class regular clerks as a branch of the regular canons.

They serve primarily the sacred ministry, not contemplation. They must cultivate the sacred sciences, which monks are not bound to by state of life. As clerics they keep clerical dress distinct from monk's habit and cowl. Their occupations leave them less given to austerity. They differ from friars in being primarily priests, and from canons regular in holding no cathedral churches and giving themselves more to ministry than to choir service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diakovar:
A place and diocesan entry on Diakovar in Slavonia, seat of the united dioceses of Bosnia and Syrmia. In 1900 its 6,824 people were mostly Catholic, about two-thirds Serb and over a quarter German. A Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, finished in 1883 from Rösner's plans by Friedrich Schmidt, runs 256 feet long. Twin towers rise near 276 feet, with a cupola near 203 feet, Seitz frescoes, and an organ of 3,000 pipes.

Roman roots show in the Certissa station on the road from Sissek to Sirmium, lost when peoples moved across Europe in the fourth and fifth centuries. A thirteenth-century gift of Possessio Diaco to the Bishop of Bosnia revived the site, and the see moved to Diakovar in 1246. Seminary, Sisters of Charity house, and episcopal palace complete the picture, with Mariaschnee as the diocese's famed pilgrimage place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dithmar:
Dithmar, also called Thietmar, was bishop of Merseburg and a medieval chronicler. He was born on 25 July 975, son of Count Siegfried of Walbeck and kin to the Saxon emperors. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his schooling at Quedlinburg, Bergen, and Magdeburg. He became provost of Walbeck in 1002, priest in 1003, and fourth bishop of Merseburg in 1009.

As bishop he labored to restore a diocese nearly ruined by his predecessor Giseler, who had chased the archbishopric of Magdeburg. He also defended the freedom of church elections against grasping princes.
