His chronicle, the great work of his life, remains a chief source for the Saxon age, and the entry lists the editions through which it has reached modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-de-sa:
Domingo de Salazar was born at La Bastida on the Ebro in 1512 and died at Madrid in 1594. He joined the Dominicans at San Esteban in Salamanca and was sent to Mexico, where he took a master's degree in theology and a professor's chair. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his wish to preach to the heathen was granted in the province of Guajaca, where he defended Indian rights with zeal.

From Mexico he passed to Florida, laboring for years in toil and privation, then back to Mexico as prior and vice-provincial. After forty years of mission life he was sent to Madrid on order business. The entry closes with his tomb's Latin praise, calling him a father to the poor and poor himself, a fitting epitaph for a defender of the Indians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-double-altar: A double altar carries a double front, allowing Mass to be said on both sides of it at once. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that such altars are often found in churches of religious communities where the choir stands behind the altar. One priest may offer the Holy Sacrifice for the choir community while another offers it for the laity in the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eleazar:
Eleazar is the name of several men in the Bible. This entry starts with the greatest. Eleazar son of Aaron succeeded his father as high priest, wearing Aaron's robes after his death. He stood beside Moses in counting Israel. He helped settle the inheritance claim of the daughters of Salphaad. He shared out the spoils from the Madianites. He heard the plea of Ruben and Gad for land east of the Jordan.

Moses himself presented Joshua, his successor, to Eleazar. Eleazar headed the list of those who divided the land west of the Jordan. He was buried at Gabaath in Mount Ephraim, on ground given to his son Phinees. Down to the Maccabees, the high priests came from his line, apart from the years from Heli to Solomon. The entry also tells of Eleazar Abaron, son of Mathathias, crushed beneath an elephant he had stabbed at Bethzacharam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friar:
Friar names a member of a mendicant order, a begging brotherhood that lives by ministry rather than by cloistered retreat. The word comes from the Latin frater, through French and Middle English forms, and by the late thirteenth century it marked the new orders in English writing. The entry draws the line between friar and monk with care.

For the monk, solitude stands first, and his order may hold property in common. For the friar, public ministry is the heart of life, and his vow of poverty once barred even corporate ownership, so friars lived on free gifts. The Council of Trent later let most mendicant orders hold property together, the Friars Minor and Capuchins alone excepted. Jesuits, though mendicant in spirit, count as clerks regular instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gibraltar:
Gibraltar is a rugged promontory in Andalusia, about six miles round, whose rock rises to 1,396 feet above the strait. The ancient Mount Calpe, paired with Abyla across the water as the Pillars of Hercules, it passed from Phoenicians and Romans to Visigoths and Moors. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces its sieges and its passage from Spain to Britain.

Tarik's Moors built a castle on the rock in 711 and gave it the name Gibel-Tarik, whence Gibraltar. After eight sieges the Spaniards retook it in 1462. In 1704 an English and Dutch force took it during the War of the Spanish Succession. The Treaty of Utrecht made it British in 1713. Its fourteenth and last siege ran from July 1779 for three years, seven months, and twelve days, and failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamar:
Norway's medieval diocese of Hamar covered Hedemarken and Christians Amt, formed in 1152 from Oslo when Arnold, former Bishop of Gardar in Greenland, became its first bishop. He began Christ Church cathedral, finished about the time of Bishop Paul in the mid-thirteenth century. The see grew a chapter of ten canons, a school, a Dominican priory, and a monastery.

Later bishops include Thorfinn, exiled to Flanders where he died, Jörund, moved to Trondhjem, and a provincial council held in 1380. Mogens, the last Catholic bishop, ruled from 1513 to 1537 before a Danish noble seized him in his castle and carried him to Antvorskov. There he lived mildly treated until his death in 1542.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-frie:
Henry of Friemar, a German theologian born at Friemar near Gotha toward the end of the thirteenth century, entered the Augustinian Hermits young and was posted to the University of Paris. There he became master of sacred theology and taught until 1318. That year he became regent of studies at St. Thomas's monastery in Prague and examiner for Germany, later provincial for Thuringia and Saxony. He probably died at Erfurt about 1355.

His printed works show wide range. They include a collection of sermons on the saints, a treatise on the fourfold instinct, divine, angelic, diabolic, and human, and additions to the Sentences. A work on spirits and their discernment, a tract on the conception of the Blessed Virgin, and a history of the origins of the Augustinian Hermits complete the list. His writings circulated in print from Cologne to Parma and Louvain across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-kalk:
Henry of Kalkar, a Carthusian writer born at Kalkar in Cleves in 1328, studied at Cologne and Paris. He became Master of Arts in 1357, procurator of the German nation, and professor of theology. After canonries at Kaiserswerth and Cologne he withdrew in 1365 to Cologne's Charterhouse. He rose to prior of Arnheim, Ruremonde, Cologne, and Strasburg, and served twenty years as visitor amid the Great Schism. Relieved of office in 1396, he lived in prayer at Cologne until his death in 1408.

Kalkar was celebrated as reformer as well as writer: at Arnheim he drew Gerard Groote into the Charterhouse. His writings influenced the school of Deventer and Windesheim, organizing the Catholic Renaissance that found expression at Trent. Many wrongly credited him with the Rosary and the Imitation, yet the Exercitatorium Monachale is certainly his, inspiring Thomas à Kempis and supplying ideas for Ignatius's Exercises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-fr:
Two German works on mysticism carry the name Hermann of Fritzlar, and this entry sorts out what belongs to him and what does not. The first, Das Heiligenleben, is a set of ninety-one short sermons on saints' lives written between 1343 and 1349. It mixes plain teaching with mystical thought on union with God and the birth of Christ in the soul. Long credited to Hermann, it was in fact compiled at his request by the Dominican preacher Gisiler of Slatheim.

The second work, Blume der Schauung, or Flower of Contemplation, survives in a Nuremberg manuscript. It gathers loosely linked questions on the contemplative life and its models. Readers interested in fourteenth-century German mysticism find here a careful untangling of authorship, sources, and the blend of first- and third-person voice in the sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-high-altar:
The high altar is the chief altar in a church, raised on an elevated plane in the sanctuary so that all the faithful can see it at once. It symbolizes Christ, and it serves as the banquet table on which Christ offers himself through the priest's hands to the Eternal Father. A sacrifice supposes both priest and altar, and the Acts of the Apostles shows the faithful sharing in the prayers and partaking of the victim.

In early days the altar usually stood in a chapel at the head of the church, facing east, following the tradition that the faithful pray toward the east. If a church could not be built that way, the altar stood opposite the chief doorway. Olden churches had but one altar, and the entry traces how the high altar's place, form, and meaning developed from those beginnings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th:
The Christian altar is an elevated, table-like surface for offering the Sacrifice of the Mass. Its earliest scriptural reference is in St. Paul, who sets the table of the Lord, trapeza Kyriou, against the table of devils, or pagan altars. Greek Fathers kept trapeza as their favourite term, while Hebrews calls the altar thysiasterion, a word used by Ignatius and later Fathers for the Christian altar.

Christians of the first age carefully avoided bomos, with its pagan associations, until Synesius used it in the early fifth century. Latin writers used altare, mensa, ara, and altarium, though ara more often meant a pagan altar. The entry traces names, forms, and fittings from those early tables through great church altars, their columns, and the iconostasis of the Greek church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-issachar:
Issachar names both a man and a tribe, and this entry sorts the two. First, he was the ninth son of Jacob and fifth son of Leah. He was named for a circumstance of his birth. Scripture tells little of him beyond his four sons at the descent into Egypt. Second, the tribe descended from him, about which knowledge stays thin. In the wilderness march the tribe camped east of the tabernacle with Judah and Zebulun.

At Sinai's first census Issachar counted 54,400 warriors, and 64,300 at the second census, figures the entry quotes from Numbers. After entering western Palestine the tribe settled its allotted land, its later story fading from the record. Readers get a careful distinction: a patriarch known mainly as a name, and a tribe known mainly through census rolls and camp order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-goar:
Dominican and Hellenist Jacques Goar was born at Paris in 1601. He died on 23 September 1653. He entered the Annunciation convent in Rue St Honoré in 1619. He professed there on 24 May 1620. Though lector of philosophy and theology, he devoted himself to Greek study. His superiors sent him to the East to serve Rome through knowledge of Greek church documents and positive theology.

He lived at Chios as missionary apostolic and prior of St Sebastian convent. He used travel to observe rites, meet Orthodox scholars, and study Catholic-Orthodox points at issue. About 1640 he returned to Rome bearing many manuscripts, some valuable. Thereafter he corresponded with the most learned Greeks of his day. The entry presents a scholar-diplomat bridging Latin and Greek Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jewish-calend:
The Jewish Calendar entry explains how Israel has reckoned time from earliest days to the present. The day runs sunset to sunset, or to the first three stars, and before exile daylight was split only into morning, midday, and evening. Babylon brought twelve varying hours, the first near six in the morning and the sixth ending at noon.

Nights were first kept in three watches, to midnight, to cock-crow near three, and to dawn. Weeks count seven numbered days, the seventh called Sabbath, a name also used for the week itself, while Friday bears the title eve of Sabbath or day of preparation. Months, feasts, and leap years complete a system binding worship to seasons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomucene Brischar was a German church historian who spent his working life as a parish priest. Born at Horb in Wurttemberg in 1819, he studied theology at Tubingen and served from 1853 until his death in 1897 as parish priest of Buhl near Rottenburg.

His chief task was continuing Count Leopold Stolberg's History of the Religion of Jesus Christ. He wrote its forty-fifth through fifty-fourth volumes. The entry judges that work below his predecessor's standard. He also wrote two volumes on the disputes between Paolo Sarpi and Pallavicini. He added a monograph on Pope Innocent III, a five-volume survey of Catholic pulpit orators in Germany, and many articles for Herder's church lexicon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ludwig:
Joseph Ludwig Colmar was the Bishop of Mainz who rebuilt its church life after the Revolution. Born at Strasbourg in 1760 and ordained in 1783, he stayed in the city through the Terror in disguise, giving the sacraments in secret. After Robespierre's fall he preached across Strasbourg, and Napoleon named him Bishop of Mainz in 1802.

Colmar found his cathedral profaned and his diocese ruined by war and confiscation. He rebuilt and reconsecrated the cathedral, saved Speyer's from demolition, opened a seminary in 1804, and visited every parish and school. During the epidemic of 1813 and 1814 he served the sick himself. He died at Mainz in 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-of-iss: Joseph of Issachar is a figure known from a single verse of the Bible. A man of the tribe of Issachar, he was the father of Igal, one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan. Their task was to report on the land and its people. The entry, citing Numbers 13:8, gives no further detail about his life, deeds, or death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madagascar:
Madagascar is the great island south-east of Africa, sighted 10 August 1500 by Diego Dias, parted from Cabral's fleet of thirteen ships out of Lisbon, and named St. Lawrence for the martyr's feast day. It stretches from about 12 to 26 degrees south, with St. Mary, Mayotte, and Nossi-Be nearby.

Sparsely settled, barely thirteen souls to the square mile, dense in the centre and thin elsewhere, its peoples now sit under a French governor-general at Tananarivo. They include Hova, Betsileo, Sakalava, and Betsimisaraka. Grandidier and most anthropologists trace them to the black Indonesian race of the Malayo-Polynesian world. Their agglutinative tongue, Malagasy, is rich in material speech and poor in abstractions, and their religion blends a mixed monotheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malabar:
Malabar, in its narrow sense, was a district of India down the west coast south of Mangalore. It ran about 145 miles, in the region of present-day Kerala. Its chief towns were Cannanore, Tellicherry, Calicut, and Palghat. Its old name, Male, meant where the pepper grows, and it gave Malayalam its name.

Widely used, Malabar Coast meant the whole south-west corner of India back to the ghats. In church terms, British Malabar fell under Mangalore. Cochin state held the Padroado diocese of Cochin, the Archdiocese of Verapoly, and three vicariates. Travancore lay under Quilon. Syrian Christians of Malabar lived chiefly in those three vicariates. The famed Malabar Rites, oddly, had nothing to do with Malabar itself. Their scene was Madura, across the peninsula.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechitar:
Mechitar, a name meaning Comforter, was taken by Peter Manuk of Sebaste when he became a monk and founded the Mechitarist order. Born at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia in 1676 to parents of reputed noble blood, he was raised to fifteen by two pious nuns. He entered the cloister of the Holy Cross near Sebaste and was ordained deacon in 1691. Thirst for learning soon drew him out toward Etchmiadzin.

On the road he met a European missionary and an Armenian whose tales of Western wonders changed his life. Fired with love for Western culture, he wandered and taught for scant wages. After eighteen months he returned to Sebaste, still bent on Western study. There he conceived a religious society, perhaps prompted by the suppressed United Brothers, that would wed Armenian faith to Western learning and win his countrymen to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuestra-senor:
Our Lady of the Pillar, a celebrated shrine at Saragossa in Spain, honors an image of the Virgin set on a marble pillar. The present Baroque church began in 1681, and the image was crowned in 1905 with a crown valued at 450,000 pesetas, a mark of devotion across the kingdom.

Tradition says Saint James built the first shrine at Mary's wish after she appeared by the Ebro, a story Duchesne and Baronius doubt and defenders support from Jerome and the Mozarabic office. Written devotion at Saragossa is traced to Pedro Librana in 1155 and to Roman-era tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portable-alta:
A portable altar is a solid slab of natural stone, hard enough to resist any fracture. A bishop, or another person with faculties, must consecrate it. The slab sits in or on the altar table, about two inches from the front edge. It is raised enough to feel under the cloths.

It must be big enough for the Sacred Host and most of the chalice's base, and for the ciborium too when Communion is given. Five Greek crosses mark it, one at each corner and one at the centre, showing where unctions fall at consecration. If the centre cross is missing, the unction still must not be skipped, though skipping it would not void the consecration. Greeks instead use the antimensium, a consecrated silk or linen cloth like a corporal. It is made by placing cloth on a consecrated altar and pouring wine and chrism over it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privileged-al:
An altar counts as privileged when each Mass said there also gains a plenary indulgence for the single soul of the Mass's intention. The privileged altar must be fixed. It need not be consecrated, so long as a consecrated stone, a portable altar, sits in its table.

The privilege clings to the structure itself, not its altar stone, by its title. Hence the privilege stands if the altar's stuff is changed, if it moves to another place, or if another altar with the same title takes its place in the same church. It stands even under the altar's desecration or profanation. To win the indulgence, the Mass must be a Requiem Mass when the rubrics allow it. If a feast's higher rite or other cause bars a Requiem, another Mass may win it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-the:
Reform of the calendar begins with nature's units, the day and the year. This encyclopedia entry defines the day as the interval between two passages of the sun across a place's meridian. Civil reckoning counts from the midnight passage, while astronomers count from the following noon. So the civil day runs twelve hours ahead of the astronomical day. The solar day runs about four minutes longer than the sidereal day.

The Julian system drifted, losing about three-quarters of a day per century, or three whole days in four centuries. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC, a misunderstanding made leap year fall every third year instead of every fourth. At the Julian reform the sun passed the spring equinox on 25 March, but by Nicaea in 325 the date had moved to the 21st, then fixed as the proper equinox date. For the Gregorian New Style's spread, the entry points to Chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatical-ye:
The sabbatical year, the seventh year, was devoted to cessation of agriculture, also called the Year of Remission. Three prescriptions were observed: the land lay fallow and all farm labour was suspended, with no plowing, sowing, or tending vines and olives. The spontaneous yield was not garnered but left in fields for common use, and what was unused was abandoned to cattle and wild animals.

The prescribed rest was for the land, not for man, so non-farm work was not forbidden. With no crops reaped, debt payment would have been a hardship. A creditor could not press an Israelite for a debt, though strangers could still be pressed. Commentators dispute whether this meant remission or mere suspension of payment during the year. During the sabbatical year the Law was read at Tabernacles to all Israel and strangers within the gates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-leodega:
Leodegar, bishop of Autun, was born about 615 to the high-ranking Sigrada and Bobilo. He died a martyr in 678 at Sarcing on the Somme. His childhood passed at the court of Clotaire II, and he later studied at Poitiers under his uncle, the bishop there, who ordained him deacon.

He became a priest, withdrew to the monastery of Saint Maxentius in 650, and was soon elected abbot, reforming the community under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Called to court in 656 by Queen Bathildis to help govern and teach her children, he was later named bishop of Autun. There he held a council in 661 that struck at Manichaeism, built three baptisteries, enlarged Saint-Nazaire, and set up a refuge for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scapular:
The scapular, from the Latin scapula, shoulder, forms part, now the chief part, of monastic habits, and many other orders and congregations, male and female, have adopted it. Worn over habit or soutane, it is essentially a cloth band about breast-width, fourteen to eighteen inches across, hanging nearly to the feet front and back. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a garment turned devotion.

A head opening sits in the middle, with narrow bands resting on the shoulders. Older forms joined front and back by cross bands under the arms, making a cross over breast and back. Shorter forms exist for layfolk, and the famous brown scapular of Carmel carries promises for its wearers. The entry traces monastic origins, confraternities, indulgences, and the many coloured scapulars of later devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anschar:
St. Anschar, or Ansgarius, called the Apostle of the North, was born in Picardy on 8 September 801 and died on 5 February 865. This entry follows a Benedictine of Corbie who passed into Westphalia. He then sailed with Harold, the newly baptized and exiled King of Denmark returning home, to preach where Ebbo of Reims had laboured with little success.

Anschar founded a school at Schleswig, but Harold's intemperate zeal provoked a storm ending in a second expulsion, and the missionaries returned. Travelling with Louis the Pious's ambassadors, Anschar then entered Sweden. Though the embassy was attacked and seemingly abandoned, he won the king's leave to preach, planting the faith that would earn him his apostolic title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-goar:
Goar, anchorite of Aquitaine, sought total detachment beside the Rhine and became a pilgrims' host instead. Born about 585 to a distinguished family, he showed sound piety from youth, with prayer filling his heart and meditation his mind. Ordained, he laboured for souls with greater authority, yet longed above all for his own sanctification. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death near Oberwesel to 6 July 649.

About 618 he settled in a lonely place at Trier's edge, near Oberwesel, beside a little chapel he built. There he lived detached from material and perishable things. Fame spread anyway, and pilgrims flocked to him, giving him chances for hospitality and good advice. Two of them denounced him to Rusticus, bishop of Trier, opening a conflict the entry leaves unfolding. Solitude, sought strictly, kept turning into service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ibar:
Ibar, pre-Patrician Irish saint of Wexford, preached before Patrick arrived and then submitted to him. Labouring in present County Wexford from 425 to 450, he recognized Patrick's jurisdiction and was confirmed in his episcopacy, becoming the national apostle's disciple after early reluctance. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 23 April 500, his feast day.

Much obscurity veils his early training, but about 480 he settled at Begerin in Wexford harbour, building an oratory and cell that soon filled with disciples from all Ireland. Aengus's Litany invokes three thousand confessors under his direction. His nephew Abban came to Begerin aged twelve in Ibar's old age and accompanied him to Rome. Patron of Begerin, variously written Ibar, Iberius, and Ivor, he stands as a saint who yielded precedence gracefully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-othmar:
Othmar, first abbot of St Gall, gathered scattered monks into a monastery and died a prisoner for defending its lands. Of Alemannic descent and schooled in Rhaetia, he was ordained priest and led a church of St Florinus. In 720 Waltram of Thurgau set him over the cell of St Gall, where he united its monks under the rule of Columban and became its first abbot.

He built a hospital and a school, and under him the Benedictine rule replaced Columban's. When Counts Warin and Ruodhart tried to seize St Gall's property, Othmar resisted fearlessly. Seized on a journey to Constance, he was held at Bodmann and then on the island of Werd in the Rhine, where he died on 16 November 759 after six months' imprisonment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stripping-of-:
On Holy Thursday evening, after the ciborium is removed, the priest strips the high altar bare. This entry describes that solemn rite step by step. Vested in a violet stole, the celebrant with deacon and subdeacon takes away cloths, flowers, and ornaments. Meanwhile the antiphon Diviserunt sibi and Psalm 21 are recited, leaving only cross and unlit candles.

Every other altar in the church is bared the same way. The altar stands for Christ, stripped of his garments before his tormentors. The bare church marks the pause in the Holy Sacrifice. An older custom of washing altars with hyssop dipped in wine and water, recalled by Isidore and Eligius, closes the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-szatmar:
Szatmar is a Hungarian diocese, suffragan of Eger, formed by King Francis I at the same time as Kassa. It covers Szatmár, Bereg, Mármaros, Ugocsa, and Ungvar counties, with a small part of Szabolcs. Its first bishop, Stephen Fischer, served from 1804 to 1807 before becoming Archbishop of Eger, and successors Klobusiczky and Hám shaped its organization and schools.

Under Hám, who served from 1827 to 1857, the cathedral was enlarged, new churches rose, and many charities were founded; his beatification is under consideration. The present bishop, Tiburtius Boromisza, appointed in 1906, lives at Szatmár-Németi. Five archdeaneries hold 95 parishes with 177 clergy, fifteen monasteries count 703 members, and Roman Catholics number 149,807 against 625,627 Greek Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thangmar:
Thangmar, or Thankmar, was a historian born about the middle of the tenth century and probably died at Hildesheim after 1022. He first appears as head of Hildesheim's cathedral school, later dean, notary, and librarian. Distinguished as scholar and statesman, he taught Bishops Bernward, Meinwerk, and Benno, as well as Emperor Henry II. He wielded great influence over Bernward, directing much episcopal business.

In 1000 he accompanied Bernward to Rome and was sent repeatedly to the imperial court as the bishop's representative, highly esteemed by Otto III. After Bernward's death in 1022 he wrote the bishop's life, gathering material earlier and probably drafting ten chapters in 1008 to 1013. An eyewitness of many events and actor in all important measures, he wrote a plain, simple, unrhetorical, and truthful narrative. Only on the Gandersheim jurisdiction dispute does he seem partisan for Bernward. His Vita Bernwardi ranks among the finest medieval biographies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-knights-t:
Military orders begin with the Templars, their model and their tragedy, and this entry marks their story in three beats: humble beginning, marvellous growth, tragic end. After Jerusalem's deliverance, crusaders went home, leaving a precarious conquest ringed by Muslim neighbours. In 1118 Hugues de Payens and eight companions vowed before Jerusalem's patriarch to defend the Christian kingdom.

Baldwin II housed them beside the Temple, hence Poor Knights of the Temple, living on alms and escorting pilgrims. Donations, banking, and castles followed, until wealth and pride drew Philip IV's prosecution and Clement V's suppression. Trial, torture, and burning close a tale that still grips the imagination.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-legend-of:
Letters exchanged between Christ and a king of Edessa form the legend examined here, recorded by Eusebius in his Church History with firm belief. Three documents carry it: Abgar's letter to the Lord, the Lord's answer, and a portrait painted from life. Eusebius thought the Syriac originals lay in Edessa's archives in his own day.

Medieval East and West loved the tale. Copies of the Lord's letter on parchment, marble, and metal served as talismans and amulets. Syriac text, Armenian translation, two shorter Greek versions, and stone inscriptions survive, and the entry weighs their relations. It is a case study in how a pious story travelled and hardened into relic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-thirty-ye:
Germany's war of 1618 to 1648, pre-eminently German yet European in reach, is the vast conflict surveyed here. Nearly every western European country took part, and its links to other wars of the era and its final results shaped the continent. Fundamental cause lay in imperial decay from 1555: weak imperial power, estates lacking patriotism, and paralysed authority among Protestant estates of the southwest.

Unrest spread through Germany, inviting Spain and the Netherlands to seize footing on the Lower Rhine during the twelve years' truce. Bohemian revolt, Danish, Swedish, and French phases, Wallenstein and Gustavus, and the Peace of Westphalia follow. Devastation, religion, and the new balance of states close one of history's longest wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-marina-de:
Marina de Escobar was a mystic and foundress of a modified branch of the Brigittine Order, born at Valladolid in Spain on 8 February 1554, who died there on 9 June 1633. Her father Iago de Escobar taught civil and canon law and served a time as governor of Osuna, a man famed for learning and saintly life. Her mother Margaret Montana was daughter to Charles V's physician. Marina was an apt scholar, reflective beyond her years even in youth.

Until her forty-fifth year she attended mainly to her own perfection, then she gave herself more to fostering others' piety. At fifty her continual bodily afflictions grew so severe that she stayed bedridden for the rest of her life. Providence gave her an admirable guide in Luis de Ponte. The entry follows her visions, her writings, and the Brigittine reform she inspired.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-joh:
John Sugar, or Suker, was a Staffordshire priest executed at Warwick in July 1604. Born at Wombourn in 1558, he entered Oxford from St Mary Hall in 1584, left without a degree, reportedly because he disliked the Oath of Supremacy. For a time served as a Protestant minister at Cannock.

Ordained from Douai in 1601, he was sent to England the same year. Arrested at Rowington in July 1603 with Robert Greswold, who attended him, Sugar spent a year in Warwick prison. Both were condemned there in July 1604, Sugar as a priest and Greswold as his helper. Sugar was cut down while still living, while Greswold was offered his life if he would promise to conform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicar:
Vicar, from Latin vicarius, one acting instead of another, is explained here as a canon-law term for the representative of a person holding ordinary church jurisdiction. Romans used the title for officials under the praetorian prefects, and the early Church knew vicars of the Apostolic See. Such as the archbishops of Thessalonica, as well as bishops' vicars like archdeacons, archpriests, and rural priests with the cure of souls outside episcopal cities.

In time these offices became part of the Church's ordinary magistracy, treated in Gratian's Decretum and Gregory IX's Decretals, while bishops' vicars-general first appear in later collections. After Trent limited archdeacons, their office nearly vanished, and the council abolished other vicarships incompatible with clerical discipline. A vicar differs from a viceregent, and without special faculties cannot appoint an equal substitute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicar-capitul:
A vicar capitular is the administrator chosen by a cathedral chapter to govern a diocese left vacant by a bishop's death. On the vacancy the canons inherit the episcopal jurisdiction as a body. Within eight days they must meet and constitute a vicar, or the right passes to the metropolitan, the senior suffragan, or the nearest bishop.

Election need not follow a strict form, though votes, if cast, must be secret and no one may vote for himself. The chosen man, ideally a doctor or licentiate in canon law, succeeds to the chapter's whole ordinary jurisdiction. The chapter may neither reserve in part nor take back, and faculties granted to bishops for a term of years pass to him as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-war:
War is defined here in its juridical sense as contention carried on by force of arms between sovereign states, or communities holding the rights of states in that regard. The word is often loosely used for civil strife, sedition, rebellion, or a state's suppression of organized outlaws. The jurist may not so use it, since those struggles lack the juridical standing of war between sovereigns. A people in revolution may, rarely, stand in like juridical case with a state.

Seeking to restore vanished civil government or to vitalize constitutional rights reserved to the people, and protect fundamental rights by arms. Later sections treat belligerency, just title, and necessity: fair opportunity of adjustment, or reasonable assurance that offence will not be rectified except under stress of war. Must precede a just resort to arms, and whether to arbitrate first lies within the aggrieved state's own competence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-dunba:
William Dunbar was a Scottish poet often called the Chaucer of Scotland. Born about 1460, he died about 1520. He took his bachelor's degree at Saint Andrews in 1479, became a Franciscan novice, preached across England, and spent time in Picardy. About 1490 he returned to Scotland and entered the service of James IV, who used him on embassies to Paris and elsewhere and granted him a small pension.

Dunbar marked James's marriage to Margaret of England with The Thrissil and the Rois of 1503, picturing friendship between the two realms as thistle and rose. His other verse includes the Goldyn Targe, an allegory of love beating reason, and a grim Dance of the seven deadly sins, plus humorous and devout pieces. He begged king and queen in vain for a country benefice, and after 1513 no trace of him survives; some guess he fell at Flodden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-seth-:
William Seth Agar was an English canon famed as one of his country's deepest guides in ascetical and mystical theology. Born at York on 25 December 1815, he died on 23 August 1872. Schooled at Prior Park, Bath, he took orders there and was posted to Lyme in Dorset in 1845. Poor health forced him from Lyme twice, and in 1852 he became chaplain to the Augustinian canonesses at Abbotsleigh, where he lived without break until his death.

In 1856 Agar was installed as canon of the Plymouth chapter. Friends called him more a deep thinker than a wide reader, yet he studied many works of theology and philosophy, above all Rosmini, whose writings he annotated with care. His name rests on his grasp of grace at work in souls and on the inner life, a reputation the Tablet marked at his death in September 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zanzibar:
Zanzibar is the East African island and town where Persian and Arab colonists mingled with natives, forming the Swahili people. At a remote unknown period Persians and Arabs settled the coast from Somaliland to Cape Delgado, often called Zanquebar, from Persian Zendj, blacks, and bara, country. Besides Lamu, Malindi, Mombasa, and Kilwa, Zanzibar town became the best-known centre.

Ungudya, the natives' name for the island, spans only 570 square miles for about 100,000 people, over half in the capital. It is famed for clove and coconut plantations held by Arabs and Swahilis, while Hindus, Parsees, Goanese, and Europeans run the town's trade. Bantu natives speak Swahili, kin to equatorial tongues. In old days Zanzibar shipped ivory, copal, skins, grain, and slaves from Bagamoyo and Kilwa across Muslim Indian Ocean lands, sending caravans inland to the Great Lakes. Vasco da Gama took Zanzibar in 1499 and set up an Augustinian convent there.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-427-volu:
A benefit club of charitable chums anchors the fiction of number 427, dated March 6, 1852, around Mr. Bowley's new inn and the house-warming where beer flowed free. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal lets the tavern world take the lead before stepping outdoors for the season's first natural history.

Rambles in search of wild-flowers and a piece on the early months of the year suit the March date. An evening in Westminster, Archbishop Whately's book of synonyms, and a mariner's wife vary the tone. Money sent to and from emigrants gets practical attention, forest-trees are surveyed, and whisky and misery are paired in a temperance piece. The number ends where many of its readers' weeks did, between home and abroad.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-428-volu:
Dinner hours start the argument in number 428, dated March 13, 1852. A Frenchman works best fed by one. A Scot thrives half-starved till two. Dinner-party hours, the essay insists, affect the health of the whole gentry. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal builds its lead piece, The Dinner-Bell, from that national timetable.

Two kinds of honesty and a decimal system of coinage take up questions of conduct and cash. Why the Scotch do not shut the door is debated from both sides. Edfou in Egypt, a New York strike told by an English workman, and a doctor set against his own medicine widen the map. A sirene used to count insect wing-beats ends the number in the laboratory.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-429-volu:
London to Calcutta in a week, by rail except for narrow sea crossings, is the boldest of the things in expectation that open number 429, dated March 20, 1852. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal imagines a station in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and lines to Baghdad and Jerusalem without blinking, in a lead piece drunk on engineering.

A tale called The Wrecker turns from future speed to old coastal crime. The Lowell Mechanics' Fair reports American making, and curiosities of chess amuse the stay-at-home. Pet birds of India, the literary circles of London, and the sky-lark's song soften the middle pages. Fanny Farmer's story and an extraordinary dog sale bring the number back to ground level.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-430-volu:
Pronouncers — people ready to decide any question on no basis at all — take the first hit in number 430, dated March 27, 1852. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal mocks the giddy certainty of company talk, where even a girl of seventeen must have an opinion or look foolish, before moving to hotter climates.

Cooling the air of rooms in hot climates answers a real colonial need. A church of the cup of cold water, London's street music-grinders, and a voice from the Australian diggings follow. The history of Jane a Poole gives the number its human story. Children's joys and sorrows, a rejected lover, and the tears of oysters — a curiosity of natural history — fill the remaining columns.
crittenden-a-kentucky-story-of-love-and-:
A Kentucky tale of love and war by John Fox Jr. fills this novel, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1911, with copyright from 1900. F. Graham Cootes drew the pictures. The hero, Crittenden, rides home at dawn through the Bluegrass as the book opens.

He has spent a month in the backwoods fishing and viewing coal lands, in flight from his worse self. Judith stands at the heart of the love story named in the title. War then takes him to sea and to a soldier's work, where action must replace thought. Fox writes of his home state with close love. The book mixes Bluegrass scenes with the call of arms that swept his generation.
doe-osti-17197400-a-review-of-best-pract:
Hillary Fishler, Alex May, and Rachad Bani Samari of Oak Ridge review best practices for sharing research data across institutions, in report ORNL/LTR-2026/4737 dated July 2026. Joint projects stall when each partner guards its data or uses clashing systems. Shared, trusted data speeds science, the authors argue.

One chapter surveys how research data assets are shared today. The next lays out practices that work: building trust through validated data, steady engagement, and clear management. Opening access more widely helps break fragmentation between groups. Further sections treat naming, access rules, and long term care of shared sets. The review closes with guidance an institution can adopt without waiting for a field wide standard.
doe-osti-17197612-fy26-progress-on-irrad:
Samantha Sabatino, Yann Le Pape, Paula Bran Anleu, and Arzu Alpan report fiscal 2026 progress on harvesting irradiated concrete. Their March 2026 report comes from Oak Ridge, under the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program. Concrete that spent decades beside a reactor core carries the true record of radiation aging. Lab tests at high dose rates cannot fully stand in for it.

One source is Canada's National Research Universal reactor, now retired. The other is the Kewaunee Power Station in Wisconsin, shut down in 2013. Work this year covered planning, dose reconstruction, and sample extraction steps at both sites. Harvested cores will be tested for strength and internal change. Results feed service life models for plants seeking to run to 80 years.
doe-osti-2573812-analysis-of-rf-surface-:
Fermilab paper FERMILAB-FN-1274-SQMS, by Andrei Lunin, Mustafa Bal, Akshay Murthy, Shaojiang Zhu, Anna Grassellino, and Alexander Romanenko of the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center, studies a quiet limit on quantum computers. A transmon qubit loses its stored information mainly through dielectric loss in the thin natural oxide on its superconductor surface. How long the qubit stays coherent sets how much computing it can do.

The team modeled microwave surface losses for several planar transmon designs, built around a 200 nanometer niobium film on a dielectric base. They propose an asymptotic method to estimate the energy participation ratio in films only nanometers thick, the share of the field's energy sitting in the lossy layer. From it they derive the lowest radio-frequency losses each design could reach. The limits depend on the oxide's electrical traits and on the film's interface with the substrate beneath.
doe-osti-2583486-backflip-a-comparison-o:
Final results report NREL/TP-5K00-80606, by Naila M. Al Hasan, Rachael L. Arnold, Jimmy M. Newkirk, and colleagues with the Colorado School of Mines, ends a two-year durability contest among solar panel backsheets. The backsheet is a module's rear skin; fluoropolymer versions dominate the market, and the BACKFLIP study raced them against new fluorine-free coextruded films. Coupons and mini-modules endured accelerated weathering out to 4,000 hours.

Flash testing measured power, electroluminescent imaging revealed dead cell areas, and tensile and dielectric tests probed the film itself. Cracking appeared in some backsheets after just 1,000 hours of weathering, and discoloration marched across sun-side surfaces. Because the same materials aged as coupons and as working mini-modules, the study could tie cheap coupon tests to real module degradation rates. That link is what manufacturers need before swapping a proven skin for a greener film.
doe-osti-2583512-inforich-vd-amp-pt-cont:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5400-94533, dated February 6, 2025, supports General Motors' InfoRich vehicle dynamics and powertrain controls project. Jeffrey Gonder was NREL's contact; Carnegie Mellon University was the third partner. The work sat under ARPA-E's NEXTCAR program, which asked what connected and automated vehicles could do for fuel economy. A car that knows the road, the traffic, and its own powertrain deeply can drive itself thriftier even before it drives itself.

The InfoRich idea is to feed controllers richer information: sensing, communication, and prediction, traded against engine and transmission decisions in real time. NREL's CRADA backed GM's cooperative agreement with modeling and analysis support. Program goals reached beyond one vehicle line: fuel savings for consumers, stronger energy security, and a domestic manufacturer leading in controls rather than following. This report closes the laboratory's supporting role in the award.
doe-osti-2584235-photosynthetically-acti:
Instrument handbook DOE/SC-ARM-TR-319, by A. B. Moyes and S. C. Biraud of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, documents the photosynthetically active radiation sensor for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility. PAR is the 400 to 700 nanometer band plants actually use, reported as photosynthetic photon flux density. For ecosystem and land-surface science, it is the light measurement that matters, and ARM sites, including the Bankhead National Forest deployment, record it continuously.

The handbook follows the ARM pattern: mentor contacts, a full instrument description with technical specifications, and the measurement theory behind the numbers. Data sections define the products, their quality and uncertainty, and the QC bit flags users will meet in the files, with examples. Maintenance and calibration plans close the volume. Handbooks like this are why a measurement taken in Alabama can be compared with one taken years later on another continent.
doe-osti-2584741-orbiting-lunar-ground-p:
Samuel Wagner's July 2025 Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report, LLNL-TR-2007904, asks whether ground penetrating radar could map lunar resources from orbit. The study explores feasibility only; it does not propose a system. The target case is a satellite flying at 10 kilometers or higher above the Moon's surface.

Working through link budget equations, Wagner finds the needed radar specifications difficult but reasonable. His example system uses a high-power radar at 500 to 800 megahertz with a 60 microsecond chirp and a 6.6 kilohertz pulse repetition rate. In synthetic aperture mode it would reach about 1 meter azimuth resolution and 0.5 meter depth resolution. Penetration in low-loss lunar regolith could reach hundreds of meters.
doe-osti-2998336-from-stewardship-to-tra:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory paper LLNL-TR-2012390, by Brad Roberts and Kim Budil, dated October 2025, argues the United States nuclear enterprise must move from stewardship to transformation. Stewardship, the post-testing practice of maintaining weapons through science and surveillance, has run for three decades. The paper contends the enterprise built for it no longer matches the century's demands.

Critical parts of the enterprise should be right-sized to urgent and emerging needs. One example given: more frequent refresh and update cycles for weapons would raise demand on transportation, logistics, storage, and warehousing, above all for special nuclear materials. The authors draw on a strategic posture review's findings to press the case. The paper is a policy agenda for laboratory and agency leadership, not a technical study.
doe-osti-2998645-greenhouse-gas-flux-res:
James Jihoon Kang and co-workers at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley wrote this final report for award DE-SC0023104, covering September 2022 to June 2025. The team measured greenhouse gas flows from lawn soil treated with biochar, compost, a blend of both, or nothing. Biochar is charred plant matter dug into soil. Tests ran in soil columns inside a controlled greenhouse.

Columns went through normal watering, half or full soaking by a raised water table, and then drying, under both laid sod and seeded grass. Compost columns gave off more carbon dioxide, near 6 units against 4.5 to 5.0 for biochar or plain soil, in the report's flux units under sod. Biochar held the most soil moisture, near 95 percent. Methane and nitrous oxide rose during soaking and draining. Blending compost with biochar may curb the extra carbon dioxide.
doe-osti-3007751-toroidal-alfven-wave-co:
Close-out report by Mark Koepke of West Virginia University for a DOE grant on toroidal Alfven wave coupling in the DIII-D tokamak. The question was whether nonlinear wave-wave interactions set the saturation level of toroidal Alfven eigenmodes, plasma waves that can drain energy from fusion reactions.

Archival work in fiscal 2019 found evidence of nonlinear interactions in 175 relevant DIII-D shots, using Mirnov coil spectrograms and bispectral analysis. An improved bispectrum code, grown from a 1995 master's thesis tool, was also tested on the TJ-II stellarator and T-10 tokamak. The run plan drove one eigenmode against others and swept driver frequency to watch amplitudes respond. The same coupling physics appears in space plasmas and radiation belts.
doe-osti-3011419-newberry-shr-demonstrat: An enhanced geothermal system at the Newberry site is planned in a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory abstract, PNNL-38048, issued under CRADA 677 in July 2025. Parker Sprinkle and five colleagues describe a Bipartisan Infrastructure Law pilot demonstration. The project will create a system of two or more wells drilled to a depth of 4.25 kilometres into superhot rock. The hosted record carries the abstract only, so it states the plan and depth without drilling results or reservoir data.
doe-osti-3011896-initial-characterizatio:
Initial characterisation of a large amplitude motion platform at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is reported by Bri Friedman, Casey Nichols, Andrew Simms, Calum Kenny, and Miles Skinner. The platform is a six degree of freedom Stewart design with six variable length actuators. Test masses and motion profiles exercised the machine across its working envelope.

An inverse kinematics solver checks whether a desired pose is achievable before a run. Pose limits are hard to state directly, while actuator length limits are simple. Joint layouts on the base and top frames, plus actuator travel ranges, fully define the system geometry. Data acquisition runs through the platform control system and an EDAS unit.
doe-osti-3012116-development-of-industri:
Rare earth master alloys made directly from native oxides are developed at industrial scale in the final report for award DE-EE0009437 from the University of Virginia. Xiaodong Li led the August 2021 to July 2024 project. Partners were Ames Laboratory, Rare Earth Salts, Materion, and Electron Energy Corp. The target products feed permanent magnet production.

Calcium reduces neodymium and samarium oxides inside a calcium chloride bath. A two step route through oxychloride intermediates was modelled in heat and rate terms. Reaction rates fall sharply below 900 degrees C, which the modelling picked as the optimal process temperature. Smaller feed particles lowered reaction resistance at lower temperatures.
doe-osti-3012391-network-of-modified-por:
A network of modified portable optical particle spectrometers is documented in an ARM instrument handbook by Sarah and Markus Petters of the University of California, Riverside. The handbook, DOE/SC-ARM-TR-328, describes instruments that size particles and count concentration optically at high time resolution. No high voltage supply or diameter scanning is needed.

Particle laden air crosses a blue violet laser beam, 405 nanometres at 100 milliwatts. A concave mirror below collects scattered light over 38 to 142 degrees and directs it into a photomultiplier tube above. The network supports ARM field campaigns including the CoURAGE and TRACER experiments listed in the handbook acronyms.
doe-osti-3015880-solvari-sr-simplifying-:
Michael Kempe of the National Laboratory of the Rockies served as technical contact for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5K00-96840, under agreement CRD-22-22484. The partner product is the Solvari SR, a home solar system designed to shrink residential solar down to a single stock-keeping unit, one standard package. Extended testing of its mounting materials is the report's core.

Laboratory work centered on accelerated weathering and material compatibility tests for the plastic and asphalt-based materials in the support structures designed by TESCI Solar. Samples faced damp heat, plus heat with humidity and ultraviolet light, then went through mechanical checks such as Izod impact testing. Bare materials and coupons fixed to asphalt shingles were both exposed. A later phase extended some tests and added new methods and materials. The results tell the maker how long the support materials should last on real roofs.
doe-osti-3016955-unraveling-the-dynamics:
Yaqing Wang of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory led project 24-LW-043, reported in LLNL-TR-2015384 in February 2026. The subject is nucleosome arrays. Nucleosomes are the spool-like units that DNA wraps around to form chromatin, and how they pack into larger structures is hard to see with standard methods that average over many molecules.

The project tested atomic force microscopy, a scanning probe method, as a way to picture single nucleosome assemblies directly. Work covered sample preparation, imaging, and qualitative analysis of multi-nucleosome systems. The results established that the approach is feasible for chromatin-like assemblies. The project also raised the lab's profile in genome organization research. Biologists studying how DNA packaging controls genes get a possible new window on structures that ensemble tools blur together.
doe-osti-3017767-temperature-of-a-tungst:
René Reifarth and Aaron Joseph Couture of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this technical report, LA-UR-26-20932, issued February 9, 2026. It calculates the temperature of a tungsten spallation target struck by an 800 megaelectronvolt proton beam. The work supports the Neutron Target project at LANSCE, where a spallation target will sit inside a graphite or beryllium cube to form a free-neutron target.

Such a target would let physicists measure neutron-induced reactions in inverse kinematics, a trick that opens reactions otherwise out of reach. The report works out equilibrium temperatures for the tungsten under beam, in a table running into the thousands of degrees at high beam loadings. It then treats a short pulse: five microcoulombs at 800 megaelectronvolts deposits at most 4,000 joules. The example target is a cylinder 3.5 centimeters in radius and 25 centimeters long. Target designers get the heat numbers their cooling must survive.
doe-osti-3019397-daisy-a-rapid-approach-:
Brian Polagye of the University of Washington led the DAISY project, award DE-EE0007823, with MarineSitu Inc and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory as partners. The final report covers a problem: marine energy converters make sound, and regulators need to know how much. Fixed hydrophone arrays are expensive to deploy and analyze. DAISY answers with drifting instruments. Each Drifting Acoustic Instrumentation SYstem floats a surface expression and listens below. Groups of drifters surround a device at sea.

Four threads structure the work. Flow noise and self-noise were minimized. Metadata streams were integrated into one acquisition system. Review routines sped up data review. Timing-based localization then identified converter sound against ambient noise. Deployments at the Wave Energy Test Site in Hawaii exercised the chain, with five units tank-tested before sailing. Permitting for tidal and wave devices runs on acoustic evidence; DAISY makes that evidence cheaper to gather well.
doe-osti-3020893-neutron-diffraction-res:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4442, by Wei Tang and seven co-authors, measures the hidden stresses locked inside two large stainless steel cylinders built by wire-arc directed energy deposition. This printing method lays down weld metal layer by layer to form big parts cheaply. The heating and cooling leave residual stresses that can drive cracking or corrosion years later, so the team mapped them with neutron diffraction.

Both shells used 316L stainless steel. Stresses along and across the cylinder were compressive at the inner wall, near neutral at mid-wall, and tensile at the outer surface, where the peak tensile stress ran along the cylinder's length. Radial stresses stayed low. The printed metal showed finely dispersed delta-ferrite, high strength, and ductile fracture at room temperature and at 250 degrees Celsius. The outer surface is flagged as most vulnerable to stress-corrosion cracking and fatigue.
doe-osti-3021461-a-brief-review-of-techn:
PNNL review PNNL-39061, by Stuart T. Arm, dated February 2026, surveys methods for pulling tritium out of the water discharged by nuclear fuel reprocessing plants. Tritium, a radioactive form of hydrogen, binds into water molecules themselves, so plain filtering cannot remove it. Plants must either manage large volumes of tritiated water or pull the tritium into a small, concentrated stream.

The review weighs the main plant options. Water distillation is mature and works well for light water but demands large capital equipment, sized here around a feed of 25 kilograms per hour carrying 1 curie of tritium per kilogram. Combined Electrolysis Catalytic Exchange, long used in Canada and Europe for heavy water and reprocessing wastewater, joins electrolysis with catalytic exchange for added efficiency. The write-up gives plant designers the trade-offs in maturity, scale, and cost.
doe-osti-3022248-exploring-offshore-regi:
Battelle's final technical report for DOE award DE-FE0032407, led by co-leads Neeraj Gupta and Joel Sminchak, weighs offshore carbon storage for the Mid-Atlantic coast of the eastern United States. The EXPLORE-ACS project studied whether carbon dioxide captured from regional industry could be stored in offshore formations, and what pipelines, wells, and hub infrastructure that would require.

Geologic profiling of candidate formations anchors the report, checked against operating offshore storage projects worldwide. That survey found reservoir permeability mostly between 80 and 1,000 millidarcies, with a wide overall range, and reservoir thickness averaging about 170 meters across projects, mostly in sandstones. Community and industry engagement for a Mid-Atlantic storage hub runs through the study beside the technical screening.
doe-osti-3029160-domestic-manufacturing-:
Amy Rose, Becca Fuchs, and Sarah Inskeep of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presented this supply summary in January 2026 for transmission components. American electricity load is growing again, and large transmission build-outs are a cheap answer, but most planning studies simply assume the equipment will be there. The authors test that assumption against domestic manufacturing and supply through 2035.

The deck works component by component, then drops to the critical materials underneath them, and gives towers their own section. One chart tracks net import reliance in millions of metric tons, with a 2023-2024 average marked at eighteen on its scale. Objectives are stated as two verbs: demonstrate methods that turn national planning models into component demand, and evaluate whether supply chains can meet the anticipated transmission development.
doe-osti-3029957-catalytic-membrane-reac:
Haiqing Lin of the University at Buffalo led this final report under award DE-FE0032209, covering October 2022 to June 2025, on a cleaner route to hydrogen. The device is a catalytic membrane reactor built from carbon molecular sieve hollow fibers. It runs the water-gas shift reaction, which turns carbon monoxide and steam into hydrogen and carbon dioxide. As hydrogen forms, the membrane pulls it out in place, pushing the reaction past its normal limit and leaving a carbon dioxide rich stream.

Tests put carbon monoxide conversion near 90 percent, steady across the heat range tried. Hydrogen permeance rose from 450 to 675 gas permeation units as heat climbed from 250 to 300 degrees Celsius, and hydrogen over carbon dioxide selectivity rose from 15 to 16. Robust reactors housed the fibers in porous ceramic tubes.
doe-osti-3030131-distributed-mafic-rock-:
Lisa A. Thompson of the Arizona Geological Survey led this final report under award DE-FE0032252, submitted in April 2026, with Northern Arizona University and Arizona State University partners. The team mapped a climate tool hiding in plain sight: mafic rocks, dark volcanic rocks rich in minerals that react with carbon dioxide. Locked together, the gas becomes stable carbonate stone. Arizona holds plenty of such rock at the surface in three young volcanic fields.

Crews sampled flows and scoria, ran whole-rock chemistry, and tested how fast the rock drinks in carbon dioxide. They also sized the deposits. Pairing capture with mineral storage on site wipes out pipeline transport costs, the report notes, though capture itself stays pricey. The team judges that viable projects need mineralization costs below 100 dollars per tonne after other gains.
doe-osti-3363286-comparison-of-commercia:
Shannon McNaul, James Clarke, Megan S. Henriksen, and colleagues at the National Energy Technology Laboratory deliver a techno-economic comparison of commercial, state-of-the-art ammonia production from fossil feedstocks (DOE/NETL-2026/5323, October 2025). All three configurations studied use natural gas as the feedstock, and the analysis, peer reviewed by three independent reviewers, models each plant in process detail down to stream compositions.

Ammonia underpins fertilizer supply, so the cost and performance of today's best plants set the baseline that cleaner routes must beat. The report documents the configurations, methods, and results in full, giving later studies a consistent reference point for comparing new production pathways against the incumbent technology.
doe-osti-3372841-machine-tool-metrology-:
A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory Micropoint report by J. Khan, dated June 2026, records how the lab measures the machine tools that grind carbide inserts for special materials work. The inserts come off legacy Micropoint Tool grinders, and much of the know-how behind those machines was never fully written down. As the lab modernizes, it needs the old process described well enough to keep production running.

Khan lays out the analysis methods, fixtures, and tools used or proposed to rate grinder performance. The report breaks machine motion into error types for each axis, such as straightness, roll, yaw, and pitch, and judges which errors can hurt a finished insert. Motions that run at right angles to the cutting direction, for instance, are shown to add no error to the ground parts.
doe-osti-3375709-generation-of-rare-eart:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0009432, filed April 27, 2026, covers a University of Wyoming project on making rare earth metals from their oxides. Maohong Fan led the work. Co-investigators were Jinke Tang, Matt Kramer of Ames Laboratory, and Patrick Taylor of the Colorado School of Mines. Eutectix LLC also took part. The project ran from September 2021 to December 2023. Standard metal making is dirty and costly, so the team tried microwave-driven plasmas instead.

Hydrogen plasma runs on neodymium oxide anchor the tests. Diffraction scans track the powder hour by hour, past ninety hours of treatment. Peaks still match the standard oxide pattern, a sign the change is slow going. Theory work covered plasma heat models, Cantera chemistry sums, and machine learning forecasts of phase paths. A tech-to-market study weighs whether the route can pay at scale.
doe-osti-3392046-reproducibility-replica:
Reproducibility, Replicability, and Research Quality in Homogeneous Catalysis collects a community's answer to a worry that hangs over all of science: can published results be repeated? Researchers from every sector of homogeneous catalysis convened for the project. They met through an in-person workshop and a webinar series that drew in the wider field. Sayak Banerjee, James Blakemore, and Caleb Brown are among the contributors named in the evidence record.

The summary gives a two-part verdict. Homogeneous catalysis is not in a reproducibility crisis. The field's work for agriculture, consumer goods, and human health proves its results land. Yet researchers do meet obstacles to repeating results. Keeping results repeatable is the community's own responsibility, in today's work and in training. Recommendations address societies, publishers, employers, research leaders, and bench researchers. They are framed to travel beyond catalysis to chemistry at large.
doe-osti-3399428-conduct-a-techno-econom:
Conduct a Techno-Economic Analysis, Solar Prize Round 7, SET Voucher, NC Solar Inverters, is the assignment recorded in CRADA final report NLR/TP-6A20-100418, dated July 2026, under agreement CRD-24-30365. Hope Wikoff is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Solar Energy Technologies Office, which runs the American-Made Solar Prize.

Solar Prize winners can spend voucher awards on laboratory help, and the SET voucher program routes specific technical tasks this way. Here the task was a techno-economic analysis for a North Carolina solar inverter participant: what the device costs to make and run, set against what the market will pay. The report closes the voucher work and stands as the public record of the assistance delivered.
doe-osti-3402856-cully-community-solar:
Verde reports on the Cully Community Solar project under award DE-EE0010128. Tatiana Siegenthaler-Rodriguez served as principal investigator for the recipient group. The project period ran from September 1, 2023 to December 31, 2025.

Crews designed and built a community solar array and worked through grid connection with the utility. Late in design, the utility required a recloser, a device that spots faults and guards the grid. Parts of the electrical design had to be redone to fit that rule. The team still won connection approval, and the report records those steps for other local solar groups.
doe-osti-3403176-analytic-expressions-fo:
ORNL/TM-2026/4688 is a June 2026 report from Oak Ridge National Laboratory that gives math formulas for transport in the far scrape-off layer of divertor tokamaks. P. C. Stangeby, J. H. Nichols, and E. A. Unterberg wrote the study. The scrape-off layer is the thin plasma edge zone that hits the wall.

The formulas pull transport rates from the shape of radial current profiles, not just their totals. Probe arrays built into window frames supply the data, with a moving probe as backup. A DIII-D case shows how wide frame spacing adds change along the ring. Plasma staff can read wall loads with less guesswork.
doe-osti-3422013-platypus-improvements-c:
Dated August 2026, report NLR/TP-5K00-100335 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies covers improvements to PLatypus, a camera system that watches solar panels. Tim Silverman was the lab contact. The work is Project 3 under CRADA number CRD-22-23303.

One fix targets the power supply for the lights that brighten panel images. Options include new converters, changed battery voltage, or new light inputs. Image gathering was also automated. Each camera node once took about five extra seconds to send images to shared storage. Faster, steadier image flow helps crews spot panel faults sooner.
doe-osti-3451859-c-her-metadata-overview:
ORNL/TM-2026/4743 is a August 19 report from Oak Ridge National Laboratory that 2026, sets the metadata approach for C-HER, a centralized health and exposome resource. Midgie MacFarland leads an eight-author team. Exposome data link environmental exposures to health outcomes.

The framework rests on FAIR data principles and readiness for AI use. Controlled word lists govern most fields, while some fields stay free text. Version codes are assigned in order as records enter the database. Two records that differ only by version code still count as distinct. Careful metadata let researchers find and trust health data sets.
doe-osti-3583412-tracer-vnats-vertically:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-030, dated August 2026, records a field study of new particle formation near Houston, Texas. Chongai Kuang of Brookhaven led the work. Co-investigators were Scott Giangrande, Michael Jensen, and Tamanna Subba of Brookhaven, plus Darielle Dexheimer of Sandia. Claire Longbottom of Sandia was an added team member. The study site was a farm field at Guy, Texas.

A tethered balloon carried a small particle counter that had been reshaped to fly within strict weight, power, and size limits. Flights ran for two weeks near the start of each month in summer 2022, from June through September. The counter tracked tiny clusters, between one and three nanometers wide, at set heights above the ground. Results show how particle counts changed with height on sample days, in both morning and afternoon air.
doe-osti-3684122-uncertainty-quantificat:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2023753, dated August 2026, compares ways to put error bars on deep learning forecasts of drug binding strength. Four authors are printed: Andre R. Goncalves, Derek Jones, Hyojin Kim, and Jonathan E. Allen. The work was first done in 2021. A three-dimensional neural network reads voxel maps of protein and drug pairs from the PDBbind 2016 set. A bare score gives no hint of its likely error.

Six methods were tested against the plain network: two ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, a Gaussian process, and two residual methods. Every setup proved overconfident. All six measure spread among models, not noise in the labels. Ensembles gave the best raw accuracy and remain the pick where thirty training runs are affordable. Their intervals still need recalibration on held-out data before use. Cheaper frozen methods varied their doubt too little to rank cases.
doe-osti-3740783-balancing-opportunity-a:
Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4351, dated July 2026, weighs onboard machine learning for the next safeguards camera system. James Garner is the sole printed author. The International Atomic Energy Agency runs more than one thousand surveillance cameras to watch nuclear sites. Missing footage can leave inspectors unable to rule out diversion of fuel. Machine learning could sharpen what cameras catch, yet it also drains batteries and fills storage. A false trigger storm could end a recording long before staff return.

Garner sorts risk by site setup: wall power with a network link is the easy case; off-grid cameras face the hardest. Each case gets guardrails, such as a floor on picture rates so baseline footage always survives. Oak Ridge is designing a learning-capable camera that sips power when alone, then leans on wall power and links when a site offers them.
early-letters-of-george-wm-curtis-to-joh:
George Willis Cooke edited the early letters of George William Curtis to John S. Dwight, with a life sketch of Curtis at Brook Farm and Concord. Curtis was born in Providence on February 24, 1824. At about the age of eleven he heard Emerson lecture, and his brother Burrill called that hearing the cardinal event of their youth.

Burrill recalls Emerson delivering The Over-Soul in a Providence schoolroom. He seemed to speak, the brother writes, as an inhabitant of heaven, with a prophet's authority. The letters then follow the young Curtis into the Brook Farm circle and Concord friendships. Dwight, a music critic and fellow reformer, receives the young man's earnest, high-toned confidences. Readers meet a future editor and orator in his forming years, drunk on Emerson and ideal work.
echoes-of-the-war:
J. M. Barrie gathers four short war plays in Echoes of the War, dated 1918. The first, The Old Lady Shows Her Medals, opens on three London charwomen and a fourth, uninvited guest over a dish of tea. Barrie's stage talk explains, with comic care, that an 'and' is a charwoman who also caretakes, a rank far above a plain charwoman like Mrs. Haggerty.

Mrs. Dowey, the hostess, has invented a soldier son to boast of, and the medals of the title hang on that tender lie. The other plays are The New Word, Barbara's Wedding, and A Well-Remembered Voice. In one scene a returned officer's liveliness alarms his mother, who presses him on whether something is wrong. Barrie writes the home front in whispers and small prides: women, old men, and the absent boys who fill every room.
england-and-the-war:
Walter Raleigh, the Oxford professor of English literature, gathered six wartime addresses in England and the War, published at Oxford in 1918. The pieces span the whole conflict, from Might Is Right, an Oxford Pamphlet of October 1914, to Shakespeare and England, the British Academy lecture of July 4, 1918. Other talks went to the Royal Colonial Institute and to Eton boys.

Raleigh argues that England fights not a tyrant caste but the united German people and their Prussian doctrine. That doctrine paid Germany well, he says, and will be dropped only when it stops paying. Later pieces weigh the press, the faith of England, and the gains of the war. The tone is plain, public, and meant to stiffen resolve.
famous-adventures-and-prison-escapes-of-:
Cable's Famous Adventures and Prison Escapes of the Civil War gathers firsthand war narratives. George Washington Cable's name heads the collection. Its pieces carry copyrights from 1885 to 1893, and this New York issue is dated 1913. A frontispiece shows a prisoner under questioning.

A war diary of a Union woman in the South opens the book. The Locomotive Chase in Georgia follows at page 83. A Romance of Morgan's Rough-Riders tells of the famous raiders. Colonel Rose's Tunnel at Libby Prison forms the centerpiece escape. A Hard Road to Travel Out of Dixie and the Escape of General Breckinridge close it. Maps and prison views illustrate the accounts. The volume preserves daring as participants told it.
fanny-goes-to-war:
Washington's Fanny Goes to War is a memoir of the First Aid Nursing Yeomanry in France. Pat Beauchamp served with the FANNYs, as the corps was nicknamed. Major-General H. N. Thompson wrote the introduction. The London book is dated 1919.

Nineteen chapters run from camp before the war to after two years. First impressions and the journey to the front come early. Typhoid wards, a Zeppelin raid, and baths fill the middle chapters. Convoy life, Christmas 1916, and commandeered lorries add color. The last ride leads to hospitals in France and England. Roehampton, a grey horse called Bob, and the Armistice close the war. Washington writes with humor about driving, nursing, and loss.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: A protected source sits at the center of this short Federal Bureau of Investigation interview record from March 2001. The source was spoken to at a place the report does not name, under a proffer pact from the United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York. Prosecutors Joseph Bianco and Michael McGovern took part, and Patrick Fitzgerald joined on March 16 and 17. The source signed the pact each day, his lawyer at hand. What he said is not in the pages that survive here.

March 2002 brings a life story in this Federal Bureau of Investigation interview report. Agents spoke with a man held at the immigration detention site on Los Angeles Street in Los Angeles. A city police officer sat in on the talk, which was typed on March 7, 2002.

The man said he was born and raised in Tunis, Tunisia. He came to the United States on January 25, 1999, on a visitor visa, with his mother, who stayed about two weeks. He studied English for ten months at a school in Los Angeles, then took computer science classes at West Los Angeles College. The sampled pages trace his friends and work: taxi drivers, a gas station, a carpet shop, and a sum of $2000 wired to free a man from custody.
forward-march-a-tale-of-the-spanish-amer:
Munroe sends young Ridge Norton off to the Spanish-American War as the Rough Riders form at San Antonio. The chapters promise the Hobson and Merrimac story, a secret mission, and a dawn firing squad escaped. Blockade duty and Cuban hospitality carry the tale forward.

On campaign, Ridge shares roasted yams with Lieutenant Navarro, a Spanish officer turned almost a friend. Navarro will not rejoin General Pando's army against a country he esteems. He had visited cousins in New Mexico a year before and been charmed by the welcome. Kirk Munroe published this tale with Harper in 1899.
found-at-blazing-star:
Bret Harte begins this California tale the morning after rain at the mining settlement of Blazing Star. Cass Beard, up early because his cabin roof leaked, crosses the highway and sees something glitter in a red pool. It is not gold quartz but a plain gold ring, and its inscription reads May to Cass, his own nickname, in a camp with no women in it.

Harte lets the find work on a superstitious man. Cass pockets the ring and asks his fellows, too casually, whether anyone lost anything in the night. The answers he gets are jokes, and the mystery of the ring's owner drives the story from there. It is a compact piece of Harte's mining-camp manner: one object, one conscience, and a settlement watching.
friends-though-divided-a-tale-of-the-civ:
Two school friends near Oxford take opposite sides when civil war begins. Harry Furness is merry, careless, and loyal to the king. Herbert Rippinghall is grave, studious, and drawn to Parliament. Their fathers' politics pull them apart in 1642. The boys vow that no cause will end their friendship.

Henty sends them through the war's full course. They brawl at Oxford, break prison, and carry state missions. One chapter follows Montrose in Scotland. Others cover a plot to rescue the king and his execution. The action runs to the siege of Drogheda and the battle of Worcester. A sea fight and capture stretch the tale overseas. It ends with rest after years of fighting.
full-revelations-of-a-professional-rat-c:
Matthews sets out twenty-five years of work as a professional rat-catcher in this plain, practical book. Ike Matthews served corporations, railway companies, and merchants, chiefly in Manchester. He describes methods of catching rats and ferreting, and the habits he watched over years of work. He warns at the start that rats cannot be wholly wiped out, above all in large towns. His methods, he says, apply to any large town.

The chapters mix instruction with stories from the job. One tells of a mother rat found to have killed her whole litter. Others cover poisons, traps, and dogs. The book is a working man's trade manual, full of observed detail.
germany-and-the-next-war:
General Friedrich von Bernhardi set out Germany's case for war in this book, Englished by Allen H. Powles in 1912. He wrote after the Morocco crisis of 1911, when, he says, patriotic Germans felt their honor and future at stake. Crowds had been ready to fight, yet the government settled by talks. Bernhardi thought the nation did not grasp the cost a bold policy would demand.

The book argues that war is a law of life for nations and that Germany must win world power or fall. Bernhardi faults soft peace talk and urges more arms, more taxes, and a will to strike. Read after 1914, the work is grimly telling. It shows, in a general's own words, the thought that helped push Europe toward the Great War.
govdocs-archive_org-TheTruthAboutGalileo: Garbled text of a work defending the Catholic Church's side of the Galileo case makes up this file; its author is not identified in the text. It opens on the schoolbook account of the Inquisition seizing and torturing the astronomer, the version the book sets out to correct as lies and errors. Much of the capture is damaged, so the argument survives only in part. It is kept as found, a partial record of Catholic apologetics on a famous trial.
